article_title: The Success Project
citation: Cowhy, J.R. & de la Torre, M. (2017). The Success Project: The Implementation and Early Outcomes of a Middle Grade Program. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://uei.uchicago.edu/
title: Protecting curriculum time through principal buy-in and flexible delivery models
description: A lesson-level implementation pattern in which schools secure a stable slot for a non-tested curriculum by obtaining administrator buy-in early and adapting delivery to existing structures. The report found "identifying and protecting time  to teach the 6to16 curriculum within their school schedules was a critical step in implementation." Coordinators succeeded by negotiating schedule changes at the start of the year and by embedding lessons in social studies, MTSS, SEL, homeroom, or prep periods, delivered to whole classes or small groups.
requirements: Principal or administrator buy-in secured at the start-of-year schedule planning
Flexibility to deliver the curriculum to a whole class or a small group
constraints: District accountability pressure privileging tested subjects squeezed out non-tested curriculum time
Where principals did not buy in, 6to16 time was lost, even during testing periods in schools with full buy-in
target_learners: Middle grades students in high-accountability urban elementary schools
target_learning_goals: College readiness knowledge and skills delivered through a non-tested curriculum
examples: One coordinator whose administration fully bought into the program never lost 6to16 time, including during testing windows, after integrating it into the year's systems during start-of-year planning.
key_sources: Cowhy, J.R. & de la Torre, M. (2017). The Success Project: The Implementation and Early Outcomes of a Middle Grade Program. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/success-project-implementation-and-early-outcomes-middle-grade-program

article_title: How Do Secondary Principals Influence Teaching and Learning?
citation: Sebastian, J., & Allensworth, E. (2013). How Do Secondary Principals Influence Teaching and Learning? Principal's Research Review, 8(4). https://www.nassp.org/prr
title: Principals should make school climate the priority in school improvement efforts
description: Because the strongest mechanism linking principal leadership to schoolwide instruction and achievement is the learning climate, principals should prioritize building a safe, orderly, academically focused climate with a college-going culture. The article states that "principals need to make school climate the priority in their school improvement efforts," and that training programs preparing principals to lead urban schools must recognize this. Climate work does not require subject-specific instructional skills, making it feasible for secondary principals.
requirements: Sustained attention to safety, order, academic expectations, and a college-going culture across the whole school
constraints: Shifts toward climate must be incorporated in a way that balances principals' other roles, such as supporting quality professional development and coherent instructional programming
target_learning_goals: schoolwide instructional quality and student achievement
examples: The review recommends principals ensure the school is safe, orderly, and focused on academics, and that principals set the stage for instruction through climate, professional development opportunities, and teacher collaboration.
key_sources: Sebastian, J., & Allensworth, E. (2013). How Do Secondary Principals Influence Teaching and Learning? Principal's Research Review, 8(4). https://www.nassp.org/prr

article_title: Instruction and Achievement in Chicago Elementary Schools
citation: Julia B. Smith, Valerie E. Lee, and Fred M. Newmann. (2001). Instruction and Achievement in Chicago Elementary Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Promote interactive instruction through teacher preparation, collegial dialogue, and principal instructional leadership
description: Because interactive instruction was associated with greater learning gains while didactic instruction and review were associated with smaller gains, the report recommends building the conditions linked to interactive teaching. These include educating teachers in interactive methods through pre-service education and high-quality professional development, supporting collegial dialogue about practice, and encouraging principals to provide instructional leadership. The authors conclude that "Chicago students’ achievement could improve further if teachers across the school system were encouraged to achieve a better balance among their use of review, interactive teaching, and didactic teaching practices."
requirements: Teachers with advanced degrees, substantial coursework in their subject, or high-quality professional development; school organizational supports of innovation orientation, reflective dialogue, and instructional leadership
constraints: The associations are observational and controlled for student, classroom, and school characteristics; causal direction for some contextual links (e.g., problem behaviors) is acknowledged as complicated
target_learners: Elementary school students in grades 2-8 in urban districts
target_learning_goals: Reading and mathematics achievement gains on standardized assessments
examples: The study found teachers reporting high-quality professional development used interactive instruction most (.21 effect-size units), and schools with strong instructional leadership showed more interactive and less didactic instruction
key_sources: Julia B. Smith, Valerie E. Lee, and Fred M. Newmann. (2001). Instruction and Achievement in Chicago Elementary Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/instruction-and-achievement-chicago-elementary-schools

article_title: School Leadership and the Bottom Line in Chicago
citation: Penny Bender Sebring and Anthony S. Bryk. (2000). School Leadership and the Bottom Line in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research. http://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Four leadership-style characteristics of principals in productive Chicago elementary schools
description: The article enumerates a recurring pattern of leadership-style characteristics shared by principals of improving schools: an inclusive, facilitative orientation in which principals articulate a "vision-in-outline" and invite teachers and parents to elaborate it; an institutional focus on student learning; efficient management; and the use of support and pressure to catalyze initiatives. As printed, "Principals in productive schools set high standards for teaching, understand how children learn, and encourage teachers to take risks and try new methods of teaching." Regular classroom visits demonstrate conviction and give principals a pulse on instruction, and efficient management ensures teachers have needed materials and students receive support services so disruptions are minimized.
requirements: Change requires the commitment, talent, and energy of many, so principals bring parents, teachers, and other staff into leadership positions
target_learners: Elementary school teachers and students in improving Chicago schools
target_learning_goals: Improved quality of teaching and student learning opportunities
examples: Principals make regular visits to classrooms and secure academic and social support services for students in need
key_sources: Penny Bender Sebring and Anthony S. Bryk. (2000). School Leadership and the Bottom Line in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/school-leadership-and-bottom-line-chicago

article_title: Seven Successful Strategies for Literate Assessment
citation: Beth Tarasawa, Amelia Wenk Gotwals, Cara Jackson. (2018). Seven successful strategies for literate assessment. Principal Leadership 18. https://www.nwea.org/research/publications/
title: Principals build teacher assessment literacy through professional development, data use in planning, and professional collaboration
description: The article presents school principals' assessment leadership as the foundation of assessment literacy among teachers. It states that evidence suggests principals' knowledge and skills in relation to assessment leadership—such as incorporating professional development, use of assessment data in classroom planning, and nurturing professional collaboration on matters of student achievement and instruction—are of fundamental importance to building assessment literacy among their teachers.
requirements: Principals must possess knowledge and skills in assessment leadership, including incorporating professional development and nurturing professional collaboration on matters of student achievement and instruction
target_learners: school principals and the teachers they lead
target_learning_goals: assessment literacy among teachers
use of assessment data in classroom planning
examples: The article identifies incorporating professional development, use of assessment data in classroom planning, and nurturing professional collaboration as the leadership practices it highlights
key_sources: Beth Tarasawa, Amelia Wenk Gotwals, Cara Jackson. (2018). Seven successful strategies for literate assessment. Principal Leadership 18. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/seven-successful-strategies-for-literate-assessment/

article_title: Practitioner's Guide to Integrating Literacy and Science
citation: Practitioner's guide to integrating literacy and science. (2025). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Build and progressively revise a class consensus model of the phenomenon across the lesson sequence
description: The guide has students sketch initial individual models, then maintain a class consensus model on chart paper that is deliberately incomplete at first — "It's OK if this initial model is inaccurate and/or incomplete" — and revised as observations, experiments, and reading accumulate. By Lesson 8 the final model represents sunlight transferring energy to objects, reflecting off light-colored surfaces and being absorbed by dark ones, with captions, and is used to explain or predict related phenomena.
requirements: Chart paper or similar visible record of student ideas and the consensus model maintained throughout the unit
target_learning_goals: Modeling and explaining scientific phenomena
Connecting new ideas to prior ideas across lessons
examples: In Lesson 8, students suggest changes so the consensus model shows sunlight reflecting off light-colored objects but absorbed by dark-colored ones.
key_sources: Practitioner's guide to integrating literacy and science. (2025). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/practitioners-guide-to-integrating-literacy-and-science/

article_title: Proportional relationships decluttered—at last!
citation: James Tanton, Ted Coe, April Ström, Kyle Pearce. (2022). Proportional relationships decluttered—at last! White paper. https://www.nwea.org
title: Six common contexts where proportional relationships arise
description: The paper enumerates the everyday and mathematical settings where, in its words, 'common sense informs us that a proportional relationship is at play': unit conversion and exchange rates, constant rates, percentages, scaled drawings and maps, similar figures in geometry, and ratios. Each context is worked with the same scaling-in-tandem reasoning rather than with cross multiplication.
requirements: Each context must involve two measurable quantities that plausibly scale in tandem
constraints: The paper cautions that constant-rate statements concern changes in quantities, not absolute values: distance from home is not proportional to clock time
target_learners: middle grades and secondary mathematics students
target_learning_goals: recognize proportional structure across varied contexts
examples: The paper works unit conversion (100 inches ↔ 254 cm), a 35-cents-per-dollar tax rate, a 135%-of-a-quantity problem, a 1:500 map scale, judging a friend's face width with fingers, and a 3:5 boy-to-girl class ratio
key_sources: James Tanton, Ted Coe, April Ström, Kyle Pearce. (2022). Proportional relationships decluttered—at last! White paper. https://www.nwea.org

article_title: Preparing early learners: Considerations for supporting the kindergarten class of 2021
citation: Beth Tarasawa, Angela Johnson, Christine Yankel. (2021). Preparing early learners: Considerations for supporting the kindergarten class of 2021. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org
title: Prioritize effectively supporting youngest students' learning because early skills are foundational to longer-term outcomes
description: The brief holds that because early academic and nonacademic skills are foundational, educators and leaders must find ways to effectively support young learners' learning, especially given pandemic-related enrollment changes. It states that "finding ways to effectively support our youngest students’ learning is critical for educators and leaders." This principle directs leader attention and resources toward early elementary grades during recovery.
requirements: Educators and leaders need an understanding of pandemic-related changes in kindergarten enrollment and early learning
target_learners: Young learners in preschool and early elementary school, including the kindergarten class of 2021
target_learning_goals: Foundational academic and nonacademic skills predictive of longer-term outcomes
examples: The brief frames its four leader considerations around this priority, noting that understanding enrollment changes and supporting young students' learning is critical

NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/preparing-early-learners-considerations-for-supporting-the-kindergarten-class-of-2021/

article_title: Estimating student growth on psychological and social-emotional constructs: A comparison of multiple scoring approaches
citation: Kuhfeld, Megan, and James Soland. (2020). Estimating Student Growth on Psychological and Social-emotional Constructs: A Comparison of Multiple Scoring Approaches. EdWorkingPaper No. 20-193. https://www.edworkingpapers.com/ai20-193
title: When survey responses from all timepoints are available, use MIRT calibration that accounts for latent variable covariances over time before fitting growth models
description: The article recommends that researchers scoring longitudinal survey measures of psychological and social-emotional constructs calibrate items with a multidimensional IRT model spanning all timepoints rather than sum scores or unidimensional calibration. The authors conclude that "a MIRT approach is likely preferable when survey responses from all timepoints are available at the time of calibration," because such models better recover true developmental trajectories and variance components. The recommendation rests on the simulation and empirical comparisons showing non-MIRT approaches understate slopes and variances.
requirements: Item responses from all timepoints available at the time of calibration
Consistent item set administered across timepoints
constraints: The article states MIRT models are "not a panacea for all measurement issues"; results were not examined under failures of longitudinal measurement invariance or shifting item composition across timepoints
target_learning_goals: accurate recovery of growth trajectories and variance components on psychological and social-emotional constructs
examples: The two simulation studies and the growth mindset empirical study each compared sum score, unidimensional IRT, and MIRT scoring approaches feeding latent growth curve models
key_sources: Kuhfeld, Megan, and James Soland. (2020). Estimating Student Growth on Psychological and Social-emotional Constructs: A Comparison of Multiple Scoring Approaches. EdWorkingPaper No. 20-193. https://www.edworkingpapers.com/ai20-193

article_title: Privacy Enhancing Technologies in Digital Learning Platforms
citation: Dorie, Vincent. (2025, December). Privacy enhancing technologies in digital learning platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/278
title: Design PETs into digital learning platforms from the ground up as core infrastructure
description: The long-term recommendation is that PETs be considered integral parts of DLPs both to protect data and further trust, and as purpose-limiting, research-enabling tools. They should be designed into DLPs from the ground up, not layered on to existing systems, with a privacy-by-design mindset applied to each step of the data lifecycle for each data source. The article argues this sustains the social license needed for long-term viability of educational research.
requirements: Data governance that considers each step of the data lifecycle for each data source
constraints: Adoption requires stakeholder buy-in and concerted efforts such as participatory design of PET adoption
target_learning_goals: sustainable, trustworthy educational research infrastructure
examples: The article recommends communities of practice discuss PETs at educational research conferences and share templated data sharing agreements
key_sources: Dorie, Vincent. (2025, December). Privacy enhancing technologies in digital learning platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/278

article_title: Interview Protocol for Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses
citation: Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses: Interview Protocol. (2025). Digital Promise / Achieving the Dream. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Probe both real-world relevance and racial-cultural connection when evaluating course engagement
description: The protocol treats two levers for engagement in statistics as worth probing separately: embedding real-world examples and scenarios into course content, and connecting course content to the racial and cultural experiences of the students. Interviewers ask how well the course makes each connection and how inclusion of real-world topics or racial identity and cultural experiences impacts learning, asking hypothetically if connections have not yet been made.
requirements: Interview questions must address both real-world connections and racial and cultural connections as distinct topics
constraints: Statistics courses can often seem very theoretical and disconnected from real life, which motivates the probes
target_learners: Undergraduate statistics students from a variety of backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Increase student interest and engagement in statistics
examples: The protocol asks students to rate how well the course makes connections to real world topics and to their own racial and cultural experiences
key_sources: Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses: Interview Protocol. (2025). Digital Promise / Achieving the Dream. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/05ccd902-1e80-4c94-9cd9-f706a98d0cc0

article_title: Fostering Market Effciency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement
citation: Morrison, J. R., Ross, S. M., Corcoran, R. P., & Reid, A. J. (2014). Fostering Market Efficiency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563768
title: Providers should seek third-party independent evidence to differentiate their products
description: The report recommends providers should seek opportunities to collect third-party (independent) evidence from evaluation studies, including both treatment-control group comparisons and case studies, to differentiate and support their products. As a practical alternative to complex and expensive RCTs, credible evidence for judging product fit and potential efficacy can come from pilots, case studies, and small comparison-group designs.
requirements: Engaging third-party evaluators for design reviews, case studies, or experimental comparison group studies
constraints: Few providers (except for the very large companies) can afford or win large grants to fund a randomized control trial
target_learning_goals: Differentiating products and supporting claims of effectiveness
examples: The report notes few providers seek opportunities for their products to be evaluated in pilots, case studies, and small comparison-group designs.
key_sources: Morrison, J. R., Ross, S. M., Corcoran, R. P., & Reid, A. J. (2014). Fostering Market Efficiency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563768

article_title: Strategic Surprise and the Future of Educational R&D
citation: Uncapher, M. & Roschelle, J. (2025, November). Strategic surprise and the future of educational R&D. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/277
title: Make solvable, high-leverage problems the organizing unit of education R&D
description: The paper recommends shifting from field-initiated to problem-focused research: invest in the discipline of problem definition, replace generic goals such as improving literacy with measurable, time-bound challenges, involve practitioners in all research stages through co-design, and build infrastructure for cumulative progress. A ripe problem is one where concerted effort could produce measurable change in the near term, with lessons that generalize.
requirements: Requires tolerating risk and failure in pursuit of breakthroughs with outsized impact, enabling bold bets that may fail but offer disproportionate upside.
constraints: The paper warns that if educational research responds to surprise only through normative, paradigmatic studies, transformative potential may not be harnessed.
target_learners: Education researchers and the practitioners who co-define research problems with them
target_learning_goals: Directing research effort toward timely, solvable challenges that drive systemic value
examples: The paper's researchers recommendation tells investigators to move beyond what interests them to what moves the needle, defining problems actionable within cycles.
key_sources: Uncapher, M. & Roschelle, J. (2025, November). Strategic surprise and the future of educational R&D. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/277

article_title: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: Briya Public Charter School, Washington, D.C.
citation: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: Briya. (2016). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Provide free or low-cost technical support and device access so families can maintain the technology they need
description: Even when families own devices, they often lack affordable technical support. Briya therefore provides "full technical support to ensure their parents and children always have the devices they need," connects learners to a local program offering low-cost laptops, lets learners use the program's IT department for device issues, and opens its devices for use before and after school. The case study names opening the program's IT division to families "a creative way to solve this need."
requirements: An IT department or technical support capacity that can be opened to learners
Devices available on site before and after school
constraints: Applies when families have their own devices but lack access to affordable technical support
target_learners: adult learners and families without affordable technical support
target_learning_goals: sustained access to digital learning tools
examples: Briya connects learners to a local program that provides low-cost laptops for families who do not have their own devices
key_sources: Lb0

article_title: Encouraging Girls in Math and Science
citation: Halpern, D., Aronson, J., Reimer, N., Simpkins, S., Star, J., and Wentzel, K. (2007). Encouraging Girls in Math and Science (NCER 2007-2003). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Research, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncer.ed.gov
title: Provide students with prescriptive, informational feedback focusing on strategies, effort, and the learning process
description: Teachers should give feedback that focuses on strategies used, effort expended, and the process of learning — for example identifying gains in strategy use or specific errors — rather than general praise such as "good job" or global intelligence praise. The guide states that "Prescriptive, informational feedback enhances students' beliefs about their abilities, typically improves persistence, and improves performance on tasks." It directs girls' attention to what to change after errors rather than letting them attribute wrong answers to lack of ability.
requirements: Multiple opportunities for students to receive feedback on their performance
Feedback that identifies specific strategies or errors rather than simply whether an answer was correct
constraints: A descriptive study of 58 third-grade mathematics classrooms found the primary form of feedback teachers actually use is general praise, which provides no useful information
target_learners: K-12 students in math and science courses
target_learning_goals: Self-efficacy beliefs about mathematics
Persistence on difficult tasks
Correcting misunderstandings and learning from mistakes
examples: The panel rated this recommendation Moderate based on small randomized experimental studies of children performing math or math-related tasks plus supporting research across many designs.
key_sources: Halpern, D., Aronson, J., Reimer, N., Simpkins, S., Star, J., and Wentzel, K. (2007). Encouraging Girls in Math and Science (NCER 2007-2003). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Research, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/5

article_title: Structuring Out-of-School Time to Improve Academic Achievement
citation: Beckett, M., Borman, G., Capizzano, J., Parsley, D., Ross, S., Schirm, A., & Taylor, J. (2009). Structuring out-of-school time to improve academic achievement: A practice guide (NCEE #2009-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. Retrieved from http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Provide engaging learning experiences in OST programs
description: OST programs should capitalize on their programming flexibility by offering activities students find especially engaging, particularly when students may be fatigued after a long school day, on Saturdays, or during summer months. The guide recommends making learning relevant by incorporating practical examples and connecting instruction to student interests and experiences, making learning active through collaborative learning and hands-on academic activities, and building adult-student relationships. To avoid the pitfalls of programs that failed to show academic effects, all activities should have a specific learning objective.
requirements: Every activity has a specific learning objective
Learning made relevant through practical examples and connections to student interests
Learning made active through collaborative and hands-on academic activities
Adult-student relationships built among OST participants
constraints: The level of evidence for this recommendation is low
target_learners: elementary and middle school OST participants, including fatigued after-school and summer program attendees
target_learning_goals: engagement in academically oriented OST activities with specific learning objectives
examples: The panel suggests engaging students when they may be fatigued after a long day of school, on Saturdays, or during the summer months, and notes 21st CCLC programs emphasized sports or extracurricular activities because those were thought more popular with students.

article_title: Designing an App to Support Families’ Joint Engagement with Media: Design Principles and Lessons from Research
citation: Digital Promise, The Jim Henson Company, Concord Evaluation Group, & Curious Media. (2021). Designing an app to support families' joint engagement with media: Design principles and lessons from research. [White Paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/121
title: Provide clear instructions for alternative ways to access content when including features like automatic sync
description: This principle holds that a second-screen app should pair an automatic content recognition sync feature with clear instructions for other ways families can access content, because some families cannot or prefer not to use sync. The team recommends incorporating sync since many who used it found it valuable, while noting "it would also be necessary to provide multiple ways to access information in the app."
requirements: The app includes a sync feature that many families find valuable for accessing episode-related content
constraints: Some families cannot use sync because they watch episodes and use the app on the same device rather than accessing the app on a second device

article_title: Changing the Principal Supervisor Role to Better Support Principals: Evidence from the Principal Supervisor Initiative
citation: Ellen B. Goldring, Melissa A. Clark, Mollie Rubin, Laura K. Rogers, Jason A. Grissom, Brian Gill, Tim Kautz, Moira McCullough, Michael Neel, Alyson Burnett. (2020). Changing the Principal Supervisor Role to Better Support Principals: Evidence from the Principal Supervisor Initiative. title: Redesign the principal supervisor role from administrative compliance toward developing principals as instructional leaders
description: The PSI demonstrates a design principle for district leadership support: shift the principal supervisor position away from a traditional focus on administration, operations, and compliance toward developing and supporting principals to be effective instructional leaders. Districts that made this shift under the PSI saw principals' perceptions of their supervisors improve, though effects did not extend to teachers' perceptions of principals.

Supervisors redirected toward developing and supporting principals rather than administration, operations, and compliance

article_title: Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through 8
citation: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Personalize and scaffold problem contexts before problem solving: reword problems into familiar contexts and clarify unfamiliar words in advance
description: The guide recommends that, so students can focus on the mathematics and reasoning, teachers ensure familiarity with a problem's context and language before solving. Concretely, "Teachers can help students by rewording problems, placing them in familiar contexts that better align with students' backgrounds, and clarifying unfamiliar words in advance." It illustrates this by recasting a grocery-shopping fraction problem as a gift-card problem at an electronics store.
requirements: Teachers need advance preparation time to review and reword problems before instruction.
constraints: These strategies are described as especially important for English language learners and students currently struggling with mathematics.
target_learning_goals: Mathematical problem solving in grades 4-8
examples: The guide rewords a Mrs. Sears grocery problem (spent 2/5, then 1/3 of the remainder, $30 left) into a Lee gift-card problem at Gadgets Galore with identical mathematics.
key_sources: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/16

article_title: Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through 8
citation: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Make problem solving an active part of classroom instruction and source supplementary problems beyond the textbook
description: The guide's overarching recommendation is that "Problem solving should not be reserved solely for homework and individual practice assignments. It should be an active part of mathematics teachers' classroom instruction." To do this, teachers must allocate preparation time for thoughtful problem selection and "will likely need to explore a variety of supplementary materials to find relevant and appropriate problems to extend the examples provided in their mathematics textbooks."
requirements: Teachers must allocate time during advance preparation to select problems thoughtfully and explore supplementary problem sources.
constraints: The textbook alone is treated as insufficient; problems must be extended with supplementary materials.
target_learning_goals: Strengthening skills and deepening understanding of math concepts through meaningful real-world problems
examples: The guide frames meaningful real-world problems as more likely to strengthen skills and deepen conceptual understanding when embedded in daily instruction.

article_title: Funding Coaching is Not Enough: The Role of the District Administrator in Coaching
citation: Hardy, A., & Bakhshaei, M. (2021). Funding coaching is not enough: The role of the district administrator in instructional coaching. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Protect coaches', principals', and teachers' time for coaching from unrelated duties and oversized caseloads
description: The report recommends that districts safeguard the time coaches and teachers spend together so they can consistently plan, implement new strategies, and reflect, and that coaches and principals get adequate time for consistent collaboration. Districts should verify before assigning unrelated tasks that coaches "will still have adequate time to meet with teachers and visit classrooms," since other duties and large caseloads diminish coaching impact.
requirements: Teachers must be assured that time spent with their coach is protected
Principals and coaches need a recurring standing meeting for consistent collaboration
target_learning_goals: sustained teacher-coach collaboration
implementation of new instructional strategies
examples: The report advises districts to encourage principals and coaches to set a recurring standing meeting and to check coaching-time availability before assigning non-coaching tasks.

article_title: Making Effective Use of Postsecondary Data in K-12 Education Settings
citation: Luke Heinkel, Kristin Hallgren, Brian Gill, Megan Shoji. (2015). Making Effective Use of Postsecondary Data in K-12 Education Settings. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Process or analyze postsecondary data beyond raw form before using them to inform K-12 policy and practice
description: This principle holds that K-12 officials should not rely on raw postsecondary data extracts alone when trying to inform policy and practice. The brief's key findings state directly that "additional processing or analysis of postsecondary data is required to use these data in more sophisticated ways." The brief presents this processing step as the bridge between descriptive reporting and the three sophisticated analytic uses it describes.
requirements: Access to postsecondary outcomes data on former students, such as through the National Student Clearinghouse StudentTracker for High Schools
Analytic capacity to process or analyze the raw data beyond descriptive reporting
target_learners: K-12 state, district, and school officials
target_learning_goals: Using postsecondary outcomes data to inform K-12 policy and practice
examples: The brief's key findings list additional processing or analysis as the requirement for moving from descriptive use to sophisticated use of postsecondary data

article_title: Towards an Evidence Framework for Emerging Educational Technologies
citation: Roschelle, J., Ruiz, P., Means, B., Griffiths, R., Lee, K. (2026 April). Towards an Evidence Framework for Emerging Educational Technologies. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/289
title: Prioritize the voice of education procurement leadership when reframing evidence frameworks
description: A core recommendation from the convening is 'the importance of involving and paying attention to perspectives and contributions of leaders in educational procurement as evidence is re-framed'. The article argues the traditional tiered approach assumes leaders want only causal impact evidence, and questions this assumption; these leaders want data on outcomes they care about plus implementation requirements so they can evaluate feasibility and return on investment.
requirements: Evidence must be anchored in student outcomes and staff use, and grounded in clearly defined student outcome goals
constraints: The article states further work with additional participants is needed to arrive at consensus recommendations
target_learning_goals: Feasibility and return-on-investment evaluation of edtech purchases
examples: A North Carolina model program organized districts by similar student populations and educational foci rather than geography; a California multi-district procurement collective demonstrated growing leadership strength in demanding evidence

article_title: Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators
citation: Ruiz, P. & Fusco, J. (2024). Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators. Educator CIRCLS Blog. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Prefer interpretable machine learning over post-hoc explainable machine learning in educational AI
description: The glossary defines interpretable machine learning as the creation of models that are inherently interpretable because "they provide their own explanations for their decisions". It recommends this approach over explainable ML, arguing we should understand what is happening from the beginning in our systems rather than try to explain black boxes after the fact, and notes we cannot know for certain whether an XAI explanation is correct.
requirements: Educators and developers evaluating AI tools should check whether interpretability is built into the model rather than added as an after-the-fact explanation.
constraints: The glossary notes that with XML/XAI "we cannot know for certain whether the explanation we are getting is correct", and presents interpretable models as the researchers' recommended alternative.
target_learning_goals: Evaluating the transparency and trustworthiness of AI systems used in education
examples: The glossary's interpretable machine learning and black boxes entries contrast IML with XAI, describing two primary ways to pull back the curtain on AI black boxes.

article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Practice-driven data: a five-lesson approach to using data for school improvement that has no playbook and no fidelity standard
description: The paper names and organizes an approach to data use in schools called practice-driven data, developed through the University of Chicago's partnership with Chicago Public Schools. It is explicitly not a scripted program: the approach has no playbook, no singular practice, no such thing as fidelity, and is instead rooted in respect for educator professionalism, context, and autonomy. The framework consists of five lessons — prepare (build capacity to facilitate hard conversations), focus (prioritize research-based indicators), make meaning (develop shared ownership over the implications of research), strategize (use the right data at the right time), and disrupt (identify and stop inequity). Together, the authors write, these lessons form an approach that focuses stakeholders on the most important goals and features of an ecosystem of data use with the potential to catalyze systematic improvement in student outcomes.
requirements: Educators and leaders must build capacity to facilitate hard data conversations, with an emphasis on trust, collaboration, and culture
Research-based indicators must be available and integrated into data that reaches schools
constraints: The approach was generated in a place-based partnership with Chicago high schools, and the authors note the high school context differs from K-8 and post-secondary education
The authors state the approach has no playbook and no fidelity standard, so implementation is inherently contextual
target_learners: high school educators and school leaders
target_learning_goals: using data to guide instructional and school improvement practice
building educator capacity for data-driven conversations
prioritizing research-based indicators of student success
examples: The paper presents the five lessons in Figure 1 and illustrates each with Chicago high school practice, such as NCS-supported Freshman Success Teams and the To&Through Online Tool
key_sources: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/practice-driven-data-lessons-chicagos-approach-research-data-and-practice-education

article_title: The Influence of Principal Leadership on Classroom Instruction and Student Learning
citation: James Sebastian and Elaine Allensworth. (2012). The Influence of Principal Leadership on Classroom Instruction and Student Learning: A Study of Mediated Pathways to Learning. Educational Administration Quarterly, 48(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/0013161X11436273
title: In high schools, principals should make school learning climate the priority in school improvement efforts
description: Because the between-school pathway from leadership to instruction and achievement runs only through learning climate, the authors argue that "principals need to make school climate the priority in their school improvement efforts" and that principal preparation programs should treat learning climate as a priority. Climate affects all classrooms, giving it the broadest schoolwide reach.
requirements: Principals must be able to shape safety, order, and college-going expectations across the whole school rather than only working with individual teachers
constraints: This does not mean other aspects of principals' roles are unimportant: within-school pathways such as professional development quality remain significant for individual teachers' instruction
target_learners: high school students, particularly in urban districts
target_learning_goals: schoolwide instructional quality
student achievement gains
examples: The study found schools with stronger leaders were more likely to be safe, orderly, and college-focused, and these climate differences yielded classrooms with better behavior and greater academic demands
key_sources: James Sebastian and Elaine Allensworth. (2012). The Influence of Principal Leadership on Classroom Instruction and Student Learning: A Study of Mediated Pathways to Learning. Educational Administration Quarterly, 48(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/0013161X11436273

article_title: A Series of Briefs: Implementing AI Literacy Across Learning Environments
citation: Ruiz, P., Liberman, B., Karim, S., Dallas, D., Zachariah, I., Peters Hinton, V., Chillmon, C., & Gonzales, L. (2025). Implementing AI literacy across learning environments: A series of briefs. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/268
title: Institutions should adopt proactive, thoughtful adaptation strategies rather than reacting to AI with urgency or fear
description: The briefs recommend that "Rather than reacting to AI developments with urgency or fear, institutions and communities need proactive, thoughtful adaptation strategies." Effective integration, they argue, requires deliberate planning with an emphasis on human connection, learning, and equity so that all learners and workers can thrive in an AI-integrated future. This principle guides the tone and pacing of the implementation guidance across the brief series.
requirements: Deliberate planning with emphasis on human connection, learning, and equity
constraints: AI technology is ever-evolving, so adaptation strategies must remain dynamic
target_learners: all learners and workers preparing for an AI-integrated future
target_learning_goals: safe and effective engagement with AI
equitable participation in AI-integrated environments
examples: The briefs advise policymakers to consider the interconnected implications of AI-related policies across settings for comprehensive, coordinated responses

article_title: Using the Freshman On-Track Indicator to Improve High Schools in Chicago
citation: Using the Freshman On-Track Indicator to Improve High Schools in Chicago. (1990). Chapter 5 of Measuring to Improve: Practical Measurement to Support Continuous Improvement in Education, Harvard Education Press. https://www.harvardeducationpress.com
title: Practical measurement should be relevant to practice, useful to practitioners, and integrated into practice
description: The chapter's parent volume defines practical measurement as "data collection and analysis that is relevant to practice, useful to practitioners, and designed to guide and even be integrated into practice". The principle holds that measurement for improvement differs from research measurement: its validity lies in whether practitioners can act on the data, as Chicago's on-track reports illustrate.
requirements: Data must be timely and formatted so school staff can act on it during the school year
target_learners: K-12 students, with the chapter focusing on ninth graders
target_learning_goals: continuous improvement of student outcomes such as graduation
examples: Chicago's Freshman Success reports were designed for staff to monitor and support ninth graders in real time, exemplifying measurement integrated into practice

article_title: Project Cal-Well: Building Sustainable School-Based Mental Health Systems
citation: Project Cal-Well: Building Sustainable School-Based Mental Health Systems. (2024). WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Project Cal-Well three-component model for sustainable school-based mental health systems
description: The brief describes the Project Cal-Well model as "anchored by three components": Component 1 improves school climate for schoolwide prevention (policy changes, mental health literacy training, universal screening, MTSS and SEL programs, student-led clubs); Component 2 increases access to school-based behavioral health services (linkage protocols, staffing, referral tracking); Component 3 enhances community collaborations (partnerships, outreach, crisis response protocols). LEAs used this multifaceted approach emphasizing collaboration, community engagement, and infrastructure development.

constraints: Developed and evaluated within a SAMHSA Project AWARE State Education Agency grant program in California local educational agencies

target_learning_goals: Student mental health awareness and access to school- and community-based mental health services
examples: Cohort 2 partnered with three county offices of education to support eight LEAs across five Northern California counties from 2019 to 2024

article_title: Del Norte Unified School District: "A Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health Services through Project Cal-Well"
citation: WestEd. (2024). Del Norte Unified School District: A Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health Services Through Project Cal-Well. https://www.wested.org/
title: Project Cal-Well three-component school mental health model implemented in DNUSD
description: Project Cal-Well is a California Department of Education program, initiated in 2014 and funded by a SAMHSA NITT-AWARE grant, that "aims to expand mental health services in schools and communities." In Cohort 2 (2019–24) it supported DNUSD's multi-tiered system of support across three components: universal Tier 1 supports for positive school climate and social–emotional skills, Tier 2 school-based mental health services, and Tier 3 partnerships and cross-system collaborations. The district used the grant as a foundation to leverage additional pandemic-era funding.

Coordination with local and county behavioral health resources
target_learners: All K-12 students, with escalating supports for students with elevated needs
target_learning_goals: Social–emotional skill development
Resilience
School safety
Access to mental health services
examples: DNUSD expanded its SEL Committee to include all 12 schools and created a Social Emotional Strategic Plan

article_title: Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics
citation: Rebecca Colina Neri, Jahneille Cunningham, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics. WestEd brief.
title: Practical measures as sensing mechanisms for CRSE implementation in mathematics
description: Practical measures are tools that "act as sensing mechanisms at the level at which work is carried out" and can be easily collected, analyzed, and used within practitioners' daily work lives. In CRSE mathematics, they help teachers gauge whether instruction resonates with diverse cultural backgrounds and adapt their practice.

constraints: The brief presents practical measures as requiring regular collection, analysis, and reflection time within teachers' work lives

target_learning_goals: assessing effectiveness of CRSE innovations
tailoring instruction to culturally and linguistically diverse learners
teacher reflection on equity-focused practice
examples: The brief lists gathering practices including formative assessment, self-reflection and peer observation, exit tickets, student feedback surveys, action research, supervisor feedback, and formative evaluations
key_sources: Rebecca Colina Neri, Jahneille Cunningham, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics. WestEd brief. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673572

article_title: What Educational Research Looked Like When Scores Were Rising: A Comparative Analysis of AERA Conference Programs, 2005-2014 and 2022-2025
citation: Quesen, S. (2026). What educational research looked like when scores were rising: A comparative analysis of AERA conference programs, 2005–2014 and 2022–2025. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Protect stable, nonpartisan federal research infrastructure because all educational research depends on it regardless of research focus
description: The principle holds that federal data systems—NAEP, longitudinal surveys, and enrollment tracking—are shared infrastructure that serves research across the ideological spectrum, so protecting them should be prioritized "independent of changing federal and state policy priorities." The author cites nearly $900 million in IES grant cuts and reports that nearly every one of the 11 most important education studies since 2002 drew on IES data infrastructure.
requirements: Sustained federal funding for data collection systems such as NAEP, longitudinal surveys, and enrollment tracking
constraints: Federal research priorities have swung in different directions across administrations, making infrastructure vulnerable to partisan shifts
target_learners: Policymakers at all levels of government
target_learning_goals: Maintaining the evidence base for educational policy and practice
examples: The report cites the elimination of nearly $900 million in IES grants and three fourths of National Science Foundation education funding as threats to fundamental data collection systems.

article_title: School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices
citation: Jackson, T., Pakhira, D., Fusco, J., Ruiz, P., Lekshmi Narayanan, A. B., Glazer, K., Eaglin, P., & Eguchi, A. (2021). School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices. CIRCLS. https://circls.org/reports/ai-policy

constraints: AI-enabled tools are designed and evaluated under specific settings and operate most reliably under those tuned constraints

examples: The brief asks educators to evaluate questions like how the AI works, for whom, and what potential biases it might have related to their students

article_title: Merging Cognitive Science and Curriculum to Strengthen Middle School Math

avoiding repeated errors

citation: A Call to Action on Behalf of U.S. Babies. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://forourbabies.org/wp/
title: Program for Infant/Toddler Care (PITC) training system for responsive, relationship-based infant/toddler care
description: The Program for Infant/Toddler Care (PITC) is a comprehensive training system developed by WestEd in collaboration with the California Department of Education that "promotes responsive, relationship-based care." requirements: Caregiver training that promotes responsive, relationship-based care of infants and toddlers

article_title: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts
citation: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela
title: Progress from familiar texts and formats to unfamiliar content and text structures
description: Rather than simplifying text or assuming students cannot identify themes, teachers differentiate instruction and help students draw on background knowledge to build deeper understandings. By progressing from analysis of more familiar ideas and formats to analyzing unfamiliar content and text structures, teachers gradually enable students to explore complex texts in a purposeful way. Each lesson takes students through similar types of texts representing similar genres and conventions, thematically designed so new lessons build on prior concepts and skills.
requirements: Lessons must be thematically designed so each new lesson builds on prior concepts and skills
target_learning_goals: comprehension and critical analysis of complex texts
examples: The unit's texts range from television commercials to Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address and pivotal speeches from the Civil Rights Movement.

article_title: What Further Research Is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools?
citation: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Strong principal leadership endorsing a change in discipline approach is essential for RJ implementation
description: Interviewed experts agreed on essential ingredients for implementing RJ in schools: strong leadership endorsing and advocating a change in the school's approach to discipline and culture, and training for school staff. The article reports that "a school principal who is committed to RJ and to creating a restorative environment in the school is essential for implementation to be successful," and that research is needed on leadership characteristics that best facilitate implementation and on sustainability.
requirements: Training for school staff alongside leadership commitment
constraints: Presented as expert consensus from interviews, not a tested relationship

article_title: Underuse of Title VII Funding for Indian Education in Arizona, Nevada, and Utah
citation: RMC Research Corporation. (2015). Underuse of Title VII funding for Indian education in Arizona, Nevada, and Utah. Phoenix, AZ: West Comprehensive Center at WestEd. http://www.westcompcenter.org
title: Because knowledge of a funding program is the primary difference between funded and unfunded eligible agencies, improving program awareness should precede expectations of participation
description: The report's central interpretive finding is that the "primary difference" between eligible LEAs that received Title VII funding and those that did not "was in terms of knowledge about the program." Unfunded respondents were generally unfamiliar with the program and its eligibility requirements, and many learned about Title VII for the first time through the study itself. This implies that outreach and information provision are preconditions for eligible agencies to access available resources.
requirements: Information about the program's purpose, eligibility criteria, and application process must reach the LEA personnel knowledgeable about grants and AI/AN education.
constraints: Based on interviews in three states with a small sample; the report states findings should not be considered broadly generalizable.
target_learners: American Indian/Alaska Native students in eligible but unfunded LEAs
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to federally funded educational and culturally related academic programming
examples: Many unfunded respondents indicated participation in the study was the first time they had learned about Title VII as a mechanism to serve AI/AN students.

article_title: Evidence-Based Improvement: A Guide for States to Strengthen Their Frameworks and Supports Aligned to the Evidence Requirements of ESSA
citation: Hale, S., Dunn, L., Filby, N., Rice, J., & Van Houten, L. (2017). Evidence-based improvement: A guide for states to strengthen their frameworks and supports aligned to the evidence requirements of ESSA. San Francisco: WestEd. http://www.wested.org/resources/evidence-based-improvement-essa-guide-for-states
title: Start continuous improvement with the problem, not the solution
description: The guide's framework principle is that improvement should begin with diagnosing needs rather than adopting a pre-chosen program: "A continuous improvement process starts with the problem, rather than the solution." The process addresses a discrete issue by systematically testing potential solutions while tracking well-defined and measurable goals, iterating as data are collected, analyzed, and discussed frequently so adjustments can be made and data collected again.
requirements: Needs assessment data used to identify and prioritize gaps, plus well-defined and measurable goals and hypotheses about causing factors
constraints: The initial effort often begins small and expands over time as fit to local conditions is better understood

article_title: High-Quality Science Instruction: Building Conceptual Understanding and Language Skills for English Learners
citation: DiRanna, K., & Gomez-Zwiep, S. (2013). High-Quality Science Instruction: Building Conceptual Understanding and Language Skills for English Learners. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Treat ELD proficiency levels as descriptions of what a student knows and can do at a stage, not as labels for students, since second-language acquisition is not strictly linear
description: The report advises structuring language development strategies to meet students' proficiency levels in California's ELD Proficiency Level Descriptors (emerging, expanding, bridging), while cautioning that the linear progression across levels is for purposes of presentation and understanding. Actual second-language acquisition does not necessarily occur in a linear fashion within or across proficiency levels. A proficiency level identifies what a student knows and can do at a particular stage, so it is inaccurate to speak of an "emerging student" but accurate to say a student's listening comprehension is at the emerging level.
requirements: Language supports should be matched to the proficiency level of the relevant skill, not applied as a blanket student label
constraints: The linear progression across proficiency levels reflects presentation conventions, not the actual course of second-language acquisition
target_learners: English learners at all proficiency levels
target_learning_goals: English proficiency
access to high-level, cognitively demanding academic work with appropriate linguistic support
examples: The report contrasts saying a teacher has an "emerging student" (inaccurate) with saying a student's listening comprehension ability is at the emerging level (accurate)
key_sources: Lb0

constraints: The program targets turnaround principals and educators preparing for that role in low-performing schools

article_title: Thought Leadership Forum Brief: Talent Development and Opportunity Culture
citation: Center on School Turnaround at WestEd. (2018). Thought Leadership Forum Brief: Talent Development and Opportunity Culture. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://WestEd.org
title: Project LIFT: public-private Opportunity Culture implementation in Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools

focus professional development to impact student achievement
increase compensation tied to student-learning factors

article_title: States' School Safety Centers: A Brief Look into History, Characteristics, and Activities
citation: McKenna, J., Russo, S., Sutherland, H., Boal, A., & Petrosino, A. (2022). States’ school safety centers: A brief look into history, characteristics, and activities. WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org
title: Proposed initial uniform definition of a state school safety center (SSSC)
description: The article proposes an initial definition of what constitutes an SSSC, based on its survey data: "A state-level resource that is funded through state appropriations, state/federal grants, or some combination of the two; that, at a minimum, serves the entire state as a central clearinghouse for school safety information and resources; and that may provide technical assistance and training and/or develop resources to support school safety efforts." The definition was developed because respondents varied in whether they counted agency-embedded offices as SSSCs.

constraints: The authors present it as at least an initial definition, subject to refinement through future data collection

article_title: Fostering Resiliency in Kids: Protective Factors in the Family, School, and Community.
citation: Benard, B. (1991). Fostering Resiliency in Kids: Protective Factors in the Family, School, and Community. Western Regional Center for Drug-Free Schools and Communities, Northwest Regional Educational Laboratory. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED335781
title: Protective-factors triad: support, high expectations, and youth participation across family, school, and community
description: The article's organizing framework holds that resiliency in youth is built by three protective factors — caring and support, high expectations, and encouragement of participation — that recur in each of the three socializing systems of family, school, and community. As the abstract states, "Support, high expectations, and encouragement of youth participation are family, school, and community protective factors." The framework rests on the transactional-ecological model, in which personality is viewed as a self-righting mechanism adapting to its environment, and it directs prevention programs toward enhancing environmental contexts rather than fixing individuals.
requirements: Prevention interventions must focus on enhancing and creating positive environmental contexts — families, schools, and communities — rather than a pathology-focused, fix-the-child approach
constraints: The review notes that most studies of vulnerable children have defined risk at only one level of organization, and data analyses exploring interplay among multiple risks and protective factors at all three levels are still rare
target_learners: children and youth at risk due to stress, adversity, or economic deprivation
target_learning_goals: social competence
problem-solving skills
autonomy
sense of purpose and future

article_title: The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers Leading Sustainable Professional Learning in Their Communities
citation: Lotan, R. A., & Burns, D. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers leading sustainable professional learning in their communities. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-teachers-leading
title: Professional capital: human, social, and decisional capital that amplifies teacher effectiveness
description: The casebook invokes Hargreaves and Fullan's concept of professional capital as a strategy for changing education and strengthening the teaching profession. It is "the confluence of three other kinds of capital—human, social, and decisional—that amplify one another." The report states that "Professional capital combines teachers' professional knowledge and skills, their collective capacity to form networks and communities of learning and practice, and their use of experience to make decisions about teaching and learning that are in the best interests of their students." The ILC's teachers-teaching-teachers approach is presented as allowing teachers to develop professional capital and lead sustainable professional development.
requirements: Investing in the professional capital of individuals, the group, and the system, which the report says improves learning and achievement
constraints: The framework is cited from Hargreaves and Fullan as background theory, not tested in this report
target_learners: Practicing K-12 teachers and teacher leaders
target_learning_goals: Building collective professional capacity for standards-aligned instruction
examples: ILC teacher leaders aligned activities with school and district improvement goals, boosting capacity for instructional choices and enhancing their decisional capital

article_title: Principal Learning Opportunities and School Outcomes: Evidence from California
citation: Campoli, A. K., & Darling-Hammond, L. (with Podolsky, A., & Levin, S.). (2022). Principal learning opportunities and school outcomes: Evidence from California. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/438.376
title: Professional Learning Theory of Action: principal learning shapes leadership behaviors that influence teacher and student outcomes
description: The report's organizing framework "assumes connections between principal professional learning—both the content of learning and strategies for learning—and principal enactment of specific leadership behaviors." Leadership behaviors in turn relate to teacher practices and retention, school climate, and student opportunities and learning, all unfolding within state, district, school, and community contexts and policies. The framework distinguishes content areas (instructional leadership, school improvement, school conditions, developing people, meeting diverse students' needs) from learning strategies (applied learning, internships, coaching and mentoring, cohorts and networks), and applies to novice principals, experienced principals, assistant principals, and teacher leaders.

Developing people
Managing change
Shaping a positive school climate
Meeting diverse students' needs

article_title: Fostering Belonging, Transforming Schools: The Impact of Restorative Practices
citation: Darling-Hammond, S. (2023). Fostering belonging, transforming schools: The impact of restorative practices. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/169.703
title: The program–practice distinction: restorative programs are training systems while restorative practices are the specific actions that drive outcomes
description: The report's central organizing framework distinguishes restorative programs—systems of training designed to encourage community members to use restorative practices—from restorative practices themselves. It states that "Restorative programs offer various kinds of training to staff to help them learn to use restorative practices" while "Restorative practices are the specific actions in which community members might engage in a restorative school." Because programs often fail to shift practices pervasively, prior research evaluating program adoption may miss the effectiveness of practices, the true target of interest. This study is designed to measure the impacts of student exposure to practices directly.
requirements: Evaluating practices rather than programs requires data that track student exposure to restorative practices over time, which the report notes few datasets have allowed
constraints: The report notes programs vary substantially in design and implementation and that there is no established definition of which program model makes a school 'restorative'
target_learning_goals: conflict resolution skills
school climate
reduction of exclusionary discipline
examples: The report identifies program quality, restorative readiness, and teacher discretion as moderators of whether a program results in student exposure to practices

article_title: Implementation and Impact of the Project with Curriculum in Juvenile Justice Facilities and Group Homes
citation: Nakamoto, J., Carter, C., & Russo, S. (2025). Implementation and impact of the Project With curriculum in juvenile justice facilities and group homes. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Project With: a 12-lesson literary-based relationship skills and self-management curriculum for justice-involved youth
description: Project With is a sexual health curriculum adapted from The Art of Loving Well in which youth read a literary selection such as a short story or poem, discuss it with peers and a facilitator with lived experience consistent with justice-involved youth, and complete an aligned activity. It comprises 12 lessons delivered in a 6-week, twice-weekly format, with each lesson carrying a "Big Idea" related to relationship skills or self-management. Groups of 5 to 10 youth sharing a meal with the facilitator between two lessons in ideal delivery

target_learning_goals: Relationship skills
Self-management and self-regulation
Goal setting and life planning
Sexual risk avoidance

article_title: A Comprehensive Review of the Changing Landscape of Academic Dishonesty in Automated Proctoring in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
citation: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). A comprehensive review of the changing landscape of academic dishonesty in automated proctoring in the era of artificial intelligence. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01275-6
title: Taxonomy of proctoring systems: offline proctoring and online proctoring subdivided into live, semi-automated, and fully automated
description: The review organizes proctoring systems into a classification derived from its literature study. It states that "various proctoring systems have been developed: offline proctoring, online proctoring", with online systems "categorized into live proctoring, semi-automated and automated proctoring systems". Offline proctoring requires a physical invigilator at an exam venue; live proctoring combines a virtual tool with a human proctor monitoring in real time; semi-automated proctoring records video and periodic images; fully automated proctoring uses AI tools without human involvement and generates a report at the end of the exam.
requirements: Fully automated proctoring requires infrastructure such as persistent internet connectivity, authentication, storage facilities, and security, which the review notes incur huge costs.
constraints: The review notes semi-automated proctoring has the drawback of lack of internet connectivity and the infrastructure required for processing images.

target_learning_goals: maintaining academic integrity during examinations
preventing cheating in online and offline assessments
examples: The review describes semi-automated image-based proctoring in which "the examinee's photos are taken at specified intervals: at the start of the exam, at the conclusion, and during the answering process, every 30 to 45 s."

citation: Zhang, Y., Jiang, J. & Tang, X. (2026). Toward Agent-Based Educational Science: Rethinking Educational Research in the Age of AI. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 113. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10209-5

Any use of simulated learners for prediction should therefore operate at the level of distributions and counterfactuals rather than individual fate.

constraints: The article states this distinction is needed to address humanistic concerns about flattening learner diversity

preserving learner diversity in simulation-based evaluation
examples: The article defines the term prediction this way in a note applying it throughout the paper

article_title: The 5P Reflection Model for Education in the Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Era
citation: Rajan Kadel, Samar Shailendra, Islam Mohammad Tahidul, Urvashi Rahul Saxena, Aakanksha Sharma, and Sabitra Kaphle. (2026). The 5P Reflection Model for Education in the Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Era. Pre-print submitted to IEEE Transactions on Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03413

description: Because GenAI challenges the authorship and authenticity of learner-produced artefacts, reflection models should focus on the reflective process rather than the product. The article argues existing models assume the product is created by learners themselves, and advocates a "process over product" philosophy so that learners' reasoning, prompts and iterations become observable and assessable even when GenAI assists.

constraints: The article frames this as necessary for authenticity assessment in GenAI-rich environments rather than as a universally tested recommendation

academic integrity
deep learning with GenAI support

article_title: Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does
citation: Hou, X., Weng, Y., Yeh, C. H., Lee, D. L., Zheng, L., Li, F., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22993
title: Preserved metacognitive demand: hold what the learner must decide constant and let carried load vary with demonstrated need
description: The principle states that "An AI learning system should hold the learner's metacognitive demand approximately constant, and let the cognitive load it carries vary with demonstrated need." It rests on the paper's separation of two quantities that giving-more-or-less designs run together: the load the system carries and the demand placed on the learner before help arrives. CoMeT implements it by escalating support at decision points on failure and fading on take-up, so the learner keeps deciding while the tutor's labour varies.
requirements: The tutor must be able to identify decision points and detect take-up from the learner's turns, via authored coverage patterns plus a take-up judgement

citation: Kazuki Kawamura. (2025). AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques. Doctoral dissertation, The University of Tokyo. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08990
title: Profy data-driven pronunciation feedback system learned from unannotated audio
description: Profy is an automated feedback system for imitation-based skill learning, instantiated for second-language pronunciation. It constructs a deep learning model that "directly learns what constitutes good and poor performance from unannotated audio data", avoiding the annotated error-pattern databases of conventional CAPT systems. The system highlights waveform regions emphasized by the classifier and shows model-derived acoustic distances from native-speaker distributions in latent space, giving learners localized feedback on where their performance deviates.

Self-supervised learning techniques for representation learning

citation: Miina Koyama, Ruiwei Xiao, and John Stamper. (2026). PromptDecipher: Supporting AI Tutor Authoring Through Editable Simulated Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16605
title: PromptDecipher: a web-based system for authoring AI tutoring chatbots through direct correction of bot responses
description: PromptDecipher is a web-based system that "enables educators to author and refine AI tutoring chatbots through direct correction of bot responses, without requiring expertise in prompt engineering." Teachers create a bot, select a foundation model (OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google), optionally upload course materials, and work in a test environment showing a simulated student chat. The primary unit of authoring is the simulated tutoring chat, not the prompt; a live prototype, an anonymized codebase, and an anonymized demo are available.

article_title: Design Principles and Observable Indicators for AI-Enabled Pedagogical Accompaniment: Evidence from the Amico Dual-Mode Prototype in Italy and China
citation: Pier Paolo Benedetti. (2026). Design Principles and Observable Indicators for AI-Enabled Pedagogical Accompaniment: Evidence from the Amico Dual-Mode Prototype in Italy and China. Accepted at the 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Education (ICAIE 2026), IEEE.
title: Principle-to-indicator mapping as an accountability device for AI-enabled pedagogical systems
description: The framework translates pedagogical design principles into observable indicators using a compact mapping (Table I) from principle to indicator to observation method: transparency of identity and limits (misinterpretation rate via survey/observation), scaffolding toward humans (transition-to-human prompts and follow-through signals via logs/observation), directional micro-mediations (micro-action formulation and completion via logs/rubrics), prevention of dependency (looping and exclusive-use signals via logs), communicative autonomy support (goal/question articulation quality via rubrics), and data minimization (sensitive-data solicitation frequency, which should be near zero). The mapping is treated as an accountability device making the system's pedagogical function testable through concrete traces, structured judgments, and participant perceptions.
requirements: Combines light quantitative traces with qualitative rubrics and facilitator observation so that accompaniment is not reduced to what is easiest to measure; indicators are treated as signals supporting professional judgment, not exhaustive KPIs.
constraints: In the pilot, transition-to-human follow-through could not be systematically verified and was not reported as a quantified metric; facilitator notes and brief post-task items require confirmation with larger samples and validated instruments.
target_learners: Learners and adult educational actors in non-clinical educational settings
target_learning_goals: Pedagogical accountability: assessing whether an AI system supports education or drifts into substitution and dependency dynamics
examples: The relational bridge loop (Table II) operationalizes the mapping in six steps: entry, micro-mediation generating 1–3 micro-actions, directionality toward a human target, exit with closure prompt, accountability checks, and risk-signal response reducing interaction and recommending human contact.
