citation: Yearim Kim, Injun Baek, and Nojun Kwak. 2026. When Saying No Makes Better Videos: Designing Dual Gatekeeping for Pedagogically Grounded AI Content Creation. In Proceedings of Understanding and Engaging Critical Resistance to AI in Education (CHI '26 Workshop). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19812
title: Principled resistance: theory-grounded, dual-layer gatekeeping of AI-generated educational content
description: The article conceptualizes "principled resistance" as "deliberate, theory-grounded pushback against AI outputs that fail pedagogical standards", taking three concrete forms: rejecting (requesting regeneration), revising (manual editing), and overriding (vetoing automated flags). Rooted in Mayer's CTML, the framework holds that educators and algorithms catch different kinds of problems—humans detect nuanced pedagogical mismatches while algorithms verify structural integrity—so building both checkpoints into one pipeline creates overlapping coverage neither could achieve alone. It reframes pedagogical friction as a site of professional accountability rather than inefficiency.
requirements: Educators must be briefed on the CTML principles the system enforces, as participants in the study were "priorly briefed on the CTML principles"
constraints: The article notes neither layer is exhaustive and the long-term viability of iterative review in daily classroom preparation remains unknown
target_learning_goals: pedagogical quality of AI-generated instructional videos
examples: PedaCo operationalizes the framework with educator script review before rendering and automated metrics after video synthesis

title: Scaffold students' GenAI dialogue with prompt scaffolding built on context, objective, and role elements to improve peer feedback quality

Context supplies argument content and background knowledge; objective specifies the evaluation tasks GenAI should perform; roles such as approvers or detractors let the model conduct thought experiments. The bug injection pipeline acts as middleware that intercepts correct generated code and replaces it with validated, runnable near-miss variants containing subtle faults. citation: Poquet, O., Nanduri, M. S., Salinas Loyer, M. X., Stadler, M., Sailer, M., Jovanovic, J. (2026). Profiling Cognitive Offloading in LLM-mediated Synthesis Writing: Volume vs. Content. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10434
title: Coding framework for the content of LLM offloading prompts (active/passive by local/global comprehension)
description: A four-way coding scheme applied to each of 564 learner prompts, capturing whether the learner "remained somewhat active or was passive during a comprehension activity, and if the comprehension within a prompt was targetting local or global level". Active prompts specify learner direction (clarifying gaps, seeking evaluation or structure); passive prompts leave the LLM to act without learner-specified constraints; local refers to micro-level items and global to whole-text or cross-text structure. Reproducibility was checked against three LLM-based labelling agents, reaching an average kappa of 0.64 (passive/global) and 0.61 (local/global).
requirements: An expert-coded prompt corpus and a coding framework with worked examples; automated agent labelling with framework-rule checking for reproducibility
constraints: The framework was not further fine-tuned to avoid overfitting; the article notes other tasks may require other lenses to represent offloading patterns
target_learners: university students using LLMs in synthesis writing
target_learning_goals: characterising comprehension-related cognitive offloading in learner-LLM interaction
examples: Example codings include 'What does the assumption mean in text A?' as active-local and 'Write me a 300-word synthesis' as passive-global

title: Three-dimensional framework for assessing problem posing ability: number, category, and quality
description: The article operationalizes students’ problem posing ability in science into three coded dimensions, defining them so that "category was used to reflect the breadth of question types and the characteristics of their knowledge sources; and quality was used to reflect the depth of cognitive processing" demonstrated in students’ questions, with number reflecting how many questions were posed. article_title: Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks
citation: Enkelejda Kasneci and Gjergji Kasneci. (2026). Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14604
title: Tutoring evaluations should report pressure-resolved failure rates, confidence-conditioned deference profiles, and judge-disagreement reliability signals
description: The paper recommends that educational LLM evaluations treat pedagogical sycophancy under social-epistemic pressure as a safety failure and measure it explicitly before deployment. It states: "We recommend that evaluations report (i) pressure-specific failure rates, (ii) confidence-conditioned “deference profiles” rather than a single aggregate, and (iii) explicitreliability signals such as judge disagreement and human-validated subsets where feasible." The rationale is that a single aggregate score can hide the most safety-relevant cases, since borderline responses mix correction with reassurance, and warm hedged correction can resemble warm wrong capitulation.
requirements: Two-judge disagreement tracking and human adjudication of ambiguous cases, because polite capitulation can resemble good pedagogy
constraints: Reported rates should be interpreted together with disagreement and audit statistics, not as judge-independent facts
target_learners: benchmark creators, model developers, and deployers of LLM tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: avoiding pressure-contingent validation of learner misconceptions in deployed tutors
examples: The paper's own evaluation reports adjudicated SYC and DISAGREE rates per tutor, per pressure mode, per confidence level, and per domain rather than a single leaderboard score

citation: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. title: Treat privacy as a capture-policy problem: record task-relevant metadata rather than full interaction replay
description: DebugTracker's privacy stance is to bound capture to the task: "it records task-relevant metadata rather than a full interaction replay". By default it does not store complete terminal output, screen video, mouse movement, or per-keystroke history, and it saves baseline and final source snapshots so instructors can compare the starting bug with the submitted fix. Reports also separate captured evidence from instructor-only interpretation.
requirements: A capture policy that limits storage to task-relevant metadata; workspace-local artifacts such as JSONL logs, Markdown reports, and snapshots
constraints: The article states this design records less than full replay, so it captures what a review task requires rather than everything a student did
target_learners: Students whose debugging sessions are recorded for assessment
target_learning_goals: Process-oriented feedback and assessment of debugging without intrusive surveillance-style capture
examples: Human labels are appended as separate events and instructor-side reports are derived from the log, keeping the student's raw assessment trace distinct from the instructor's interpretation

citation: Meghna Manoj Nair, Rachel Greenstadt. (2026). "We'll Fix It Later": Education, AI, and the Deferral of Student Privacy in EdTech. New York University. https://www.nyu.edu
title: The privacy deferral cycle in EdTech
description: A theory-building framework from the interview study, summarized in Figure 1, in which privacy deferral reproduces itself across the product lifecycle. As the article puts it, "Figure 1 summarizes the resulting theory": privacy struggles to enter the business case at strategy and funding stages, cloud delegation substitutes for internal engineering during build, pilots surface usability rather than privacy concerns, procurement can shift responsibility to schools with uneven capacity, AI introduces less visible downstream uses, and incidents finally create reactive attention. The cycle continues because underlying incentive, ownership, and feedback structures remain unchanged.
requirements: The framework was built from 12 interviews using Charmaz's grounded theory principles, with credibility grounded in convergence across roles and contexts rather than saturation
constraints: The article states the categories are an explanatory structure for findings, not evidence that every EdTech organization exhibits each pattern
The article does not claim analytical saturation or generalizability from the 12-person sample
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students using institutionally mandated EdTech platforms
target_learning_goals: Protection of student data privacy and governance of AI-enabled learning tools
examples: Figure 1 depicts privacy deferral across the EdTech product lifecycle, where market pressure and delegation stabilize deferral and weak feedback loops sustain it

citation: Shen, N., Lee, L. S., and He, A. (2026). Generative AI in creative education: baseline-linked evidence on learning processes, artistic performance, and authorship. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1956939
title: Process–outcome decoupling in AI-supported creative education
description: The article develops process–outcome decoupling as an explanatory account for AI-supported creative learning: perceived support, fluency, and confidence can rise while assessed artistic competence, authorship, and judgment do not. The authors write that "This tension can be understood as a process–outcome decoupling pattern: AI may intensify the visible activity of creative learning without necessarily strengthening the artistic competence, ownership, or judgment through that learning is evaluated." The framework draws on illusions of learning and cognitive offloading research and motivates evaluating AI use by authorship, internalization, and transferable agency, not output quality alone.
requirements: Evidence must link reported learning-process experience with assessed performance rather than perceptions alone, as the study does by combining prior performance, final assessment, and questionnaire data.
constraints: The article frames the pattern as an association-based account from a single-institution, course-based design, not a causal demonstration.
target_learners: undergraduate art and design students in studio-based courses
target_learning_goals: creative agency and authorship
internalization of creative decisions
transferable artistic judgment
examples: The study operationalizes the framework by comparing AI-use associations with perceived support and skill transfer against baseline-adjusted final performance and performance-change models.
key_sources: Shen, N., Lee, L. S., and He, A. (2026). Generative AI in creative education: baseline-linked evidence on learning processes, artistic performance, and authorship. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1956939

article_title: From Unified to Differentiated Materials: Generative AI–Supported Adaptation of EAP Reading Materials
citation: Gao X (2026) From unified to differentiated materials: generative AI–supported adaptation of EAP reading materials. Front. Psychol. 17:1887565. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1887565
title: Proficiency-sensitive barrier-to-support mapping for EAP reading materials
description: The article organizes EAP reading adaptation around a mapping from proficiency-specific reading barriers to text-embedded supports, process indicators, and outcome foci. Low-proficiency learners face vocabulary and syntax load addressed by "glosses, short paraphrases, sentence unpacking, and clause segmentation"; intermediate learners face discourse navigation addressed by rhetorical labels, paragraph-function notes, and claim–evidence outlines; high-proficiency learners face evidence and stance evaluation addressed by critical prompts. Each pathway assigns a distinct process indicator (cognitive load, discourse awareness, critical engagement) so process variables are not treated as interchangeable.
requirements: Supports must be fixed, text-embedded, and task-bound, printed into the material as glosses, labels, notes, outlines, or prompts.
The dominant barrier for each proficiency group must be identified before selecting the support layer.
constraints: Teacher mediation during reading falls outside this operationalization of scaffolding.
The mapping was evaluated in one EAP instructional context with three source passages and 15 reviewed material versions.
target_learners: Adult undergraduate EAP readers at low, intermediate, and high proficiency
target_learning_goals: Academic reading comprehension
EAP task performance including summary, claim–evidence use, and critical response
examples: Low-proficiency versions added inline glosses such as "glucose = a typeofsugar" and process breakdowns listing stages of glycolysis; high-proficiency versions added stance and evidence prompts such as evaluating the power-plant analogy and considering counterexamples.
key_sources: Gao X (2026) From unified to differentiated materials: generative AI–supported adaptation of EAP reading materials. Front. Psychol. 17:1887565. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1887565

article_title: Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific argumentation
citation: Ates, H. (2026). Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific argumentation. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00614-9
title: Design GenAI feedback environments to preserve student agency, evaluative judgment, and ownership during revision
description: The article's central design principle is that the educational value of GenAI feedback depends less on AI access than on whether the feedback environment keeps learners responsible for judging quality. The abstract states that value "may depend less on AI access per se than on whether feedback environments preserve student agency, evaluative judgment, and ownership during revision." Designs that require students to articulate an initial judgment before receiving AI critique position AI feedback as a resource for comparison rather than a substitute for judgment.
requirements: Students must be positioned to interpret critique, compare it against criteria, and decide how revision should proceed
constraints: Reflective and hybrid designs require additional evaluative activity and time-on-task, so advantages reflect the whole designed process
target_learners: higher education students in science courses
target_learning_goals: feedback uptake
evaluative judgment
durable transfer of argumentation skill
examples: The hybrid condition required a 100–150 word revision memo explaining which suggestions students accepted, rejected, or modified
key_sources: Ates, H. (2026). Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific argumentation. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00614-9

article_title: A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers based on goals, models
citation: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder.
title: A principled framework bridging educational goals, models of human learning, and technology use in AI-era higher education
description: The article advances a framework positioned as a third path between discourse on AI's promise and peril and immediate implementation advice. It states: "a set of guiding principles can bridge the gap, connecting our implementation approaches to the large-scale goals we have for education." The framework connects broad goals (individual development, societal infrastructure, workforce) to actionable practices for educators, learners, and administrators, and is designed to be flexible across contexts.
requirements: Educators and policy makers must be explicit about the goals they are advancing before choosing technologies
constraints: The framework presupposes the value of institutions of higher education and focuses on colleges and universities, though the author notes many approaches will likely apply to pre- and post-college environments
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning, discernment, empathy, sense of self, preparation for dynamic futures
examples: The article applies the framework through scenarios including ubiquitous institution-supported AI access, basic skills catch-up, students training AI agents, and addressing TA shortages
key_sources: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01467

article_title: Thoughtless Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence and College Students' Self-Directed Learning: A Multi-Group SEM Analysis of Gender Differences
citation: Hui Zhao & Huijuan Gu. (2026). Thoughtless use of generative artificial intelligence and college students’ self-directed learning: a multi-group SEM analysis of gender differences. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-54337-y
title: Higher education institutions should promote responsible AI use to protect students’ self-directed learning
description: Because thoughtless use of generative AI was found to undermine self-directed learning directly and through lowered self-efficacy and motivation, the article positions its findings as guidance for institutions. It states the study offers "practical implications for higher education institutions seeking to promote responsible AI use and strengthen students’ SDL." The principle directs institutions to address unreflective adoption of AI outputs rather than only expanding AI access.
requirements: Institutional attention to how students engage with AI outputs, not merely whether they use AI tools
constraints: Evidence base is a self-reported cross-sectional survey from four universities in Henan Province, China, using snowball sampling; causality is not established
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning
responsible AI use
examples: The survey documented students using conversational AI for generating assignment ideas, obtaining explanations, assisting writing, and solving academic problems
key_sources: Hui Zhao & Huijuan Gu. (2026). Thoughtless use of generative artificial intelligence and college students’ self-directed learning: a multi-group SEM analysis of gender differences. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-54337-y

article_title: Under surveillance: Mapping remote proctoring practices in the assessment of nursing students — a scoping review
citation: Harerimana A, Mtshali N, Mchunu G. (2026). Under surveillance: mapping remote proctoring practices in the assessment of nursing students— a scoping review. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00229-7
title: Remote proctoring as a spectrum of technologically mediated assessment security strategies
description: The review organizes remote proctoring into a spectrum of modalities rather than a monolithic practice: AI-based automated/recorded systems (Honorlock, Respondus Monitor with LockDown Browser), live human invigilation (ProctorU), webcam/video proctoring with lockdown browsers, mobile-phone-based invigilation (the Invigilator app), and electronic test-center surveillance. It states remote proctoring "constitutes a spectrum of technologically mediated assessment security strategies, each with distinct trade-offs", reflecting disparities in infrastructure, institutional capacity, and assessment context. Context-adapted approaches in resource-constrained settings illustrate pragmatic alternatives to proprietary AI systems.
requirements: Depends on reliable internet connectivity, suitable devices, user-friendly platforms, adequate technical support, and assessment approaches aligned with student expectations
constraints: No single proctoring approach is universally effective; success is highly context-dependent
target_learning_goals: upholding academic integrity in online assessment
examples: Six included studies deployed Honorlock (UK), ProctorU and Respondus Monitor (USA), the Invigilator mobile app (Southern Africa), webcam proctoring with lockdown browser (USA), and electronic test-center surveillance (Egypt)
key_sources: Harerimana A, Mtshali N, Mchunu G. (2026). Under surveillance: mapping remote proctoring practices in the assessment of nursing students— a scoping review. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00229-7

article_title: ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming
citation: Anahita Golrang, Kshitij Sharma, Simon Dehaen, Olga Viberg. (2026). ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02703
title: ProPACT: forecast-driven dyadic learner modeling treating collaboration as the object of instruction
description: ProPACT is an AI-driven adaptive collaborative tutor that treats collaboration itself, rather than the individual learner, as the object of instruction. It builds a dyadic learner model in which "ProPACT constructs a dyadic learner model based on Joint Visual Attention (JVA) and Joint Mental Effort (JME), alongside individual mental effort (ME)", and uses an XGBoost forecasting model to predict suboptimal collaboration states up to 30 seconds ahead. Predictions drive a hierarchical adaptive policy that orchestrates dialogue prompts, gaze-awareness cues, AI-assisted code suggestions, and task-based hints while fading support during productive collaboration.
requirements: Dual eye-tracking and pupillometry sensing infrastructure to measure JVA, ME, and JME in real time
Empirically validated thresholds from prior DUET and eye-tracking research for discretizing indicators into High, Average, and Low levels
constraints: The study was conducted in a controlled laboratory setting with a relatively small sample size and short-duration debugging tasks
The system relies on specialized sensing infrastructure, including dual eye-tracking and pupillometry, which poses practical and financial constraints for large-scale deployment
target_learners: Undergraduate or master's students in computer science or engineering learning pair programming
target_learning_goals: Collaborative debugging and pair-programming regulation, including attention alignment and cognitive-effort balance
examples: In the evaluation, 26 dyads debugged tasks containing only logical bugs under control and ProPACT feedback conditions with eye trackers individually calibrated
key_sources: Anahita Golrang, Kshitij Sharma, Simon Dehaen, Olga Viberg. (2026). ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02703

article_title: ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming
citation: Anahita Golrang, Kshitij Sharma, Simon Dehaen, Olga Viberg. (2026). ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02703
title: ProPACT Hybrid-AI feedback system with five feedback tools and hierarchical trigger policy
description: The feedback system is a Hybrid-AI framework that "combines data-driven forecasting with rule-based pedagogical decision-making". An XGBoost model predicts JVA, JME, and ME over a 30-second horizon; predictions are discretized against each participant's resting baseline using a ±2SD criterion and mapped against a desired collaboration matrix to predefined trigger conditions. Five feedback tools are integrated: GitHub Copilot autocomplete, dual text selection, a gaze-awareness tool, a dialogue prompt, and a last-resort task-based hint, selected via a top-down hierarchical policy prioritizing minimal intervention.
requirements: A desired collaboration matrix and predefined trigger conditions (e.g., gaze-awareness triggered when JVA = Low, dialogue prompt when JME = Low, task-based hint when both MEs = High)
Per-participant resting baselines for the ±2SD discretization of predicted states
constraints: The task-based hint is used only as a last-resort intervention, triggered when less intrusive scaffolds fail and both collaborators exhibit sustained extreme mental-effort levels
target_learners: Undergraduate or master's computer science and engineering students pair programming on debugging tasks
target_learning_goals: Restoring joint attention and cognitive alignment during collaborative debugging
examples: The gaze-awareness tool visualizes a partner's gaze as a translucent colored rectangle highlighting the current attention region (nine lines of code), triggered when JVA is low
key_sources: Anahita Golrang, Kshitij Sharma, Simon Dehaen, Olga Viberg. (2026). ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02703

article_title: LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning
citation: Nizam Kadir. (2026). LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning. Technical research report. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02699
title: LearnAdapt Praxis five-stage learning workspace (Frame, Learn, Build, Validate, Transfer)
description: Praxis is a web application in the LearnAdapt ecosystem that structures an adult workplace-learning project across five stages: Frame, Learn, Build, Validate and Transfer. Learners "begin with their own starting response, engage with course material, develop a five-field specification, record validation observations and respond to a different scenario." The server stores a locked baseline, versioned specifications, hint records, validation observations and a separate transfer response, and enforces prerequisites such as a saved specification and validation observations before transfer begins.
requirements: A saved specification and validation observations are server prerequisites before transfer begins; a locked baseline is required before later substantive commands
constraints: The specification is a structured learning artefact, not an executable workplace application; the system does not execute external tests or certify deployment readiness
target_learning_goals: framing workplace problems, designing AI-supported services, validation reasoning, independent transfer
examples: The report's Table 1 relates each visible stage to its stored evidence and its interpretation limit, such as a saved reflection not establishing understanding
key_sources: Nizam Kadir. (2026). LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning. Technical research report. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02699

article_title: LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning
citation: Nizam Kadir. (2026). LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning. Technical research report. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02699
title: Retain inspectable provenance records of assisted and independent work, while treating them as application evidence rather than learning-gain evidence
description: The report argues that retaining versions, activity events, coaching records and authenticated actors makes future studies more interpretable by preserving the conditions under which an artefact was produced, but that these records support only limited inferences. It states that "an event label such as authenticated learning activity describes an application provenance category, not a psychological finding", and Table 5 distinguishes supported interpretations (e.g. text was saved in a particular sequence) from unsupported ones (e.g. that a change measures a learning gain).
requirements: Study design and collection context determine the evidential status of records; a course protocol must determine when facilitator feedback is delivered if unaided performance is an outcome of interest
constraints: The JSON schema is not a conformant W3C PROV serialisation, does not capture every interaction, and does not store a tamper-evident audit log or full model-request archive
target_learning_goals: independent reasoning and transfer in AI-supported design work
examples: The rehearsal's final exports retained the submitted transfer state, server-assigned reviewer identity, source-labelled timestamped events and notices separating activity records from learning-gain inference
key_sources: Nizam Kadir. (2026). LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning. Technical research report. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02699

article_title: Automated Grading of Handwritten Mathematics Using Vision-Capable LLMs
citation: Jacob Levine, Miguel Aenlle, Craig Zilles, Matthew West, and Mariana Silva. (2026). Automated Grading of Handwritten Mathematics Using Vision-Capable LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19043
title: PrairieLearn-integrated AI grading tool for handwritten mathematics with single-call transcription and rubric evaluation
description: The article presents a prototype AI-assisted grading tool integrated into PrairieLearn, an open-source online assessment platform, that evaluates open-ended mathematical responses submitted as handwritten photographs. It extends a prior typed-response pipeline by introducing an image-based grading pipeline and prompt structure that jointly perform transcription and rubric-based evaluation. The prompt includes the problem statement, rubric, optional reference solutions, and explicit directives for both transcription and assessment. Human graders may review and override AI evaluations, and human-assigned grades always take precedence.
requirements: The LLM prompt includes the problem statement, rubric, optional reference solutions and instructions, and explicit directives for both transcription and assessment
The grader operates asynchronously, executing only after submissions close and the grading configuration is finalized
constraints: Only the final uploaded image is graded
Randomized problem instances preclude retrieval-augmented grading, as the variability across problem instances prevents reliable reuse of previously graded examples
target_learners: university STEM students in numerical methods and introductory dynamics courses
target_learning_goals: grading of multi-step handwritten mathematical derivations against instructor-defined rubrics
examples: Students captured images using a laptop webcam or mobile phone in Course 1, and uploaded scratch-paper work via document cameras in proctored Course 2 midterms
key_sources: Jacob Levine, Miguel Aenlle, Craig Zilles, Matthew West, and Mariana Silva. (2026). Automated Grading of Handwritten Mathematics Using Vision-Capable LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19043

article_title: A Classroom Study of LLM-Generated Feedback Intervention in Introductory Programming
citation: Hasnain Heickal and Andrew Lan. (2026). A Classroom Study of LLM-Generated Feedback Intervention in Introductory Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08807
title: PROGFEED: a longitudinal dataset of randomized AI feedback conditions in introductory programming
description: PROGFEED is a released dataset from an IRB-approved classroom study in an introductory Python course, capturing "6,693 submissions from 215 consenting students across 17 labs and 43 problems". It links complete submission histories to feedback conditions, execution outcomes, and temporal ordering, and includes source code, test case outcomes, demographic and weekly survey responses, and course performance measures. The dataset is publicly available on GitHub and supports hierarchical analysis at student, problem, and lab levels.
requirements: Feedback conditions were randomized at the submission level within each lab, with students reassigned between labs; feedback was conditionally triggered only on failing submissions.
constraints: Because feedback delivery is conditionally triggered rather than fully randomized, all analyses on the dataset are associative, not causal.
target_learners: first-year introductory programming students, primarily computer science majors
target_learning_goals: debugging and reaching correct solutions on introductory Python programming problems
examples: The study randomized submissions across no-AI, failing test case, and natural language feedback conditions generated by gpt-4o-mini with fixed prompts across all labs.
key_sources: Hasnain Heickal and Andrew Lan. (2026). A Classroom Study of LLM-Generated Feedback Intervention in Introductory Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08807

article_title: To Facilitate or not to Facilitate: Human and LLM Facilitator Tendencies in Online Discussions
citation: Dimitris Tsirmpas, Katerina Korre, John Pavlopoulos. (2026). To Facilitate or not to Facilitate: Human and LLM Facilitator Tendencies in Online Discussions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28643
title: Prefer trained encoder-only classifiers over out-of-the-box LLMs for facilitation timing prediction
description: The article recommends that, for predicting when a facilitator would intervene, trained encoder-only classifiers such as ModernBert may be "a much more scalable, reliable and viable solution compared to LLMs for the task, even though they have been overlooked in current literature". The recommendation rests on the finding that out-of-the-box LLMs with generic prompting are inconsistent, while ModernBert classifiers are more consistent and score the highest F1p across all datasets. An additional advantage the authors note is that the probability threshold can be tuned to configure how proactive or cautious the classifier is.
requirements: Training data from established facilitation datasets with facilitator information; separate models for oral and written datasets due to substantial differences in text format
constraints: Performance remains bounded by the low ceiling imposed by current datasets; boosting LLM classifier performance was outside the scope of this work
target_learners: developers of automated facilitation and moderation systems for online discussions
target_learning_goals: reliably predicting when facilitative intervention is needed in online discussions
examples: The authors trained ModernBert classifiers on PEFK subsets with a 60–20–20 split and evaluated six open-source LLMs on 2,000 randomly sampled test instances
key_sources: Dimitris Tsirmpas, Katerina Korre, John Pavlopoulos. (2026). To Facilitate or not to Facilitate: Human and LLM Facilitator Tendencies in Online Discussions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28643

article_title: Five Guiding Principles for Navigating Artificial Intelligence in Students as Partners Practice to Preserve Pedagogical Trust
citation: Matthews, K. E. (2025). Five guiding principles for navigating artificial intelligence in students as partners practice to preserve pedagogical trust: Navigating artificial intelligence in students as partners practice. International Journal for Students as Partners, 9(2), 1–8. https://doi.org/10.15173/ijsap.v9i2.6871
title: Preserve pedagogical trust when bringing AI into students as partners practice
description: This principle holds that any navigation of artificial intelligence within students as partners practice should be judged by whether it preserves pedagogical trust. The article's title makes preservation of "pedagogical trust" the stated purpose of its five principles for "navigating artificial intelligence in students as partners practice", and the keyword "trust" signals that trust is the outcome the guidance protects. It functions as a design criterion: AI-related partnership decisions are evaluated against their effect on trust.
requirements: AI-related decisions in partnership practice must be checked against their effect on pedagogical trust
target_learners: higher education students and staff in pedagogical partnership
target_learning_goals: sustaining trustworthy partnership relationships amid generative AI use
examples: The editorial's five principles are explicitly framed as serving the preservation of pedagogical trust

article_title: Designing an Aligned Generative AI Course Policy: An Equitable and Transparent Learner-Centered Approach
citation: McCorkle, S. (2025). Designing an Aligned Generative AI Course Policy: An Equitable and Transparent Learner-Centered Approach. International Journal of Designs for Learning, 16(2), 96–110. https://doi.org/10.14434/ijdl.v16i2.41058
title: Prioritize between assessing a task and building a GenAI workforce competency for each inventoried task
description: For every task in the inventory, the instructor makes an explicit priority decision. "A determination is then made to prioritize either the need to assess student performance of the task or build the GenAI workforce competency." This principle makes GenAI permissions follow from that priority: where assessment of a task matters less, competency-building can take precedence and GenAI use can be permitted. The article frames this as the mechanism that aligns the policy with course goals rather than applying uniform restrictions.
requirements: A completed task inventory with each task classified as assessed or unassessed
constraints: The priority determination is made task by task, so a single course-wide GenAI rule cannot implement this principle
target_learning_goals: student performance of assessed tasks
GenAI workforce competency development
examples: The design case describes the instructor making a determination for each task in the inventory between assessing performance and building the GenAI workforce competency

article_title: Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement
citation: April Joy Miles, Paige Haber-Curran, Khalid Arar. (2026). Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement. Open Praxis, 18(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1191
title: Prompt Literacy Cycle: a five-stage recursive structure for daily prompting practice
description: The Prompt Literacy Cycle is the instructional tool nested within Phase Two of the framework, giving students a concrete, repeatable structure for developing prompt literacy at the level of daily practice. It guides students through five recursive stages: clarify purpose, craft the prompt, engage with output, refine the prompt, and reflect. The authors state it encourages experimentation, reflection, and interactive improvement in students' interactions with LLMs, and can be introduced through demonstrations, scaffolded assignments, or workshops.
requirements: Instructors introduce it through demonstrations, scaffolded assignments, or workshops so students internalize both the mechanics of prompting and the ethical and epistemological dimensions of LLM engagement
constraints: It operates at the level of daily practice, while the five-phase model guides the overall arc of LLM-integrated learning
target_learning_goals: prompt literacy
critical interpretation of LLM outputs
reflective revision
examples: Instructors model the same five stages in their own work, demonstrating how vague prompts produce generic results and how minor revisions yield more nuanced responses
key_sources: April Joy Miles, Paige Haber-Curran, Khalid Arar. (2026). Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement. Open Praxis, 18(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1191

article_title: Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement
citation: April Joy Miles, Paige Haber-Curran, Khalid Arar. (2026). Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement. Open Praxis, 18(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1191
title: Teach prompt literacy, not just prompt engineering: rhetorical and ethical engagement over technical optimization
description: The framework's central conceptual distinction is that prompt engineering is a technical skill set focused on fine-tuning inputs for performance, while prompt literacy is rooted in student-centered pedagogy, emphasizing clarity of purpose, ethical responsibility, and critical reflection in designing prompts and interpreting outputs. The article argues this distinction makes prompt literacy a foundational literacy for contemporary learners and treats it as the central pedagogical mechanism of the framework.
requirements: Instructors must explicitly teach the distinction, for example through the Compare Prompt Literacy vs. Prompt Engineering activity
constraints: The distinction is argued conceptually from existing scholarship rather than tested empirically in this article
target_learning_goals: rhetorical intentionality
ethical responsibility in AI use
critical interpretation of AI outputs
examples: A class debate or Venn diagram activity asks students to map how prompt literacy differs from technical prompt engineering
key_sources: April Joy Miles, Paige Haber-Curran, Khalid Arar. (2026). Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement. Open Praxis, 18(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1191

article_title: Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement
citation: April Joy Miles, Paige Haber-Curran, Khalid Arar. (2026). Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement. Open Praxis, 18(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1191
title: Sample rubric for assessing prompt literacy as a process rather than a product
description: Table 1 offers a sample rubric that evaluates the student's engagement with the tool rather than grading the AI-generated output itself. It assesses three criteria: iterative refinement of prompts, critical interpretation of output for accuracy, bias, and relevance, and reflective revision that integrates and transforms output. Instructors can adapt these criteria to discipline-specific assignments while keeping human reasoning and judgment at the center of evaluation.
requirements: Instructors adapt the criteria to discipline-specific assignments
constraints: The rubric is offered as a sample to illustrate process-oriented assessment, not as a validated instrument
target_learning_goals: prompt literacy assessed as process
critical evaluation of AI output
reflective revision
examples: An exemplary-level student systematically refines prompts, articulating why each change improves the response, and rigorously evaluates output for accuracy, bias, and relevance

article_title: Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning
citation: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047
title: Prioritize hands-on experiential activities over lecture-based instruction when cultivating metacognitive awareness of AI-assisted learning
description: The article advises that "Practitioners are thus advised to primarily rely on experiential and hands-on approaches for cultivating metacognitive awareness in AI-assisted learning." Experiential instruction produced larger immediate gains in knowledge of cognition and engagement, and although instructional approaches eventually reached comparable levels, that convergence took weeks to unfold. The principle holds that hands-on experience of productive and unproductive GenAI use builds strategy knowledge faster than lecture while also supporting slower-developing regulatory behaviour.
requirements: Experiential sessions must be matched on total instruction time with lecture alternatives so differences reflect the mode of learning rather than exposure or time on task.
constraints: Immediate gains in knowledge and engagement were not matched by an immediate rise in regulation of cognition; the authors warn that greater engagement without regulation may itself lead to cognitive offloading.
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge and regulation of cognition in AI-assisted learning
examples: The study's experiential condition replaced a full lecture with a condensed introduction followed by four structured exercises enacting productive and unproductive GenAI interactions.

title: Precision Education: a healthcare-inspired framework of five analytics maturity stages culminating in autonomous, adaptive student success
description: Precision Education is a paradigm in which AI continuously analyzes academic, behavioral, financial, and career data to identify emerging risks, recommend personalized interventions, and align academic decisions with career success. The paper organizes the field's evolution across five stages, from descriptive reporting to what it calls "Stage 5: Autonomous and adaptive student success." It argues the field has invested heavily in Stage 3 predictive analytics while "The value proposition of Precision Education lives in Stages 4 and 5." The framing pairs data science with "warm humanity": technology identifies the signal, human judgment shapes the response.

constraints: Stages 4 and 5 require causal reasoning, not only correlation, per the article's own stage definitions

student retention
career-aligned academic planning

citation: Hunter McNichols, Kai Du, Andrew Lan. (2026). PRINCIPAL TRAIT ANALYSIS: TOWARDS DERIVING "SKILLS" IN HUMAN-AI COLLABORATION. A preprint - August 13, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11460
title: Principal Trait Analysis (PTA): a four-stage, PCA-inspired pipeline for deriving behavioral traits from human-AI conversation corpora
description: PTA is a data-driven methodology that "produces a representative set of textual descriptions we callprincipal traitsfrom a corpus of human collaborator-AI collaborative conversation sessions." It runs four stages: LLM-prompted behavior-observation extraction (generic or theory-lens), embedding-based top-down and agglomerative clustering into candidate traits, LLM-as-a-judge scoring of each session on a 1-5 Likert scale, and greedy principal-trait selection trading off relevance (item-total correlation plus factor-analysis communality) against redundancy in score and text-embedding space. Trait selection mirrors PCA's variance-maximizing criterion adapted to text, where orthogonality is undefined.
requirements: A corpus of human collaborator-AI conversation sessions with an outcome signal for outcome-aligned evaluation
LLM prompting and text-embedding infrastructure for extraction, clustering, scoring, and selection
constraints: The authors caution the derived traits "do not, by themselves, appear to be grounded enough to be interpreted as a definitive skill taxonomy in human-AI collaboration"
The work is described as early stage, preliminary work with a principled version forthcoming

Professional software developers using AI coding agents
target_learning_goals: Effective collaboration with LLM-based tutors and coding agents
AI use skills for computer science students and professionals
examples: Applied to StudyChat (1,540 tutoring sessions, 171 students) and SWE-Chat (2,774 developer-agent sessions) with K=10 principal traits selected per dataset

article_title: Privacy-Preserving Heterogeneous Multi-LLM Federated Inference for Cognitive Diagnosis
citation: Yagna Manasa Boyapati, Chong Yu, Tianyu Jiang, Justin Zhan. (2026). Privacy-Preserving Heterogeneous Multi-LLM Federated Inference for Cognitive Diagnosis. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02947
title: Privacy-preserving heterogeneous multi-LLM federated inference framework for cognitive diagnosis
description: A four-stage framework in which heterogeneous commercial LLMs (LLaMA-3.3-70B, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3-Haiku) independently predict student knowledge states via engineered prompts, add calibrated Laplace noise locally to their prediction outputs, and aggregate with residual correction. The article describes it as "the first privacy-preserving heterogeneous multi-LLM federated inference framework for cognitive diagnosis", operating entirely at the prediction level with models frozen and accessible only via black-box APIs. It integrates Q-matrix theory to constrain prompts to relevant concepts and rests on an honest-but-curious trust paradigm.
requirements: Commercial LLM API access for each federated entity; a Q-matrix (expert-crafted or automatically generated) mapping questions to knowledge concepts; local calibration data per entity for residual correction terms.
constraints: The privacy guarantee follows an honest-but-curious trust paradigm: LDP shields published diagnostic outputs but does not prevent commercial API providers from logging submitted queries.
The framework is evaluated on structured educational domains; extension to open-ended assessment tasks may require adapted prompt engineering.
Residual correction may require periodic recalibration when providers release model updates.
target_learners: K-12 and secondary students in mathematics and academic assessment settings (ASSIST09, GSM8K, UCI Student Performance populations)
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing student mastery of specific knowledge concepts and skills to support intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning
examples: The framework was instantiated with LLaMA-3.3-70B via Groq API, GPT-4o-mini via OpenAI API, and Claude-3-Haiku via Anthropic API, each holding a disjoint local dataset subset for calibration, and evaluated on ASSIST09, GSM8K, and UCI Student Performance.

article_title: PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews
citation: Zabaleta, M. & Lin, B. (2026). PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11559
title: PRISMA-LLM: a three-layer reporting framework for LLM-assisted systematic reviews
description: PRISMA-LLM is an evidence-informed reporting framework for LLM-assisted and AI-enabled systematic-review workflows, organized to complement PRISMA 2020. It has three layers: "a universal checklist specifies the information that should be reported across LLM-assisted review workflows"; five implementation-disclosure levels organize technical detail needed to reconstruct workflows; and consequence-sensitive evaluation expectations determine when validation should exceed the minimum associated with a disclosure level. Its empirical basis is the recurring evaluation and limitation dimensions observed in SciLitBench and the association between workflow type and reporting coverage.
requirements: Every LLM-assisted review should identify the system and task, describe inputs and outputs, report human oversight, disclose evaluation and failures, and provide reproducibility materials where possible
constraints: The levels are disclosure tiers, not risk tiers
It is not presently an official extension endorsed by the PRISMA Executive and has not undergone formal consensus development or prospective user testing
Its purpose is not to certify the quality or safety of an AI workflow
target_learners: review authors and auditors in evidence synthesis
target_learning_goals: transparent, auditable reporting of AI-assisted review workflows
distinguishing implementation disclosure from consequence-sensitive evaluation
examples: The framework was developed from SciLitBench reporting patterns, workflow choices encountered while building SciLitBench, and comparison with PRISMA 2020, PRISMA-S, and adjacent AI-reporting proposals

title: PRISMA-LLM 16-item universal reporting checklist (Table 1)
description: The PRISMA-LLM checklist is a page-sized, user-facing set of 16 items (LLM-1 through LLM-16) spanning identification, rationale, methods, results, discussion, availability, and disclosure sections. It asks authors to report system identity and version, task and disclosure level, inputs and document processing, prompts and settings, outputs and post-processing, human oversight, evaluation and errors, limitations, reproducibility materials, and support or competing interests. It is "intended to be used alongside PRISMA 2020 rather than as a replacement for it."

article_title: PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews
citation: Zabaleta, M. & Lin, B. (2026). PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11559
title: Five cumulative implementation-disclosure levels with a consequence-sensitive evaluation override
description: PRISMA-LLM organizes implementation disclosure into five cumulative levels: off-the-shelf software; prompt-only LLM; structured/engineered workflows; retrieval/adapted/single-agent workflows; and multi-agent/swarm systems, each adding the technical detail needed to reconstruct the workflow. Minimum evaluation breadth increases with implementation complexity, but "implementation level is not a risk score": a consequence override requires stronger validation at any level when outputs can change the evidence base, human verification is limited, the system is proprietary or mutable, or errors are hard to reconstruct or reverse.
requirements: Each level adds the implementation detail of the previous level, from product/version and settings at Level 1 to agent roles, coordination, handoffs, and cross-agent audit logs at Level 5
constraints: The levels summarize implementation complexity rather than methodological risk
Reporting richness remains a descriptive empirical index because no compliance cutoff has undergone prospective validation
target_learners: review teams using LLM or AI-enabled automation
target_learning_goals: graded, reconstructable disclosure of AI workflow implementation
calibrating evaluation expectations to task consequence
examples: Supplementary Figure S6 maps the cumulative minimum reporting dimensions associated with the five implementation levels

description: Before finalizing an AI-assisted answer, students respond to short prompts evaluating their own understanding, the AI's trustworthiness, and reasons for accepting or rejecting the recommendation. article_title: ProPRL: Property-Aware Prerequisite Relation Learning in Educational Knowledge Graphs
citation: Xinghe Cheng, Jiapu Wang, Chaobo He, Ruihai Dong, Quanlong Guan. (2026). ProPRL: Property-Aware Prerequisite Relation Learning in Educational Knowledge Graphs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03006
title: ProPRL: a property-aware framework for prerequisite relation learning with multi-view representation, pair-conditioned gating, and an irreversibility constraint
description: ProPRL is a framework that learns prerequisite relations over ordered concept pairs in educational knowledge graphs. It learns complementary concept embeddings from a concept-resource hypergraph and a directed learning-behavior graph, using "direction-preserving personalized multi-hop propagation to aggregate multi-hop behavioral evidence". A Pair-conditioned Gate constructs view-specific representations for each candidate ordered pair and adaptively weights the two views, and an Irreversibility Constraint applies "an anti-symmetry regularizer that penalizes simultaneously highpredictionsfor(ci,cj)and(cj,ci)". Training jointly optimizes resource-aware, behavior-aware, and fused branches with a teacher-detached consistency loss.
requirements: Requires an educational dataset with a concept set, resources, learner interaction sequences, and observed prerequisite labels for training
constraints: Hyperparameters such as α and λ are dataset-dependent and selected on a validation set
Requires an appropriately small learning rate for reliable optimization
target_learners: learners in MOOC, university course, and lecture-bank educational settings
target_learning_goals: accurate prerequisite relation prediction to support curriculum planning, learning path recommendation, and adaptive instruction
examples: Evaluated on MOOC, LectureBank, and UCD benchmarks against general-purpose and task-specific baselines, with ablation, case study, hyperparameter, and efficiency studies

article_title: Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access
citation: Lier Jin, Lan Hu, Binqi Shen, Hanyu Cai, and Yuting Xin. (2026). Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08942
title: Prompt privilege and prompt equity: framing prompt-formulation sensitivity as an AI accessibility problem
description: The article names prompt privilege as an accessibility challenge in which users with greater prompting expertise systematically obtain better model performance despite expressing the same underlying intent, and prompt equity as the counterpart property of consistent performance across users expressing semantically equivalent requests in different communication styles. It reframes prompt-formulation sensitivity as an accessibility problem in addition to a security or optimization one, and operationalizes equity with the Prompt Equity Score, where higher PES values indicate smaller performance disparities across user cohorts and therefore greater prompt equity, whereas lower values indicate stronger prompt privilege.
requirements: Measurement requires systematically varying user communication styles while holding the underlying task and language model fixed, so observed differences are attributable to prompt formulation rather than task difficulty or information content.
constraints: Existing prompt-robustness research the article builds on addresses adversarial settings; the framework concerns non-adversarial, naturally occurring communication-style differences.
target_learners: users with limited health and digital literacy
everyday users without formal medical training or prompt-engineering expertise
target_learning_goals: obtaining comparable AI assistance for the same underlying information need
equitable access to medical information and decision support through LLMs
examples: The framework is instantiated on MedQA with cohorts from Low Literacy to Prompt Engineer, quantified by a baseline Prompt Equity Score of 0.9959

citation: Lier Jin, Lan Hu, Binqi Shen, Hanyu Cai, and Yuting Xin. (2026). Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08942
title: Prompt Equity Transformer (PET), an accessibility-oriented prompt normalization agent
description: PET is an LLM-based agent that automatically transforms heterogeneous user inputs into semantically equivalent prompts with standardized reasoning guidance while preserving the user's original intent. It optimizes expected downstream task performance subject to a predefined semantic-preservation threshold, and does not introduce new information or modify the user's underlying request. Positioned as middleware, it functions as an intelligent accessibility layer between users and foundation models, shifting prompt-optimization responsibility from user to system without modifying the underlying foundation model.
requirements: Semantic similarity between the original and transformed prompts must meet a predefined semantic-preservation threshold, and rewriting must preserve the user's original intent.
constraints: Experiments are limited to the healthcare domain (MedQA) and to GPT-5.4-mini; PET currently operates as a static normalization agent, leaving adaptive capabilities such as clarification questions or personalized rewriting strategies for future versions.
target_learners: users with limited health literacy and limited digital literacy
target_learning_goals: receiving comparable model performance regardless of communication style
obtaining high-quality AI assistance without specialized prompting skills
examples: Applied as a preprocessing step to normalize prompts from the Low Literacy, Everyday User, and Educated User cohorts, while the Prompt Engineer cohort serves as an upper-bound reference

article_title: Literacy demands placed on students in student–GenAI entanglements in higher education
citation: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7
title: Sequence GenAI activities across the entanglement spectrum, starting from coherent types and moving toward more distributed forms (progression)
description: The second design principle is progression: "teachers could consider designing activities that span multiple entanglement types." Because Assistant and Enabler entanglements dominate, many students encounter mainly institutionally coherent distributions of epistemic work and may graduate into professional contexts where Generator, Reimaginator, and Synthesizer entanglements are common without the literacy to navigate them. A workable starting point is Assistant or Enabler activities, from which teachers can then introduce Synthesizer, Generator, and Reimaginator activities to develop confidence, critical awareness, and capacity to manage more distributed epistemic work.
requirements: Activity sequences must move gradually across the entanglement spectrum, beginning with types whose literacy demands are relatively coherent
constraints: The progression is not simply about exposure to different GenAI tools; its purpose is developing competence to recognize, evaluate, and take responsibility for epistemic work distribution
target_learning_goals: navigating a broader range of epistemic distributions and exercising a broader range of literacy forms
examples: Starting with Assistant or Enabler activities where students can focus on calibrating GenAI's role in relation to their own work, then introducing Synthesizer, Generator, and Reimaginator activities

title: Prefer explainable models for predicting student exam performance when overall ability is the dominant factor
description: The article argues that when overall ability is the leading factor in prediction, simpler explainable models should be preferred over less explainable ones. The authors state: "If ability is the leading factor, less explainable models may be highly undesirable as they could introduce biases into the predictions and reduce accountability to the students impacted." Their explainable models reached competitive accuracy of around 78%, offering a benchmark showing explainability need not sacrifice performance.

article_title: Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem
citation: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527
title: Engagement friction must be proportional, adaptive, transparent, non-paternalistic, and treated as an empirical hypothesis
description: The article states five principles governing engagement mechanisms in use: "Friction must be proportional, so that low-stakes queries stay frictionless while high-stakes queries carry more." Mechanisms must be adaptive to the user profile, transparent about why they slow the user down, non-paternalistic so users can always override them, and treated as empirical hypotheses with testable effects on calibration, accuracy, and satisfaction. An operating rule adds that interpretability stays on for everyone while friction is off by default.
requirements: Friction triggers only when the query is high stakes and recent behavior suggests uncritical acceptance, escalating in small steps and stopping at the first step that produces verification
constraints: A rising skip rate is the signal that the dose has gone too far
target_learners: All chatbot users, with friction dosed by observed behavior
target_learning_goals: Calibrating trust without rationing information
examples: Figure 2 translates the operating rule into a candidate adaptive design sequence responding to query stakes and observable interaction behavior

article_title: Computer Science Achievement and Writing Skills Predict Vibe Coding Proficiency
citation: Sverrir Thorgeirsson, Theo B. Weidmann, and Zhendong Su. 2026. Computer Science Achievement and Writing Skills Predict Vibe Coding Proficiency. Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791666
title: Use predictor profiles (writing vs. CS fundamentals) to decide where tool and curriculum design should emphasize support for future software creators
description: Because both written communication and CS achievement independently predict vibe-coding performance, the article argues its results can guide when educators and tool builders should emphasize prompt-writing versus CS fundamentals. The authors state that "The results have implications for both tool design and curriculum design (e.g., where to emphasize writing versus CS fundamentals)", for example in designing systems that teach users to write better prompts. The principle treats the two predictors as complementary levers rather than substitutes, with CS achievement carrying more unique variance in a joint model.
requirements: Local measurement of both written-communication proficiency and CS achievement is needed to identify which lever matters for a given cohort.
constraints: Evidence is cross-sectional and correlational from a single study of tertiary students in one metropolitan area; the article makes no causal claim about instruction.
target_learners: tertiary-level students learning LLM-based software development
target_learning_goals: effective natural-language specification of software; computer-science fundamentals
examples: The study operationalized vibe coding as programming through LLM interaction without viewing source code, and analyzed prompts as a candidate mechanism linking writing skills to performance.

article_title: Balancing Teacher and Student Agency: Co-Orchestration Tool Design Supporting Real-Time Dynamic Pairing
citation: Kexin Bella Yang, Menghan Liu, Liyi Xu, Nikol Rummel, and Vincent Aleven. (2026). Balancing Teacher and Student Agency: Co-Orchestration Tool Design Supporting Real-Time Dynamic Pairing. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Balancing+Teacher+and+Student+Agency+Co-Orchestration+Tool+Design+Supporting+Real-Time+Dynamic+Pairing
title: Design hybrid-control orchestration tools by starting with structured teacher guidance and progressively increasing student autonomy as activities unfold.
description: The article recommends hybrid-control designs for analytic-based orchestration tools in pairing contexts: "We recommend ensuring structured teacher guidance in the beginning, while progressively increasing student autonomy over time as activities unfold." This follows from findings that neither teachers nor students favored full student control, and that preferences varied across the pairing stages. The principle guides designers to scaffold authority early and open more student decision space as collaboration becomes established.
requirements: A context where teachers and students dynamically transition between individual and collaborative learning, supported by analytics from tutoring systems.
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem-solving
algebra equation solving
examples: Teachers and students ranked readiness-based timing, shared role assignment, and hybrid content selection above full student control in the PSD sessions.

article_title: A Durability and Cross-Language Transfer Benchmark for a Validated Teaching-Feedback Classification Protocol
citation: Esteban U. Vega Barajas. (2026). A Durability and Cross-Language Transfer Benchmark for a Validated Teaching-Feedback Classification Protocol. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11873
title: Carry forward the documented protocol, not the model: annotation guide, reliability measurement, validation design, and auditability survive model and language change
description: The article's central design principle for institutional NLP adoption: what an institution carries forward is the documented procedure rather than any particular model. The authors argue that if a modern LLM wins on raw accuracy, "that is an expected finding, and it reinforces the claim that what an institution carries forward is the documented procedure: the annotation guide, the reliability measurement, the validation design, and the interpretability analysis." The benchmark operationalizes this by holding the protocol fixed while varying model generation and language, showing the protocol holds across all arms with "no single arm is load-bearing".
requirements: A written annotation guide, an explicit reliability measurement, stratified cross-validation for model selection, and a held-out test set untouched until final reporting
constraints: The article reports paired comparisons as descriptive only and claims no statistical significance; the Spanish ordering rests on a single stratified split with a 233-comment held-out set
target_learners: institutional staff and researchers processing open-ended teaching-evaluation feedback in higher education
target_learning_goals: building durable, auditable, reliability-checked classification procedures for teaching-feedback analysis that survive changes of model and language
examples: The benchmark slotted every newer model, from TF-IDF through frozen BETO and e5 encoders to prompted LLMs, into the same annotation guide, splits, and held-out evaluation, and none forced the auditability or cost story to collapse
key_sources: Esteban U. Vega Barajas. (2026). A Durability and Cross-Language Transfer Benchmark for a Validated Teaching-Feedback Classification Protocol. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11873

article_title: Against frictionless AI
citation: Emily Zohar, Paul Bloom & Michael Inzlicht. (2026). Against frictionless AI. Communications Psychology 4:39. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-026-00402-1
title: Harness AI's benefits while preserving the friction that drives learning, connection, and meaning
description: The article recommends preserving beneficial friction when adopting AI: "The goal should be to harness AI'sb e n eﬁts while preserving the friction that makes us human— the struggle that teaches us, the loneliness that connects us, and the effort that gives our achievements meaning." It applies this by timing AI use to developmental stage and reserving frictionless AI for cases where friction offers little benefit.
requirements: Distinguish excess friction, which offers little benefit, from beneficial friction worth preserving
Match AI use to the user's developmental stage and existing skills
constraints: The authors concede AI's benefits are often overwhelming in intellectual work and it would be perverse to abandon it in some cases, even if valuable friction is sacrificed
target_learners: younger learners in earlier developmental stages
professionals in later career stages using AI as a supplement
target_learning_goals: deeper comprehension and retention
perseverance and willingness to strive
meaningful engagement
examples: The article recommends that younger learners, like students asked to show their work even when calculators exist, need to struggle, reason, and revise through the full process before benefiting from shortcuts
key_sources: Emily Zohar, Paul Bloom & Michael Inzlicht. (2026). Against frictionless AI. Communications Psychology 4:39. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-026-00402-1

article_title: \"Is this a trap?\": Student teachers' perceptions and adoption of GenAI in assessments in three teacher education courses
citation: Zou, T. X. P., Hounsell, D., Huijser, H., & Tse, R. T. L. (2026). “Is this a trap?”: Student teachers’ perceptions and adoption of GenAI in assessments in three teacher education courses. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 1–17. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10549
title: Design GenAI assessment policies with a programme-level view rather than course by course
description: The article argues that GenAI policy should not be set in isolation within single courses: "it is important for instructors to have a programme-level view when designing GenAI-related assessment policies." Its implications add that "Course leaders should consider the overall policy and context for using GenAI in assessment beyond their own courses." This addresses inconsistency students encounter when policies differ across a programme.
requirements: Course leaders must coordinate GenAI assessment policy across courses in a programme rather than only within their own courses.
target_learners: teacher education students in higher education
target_learning_goals: coherent understanding of permitted GenAI use across a programme of study
examples: The study sampled three teacher education courses and drew the programme-level recommendation from inconsistencies in GenAI-related assessment policies and communication across them.
key_sources: Zou, T. X. P., Hounsell, D., Huijser, H., & Tse, R. T. L. (2026). “Is this a trap?”: Student teachers’ perceptions and adoption of GenAI in assessments in three teacher education courses. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 1–17. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10549

article_title: Leveraging AI for Rapid Generation of Physics Simulations in Education: Building Your Own Virtual Lab
citation: Yossi Ben-Zion, Roi Einhorn Zarzecki, Joshua Glazer, Noah D. Finkelstein. (2024). Leveraging AI for Rapid Generation of Physics Simulations in Education: Building Your Own Virtual Lab. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07482
title: Prompt-based LLM workflow for generating interactive physics simulations without programming expertise
description: The article describes a workflow in which educators or students give a predefined prompt to an LLM (ChatGPT or Claude), receive HTML and JavaScript code, and run it in a browser. The authors state the process "requires no advanced programming knowledge" and that iterative dialogue with the model yields simulations "customized for different educational contexts". It is offered as a complement to professionally developed simulations.
requirements: Access to an LLM such as ChatGPT or Claude and a modern web browser to open the generated .html file
constraints: The authors state it is not intended to replace robust simulations like PhET, and some corrections through human supervision typically remain necessary
target_learning_goals: exploring physical systems through interactive simulations
hands-on experience with large language models
examples: Simulations generated for the simple pendulum, the 2D Ising model, and the 2D and 3D random walker using OpenAI's O1 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet
