article_title: GLAT: The Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test
citation: Yueqiao Jin, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Dragan Gašević and Lixiang Yan. (2024). GLAT: The Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00283
title: Prefer performance-based GenAI literacy assessment over self-report instruments when measuring actual competencies
description: The article argues that self-reported AI literacy instruments capture perceived abilities but "may introduce biases that obscure a more reliable measure of literacy levels", and that performance-based assessments evaluate actual competencies through direct engagement. It developed GLAT as a performance-based alternative and showed its scores predicted GenAI-supported task performance better than a validated self-report scale. The principle directs educators and researchers toward performance measures when the goal is assessing real capability to use generative tools.
requirements: Items must be developed and validated against established psychological and educational measurement standards, including content validity review and item analysis
constraints: Evidence for the predictive advantage comes from one study with 83 higher education students on a single chatbot-supported task
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of generative AI literacy competencies
examples: The study compared GLAT against the ChatGPT Literacy Scale (Lee and Park, 2024) as predictors of AI-assisted task performance in an OLS regression
key_sources: Yueqiao Jin, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Dragan Gašević and Lixiang Yan. (2024). GLAT: The Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00283

article_title: LUDIA: A Design and Evidence Statement
citation: Stark, B., & Rostan, J. (2026). LUDIA: A design and evidence statement (Version 1.0). Ask LUDIA. https://askludia.com/en
title: Privacy and accessibility as architecture, not settings, in an educator AI tool
description: The relaunched LUDIA embodies a design pattern in which privacy and accessibility are treated as "the architecture" rather than settings: no cookies, no accounts, no server-side chat content, no data collected for model training, and exchanges that are downloadable and re-uploadable. Accessibility is designed to WCAG 2.2 Level AA with keyboard-only operation, screen reader support tested with four screen readers, browser zoom to 400 percent with content reflowing, light and dark schemes, and adjustable notification dismiss timing. The absence of an account is itself framed as barrier removal, letting educators without institutional backing use the tool on the same terms as anyone else.
requirements: Owning and overseeing the platform is what makes these commitments keepable; on a third-party platform retention and allowances were not the authors' to determine
constraints: The same self-funded architecture that keeps LUDIA free limits how many educators it can serve at one moment and caps monthly running costs
Accessibility is tested but not independently certified; no independent audit exists yet
target_learners: Educators in schools, community or non-formal programmes, refugee or emergency settings, or working independently
target_learning_goals: Universal access to inclusive design support regardless of institutional backing, connectivity, or language
examples: The relaunched build sets no cookies, requires no account, writes no chat content to the authors' servers, and relaunches in 13 languages
key_sources: Stark, B., & Rostan, J. (2026). LUDIA: A design and evidence statement (Version 1.0). Ask LUDIA. https://askludia.com/en

article_title: Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence
citation: Lixiang Yan and Dragan Gašević. (2026). Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07813
title: Design AI-supported learning so the learner remains responsible for framing, criteria, evidence comparison, and justification
description: This pedagogical principle holds that productive use of AI depends less on whether AI is present than on whether the learning design preserves the learner's responsibility for judgment. The article recommends that "Instructors should therefore prefer tasks and supports that require learners to frame the problem, articulate criteria, compare AI suggestions with evidence, and explain why accepted outputs are appropriate". For assessment, it argues that final products are increasingly insufficient indicators of learning and that "valid assessment requires evidence of the process through which the learner engaged that support, including revision patterns, justification, source checking, and what can later be reproduced or adapted with less assistance".
requirements: Tasks must require learners to frame the problem, articulate criteria, compare AI suggestions with evidence, and explain why accepted outputs are appropriate.
constraints: The article states the educational aim should not be to eliminate assistance but to ensure that assistance does not replace the learner's role as author, evaluator, and explainer.
target_learners: Instructors and assessment designers in writing, inquiry, and problem solving with AI
target_learning_goals: Reconstructive internalization of AI-assisted outputs into independently usable knowledge and skill
examples: The article cites well-designed AI tutoring that scaffolds reasoning sequentially, AI-enhanced simulations that require problem decomposition, and AI-supported writing that requires source comparison as showing learning gains when the learner remains responsible for judgment and integration.
key_sources: Lixiang Yan and Dragan Gašević. (2026). Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07813

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework
citation: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513
title: Process view of feedback engagement across eliciting, processing and enacting stages
description: Adopting Malecka et al.'s three stages of feedback (eliciting, processing, enacting), the paper offers a process view of feedback engagement that differs from holistic models. 'The process view identifies opportunities and constraints of GenAI at each feedback stage, enabling educators and researchers to tailor scaffolds for stage-specific feedback engagement.' Active engagement may take different forms at each stage, from overt question-asking in eliciting to invisible critical judgement in processing.
requirements: Educators and researchers must analyse each feedback stage separately to design stage-specific scaffolds
constraints: The paper notes student feedback engagement had previously 'not been specified regarding different stages of the feedback process' in the literature
target_learning_goals: seeking, making sense of, and acting on feedback
examples: The paper scrutinises GenAI's influence separately at the eliciting, processing and enacting stages
key_sources: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513

article_title: A systematic review of AI-powered collaborative learning in higher education: Trends and outcomes from the last decade
citation: Kovari, A. (2025). A systematic review of AI-powered collaborative learning in higher education: Trends and outcomes from the last decade. Social Sciences & Humanities Open, 11, 101335. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssaho.2025.101335
title: PRISMA 2020 systematic review corpus of 27 studies on AI-based collaborative learning in higher education
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 27 studies selected with the PRISMA 2020 methodology from a Scopus search conducted on July 16, 2024. The search query targeted "artificial intelligence" AND collaborative AND learning AND higher AND education, yielding 163 articles, of which 27 studies were included after screening. Studies were coded by focus area, methodology, application, key findings, and AI methods.
requirements: Studies published 2014–2024 in English, focused on AI-based collaborative learning in higher education, with empirical, case-study, or meta-analytic designs
constraints: Single-database (Scopus) search; findings are described by the author as status-quo in nature, reflecting the present state of research
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning outcomes
student engagement
academic performance
examples: 163 records identified, 145 screened, 59 retrieved, 30 excluded, 27 studies included in the review
key_sources: Kovari, A. (2025). A systematic review of AI-powered collaborative learning in higher education: Trends and outcomes from the last decade. Social Sciences & Humanities Open, 11, 101335. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssaho.2025.101335

article_title: Beyond Detection: Redesigning Authentic Assessment in an AI-Mediated World
citation: Kickbusch, S., Ashford-Rowe, K., Kemp, A., Boreland, J., & Huijser, H. (2025). Beyond Detection: Redesigning Authentic Assessment in an AI-Mediated World. Education Sciences, 15(11), 1537. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci15111537
title: Progressive release of assessment complexity across a program of study
description: The paper proposes that authenticity should build across a program via a progressive release of complexity. Early-stage units emphasise transparency artefacts such as process logs, prompt records and short oral defences; mid-stage units add collaboration, negotiated briefs and peer review; capstones introduce external stakeholders, open-ended briefs, and negotiated criteria with explicit ethical framing and critical use of digital tools. This sequences authenticity to student readiness.
requirements: Program-level coordination across units so complexity is staged rather than introduced all at once
constraints: The appropriate level of authenticity is stage-appropriate: early units warrant constrained, well-scaffolded tasks
target_learners: higher education students progressing through a degree program
target_learning_goals: increasing professional judgement under uncertainty
collaboration and stakeholder engagement
examples: Capstone units introduce external stakeholders and negotiated criteria with explicit ethical framing
key_sources: Kickbusch, S., Ashford-Rowe, K., Kemp, A., Boreland, J., & Huijser, H. (2025). Beyond Detection: Redesigning Authentic Assessment in an AI-Mediated World. Education Sciences, 15(11), 1537. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci15111537

article_title: GenAI Knowledge, Epistemic Orientation, and Intellectual Values Predict Undergraduate Students' Critical GenAI Use
citation: Markus H. Hefter, Benjamin Paaßen, Kirsten Berthold. (2026). GenAI Knowledge, Epistemic Orientation, and Intellectual Values Predict Undergraduate Students’ Critical GenAI Use. AI Educ. 2026, 2, 27. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030027
title: Multifaceted framework of individual protective factors against uncritical genAI overreliance
description: The article proposes a framework in which two kinds of individual factors protect students from the risks of uncritical genAI use (reduced cognitive processing and unnoticed inaccuracy): knowledge about genAI and the disposition to engage in critical thinking, comprising epistemic orientation (“a tendency to move away from more absolutist beliefs toward more evaluativist beliefs”) and intellectual values (viewing intellectual engagement as worthwhile). The study empirically tested both factor families as predictors of critical genAI use, with need for cognition as an additional motivational disposition contextualizing the main hypotheses.
requirements: Both protective factors are assessed or addressed together; the article treats knowledge and critical-thinking disposition as complementary predictors
constraints: Established with a small, non-representative correlational sample; causality not yet established
target_learning_goals: critical and responsible use of generative AI tools
critical thinking
examples: The study measured both subjective and objective genAI knowledge, epistemic orientation, intellectual values, NFC, and a newly developed 10-item critical-use scale in one online questionnaire
key_sources: Markus H. Hefter, Benjamin Paaßen, Kirsten Berthold. (2026). GenAI Knowledge, Epistemic Orientation, and Intellectual Values Predict Undergraduate Students’ Critical GenAI Use. AI Educ. 2026, 2, 27. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030027

article_title: Transfer of test-enhanced learning: Meta-analytic review and synthesis.
citation: Steven C. Pan and Timothy C. Rickard. (2018). Transfer of Test-Enhanced Learning: Meta-Analytic Review and Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/bul0000151
title: Process accounts of transfer of test-enhanced learning: elaborative retrieval, mediator effectiveness, and dual memory theories
description: The review summarizes three process-based theoretical accounts that incorporate transfer. The elaborative retrieval hypothesis "posits that a process of spreading activation occurs during the search for correct answers on tests," creating multiple retrieval routes that can aid recall of semantically related information on transfer tests. The mediator effectiveness hypothesis "posits that mediators (i.e., a word, phrase, or concept that links a cue with a target) activated during testing support improved final test performance," including when mediators or linked information must be recalled on a transfer test. Dual memory theory holds that "two routes to retrieval are accessible for a tested response," but predicts only study memory is accessible when different responses are required, yielding no positive transfer.
requirements: Each account addresses specific transfer categories: mediator and related word cues for the first two, rearranged responses for dual memory theory
constraints: The review notes many theoretical accounts of test-enhanced learning do not directly address transfer; dual memory theory predicts no positive transfer when different responses are required on a transfer test
target_learners: Learners in laboratory and educational studies of retrieval practice
target_learning_goals: Recall of tested and semantically related, untested information
examples: The review cites Carpenter (2011) and Chan (2009) for spreading-activation accounts of transfer to semantically related cues, and Rickard and Pan (2017) for dual memory theory
key_sources: Steven C. Pan and Timothy C. Rickard. (2018). Transfer of Test-Enhanced Learning: Meta-Analytic Review and Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/bul0000151

article_title: When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure
citation: Tanmay Sinha and Manu Kapur. (2021). When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211019105
title: Productive Failure as a high-fidelity subset of PS-I designs within preparation for future learning
description: Productive Failure (PF) is a design paradigm in which an initial generation-and-exploration phase has students activate prior knowledge and generate multiple, typically failing, representations and solution methods for problems on not-yet-taught concepts, followed by a consolidation phase in which instruction builds on student-generated solutions. The article situates PF as "a subset of PS-I designs that fall under the broader design paradigm of preparation for future learning", and defines PF design fidelity as "the extent to which these criteria are implemented within a PS-I design". The rationale is "to design for failure in the initial learning to minimize failure in the longer term".
requirements: Seven coded fidelity criteria: problems affording multiple RSMs, evidence of multiple RSM generation, affective draw of the problem, group work as participation structure, instruction building on student solutions, and social surround facilitation in both the problem-solving and instruction phases
constraints: Not all PS-I designs are PF; only those following the PF design principles of Kapur and Bielaczyc (2012) count, and the article notes the least represented criteria are social surround facilitation, instruction building on student solutions, and group work
target_learners: Students from 2nd grade through undergraduates and professionals learning new concepts in math, science, medicine, and other domains
target_learning_goals: Conceptual knowledge and transfer of newly taught concepts
key_sources: Tanmay Sinha and Manu Kapur. (2021). When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211019105

article_title: Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning
citation: Manu Kapur (2016). Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning. Educational Psychologist, 51(2), 289-299. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1155457
title: Four design features for realizing the benefits of productive failure
description: A synthesis across productive failure studies yields four interdependent design features for the initial problem-solving phase and subsequent consolidation. The article states the task "should be challenging enough to engage the learner in the exploration, but not so challenging that the learner gives up," must "admit multiple solutions, strategies, and representations," should "activate learner's prior knowledge—formal as well as intuitive," and requires a teacher or expert to build on student-generated solutions by comparing and contrasting them with the correct solution. In classrooms, disciplinary norms and expectations for problem solving should also be set and reinforced.
requirements: A consolidation phase in which a teacher or expert compares and contrasts student-generated solutions with the correct solution, directing attention to critical features of the targeted concept
constraints: Benefits depend on the problem activating prior knowledge even when learners have not formally learned the concept; in classroom ecologies, disciplinary norms and expectations must be set and reinforced
target_learners: school students learning novel concepts in domains such as mathematics
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding
transfer
encoding of critical features
examples: The pattern derives from a synthesis of quasi-experimental classroom studies and controlled experiments on productive failure and preparation for future learning cited in the article
key_sources: Manu Kapur (2016). Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning. Educational Psychologist, 51(2), 289-299. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1155457

article_title: Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing
citation: Andrew C. Butler and Henry L. Roediger III. (2008). Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing. Memory & Cognition, 36(3), 604-616. https://doi.org/10.3758/MC.36.3.604
title: Provide feedback on multiple-choice tests to boost retention and prevent acquisition of misinformation
description: The article recommends that educators give feedback after multiple-choice tests because feedback lets students correct errors and maintain correct responses. In the experiment, "both immediate and delayed feedback increased the proportion of correct responses and reduced the proportion of intrusions" on a delayed cued recall test, and delayed feedback produced the best retention. Feedback also improved students' calibration of what they actually knew.
requirements: Feedback must include the correct response, not merely correct–incorrect indication, for students to encode the right answer
constraints: Without prior study and without feedback, multiple-choice testing was net harmful (intrusions exceeded correct responses)
Delayed feedback outperformed immediate feedback for correct responses, though both equally reduced intrusions
target_learners: higher education students studying prose passages
target_learning_goals: retention of factual material from texts
avoiding acquisition of false knowledge from lure items
examples: Subjects received feedback consisting of accuracy indication, re-presentation of the question, the response selected, and the correct response, either immediately or at the end of the test
key_sources: Andrew C. Butler and Henry L. Roediger III. (2008). Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing. Memory & Cognition, 36(3), 604-616. https://doi.org/10.3758/MC.36.3.604

article_title: A further study of productive failure in mathematical problem solving: unpacking the design components
citation: Kapur, M. (2011). A further study of productive failure in mathematical problem solving: unpacking the design components. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9144-3
title: Productive failure: complex problem solving in small groups without instructional facilitation until teacher-led consolidation
description: Productive failure is a learning design in which students first solve complex problems in small groups without instructional facilitation, and instruction follows only afterwards. As the article defines it, PF is a design "where they solved complex problems in small groups without any instructional facilitation up until a teacher-led consolidation." The design deliberately allows seemingly failing exploration before consolidation, and this study unpacks its design components by comparing it against fully facilitated and lecture-practice variants.
requirements: Complex problems solved in small groups before any instructional facilitation
A teacher-led consolidation phase following the unguided problem-solving phase
target_learning_goals: Mathematical problem solving, including well-structured and higher-order application problems and flexible use of representations
examples: In this study, seventh-grade students in the PF condition solved complex problems in small groups without facilitation until a teacher-led consolidation, and were then post-tested on well-structured, higher-order application, and representational flexibility items.
key_sources: Kapur, M. (2011). A further study of productive failure in mathematical problem solving: unpacking the design components. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9144-3

article_title: Professional communities and student achievement – a meta-analysis
citation: Lomos, C., Hofman, R. H., & Bosker, R. J. (2011). Professional communities and student achievement - a meta-analysis. School Effectiveness and School Improvement, 22(2), 121-148. https://doi.org/10.1080/09243453.2010.550467
title: Professional community as a school-level construct whose conceptualization and operationalization vary across empirical studies
description: Professional community is a school-environment construct studied over three decades; the article notes it "has gained considerable momentum in the theoretical and empirical studies in this field". The article presents a comprehensive synthesis of available theories and their implications for how the concept should be conceptualized and operationalized, and then tests its relationship to student achievement meta-analytically. The construct lacks a universal definition, so its measurement differs across studies.
requirements: Conceptual and empirical validation of the concept's key dimensions, as the article discusses
constraints: No universal definition has been formulated
Operationalization differs across the various empirical studies conducted on the subject
target_learners: Students in elementary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Student achievement
examples: The article synthesizes theories of professional community and meta-analyzes studies of its effect on student achievement
key_sources: Lomos, C., Hofman, R. H., & Bosker, R. J. (2011). Professional communities and student achievement - a meta-analysis. School Effectiveness and School Improvement, 22(2), 121-148. https://doi.org/10.1080/09243453.2010.550467

article_title: Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks
citation: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0
title: Process models: theoretical approaches that describe and/or guide the process of translating research into practice
description: Process models are the first category in the taxonomy. They "specify steps (stages, phases) in the process of translating research into practice", aiming to describe and/or guide that process. A subtype, action (or planned action) models, "provides practical guidance in the planning and execution of implementation endeavours". Examples include the Stetler Model, the ACE Star Model, the Knowledge-to-Action Framework, the Iowa Model, the Ottawa Model, the Quality Implementation Framework and models by Grol and Wensing and by Pronovost et al. Early models depicted rational, linear transfer from producers to users, while later models emphasize facilitation and context.
requirements: Careful, deliberate planning, especially in the early stages of implementation endeavours
constraints: The actual process is not necessarily sequential, even though the models present an ideal step-wise, orderly, linear view
target_learning_goals: planning and managing the translation of research into practice
examples: Many action models originate from the nursing-led field of research use, e.g. the Stetler Model and the Iowa Model
key_sources: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0

article_title: Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments
citation: Wang, F., & Hannafin, M. J. (2005). Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments. ETR&D, 53, 5–23. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504682
title: Implement design-based research with TELEs according to proposed principles
description: The article proposes principles for implementing design-based research in work on technology-enhanced learning environments. The abstract states that the authors "propose principles for implementing design-based research with TELEs", offering guidance for researchers who conduct DBR studies of TELEs. These principles are intended to make DBR implementation with TELEs systematic and disciplined.
requirements: Researchers implementing DBR with TELEs should follow the article's proposed principles for that implementation.
target_learners: Educational researchers and instructional designers conducting DBR studies of TELEs
target_learning_goals: Conducting design-based research on technology-enhanced learning environments
key_sources: Wang, F., & Hannafin, M. J. (2005). Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments. ETR&D, 53, 5–23. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504682

article_title: Assisting self-explanation prompts are more effective than open prompts when learning with multiple representations
citation: Berthold, K., Eysink, T.H.S. & Renkl, A. (2009). Assisting self-explanation prompts are more effective than open prompts when learning with multiple representations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9051-z
title: Provide assisting self-explanation prompts (assistance-giving-assistance-withholding) rather than open prompts when learners study multiple representations
description: The article recommends that, for enhancing high-quality self-explanations and both procedural knowledge and conceptual understanding, assisting self-explanation prompts should be provided. These prompts embed self-explanation support in an "assistance-giving-assistance-withholding procedure", gradually withdrawing help as learners explain the connections among multiple representations. The recommendation rests on the experiment showing assisting prompts particularly fostered conceptual knowledge.
requirements: Learning materials with multiple representations whose integration must be supported
Prompts implemented as an assistance-giving-assistance-withholding procedure
constraints: Evidence reported for probability theory learning with multi-representational worked-out examples in the studied experiment
target_learners: Learners studying probability theory from multi-representational worked-out examples
target_learning_goals: Procedural knowledge
Conceptual understanding of domain principles
examples: Participants (N = 62) learned probability theory under open prompts, assisting prompts, or no prompts, with assisting prompts implemented as an assistance-giving-assistance-withholding procedure
key_sources: Berthold, K., Eysink, T.H.S. & Renkl, A. (2009). Assisting self-explanation prompts are more effective than open prompts when learning with multiple representations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9051-z

article_title: Improving Young Children’s Social and Emotional Competence: A Randomized Trial of the Preschool “PATHS” Curriculum
citation: Domitrovich, C. E., Cortes, R. C., & Greenberg, M. T. (2007). Improving Young Children's Social and Emotional Competence: A Randomized Trial of the Preschool "PATHS" Curriculum. Journal of Primary Prevention, 28, 67–91. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10935-007-0081-0
title: Preschool PATHS curriculum
description: Preschool PATHS is "a universal, teacher-taught social-emotional curriculum that is designed to improve children's social competence and reduce problem behavior." In the trial, "Teachers in the 10 intervention classrooms implemented weekly lessons and extension activities across a 9-month period." It is an adaptation of the Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies curriculum for preschool-age children in Head Start, delivered by classroom teachers as part of the universal program.
requirements: Teacher delivery of weekly lessons plus extension activities across the school year, supported by implementation coordinators
target_learning_goals: social competence
emotion knowledge
reduction of problem behavior
examples: Ten intervention Head Start classrooms implemented weekly lessons and extension activities across a 9-month period, with coordinator-rated fidelity averaging high across dimensions

article_title: Financial Incentives and Student Achievement: Evidence from Randomized Trials *
citation: Roland G. Fryer, Jr. (2010). Financial Incentives and Student Achievement: Evidence from Randomized Trials. NBER Working Paper No. 15898. http://www.nber.org/papers/w15898
title: Students lack knowledge of the educational production function, explaining why input incentives outperform output incentives
description: This theory holds that students do not understand how inputs map to achievement outputs, so they cannot translate excitement about rewards into improved performance. Students paid for inputs (reading books, attending class) did not need to know the production function — they simply needed to perform the incentivized behavior. The article calls this the "leading theory" because it is the only one confirmed by significant qualitative observations. Three alternative theories — lack of self-control, noisy output with risk aversion, and complementary inputs — are also consistent with the data.
requirements: Students must be incentivized for specific, actionable inputs rather than for distal outputs like test scores
constraints: The article states the theory is supported by qualitative observations but acknowledges three competing theories also fit the experimental data
target_learners: urban public school students in elementary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: reading achievement
mathematics achievement
attendance and behavior
examples: A qualitative team of seven researchers observed twelve students and their families and ten classrooms in NYC, finding students were elated by incentives but did not know how to convert excitement into achievement
key_sources: Roland G. Fryer, Jr. (2010). Financial Incentives and Student Achievement: Evidence from Randomized Trials. NBER Working Paper No. 15898. http://www.nber.org/papers/w15898

article_title: Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise
citation: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1
title: Two complementary facets of negative knowledge: procedural and declarative
description: The article distinguishes two complementary facets. The procedural aspect is "to know what not to do" — part of professionals' practical know-how about workplace tasks, drawing on Minsky's negative expertise and Oser and Spychiger's contrastive definition. The declarative aspect is "to know what not to know" — awareness of deficient aspects of one's own knowledge, including informed versus uninformed not-knowing and trivial versus non-trivial incompetence (Heid 1996). Both facets are advanced together for research on professional learning.
requirements: Both facets should be considered together, as the article treats them as complementary
constraints: The declarative aspect is not focused on actions or strategies
target_learning_goals: awareness of one's own knowledge deficits
avoiding ineffective actions
examples: The Nepalese hospital example of "Seven easy ways to kill a newborn infant" illustrates procedural negative knowledge arising from practical experience
key_sources: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1

article_title: Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise
citation: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1
title: Prompting task technique (PTT) for eliciting workplace negative knowledge
description: The PTT is an experimental elicitation technique in which individuals are presented keywords or small phrases that activate related cognitive content. In an ongoing aged care nursing study, subjects are confronted with 20 diagnoses of varying typicality, each accompanied by the questions "What should be avoided?" and what one should pay special attention to. The pairing with a more general question was adopted because the avoidance question alone was experienced as difficult to answer.
requirements: Prompts paired with a general reflection question, since the direct avoidance question was experienced as quite difficult to answer
constraints: The PTT does not permit any directive intervention during data collection, and its broad focus may make it hard for subjects to dig up their negative knowledge
target_learning_goals: eliciting and studying the structure and function of negative knowledge
examples: A quasi-longitudinal PTT study compares bank employees: novices with less than two years of experience, semi-experts up to ten years, and experts with more than ten years
key_sources: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1

article_title: Leveraging the Potential of Large Language Models in Education Through Playful and Game-Based Learning
citation: Huber, S. E., Kiili, K., Nebel, S., Ryan, R. M., Sailer, M., & Ninaus, M. (2024). Leveraging the Potential of Large Language Models in Education Through Playful and Game-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09868-z
title: Problem-based gaming model emphasizing experiential learning and reflection
description: The article presents the problem-based gaming model (Kiili, 2007), which "emphasizes the meaning of experiential learning and reflection in educational games." In the model, the level of reflection concerns whether the player considers consequences of actions and changes in the game world to create better playing strategies (double-loop learning) or merely applies a previously formed strategy (single-loop learning). Games triggering double-loop learning persuade players to test hypotheses and consider learning content deeply from several perspectives.
requirements: Educational game design must create game mechanics that trigger meaningful reflection practices.
constraints: Reflection is especially important for games that require problem-solving, such as simulation games.
target_learners: players of educational games in formal and informal learning
target_learning_goals: problem-solving strategies
reflection on learning content
examples: The article argues the ability to reflect may be the main factor determining who learns effectively from experience.
key_sources: Huber, S. E., Kiili, K., Nebel, S., Ryan, R. M., Sailer, M., & Ninaus, M. (2024). Leveraging the Potential of Large Language Models in Education Through Playful and Game-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09868-z

article_title: Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education
citation: Agran, M., Blanchard, C., Wehmeyer, M., & Hughes, C. (2002). Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education. Remedial and Special Education, 23(5), 279-288. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Problem-solving cue cards
description: Cue cards were a support element of the training: "Cue cards were developed to teach students the steps and their sequence in the process, and students were instructed to refer to the cards if they forgot the steps in the strategy." They served as a memory scaffold so students did not need to ask the questions aloud in the general education classroom; students used the steps and, when necessary, a cue card to work through each daily challenge.
requirements: Students first rehearse the problem-solving questions out loud until they can recall the steps and their sequence
target_learners: students with intellectual or developmental disabilities
target_learning_goals: recalling and sequencing problem-solving steps independently in class
key_sources: Agran, M., Blanchard, C., Wehmeyer, M., & Hughes, C. (2002). Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education. Remedial and Special Education, 23(5), 279-288. https://doi.org/10.1177/07419325020230050301

article_title: Promoting Learning and Achievement Through Self-Assessment
citation: Arciniegas Trejos, C. M. (2008). Using Journals for Learners' Reflection and Self-Assessment. The Internet TESL Journal, Vol. XIV, No. 10. http://iteslj.org/Techniques/Arciniegas-LearnersJournals.html
title: Provide explicit guidelines for reflection and self-assessment so learners know what to evaluate
description: The article recommends that teachers provide the guidelines learners will follow for reflection and self-assessment, stating it is 'of primary importance' so learners have a clear idea of what elements are involved in developing and assessing tasks. In the reported class, guidelines asked learners whether they contributed actively, integrated new language orally and in writing, activated target expressions, and identified similarities and differences across groups.
requirements: Teachers must define tasks in advance and explain how learners are expected to work through them gradually.
Guidelines should be explained from the beginning along with the journal's purpose and role in the course.
constraints: The article notes some learners still did not know how to reflect despite guidelines, so guidelines alone may not suffice without teacher help.
target_learning_goals: self-assessment of communicative performance
reflection on learning process
examples: The walking-tour task used five guideline questions, including 'Did I integrate the new language I learned in the unit orally and in writing? Give examples.'
key_sources: Arciniegas Trejos, C. M. (2008). Using Journals for Learners' Reflection and Self-Assessment. The Internet TESL Journal, Vol. XIV, No. 10. http://iteslj.org/Techniques/Arciniegas-LearnersJournals.html

article_title: The Effectiveness of "Teach for America" and Other Under-certified Teachers
citation: Laczko-Kerr, I., & Berliner, D. C. (2002, September 6). The Effectiveness of "Teach for America" and Other Under-certified Teachers on Student Academic Achievement: A Case of Harmful Public Policy. Education Policy Analysis Archives, 10(37). http://epaa.asu.edu/epaa/v10n37/
title: Professional control versus popular control of entry into teaching
description: The article describes, citing Wise (1994a), two methods of controlling entry into the teaching profession. "Professional control allows the teaching profession to monitor who becomes a teacher" through specified certification standards, while "popular control allows public demand to control who is placed in classrooms, with much less concern for their qualifications" — emergency certificates being an example of the latter. The article uses this framework to argue that demand-based policies allowing uncertified teachers downgrade certification and prevent teaching from meeting a criterion of a profession.
requirements: Certification standards and political mechanisms through which the profession monitors who becomes a teacher
constraints: The article frames the framework as contested: interpretations of this literature are intertwined with the ideology of the researchers
target_learners: K-12 public school students, particularly those in low-income urban and rural districts
target_learning_goals: Access to qualified teachers of record supporting academic achievement in reading, mathematics, and language arts
examples: The article treats Arizona's issuance of emergency certificates during teacher shortages as an instance of popular control
key_sources: Laczko-Kerr, I., & Berliner, D. C. (2002, September 6). The Effectiveness of "Teach for America" and Other Under-certified Teachers on Student Academic Achievement: A Case of Harmful Public Policy. Education Policy Analysis Archives, 10(37). http://epaa.asu.edu/epaa/v10n37/

article_title: Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process
citation: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244
title: The choice-points model mapping participation decisions onto the research process
description: The article's central organizing model depicts "choice points" — "the intersection between participation and steps in the research cycle". At each and all phases of research, partners decide which tools and methods will produce the desired level of participation: stakeholders identify their needs and goals, researchers identify the fundamental needs of research, and academic-community partnerships work together to make choices meeting both. Choices may yield highly participatory strategies at some steps and more researcher-driven strategies at others; the article stresses "there is no prescription for the "right" way to do PR".
requirements: Stakeholders must identify their needs and goals of the research process
Researchers must identify the fundamental needs of research to provide the desired evidence, outcome, or impact
Academic-community partnerships must collaborate on the choices
constraints: Choices might lead to highly participatory strategies for some steps and more researcher-driven strategies at others; no single right way is prescribed
target_learning_goals: Choosing research tools and methods that achieve the desired level of stakeholder participation at each research stage
examples: Figure 1 depicts participation choice points across the research process, and Figure 2 gives example participatory methods for each step
key_sources: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244

article_title: Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process
citation: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244
title: Table 1 taxonomy of participatory research frameworks, orientations, and approaches
description: Table 1 compiles the article's taxonomy of PR frameworks across disciplines, including action research, action learning, appreciative inquiry, asset-based community development, citizen science, community-based participatory research, decolonizing methodologies, participatory action research, participatory evaluation, popular education, practitioner inquiry, and user-centered design research. Each entry carries a definition, variations, and key sources. The article notes "the breadth of terms describing the PR orientation is vast", but the frameworks "share in common a value in doing research with those who are typically the subjects of research, rather than on them".
requirements: Used as a demonstration that researchers within almost every discipline view research as collaborative inquiry with goals beyond knowledge generation
constraints: The article states the table is not intended to be an exhaustive list of PR frameworks
target_learners: Researchers new to participatory research seeking an entry point into PR traditions
target_learning_goals: Recognizing PR orientations across disciplines and locating source literature
examples: Educational action research is listed as action research conducted in educational and school settings, with teacher action research as a variation
key_sources: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244

article_title: Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors and Their Association with Self-Regulation in Chilean Children
citation: López-Gil, J.F., Oriol-Granado, X., Izquierdo, M., Ramírez-Vélez, R., Fernández-Vergara, O., Olloquequi, J., & García-Hermoso, A. (2020). Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors and Their Association with Self-Regulation in Chilean Children. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17165676
title: Promote regular physical activity, limited screen time and healthy nutrition together, not in isolation, to support children's self-regulation
description: The article proposes that fostering multiple healthy lifestyle behaviors during childhood may be one potential strategy to promote child social-emotional development, since a greater number of healthy habits was associated with higher self-regulation. It states that "healthy lifestyles, such as regular PA, limited ST, and healthy nutrition promotion, should not be pursued in isolation, but rather as a part of a larger promotion". Regular physical activity emerges as the main habit to emphasize.
requirements: Interventions should integrate multiple components of SR development, which the authors note seems more successful in decreasing health risk behaviors.
constraints: Evidence is cross-sectional; the authors state results need to be confirmed in longitudinal and interventional research.
target_learners: Children aged 8–12 years in low-SES public schools
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation and social-emotional development
examples: The study compared self-regulation across children meeting different numbers and combinations of healthy habits (PA, screen time, Mediterranean Diet) in 1561 Chilean schoolchildren.

Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors and Their Association with Self-Regulation in Chilean Children. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17165676

article_title: Game-based assessment: an integrated model for capturing evidence of learning in play
citation: Richard Halverson, Elizabeth Owen, Nathan Wills, R. Benjamin Shapiro. (2012). Game-Based Assessment: An integrated model for capturing evidence of learning in play. ERIA Working Paper. http://www.eriainteractive.com/index.php
title: Progenitor X: a narrative-based, turn-based puzzle game teaching stem-cell science practices
description: Progenitor X is a GLS game "developed in partnership with the Regenerative Medicine research team to present core ideas of cutting edge sciences in context of a game." Players are challenged to cultivate and differentiate stem cells, assemble tissues, and replace organs contaminated with a zombie virus. Completing game play requires solving 10-12 cell, tissue, and organ puzzle cycles, with the final organ cycle functioning as a boss-level requiring a cell-cell-tissue-cell-tissue cycle sequence using all skills learned earlier. Its content model invites players to dissect, collect, cultivate, differentiate and treat diseased tissues with stem cells.
requirements: Requires players to repeat cell-tissue and cell-cell-tissue-cell cycles to complete the game
target_learners: younger players considering stem-cell research careers
target_learning_goals: lab processes by which scientists manipulate stem cells and use them in treatment
examples: The cell cycle requires populating a grid with ips cells that can be transformed into the target population, and manipulating the cells toward the appropriate transformation
key_sources: Richard Halverson, Elizabeth Owen, Nathan Wills, R. Benjamin Shapiro. (2012). Game-Based Assessment: An integrated model for capturing evidence of learning in play. ERIA Working Paper. http://www.eriainteractive.com/index.php

article_title: Seductive details hamper learning even when they do not disrupt
citation: Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Eitel, A. (2023). Seductive details hamper learning even when they do not disrupt. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09632-w
title: Prompt learners that seductive details are irrelevant to the learning objective to protect recall of pertinent content
description: Before learning, tell learners explicitly that interesting but irrelevant material will not be tested and is not relevant to the learning objective. In this study, such a prompt "reduced students’ perceived relevance and relative processing time for seductive details, which in turn fostered recall performance", and "prompting students about the irrelevance of seductive details made the seductive details effect disappear for recall". The article frames this as reducing the details' diverting potential.
requirements: The prompt must identify which material is irrelevant and which is relevant (e.g., relevant content marked in a red frame) before the learning phase.
constraints: The benefit was demonstrated for recall, not transfer, in an online setting with adult undergraduates.
target_learners: undergraduate students in self-directed online learning
target_learning_goals: recall of pertinent instructional content (lightning formation)
examples: Participants in the irrelevance-prompt condition read that the photographs of lightning-strike consequences were "not relevant to the learning objective and will not be tested later" before a 6.5-minute learning phase.
key_sources: Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Eitel, A. (2023). Seductive details hamper learning even when they do not disrupt. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09632-w

article_title: The knowledge-learning-instruction (KLI) framework: Toward bridging the science-practice chasm to enhance robust student learning
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki
title: State instructional principles in terms of knowledge component types rather than subject-matter domains
description: A fundamental KLI assumption is that many learning processes and instructional design decisions 'are not intrinsically domain-based, but are determined by the type of KCs being learned'. The article argues a hypothetical principle like 'drill and practice is not effective for mathematics' is at the wrong level of analysis because it does not say what it is about mathematics that makes the method unsuitable. Instead, design decisions should be associated with KC types and their associated learning processes, such as study-practice trials for fact encoding and prompted self-explanations for explicit concepts and integrative knowledge.
requirements: Instructional design decisions must be tied to an analysis of the target course's knowledge components and their types
constraints: The article leaves open whether domain specificity constrains KC form qualitatively or only quantitatively
target_learners: instructional designers and researchers across academic domains
target_learning_goals: selecting instructional methods matched to the kind of knowledge being taught
examples: The article maps study-practice trials to constant-constant fact encoding, worked examples and tutored practice to implicit category and production learning, and self-explanation prompts to explicit and integrative knowledge
key_sources: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki

article_title: The Effects of Generative Learning Strategy Prompts and Metacognitive Feedback on Learners' Self-Regulation, Generation Process, and Achievement
citation: Lee, Hyeon Woo. (2008). The effects of generative learning strategy prompts and metacognitive feedback on learners' self-regulation, generation process, and achievement. Dissertation in Instructional Systems, The Pennsylvania State University. https://etda.libraries.psu.edu
title: Provide cognitive and metacognitive prompts while learners study in computer-based learning environments
description: Because providing generative strategy tools alone may not lead learners to monitor or adjust their learning, designers should pair strategy tools with prompts to use the strategies and with metacognitive feedback on strategy decisions. The study concludes that its positive effects from metacognitive feedback suggest "instructional designers or teachers should provide cognitive and metacognitive prompts while learners study". Prompts direct learners to underline, summarize, and answer adjunct questions; metacognitive feedback reminds learners to evaluate the adequacy of their strategy use.
requirements: Learners must be working with generative learning strategy tools in a computer-based environment so that prompts and feedback can direct and refine strategy use
constraints: Simple prompting alone may not be enough to help learners monitor, be aware of, or adjust their learning processes according to how well they are learning
target_learners: undergraduate students learning from computer-based static visualized instruction
target_learning_goals: self-regulation, quality of generative strategy use, recall and comprehension
examples: Treatment 3 combined strategy tools, written prompts directing underlining, summarizing and adjunct questions, and feedback on students' adjunct-question responses reminding them to evaluate and correct strategy execution
key_sources: Lee, Hyeon Woo. (2008). The effects of generative learning strategy prompts and metacognitive feedback on learners' self-regulation, generation process, and achievement. Dissertation in Instructional Systems, The Pennsylvania State University. https://etda.libraries.psu.edu

article_title: Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs
citation: Chris Piech, Jonathan Huang, Zhenghao Chen, Chuong Do, Andrew Ng, Daphne Koller. (2013). Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.2579
title: Probabilistic peer grading models (PG1, PG2, PG3) representing grader bias, reliability, temporal coherence, and coupled score-reliability
description: The article introduces a family of Bayesian models in which each submission has a latent true score, each grader a bias (tendency to "inﬂate or deﬂate her assessment") and a reliability (precision of assessments after bias correction). PG1 places priors over these latents; PG2 adds temporal coherence of bias across assignments (consecutive-assignment bias correlation of 0.33); PG3 couples a grader's reliability to her own grade. Inference uses Gibbs sampling or EM, producing posterior belief distributions over grades rather than single scores.
requirements: Multiple peer grades per submission (the studied courses used four peer grades per student)
Grades normalized to a consistent scale across assignments for the temporal-coherence model (z-scores)
constraints: The article focuses only on the dynamics of bias, not true scores or reliabilities, across assignments

PG3's dependence of a submission's score on graders' scores is weak by design; the authors exclude variables like race, ethnicity, gender, and student-grade temporal coherence (0.46 Pearson) on fairness grounds
target_learners: MOOC students grading peers in large open online courses
target_learning_goals: Accurate and fair assessment of complex, open-ended assignments such as design tasks, essays, and proofs
examples: The models were evaluated on two Coursera HCI offerings with 63,199 peer grades, using supergraded ground-truth submissions averaging 160 assessments each
key_sources: Chris Piech, Jonathan Huang, Zhenghao Chen, Chuong Do, Andrew Ng, Daphne Koller. (2013). Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.2579

article_title: <p>Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation</p>
citation: Biotteau M, Danna J, Baudou É, Puyjarinet F, Velay J-L, Albaret J-M, Chaix Y. (2019). Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. https://doi.org/10.2147/NDT.S120514
title: Two-category framework of DCD interventions: bottom-up process-oriented versus top-down task-oriented approaches
description: The review organizes DCD intervention methods into two main categories. The bottom-up category contains process-oriented (deficit-oriented) approaches such as kinesthetic training and sensory integration, which assume "a deficit in a specific body function or part ... is responsible for the impaired motor skills" and aim to remediate that underlying deficit. The top-down category contains task-oriented (functional skill) approaches such as neuromotor task training and CO-OP, which teach children the ADLs they need, with children as actors encouraged to think about difficulties and find solutions while adults help explore and validate strategies.
requirements: Interventions supporting participation and activity are key to remediating motor impairments and associated problems in DCD
constraints: Process-oriented approaches were not included in European Academy of Childhood Disabilities recommendations or the 2012 American Academy of Pediatrics policy statement due to weak effects
target_learning_goals: Improving coordinated motor skills and activities of daily living
examples: Neuromotor task training and cognitive orientation to daily occupational performance (CO-OP) as named task-oriented approaches
key_sources: Biotteau M, Danna J, Baudou É, Puyjarinet F, Velay J-L, Albaret J-M, Chaix Y. (2019). Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. https://doi.org/10.2147/NDT.S120514

article_title: Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood
citation: Checa, P., & Rueda, M. R. (2011). Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2011.591857
title: Promote executive attention and effortful control to help children succeed at school
description: The article recommends that educators and intervention designers attend to children's executive attention and effortful control as foundations for school competence. It states: "Our data point out the importance of promoting executive attention and effortful control in order to help children to be successful at school." The authors argue this evidence "has the potential to guide the design of intervention programs aiming at enhancing school readiness."
requirements: Interventions should target the executive attention network and temperamental effortful control, which the study links to grades and schooling skills.
constraints: The authors note future research is needed to test whether attention training actually results in better academic performance and schooling competence.
target_learners: children in late childhood and early adolescence (around age 12)
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in mathematics and literacy
schooling skills such as rule following and student-role understanding
examples: The study measured executive attention with a combined Flanker-Go/No-Go task and linked interference suppression efficiency to math grades and schooling skills.
key_sources: Checa, P., & Rueda, M. R. (2011). Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2011.591857

article_title: Parent praise to toddlers predicts fourth grade academic achievement via children’s incremental mindsets.
citation: Gunderson, E. A., Sorhagen, N. S., Gripshover, S. J., Dweck, C. S., Goldin-Meadow, S., & Levine, S. C. (2018). Parent Praise to Toddlers Predicts Fourth Grade Academic Achievement via Children's Incremental Mindsets. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000444
title: Praise young children's effort and strategies (process) rather than fixed personal qualities to foster incremental mindsets and long-term achievement
description: The article's central design implication for caregivers and teachers is that praise emphasizing children's effort, strategies, and specific actions predicts incremental motivational frameworks, which in turn predict achievement growth years later. Person praise (e.g., "you're so smart") was not related to children's motivational frameworks or achievement in this sample. Interventions "constructed to increase the proportion of praise children hear that emphasizes how their effort and strategies lead to learning may be a fruitful way to foster incremental mindsets and long-term academic achievement."
requirements: Praise should connect effort and strategies to learning outcomes rather than merely noting effort
constraints: Hyperbolic or excessive praise can discourage challenge-seeking, especially for children with low self-esteem; consoling effort without learning outcomes may deflate self-efficacy
target_learners: toddlers and young children (ages 1–3 in the study)
target_learning_goals: fostering incremental mindsets about intelligence
long-term academic achievement in math and reading
examples: Parents' process praise was observed naturalistically at ages 14, 26, and 38 months and coded as a proportion of total praise (18.0% on average)
key_sources: Gunderson, E. A., Sorhagen, N. S., Gripshover, S. J., Dweck, C. S., Goldin-Meadow, S., & Levine, S. C. (2018). Parent Praise to Toddlers Predicts Fourth Grade Academic Achievement via Children's Incremental Mindsets. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000444

article_title: Working memory influences processing speed and reading fluency in ADHD
citation: Jacobson, L. A., Ryan, M., Martin, R. B., Ewen, J., Mostofsky, S. H., Denckla, M. B., & Mahone, E. M. (2011). Working Memory Influences Processing Speed and Reading Fluency in ADHD. Child Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2010.532204
title: Processing speed as a deconstructable chain: sensory registration, response selection/preparation, and motor output components
description: The article proposes that processing speed, defined as "the time between stimulus onset and response completion", can be decomposed into separable components: sensory registration and perception, response selection and preparation, and response execution (Figure 1). Using the WISC-IV-I Coding and Coding Copy subtests, the study dissociates graphomotor output speed from executive response-selection components, arguing that ADHD-related slowing arises "between sensation/perception and action" in frontally-mediated circuits rather than in posterior perceptual systems.
requirements: Measures permitting dissociation of response components, such as the WISC-IV-I process analysis subtests pairing Coding with Coding Copy
constraints: The authors note the Coding task presents greater vertical scanning demand than Coding Copy, so perceptual demand differences may contribute to group differences on these tasks
target_learning_goals: reading fluency development
processing speed and executive control
examples: The study regressed sex and Coding Copy performance on Coding to create a residualized CodingR score reflecting response selection and preparation separable from graphomotor output speed
key_sources: Jacobson, L. A., Ryan, M., Martin, R. B., Ewen, J., Mostofsky, S. H., Denckla, M. B., & Mahone, E. M. (2011). Working Memory Influences Processing Speed and Reading Fluency in ADHD. Child Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2010.532204

article_title: Visual processing speed
citation: Owsley Cynthia. (2012). Visual Processing Speed. Vision Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visres.2012.11.014
title: Processing-inefficiency and attentional-disengagement account of UFOV task difficulties
description: This mechanistic account holds that older adults' UFOV task problems arise not from a shrinking attentional field but from inefficient visual search and difficulty disengaging attention, which slow the processing time needed to complete a task. The review states the fundamental problem "is more likely due to inefficiencies in visual search and problems with attentional disengagement, which in turn slow the visual processing time needed to complete the task at hand". This supports the evolution of the UFOV metric from field size to a duration-threshold measure of processing speed. It contrasts with the earlier field-constriction view and with speed-accuracy trade-off explanations.
requirements: Explanation rests on duration-threshold paradigms where response time is not the dependent measure
constraints: The review notes speed-accuracy trade-off differences may still contribute in laboratory paradigms where reaction time is the dependent measure
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms of age-related slowing in visual processing
examples: Cosman and colleagues found older adults with slowed processing in UFOV subtests 2–4 tended to also have problems attentionally disengaging from a cued location
key_sources: Owsley Cynthia. (2012). Visual Processing Speed. Vision Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visres.2012.11.014

article_title: Emergent Writing in Preschoolers: Preliminary Evidence for a Theoretical Framework
citation: Puranik, C. S., & Lonigan, C. J. (2014). Emergent Writing in Preschoolers: Preliminary Evidence for a Theoretical Framework. Reading Research Quarterly, 49(4). https://doi.org/10.1002/rrq.79
title: Emergent writing assessment battery of conceptual, procedural, and generative subtests for preschoolers
description: A battery of individually administered writing tasks designed to index the three hypothesized emergent writing domains. Conceptual knowledge was measured by Universal Principles of Print, Concepts about Writing, and Functions of Print subtests; procedural knowledge by Identify Letters, Write Letters, Write Name, and Write Words subtests; generative knowledge by Picture Description and Sentence Retell tasks scored for features such as "linearity, segmentation, presence of simple units, left-to-right orientation." Inter-rater reliability on a random 30 percent of responses ranged from 93% to 100%. The closed-ended generative tasks were chosen because pilot work showed preschoolers had difficulty with spontaneous writing.
requirements: Trained examiners administering tasks individually; scoring rubrics for name writing (9-point) and word spelling (7-point) based on prior research
constraints: Several younger children were unable to complete the generative knowledge tasks, resulting in floor effects; internal consistencies for the conceptual knowledge tasks were lower than desirable
target_learning_goals: Assessment of early writing skills across print concepts, transcription mechanics, and early composition
examples: Children wrote six common words scored with a modified Tangel and Blachman spelling rubric crediting phonemes represented
key_sources: Puranik, C. S., & Lonigan, C. J. (2014). Emergent Writing in Preschoolers: Preliminary Evidence for a Theoretical Framework. Reading Research Quarterly, 49(4). https://doi.org/10.1002/rrq.79

article_title: Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students’ Math Achievement
citation: Ramirez Gerardo, Hooper Sophia Yang, Kersting Nicole B., Ferguson Ronald, Yeager David. (2018). Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students' Math Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858418756052
title: Teachers should hold the conviction that math can be learned by everyone and use instructional strategies emphasizing learning over memorization and ability
description: To combat negative expectancy ("Golem") effects, the article recommends that "teachers must have the conviction that math material can be learned by everyone and use instructional strategies that emphasize learning rather than memorization and abilities." Practices communicating high expectations and personal assurance in students' ability may position students to respond more adaptively to struggle experiences in mathematics. This follows from the finding that reduced process-oriented practices, not lacking knowledge, carried the anxiety effect.
requirements: Teachers must communicate high expectations for math and personal assurance in students' ability to meet those expectations
constraints: The article states its evidence is correlational, so the recommendation rests on mediation models rather than causal manipulation
target_learners: adolescent mathematics students, particularly ninth graders
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
adaptive responses to academic struggle
examples: The study's process-oriented practice items included statements such as "My math teacher wants us to use our thinking skills, not just memorize things" and "My math teacher doesn't let people give up when the work gets hard."
key_sources: Ramirez Gerardo, Hooper Sophia Yang, Kersting Nicole B., Ferguson Ronald, Yeager David. (2018). Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students' Math Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858418756052

article_title: Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults
citation: Rogge, A.-K., Röder, B., Zech, A., Nagel, V., Hollander, K., Braumann, K.-M. & Hötting, K. (2017). Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults. Scientific Reports 7:5661. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06071-9
title: Progressive, varied balance circuit training with reactive postural challenges
description: The intervention was a balance circuit training on varying surfaces with eight stations per session of 5 minutes each, designed to "induce reactive postural adjustments, forcing participants to permanently re-stabilize". Exercises were progressively adjustable by increasing strap tension, partner distance or removing vision, and were replaced with a new set after six weeks to keep training challenging. Sessions ran twice weekly for 12 weeks in groups of 10–12.
requirements: Progressive difficulty adjustment to participant skill level; new exercise sets after six weeks to maintain challenge
constraints: No explicit strategies were taught; effects were demonstrated against an active relaxation control, not a passive control
target_learners: healthy adults without extensive balance-training experience
target_learning_goals: balance performance
memory
spatial cognition
examples: One task was single-leg stance while being pulled sideways with a strong elastic strap; another was throwing a medicine ball on a wobble board in tandems
key_sources: Rogge, A.-K., Röder, B., Zech, A., Nagel, V., Hollander, K., Braumann, K.-M. & Hötting, K. (2017). Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults. Scientific Reports 7:5661. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06071-9

article_title: When did you stop speaking to yourself? Age-related differences in adolescents’ world knowledge-based audience design
citation: Arvidsson C., Pagmar D., Uddén J. (2022). When did you stop speaking to yourself? Age-related differences in adolescents' world knowledge-based audience design. Royal Society Open Science 9(11): 220305. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.220305
title: Processing model distinguishing representation of others' knowledge from its online use in production
description: Following Clark's processing perspective, the article distinguishes assumed knowledge — the speaker's assumption about the addressee's knowledge state — from audience design, the process of adapting utterances to those assumptions during online communication. The findings support "an AD model distinguishing between the representation of others' knowledge as such and the usage of these representations online, where the latter develops later": 11–12-year-olds held adult-like assumptions (KAS near maximum) yet failed to deploy them consistently during production. The model treats listener-specific adjustment as relying on knowledge attribution, executive functions and social interaction experience.
requirements: Distinguishing these two components requires tasks that separately measure assumptions (e.g. prompted post-test surveys) and online production behaviour
constraints: The article states the development of audience design cannot be reduced to possessing relevant knowledge and high executive function; social experience is difficult to measure directly
target_learning_goals: pragmatic competence
use of common ground during online communication
examples: The authors argue pragmatic competence should be regarded as a specific capability with its own developmental trajectory and neurophysiological correlates rather than a composition of domain-general skills
key_sources: Arvidsson C., Pagmar D., Uddén J. (2022). When did you stop speaking to yourself? Age-related differences in adolescents' world knowledge-based audience design. Royal Society Open Science 9(11): 220305. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.220305

article_title: Trajectories of parental engagement in early childhood among dual-earner families: Effects on child self-control.
citation: Tiago Ferreira, Joana Cadima, Marisa Matias, Joana Marina Vieira, and Teresa Leal; Karine Verschueren; Paula Mena Matos. (2018). Trajectories of Parental Engagement in Early Childhood Among Dual-Earner Families: Effects on Child Self-Control. Developmental Psychology, 54(4), 731–743. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000458
title: PRQ involvement subscale as a measure of parental engagement in positive activities
description: The study used the eight-item involvement subscale from the Parenting Relationship Questionnaire—Preschool Form to measure parental engagement. Items tap "parents’ active participation in positive engagement activities, along with the parent’s knowledge of the child’s activities," including planning things to do together, teaching new games, working on projects, taking walks, and doing arts and crafts. Parents rated items on a 4-point Likert scale from never to always. Confirmatory factor analysis showed adequate fit at all three waves for both parents, and measurement invariance held across time and between mothers and fathers. Cronbach's alphas ranged from .84 to .90 for mothers and .84 to .87 for fathers.
requirements: Both mothers and fathers independently self-report on the same items
Measurement invariance across time and between parents must be established before comparing trajectories
constraints: The subscale captures frequency of positive engagement activities and knowledge of the child's activities, not the interactive quality of engagement
target_learning_goals: measuring frequency of parental engagement in developmentally supportive activities
examples: Sample items include "My child and I plan things to do together" and "My child and I work on projects together"
key_sources: Tiago Ferreira, Joana Cadima, Marisa Matias, Joana Marina Vieira, and Teresa Leal; Karine Verschueren; Paula Mena Matos. (2018). Trajectories of Parental Engagement in Early Childhood Among Dual-Earner Families: Effects on Child Self-Control. Developmental Psychology, 54(4), 731–743. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000458

article_title: Inhibitory Control and Information Processing in ADHD: Comparing the Dual Task and Performance Adjustment Hypotheses
citation: Fosco, W. D., Kofler, M. J., Alderson, R. M., Tarle, S. J., Raiker, J. S., & Sarver, D. E. (2019). Inhibitory Control and Information Processing in ADHD: Comparing the Dual Task and Performance Adjustment Hypotheses. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-018-0504-9
title: Use performance metrics with clearer cognitive interpretations (e.g., diffusion parameters) rather than raw mean reaction time
description: Because mean reaction time conflates distinct cognitive processes, the authors recommend that researchers interpret standard metrics cautiously and prefer measures with clearer cognitive interpretations, such as drift diffusion parameters. In this study, MRT alone would have suggested that stop signals slow processing speed, whereas decomposition showed drift rate was unchanged and slowing reflected increased response caution. As the authors write, "We therefore urge researchers to exercise caution when interpreting standard performance metrics, such as RT and error rates, and to utilize metrics that have clearer cognitive interpretations whenever possible".
