requirements: Requires tasks yielding sufficient trial-level RT and accuracy data for diffusion modeling (the article notes excellent parameter recovery with as few as 20 trials per participant)
constraints: Group-difference conclusions are not significantly affected by inflated MRT estimates; the concern applies mainly to aggregating or comparing MRT across studies differing in inhibitory demands
target_learners: children ages 8-13 with and without ADHD
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement and interpretation of cognitive processing in research on attention and self-regulation
examples: If MRT had been the primary outcome in this study, the authors state they would likely have concluded that introducing stop signals slows processing speed, yet drift rate was equivalent across tasks
key_sources: Fosco, W. D., Kofler, M. J., Alderson, R. M., Tarle, S. J., Raiker, J. S., & Sarver, D. E. (2019). Inhibitory Control and Information Processing in ADHD: Comparing the Dual Task and Performance Adjustment Hypotheses. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-018-0504-9

article_title: Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry
citation: Kingir, S. (2013). Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 9(2), 101-114. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2013.922a
title: Prain and Hand's five-element framework for learning from writing in science
description: The article presents Prain and Hand's (1996) framework of five elements guiding learning from writing in science: writing type, writing purpose, audience, topic, and method of text production. Writing type covers varied formats such as letters and brochures; purpose spans reviewing, clarifying, and persuading; audience involves writing for a wide range of readers so students clarify understanding; topic demands that students analyze, represent, or manipulate understanding in a new version; and production method concerns individual or group composing by hand or computer. The study operationalizes the audience element by assigning letter audiences.
requirements: Effective combinations of the five elements are needed for an increased science understanding, as the article states these elements can be combined in a writing activity
constraints: The article notes audience and writing type were the elements most frequently manipulated in writing-to-learn studies, so the framework's other elements are less empirically tested here
target_learners: science students at all levels of education
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of science content
science literacy
meaning-making through writing
examples: The study assigned 9th graders to write letters to younger students (6th graders), peers (9th graders), or their teacher after a mixture unit, manipulating the audience element while holding writing type (letter) constant
key_sources: Kingir, S. (2013). Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 9(2), 101-114. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2013.922a

article_title: Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents
citation: Pandey A, Hale D, Das S, Goddings A-L, Blakemore S-J, Viner RM. (2018). Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6059379/
title: Prefer curriculum-based self-regulation interventions in schools because they require no considerable additional time or staff resources and reach children where they already are.
description: The review recommends curriculum-based interventions as the preferred delivery model for self-regulation improvement in schools. This recommendation rests on three factors the article states: curriculum interventions were "delivered in schools by training of teachers without a need for considerable additional resource in terms of time and staff"; children and adolescents "spend a considerable part of their time at school between the ages of 5 and 18 years and thus are easily accessible for interventions"; and curriculum-based approaches were the most common type used (21 of 50 interventions, 42%), with 16 of 21 (76%) reporting consistent SR improvements.
requirements: Teachers receive professional training to implement the predefined curriculum in classrooms
constraints: Fidelity was infrequently measured and reported (11 of 21 curriculum interventions; 52%)
target_learners: Children and adolescents aged 5 to 18 years in school settings
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation skills including emotion control, positive interactions, avoiding inappropriate actions, and self-directed learning
examples: Curriculum-based interventions included a combination of teachers' professional training and classroom-based activities based on a predefined curriculum, embedded within the existing school routine, using strategies such as circle-time games, storytelling, book reading, and self-talk in preschool and kindergarten, and role play, cognitive modeling, and psychoeducational group therapeutic lessons in older children
key_sources: Pandey A, Hale D, Das S, Goddings A-L, Blakemore S-J, Viner RM. (2018). Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6059379/

article_title: Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers?
citation: Michelle S. Peter, Samantha Durrant, Andrew Jessop, Amy Bidgood, Julian M. Pine, Caroline F. Rowland. (2019). Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers? Cognitive Psychology 115 (2019) 101238. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2019.101238
title: Two competing accounts of the processing speed–vocabulary relationship: facilitation versus lexical entrenchment
description: The article frames two hypotheses about why processing speed relates to vocabulary. On the facilitation account, "faster processing of familiar words frees up resources that can then be dedicated to the learning of new words". On the reverse account, drawn from the adult literature, larger vocabularies yield stronger, more entrenched lexical representations that are accessed faster, so children with large vocabularies are simply better at processing familiar words with no implications for later growth. The study tests these by asking whether processing speed predicts future vocabulary growth over and above concurrent vocabulary size.
requirements: Testing requires showing that processing speed predicts the rate of future vocabulary growth, not just concurrent correlations with vocabulary size
constraints: Most prior work reports only concurrent relationships or does not control for concurrent vocabulary, limiting causal interpretation
target_learners: toddlers in the second and third year of life
target_learning_goals: vocabulary acquisition
lexical processing efficiency
examples: The study tested whether children with faster processing speed grow their vocabularies faster against the alternative that large-vocabulary children are merely faster to process familiar words
key_sources: Michelle S. Peter, Samantha Durrant, Andrew Jessop, Amy Bidgood, Julian M. Pine, Caroline F. Rowland. (2019). Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers? Cognitive Psychology 115 (2019) 101238. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2019.101238

article_title: Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers?
citation: Michelle S. Peter, Samantha Durrant, Andrew Jessop, Amy Bidgood, Julian M. Pine, Caroline F. Rowland. (2019). Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers? Cognitive Psychology 115 (2019) 101238. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2019.101238
title: Direct versus indirect routes from processing speed to syntax acquisition
description: The article outlines two models by which processing speed could affect syntax acquisition. On the indirect route, syntax emerges from lexical knowledge, so processing speed would act on syntax via vocabulary learning and its relationship with syntax "would disappear once we control for vocabulary". On the direct route, more efficient processing of familiar words helps track relations and co-occurrences between words, a skill necessary for syntactic development, so faster processing should predict syntactic growth even after concurrent vocabulary is taken into account. The study's syntax analyses were designed to adjudicate between these accounts.
requirements: Adjudicating the accounts requires growth curve analysis of syntactic growth with concurrent vocabulary controlled
constraints: Only one prior study (Fernald et al., 2006) had reported concurrent relations between processing speed and syntactic measures, not predictive ones
target_learners: toddlers in the second and third year of life
target_learning_goals: syntactic development
productive syntax measured via M3L and syntactic complexity
examples: The article contrasts the lexical-emergence view (Bates & Goodman, 1999; Marchman & Bates, 1994) with the direct-tracking view (Marchman & Fernald, 2008)
key_sources: Michelle S. Peter, Samantha Durrant, Andrew Jessop, Amy Bidgood, Julian M. Pine, Caroline F. Rowland. (2019). Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers? Cognitive Psychology 115 (2019) 101238. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2019.101238

article_title: Physical Exercise and Fitness Level Are Related to Cognitive and Psychosocial Functioning in Adolescents
citation: Reigal, R. E., Hernández-Mendo, A., Juárez-Ruiz de Mier, R., and Morales-Sánchez, V. (2020). Physical Exercise and Fitness Level Are Related to Cognitive and Psychosocial Functioning in Adolescents. Front. Psychol. 11:1777. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01777
title: Promote regular physical exercise and fitness development among adolescents to support cognitive and psychosocial functioning
description: The article concludes that adolescents who practiced more weekly exercise and had higher fitness scored better on cognitive and psychosocial tests, and recommends promoting exercise: "it is necessary to continue promoting the practice of physical exercise among the young population." It frames active lifestyle habits as bringing "the most direct and indirect beneﬁts to their health and well-being," supporting academic and social functioning.
requirements: Exercise should be sufficient in intensity and frequency to raise physical fitness, since fitness level rather than hours alone was the stronger correlate.
constraints: The study's comparative and predictive design does not allow causal relationships to be established; results come from a convenience sample of 14–16-year-olds in Malaga, Spain.
target_learning_goals: Cognitive functioning (selective attention, concentration, processing speed)
Psychosocial well-being (self-efficacy, self-rated health, life satisfaction)
examples: Adolescents were divided into low (less than 2 h/week), moderate (2–4 h/week), and high (more than 4 h/week) exercise groups and compared on cognitive and psychosocial measures.
key_sources: Reigal, R. E., Hernández-Mendo, A., Juárez-Ruiz de Mier, R., and Morales-Sánchez, V. (2020). Physical Exercise and Fitness Level Are Related to Cognitive and Psychosocial Functioning in Adolescents. Front. Psychol. 11:1777. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01777

article_title: Prospective Study of Insufficient Sleep and Neurobehavioral Functioning Among School-Age Children
citation: Taveras Elsie M. MD, MPH; Rifas-Shiman Sheryl L. MPH; Bub Kristen L. EdD; Gillman Matthew W. MD, SM; Oken Emily MD, MPH. (2017). Prospective Study of Insufficient Sleep and Neurobehavioral Functioning among School-Age Children. Academic Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5545152/
title: Promote optimal age-specific sleep duration in early childhood to support cognitive and behavioral functioning
description: The article concludes that insufficient sleep in the preschool and early school years is associated with poorer mother- and teacher-reported neurobehavioral functioning in mid-childhood, and states that "our results indicate that interventions to promote optimal sleep duration in early childhood could have positive effects on cognitive and behavioral functioning." The principle directs caregivers, educators, and health providers to treat age-appropriate sleep duration (≥11 h/day at 3-4 years; ≥10 h/day at 5-7 years, per National Sleep Foundation recommendations used in the study) as a foundational condition for executive function and social-emotional development.
requirements: Sleep duration must meet age-specific recommendations (e.g., ≥11 hours/day at ages 3-4; ≥10 hours/day at ages 5-7) as categorized from maternal reports in the study
constraints: Evidence is observational; the article notes residual confounding and reverse causation (e.g., anxiety or depression preceding poor sleep) cannot be ruled out
Sleep duration was estimated by maternal questionnaire rather than objective measures such as accelerometers or diaries
The cohort is of relatively high socioeconomic status, potentially limiting generalizability to lower socioeconomic environments
target_learners: children ages 3-7 years in preschool and early school years
target_learning_goals: executive function (attention shifting, working memory, inhibitory control)
behavioral and social-emotional functioning
examples: The study categorized sleep against National Sleep Foundation age-specific recommendations and found children below those thresholds at ages 3-4 and 5-7 had worse BRIEF and SDQ scores at age 7
key_sources: Taveras Elsie M. MD, MPH; Rifas-Shiman Sheryl L. MPH; Bub Kristen L. EdD; Gillman Matthew W. MD, SM; Oken Emily MD, MPH. (2017). Prospective Study of Insufficient Sleep and Neurobehavioral Functioning among School-Age Children. Academic Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5545152/

article_title: Metaphorically speaking: cognitive abilities and the production of figurative language
citation: Roger E. Beaty & Paul J. Silvia. (2013). Metaphorically speaking: cognitive abilities and the production of figurative language. Memory & Cognition. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0258-5
title: Property attribution model as a framework for metaphor generation
description: The article adopts Glucksberg's property attribution model of metaphor comprehension as a framework for conceptualizing metaphor production. Composing a metaphor involves "making an abstract link between a topic and a vehicle by relating similar characteristics", with a superordinate attributive category (e.g., "something that is healing" for music) maintained while searching semantic memory for a vehicle. The authors map this onto CHC abilities: attributive-category formation parallels broad retrieval ability (Gr), and top-down oversight of the search parallels fluid intelligence (Gf).
requirements: A superordinate attributive category must be formed and maintained while searching semantic memory for an appropriate vehicle
constraints: The model is a comprehension framework adopted by analogy for production; the article states an empirical understanding of figurative language production remains elusive
target_learning_goals: creative figurative language production
selective retrieval from semantic memory
examples: Participants forming an attributive category for "things that are gross" and selectively retrieving exemplars satisfying those criteria in the creative metaphor task
key_sources: Roger E. Beaty & Paul J. Silvia. (2013). Metaphorically speaking: cognitive abilities and the production of figurative language. Memory & Cognition. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0258-5

article_title: Neural Substrates of Inhibitory Control Maturation in Adolescence
citation: Constantinidis Christos, Luna Beatriz. (2019). Neural Substrates of Inhibitory Control Maturation in Adolescence. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2019.07.004
title: Preparatory-state model of inhibitory control maturation
description: The review proposes an integrative model in which inhibitory control matures primarily through the emergence of neural activity patterns establishing a ready preparatory state, supported by improved inhibitory circuitry and systems-level integration. As the review states, "a primary way in which inhibitory control matures is the emergence of neural activity patterns that establish a ready preparatory state to inhibit a response." These changes support PFC integration, error processing, and planning of effective responses, while leaving the ability to generate single inhibitory responses intact from early development.
requirements: Mature inhibitory circuitry and systems-level integration of prefrontal with oculomotor and subcortical systems
constraints: Adolescent immaturities do not undermine the ability to generate inhibitory responses but limit sustained, controlled engagement of cognitive control
target_learning_goals: development of inhibitory control and executive function
examples: Human longitudinal fMRI growth curves of dlPFC and dACC engagement; monkey single-neuron recordings of preparatory ramping and goal representation across adolescence and adulthood
key_sources: Constantinidis Christos, Luna Beatriz. (2019). Neural Substrates of Inhibitory Control Maturation in Adolescence. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2019.07.004

article_title: Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades
citation: Denton Carolyn A. (2012). Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades: Some Answers and Lingering Questions. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219412442155
title: Provide intensive Tier 3 intervention promptly to students with the most severe reading difficulties rather than delaying through less intensive tiers
description: The article argues, citing Vaughn, Denton, and Fletcher (2010), that students in Grade 2 and higher performing substantially below grade level may need immediate Tier 3 intensive intervention rather than progressing through Tiers 1 and 2. It is "supported by research evidence that students with the lowest preintervention performance levels require more intensive interventions to close the gap with typically developing students," and delaying intensive intervention may substantially decrease the likelihood that seriously impaired readers learn to read adequately.
requirements: Well-qualified teachers for Tier 3, as recommended by Gersten et al. (2008), given students' severe deficits in phonological processing, processing speed, and verbal working memory
constraints: The article notes Tier 3 group size (1:1 vs. very small groups) may best be decided individually by RTI problem-solving teams
target_learners: Students with severe, persistent reading difficulties in Grade 2 and higher
target_learning_goals: Word reading, decoding, and reading fluency remediation
examples: Torgesen et al. (2001) delivered 1:1 intervention for about 2 hours per day for 8 weeks to Grade 3–5 students with severe reading problems, producing large standard score gains in word reading and comprehension maintained 2 years later, with weaker fluency outcomes
key_sources: Denton Carolyn A. (2012). Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades: Some Answers and Lingering Questions. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219412442155

article_title: Sensori‐motor experience leads to changes in visual processing in the developing brain
citation: James, K. H. (2010). Sensori-motor experience leads to changes in visual processing in the developing brain. Developmental Science, 13(2), 279-288. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00883.x
title: Teach letter recognition through printing practice that couples visual and motor systems
description: Because printing practice couples visual and motor systems and produced neural specialization for letters where visual-only practice did not, the article supports sensori-motor learning strategies for letter instruction. It notes "Educators have implemented sensori-motor learning strategies when teaching children to recognize shapes, including letters" and that "children recognize letters more efficiently after printing practice than when printing is not involved in learning." The principle is to include handwriting/copied-letter production, not just visual recognition drills, in early literacy instruction.
requirements: Training must involve active letter production (copying/writing) with feedback, with stimulus exposure held comparable to comparison conditions
constraints: Behavioural recognition gains in this study were only a non-significant trend; behavioural benefits rest partly on cited work with larger samples
The visual-only comparison condition also involved oral naming, so the critical contrast is manual versus oral motor association
target_learners: pre-school and early-elementary children learning letters
target_learning_goals: letter recognition
early literacy foundations
examples: Children copied highlighted letters and words from a story across four weekly 30-minute training sessions, with feedback on writing accuracy
key_sources: James, K. H. (2010). Sensori-motor experience leads to changes in visual processing in the developing brain. Developmental Science, 13(2), 279-288. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00883.x

article_title: Print awareness of adult illiterates: a comparison with young pre-readers and low-educated adult readers
citation: Kurvers, J., Van Hout, R., & Vallen, T. (2009). Print awareness of adult illiterates: a comparison with young pre-readers and low-educated adult readers. Read Writ 22, 863-887. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-008-9129-7
title: Print awareness as a construct separate from language awareness, with three sub-domains
description: The article treats print awareness as a pre-reading construct distinct from language awareness, defining it as follows: "Print awareness refers to knowledge about environmental print, knowledge of written signs and graphemes, and knowledge about relationships between speech and writing". It operationalizes this in three sub-domains — environmental print (inscriptions, logos), the writing system (graphemes, signs), and the written register — each assessed with dedicated instruments whose internal consistencies ranged from Cronbach's alpha 0.75 to 0.99. The construct is used to compare unschooled illiterate adults with young pre-readers and low-educated literate adults.
requirements: Assessments must be administered in the participant's preferred first or second language
constraints: The article distinguishes print awareness from language awareness, the ability to reflect on spoken language forms separately from their meanings
target_learning_goals: concepts about print and written language
recognition of environmental print
understanding how writing represents speech
examples: Six assessment tasks: inscriptions (18 items), logos (9), graphemes (34), signs (14), writing/speech correspondence (7), and characteristics of written language (12)
key_sources: Kurvers, J., Van Hout, R., & Vallen, T. (2009). Print awareness of adult illiterates: a comparison with young pre-readers and low-educated adult readers. Read Writ 22, 863-887. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-008-9129-7

article_title: Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence
citation: Emily Grossnickle Peterson, Adam B. Weinberger, David H. Uttal, Bob Kolvoord and Adam E. Green. (2020). Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41235-020-00239-0
title: Attend to spatial activity participation during childhood, especially for girls, when planning spatial-thinking supports
description: The article recommends that educators and researchers consider when in development spatial activity participation matters, concluding that "Results highlight the importance of participating in spatial activities during childhood." Because childhood participation predicted later participation and later habits of mind, the authors argue that "spatial activity participation among young girls may be particularly important to consider in future research." Interventions should therefore target childhood participation rather than assuming adolescent participation can compensate for a childhood gap.
requirements: Opportunities for children to engage in spatial activities such as block play, puzzles, sports, and dance, with attention to activity participation across developmental stages
constraints: The study is cross-sectional and correlational; the authors note that future research will be necessary to directly assess whether interventions promoting childhood spatial activities increase later participation
target_learning_goals: Spatial thinking
Spatial habits of mind
STEM readiness
examples: The study found childhood activities predicted habits of mind even after controlling for adolescent activities, gender, and academic performance, and found no compensatory benefit of later participation
key_sources: Emily Grossnickle Peterson, Adam B. Weinberger, David H. Uttal, Bob Kolvoord and Adam E. Green. (2020). Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41235-020-00239-0

article_title: Metacognition and self-regulation in young children: does it matter if metacognitive experiences are communicated?
citation: Ventura, Ana Clara. (2022). Metacognition and self-regulation in young children: does it matter if metacognitive experiences are communicated?. Early Years. https://doi.org/10.1080/09575146.2022.2065666
title: Promote and hear young children's voices and judgments about their metacognitive experiences to help them solve activities in educational contexts
description: The article argues that educational contexts should actively promote and attend to children's spoken judgments about their metacognitive experiences, particularly feelings of difficulty. Because communicating FOD "allowed children to mobilize resources and to achieve their goals", adults should invite and respond to these comments during challenging task engagement rather than treating them as off-task talk.
requirements: Tasks must be challenging enough to elicit feelings of difficulty that children can communicate
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge
metacognitive regulation
emotional and motivational regulation
examples: Sixty first graders were individually interviewed while engaged in an ecological and challenging graphic task, and their spontaneous comments of FOD were coded
key_sources: Ventura, Ana Clara. (2022). Metacognition and self-regulation in young children: does it matter if metacognitive experiences are communicated?. Early Years. https://doi.org/10.1080/09575146.2022.2065666

article_title: Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference
citation: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287
title: Projection model of markedness-based acquisition (Zobl)
description: The article presents Zobl's projection model, in which markedness conditions in the input allow learners to acquire properties of the target language not represented in the input data, via "acquisition via markedness implications and ... acquisition via correlations between markedness of different but related parameters". The article draws the instructional implication that sequencing should let learners "profit from markedness conditions" rather than proceed from simplest to most difficult.
requirements: Instructional materials sequenced so learners can project from one linguistic context with available data to another without data
constraints: The model's applicability rests on structures entering into implicational markedness relations
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of grammatical subsystems such as relativization
examples: Zobl's studies of the acquisition of English possessive determiners generally supported the projection model
key_sources: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287

article_title: Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Castro-Alonso, J. C., Wong, R. M., Adesope, O. O., & Paas, F. (2021). Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09587-1
title: Prefer simpler 2D pedagogical agents over 3D agents in multimedia learning environments
description: Because the meta-analysis found that 2D agents (g+ = 0.38) tended to be more effective than 3D agents (g+ = 0.11), consistent with the redundancy effect and the coherence principle, designers of multimedia learning environments should default to simpler 2D on-screen characters rather than more elaborate 3D ones. The article's own conclusion is that "students may be able to learn similarly from different types of agents", so the recommendation is a conservative default, not a claim that 3D agents harm learning.
requirements: A multimedia learning environment in which an on-screen pedagogical agent is used to support learning.
constraints: The supporting difference is hedged as a tendency, and the article notes students may learn similarly from different types of agents; 3D agents are not shown to be harmful.
target_learning_goals: Multimedia learning outcomes
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 32 effect sizes and compared 2D versus 3D agent conditions, finding g+ = 0.38 versus g+ = 0.11.
key_sources: Castro-Alonso, J. C., Wong, R. M., Adesope, O. O., & Paas, F. (2021). Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09587-1

article_title: Practice perspectives in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Practice perspectives in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9065-9
title: Practice perspective in CSCL research
description: The practice perspective holds that CSCL research should attend to how people actually interact in dyads and small groups rather than only to controlled variables. It draws on the 'practice turn' in contemporary theory, where focus shifted to 'practices as embodied, materially mediated arrays of human activity centrally organized around shared practical understanding'. The editorial applies it at individual, group, and community levels of description.
requirements: Powerful theories and analytical approaches are required to study practices reflectively
constraints: Practices are not commonly described in terms of regularity among controlled variables
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building
examples: The editorial introduces a special issue of ijCSCL whose articles analyze the role of practices in CSCL at individual, group, and community levels.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Practice perspectives in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9065-9

article_title: From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y
title: Biologically primary versus biologically secondary knowledge distinction
description: Drawing on Geary's evolutionary educational psychology, the article distinguishes knowledge we evolved to acquire (primary, modular, acquired 'easily, unconsciously, and without explicit instruction', including generic-cognitive skills like problem solving and communication) from biologically secondary skills such as reading, mathematics, and computer use, which are domain-specific, acquired consciously with effort, and require explicit instruction. Primary knowledge is used to leverage acquisition of secondary knowledge, so collaboration, being biologically primary, may under some circumstances improve acquisition of secondary knowledge.
requirements: Biologically secondary skills require explicit instruction and considerable effort to acquire
constraints: Most generic-cognitive skills such as problem-solving, planning, or generalising are biologically primary and not the appropriate target of formal instruction
target_learners: learners in education and training institutions
target_learning_goals: domain-specific biologically secondary knowledge
examples: The article notes learning the French word-pair for cat does not interact with the word-pair for dog, while writing sentences in French involves interacting elements
key_sources: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y

article_title: Different technologies, methodologies and epistemologies—is CSCL a community or communities?
citation: Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rose, Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen. (2018). Different technologies, methodologies and epistemologies—is CSCL a community or communities? Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9280-3
title: Support theoretical and methodological diversity in CSCL and use squib-format venues to foster productive multivocality
description: The editors hold that CSCL as a field advances through multivocal conversations and debates rather than a single framework. They write that "theoretical and methodological diversity are essential to advances in CSCL" and that co-habitation of different approaches should stimulate debate. The journal's squib format was created specifically "to serve as a venue for scholarly interactions to achieve productive multivocality and avoid co-alienation".
requirements: Venues that publish quality- and rigor-grounded work regardless of theoretical grounds, plus debate formats such as squibs, to carry disagreements forward
constraints: The editorial cautions against a single comprehensive framework as the assumed goal; Rummel's proposed "kernel" taxonomy is treated as one conversation move rather than a resolution
target_learners: CSCL researchers and the learning sciences community
target_learning_goals: advancing the field of computer-supported collaborative learning through scholarly dialogue
examples: This editorial uses the four issue papers to map competing positions on Wise and Schwarz's provocations (e.g., learner agency vs. scripting, SparkNotes of orchestration vs. emergence) rather than adjudicating a winner
key_sources: Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rose, Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen. (2018). Different technologies, methodologies and epistemologies—is CSCL a community or communities? Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9280-3

article_title: Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments
citation: Peter Holtz & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress. (2018). Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9285-y
title: Productive friction: socio-cognitive conflicts resolved productively drive learning and knowledge construction
description: The article defines productive friction, adapted from organization science, as "the process of overcoming obstacles in a productive way that, in turn, leads to individual learning and collaborative knowledge construction." It uses the term broadly for discrepancies between individuals' thoughts, values, and attitudes, or between an individual's schemas and a group's view, that can be resolved so as to foster epistemic growth. Building on Piaget's socio-cognitive conflict, the article applies the concept to large-scale mass collaboration, arguing that too little friction limits learning while too much risks polarization or community rift.
requirements: Resolution of discrepancies must occur in a way that productively fosters epistemic growth rather than ignoring ideas or splitting the community
constraints: If friction is too low, chances for learning are limited; if too high on the individual level, learners will most likely fail to adapt; too much friction at the social level can lead to ignored ideas or a rift in the community
target_learners: individual contributors in large-scale online collaboration environments such as Wikipedia
target_learning_goals: individual learning and collaborative knowledge construction through resolving socio-cognitive conflicts
examples: The article operationalizes friction in Wikipedia as the difference between an author's and an article's view, betweenness scores of boundary-spanning articles, and editors contributing to articles representing opinions other than their own
key_sources: Peter Holtz & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress. (2018). Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9285-y

article_title: Data to decision-making: how elementary students use their Community and Citizen Science project to reimagine their school campus
citation: Erin Bridges Bird · Heidi L. Ballard · Margaret Harte. (2023). Data to decision-making: how elementary students use their Community and Citizen Science project to reimagine their school campus. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09612-6
title: Problem-posing spaces: four socio-ecological themes students pursued in a campus bird-monitoring CCS project
description: Problem-posing spaces, adapted from Freire, are figurative spaces that stimulate critical questioning and action. In this study they were "the four main themes or 'problem-posing spaces' we identified as key areas that student-ornithologists pursued through discussion and investigations": (1) predator-prey relations, (2) "who belongs" (native/non-native status and which birds "should" be present), (3) bird diets (trash, Hot Cheetos, sugar water, and the seagull named Jeff), and (4) the Bird Sanctuary. They are not bound to a single issue or location.
requirements: Educators should identify and surface student-generated socio-ecological questions as recurring investigation themes
constraints: They are not necessarily bound by a particular environmental issue or physical location
target_learners: elementary students in school-based CCS projects
target_learning_goals: critical questioning of socio-ecological issues
environmental problem identification
examples: Students debated House Sparrow "overpopulation", classified species by range rather than native status (Candice), and acted on bird diets by telling Kindergarteners to put trash in the trash can and considering lids on trashcans
key_sources: Erin Bridges Bird · Heidi L. Ballard · Margaret Harte. (2023). Data to decision-making: how elementary students use their Community and Citizen Science project to reimagine their school campus. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09612-6

article_title: Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers’ video analysis
citation: Meg Farrell, Monika Martin, Ricardo Böheim, Alexander Renkl, Werner Rieß, Karen D. Könings, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer, Tina Seidel. (2024). Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers' video analysis. Instructional Science (2024) 52:879–917. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09662-y
title: Professional vision conceptualized and operationalized as noticing plus reasoning components
description: The article defines professional vision, with overlap to the teacher-noticing construct, as two trainable components. "The noticing component of professional vision involves the attention allocation and selection of teaching and learning events, relevant for the given learning goals in the respective context" and is operationalized via description skills; the reasoning component is assessed through interpretations, including "cause-and-effect explanations, predictions of cognitive/motivational learning consequences" (Santagata et al., 2007; Schäfer & Seidel, 2015, as cited). The study measures each component with a scaled qualitative coding scheme.
requirements: eliciting learners' noticing reflectively, "with oral or written accounts of what was selected by the observer"
constraints: the article notes terminology varies across the literature, "e.g., noticing, noticing focus, attending/perceiving, describing" (Chan et al., 2021; Santagata et al., 2021, as cited)
target_learning_goals: describing and interpreting relevant teaching and learning events with knowledge-based reasoning
examples: Pretest and posttest video-analysis responses were scored 0-3 per noticed event on description and interpretation components.
key_sources: Meg Farrell, Monika Martin, Ricardo Böheim, Alexander Renkl, Werner Rieß, Karen D. Könings, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer, Tina Seidel. (2024). Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers' video analysis. Instructional Science (2024) 52:879–917. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09662-y

article_title: Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld
citation: Lajoie, S. P., Lavigne, N. C., Guerrera, C., & Munsie, S. D. (2001). Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld. Instructional Science, 29(2), 155-186. http://www.jstor.org/stable/41953546
title: Allow students working alone in inquiry environments to pursue their own hypotheses, including unlikely ones
description: In the BioWorld-alone condition students generated their own hypotheses and "would pursue differential hypotheses in that they collected information on more than one hypothesis at a time", whereas coached students were sometimes thwarted from following hypotheses perceived as unlikely. The authors caution that coaches' redirections prevent wrong paths "However, there may be times that such explorations allow students to build their own conceptual understandings of the problem case". Coaches should therefore weigh closing the problem space against preserving exploratory learning.
requirements: An environment rich enough (e.g., an on-line library) that students working without a coach can find information and clarify misconceptions themselves
constraints: In the alone condition students initially spent time on insignificant details and did not use the on-line consult button; the trade-off with efficiency is stated, not resolved
target_learners: high school biology students working collaboratively
target_learning_goals: hypothesis generation and scientific inquiry
conceptual understanding built through own exploration
examples: A teacher deflected a student's cirrhosis hypothesis by noting the patient had no drinking problem, and the graduate student similarly ruled out cirrhosis for a baby, cutting off that exploration
key_sources: Lajoie, S. P., Lavigne, N. C., Guerrera, C., & Munsie, S. D. (2001). Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld. Instructional Science, 29(2), 155-186. http://www.jstor.org/stable/41953546

article_title: The Relationship Between Tutoring Mode and Learners’ use of Help Tools in Distance Education
citation: Bruno De Lièvre, Christian Depover & Pierre Dillenbourg. (2006). The relationship between tutoring mode and learners' use of help tools in distance education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-6076-4
title: Proactivity intensifies the effect of a help tool's intrinsic qualities: contextualisation and ease of use matter
description: The article argues that learners are not always compliant with tutor promptings; their spontaneous use "seems to be linked to two characteristics of the tool: the contextualisation of help and its ease of use." Metacognitive help, which delivered information updated to the learner's progress, was much more contextualised than tools requiring learners to select information from an index. A given tutoring mode can only affect help use if the tools themselves have the necessary intrinsic quality.
requirements: Help tools must possess intrinsic quality — contextualisation to the learner's current difficulty and ease of access to information — for tutoring mode to influence their use
constraints: Tools requiring learners to identify relevant information on their own initiative were scarcely used without prompting
target_learners: distance education learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: spontaneous, self-initiated use of help resources
examples: Metacognitive help displayed answers given since the beginning of the session, making it more contextualised than the glossary or conceptual help, which required index or heading navigation
key_sources: Bruno De Lièvre, Christian Depover & Pierre Dillenbourg. (2006). The relationship between tutoring mode and learners' use of help tools in distance education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-6076-4

article_title: Productive failure in learning from generation and invention activities
citation: Manu Kapur, Nikol Rummel. (2012). Productive failure in learning from generation and invention activities. Instr Sci 40:645-650. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9235-4
title: Productive failure: a two-phase instructional design of generation followed by consolidation
description: Productive failure designs instruction that may not maximize short-term performance but maximizes longer-term learning. It involves "a generation (or invention) phase followed by a consolidation (or instruction) phase": the generation phase lets students explore affordances and constraints of multiple representations and solution methods on novel problems, and the consolidation phase assembles student-generated RSMs into canonical ones. The special issue consolidates research on this design.
requirements: Generation tasks on novel concepts for which students possess relevant prior skills and knowledge they can apply even without canonical knowledge
constraints: The authors state PF work is still in its infancy and the concept remains largely underdetermined and under-researched
target_learning_goals: canonical concepts in mathematics and statistics, e.g. variance
conceptual understanding and transfer
examples: The four constituent studies applied PF to variance (Kapur), mathematical analysis relearning (Westermann and Rummel), uncertainty in best-fit line slopes (Roll et al.), and variance invention tasks (Wiedmann et al.)
key_sources: Manu Kapur, Nikol Rummel. (2012). Productive failure in learning from generation and invention activities. Instr Sci 40:645-650. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9235-4

article_title: Effects of person praise on students’ motivation and performance under ego-involving and task-involving feedback conditions
citation: Cheng-Hong Liu, Xian-Rui Yin. (2026). Effects of person praise on students' motivation and performance under ego-involving and task-involving feedback conditions. Instructional Science (2026) 54:34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09789-0
title: Avoid pre-task person praise for tasks with anticipated task-involving feedback; it is a strategic option only when ego-involving feedback (public comparison) is expected
description: The article offers educators a decision rule grounded in its experiment: when the anticipated feedback is ego-involving and competitive, praising students' qualities before a new task may raise participation motivation, but "if a task is likely to employ task-involving feedback, which emphasizes student learning and improvement (e.g., learning tasks in classrooms), praising students' qualities should likely be avoided" because it activates a distraction mechanism. Teachers should nonetheless prioritize task-involving feedback generally, since students were more motivated under it.
requirements: Apply only to praise given before task engagement combined with anticipated feedback structure, not to post-task praise or feedback content
constraints: Findings come from one task (subtle difference detection) with Taiwanese junior high students; the praise used targeted personality, not ability; results should not be extrapolated to praise or feedback given after task completion
target_learners: junior high school students facing a new learning task
target_learning_goals: engagement and participation motivation in a new task
task performance
examples: In the experiment, pre-task person praise before a 5-minute subtle difference detection task reduced trials attempted under expected teacher comments but increased trials under expected score-and-ranking lists
key_sources: Cheng-Hong Liu, Xian-Rui Yin. (2026). Effects of person praise on students' motivation and performance under ego-involving and task-involving feedback conditions. Instructional Science (2026) 54:34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09789-0

article_title: Effects of problem-based discussion on studying a subsequent text: A randomized trial among first year medical students
citation: W.S. de Grave, H.G. Schmidt & H.P.A. Boshuizen. (2001). Effects of problem-based discussion on studying a subsequent text: A randomized trial among first year medical students. Instructional Science 29: 33-44. https://link.springer.com/journal/11251
title: Activate prior knowledge through small-group problem discussion before assigning a text to study
description: Because discussing a relevant problem before individual study improved recall of the text in this randomized trial, the article supports the practice of having small tutorial groups analyze and brainstorm explanations for a problem that relates to a subsequently assigned expository text. The discussion procedure used problem definition, a 30-minute brainstorming session, and tutor summaries on a flip-chart, with tutors giving no clues about correctness. The authors conclude that "it is the opportunity for problem-based elaboration on existing knowledge, prior to studying a relevant text, that is responsible for the strong effect demonstrated".
requirements: The problem discussed must be relevant to the text topic
Students should have prior experience with problem-based tutorial work
Tutors must not give clues revealing whether statements are correct or relevant
constraints: Demonstrated with first-year medical students at a single European problem-based medical school; effects measured immediately after study, which the authors say may underestimate true learning effects
target_learning_goals: comprehension and retention of expository texts
examples: Students first defined the 'Stinging incident' problem in 5 minutes, then brainstormed explanations for 30 minutes, then studied a 10-page blood pressure regulation text for 30 minutes.
key_sources: W.S. de Grave, H.G. Schmidt & H.P.A. Boshuizen. (2001). Effects of problem-based discussion on studying a subsequent text: A randomized trial among first year medical students. Instructional Science 29: 33-44. https://link.springer.com/journal/11251

article_title: The effects of constructivist learning environments: a commentary
citation: Remy M. J. P. Rikers, Tamara van Gog, Fred Paas. (2008). The effects of constructivist learning environments: a commentary. Instr Sci (2008) 36:463–467. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9067-4
title: Effective instruction blends practices from different theoretical perspectives rather than forcing a constructivist/direct-instruction dichotomy
description: The commentary endorses the Harris, Santangelo, and Graham position that effective instruction is not a forced choice between theoretical camps. It quotes their view that instruction should be "a thoughtful, pragmatic blending of practices based on evidence gained from various perspectives and lines of research". The commentary agrees and notes SRSD may not even count as constructivist, yet its evidence base justifies its use. This mirrors the finding that deep processing does not necessarily exclude stepwise processing such as memorization and rehearsal.
requirements: Practices should be selected on evidence gained from research rather than on adherence to a single theoretical perspective.
target_learning_goals: writing skills
deep and meaningful learning
examples: The commentary endorses Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) as a pragmatic instructional approach with substantial empirical evidence, even though some would argue it is not a constructivist learning environment.
key_sources: Remy M. J. P. Rikers, Tamara van Gog, Fred Paas. (2008). The effects of constructivist learning environments: a commentary. Instr Sci (2008) 36:463–467. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9067-4

article_title: Investigating students’ perceived authenticity of learning activities in an out-of-school lab for social sciences: a replication study
citation: Valentina Nachtigall, Nikol Rummel. (2021). Investigating students' perceived authenticity of learning activities in an out-of-school lab for social sciences: a replication study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09556-3
title: Productive Failure as an authentic learning activity that emulates scientific inquiry
description: The article characterizes PF as highly authentic because it mirrors how scientists work: "In PF, students are asked to explore solutions to a complex problem before they have to falsify their solutions during instruction." Failure, struggle and falsifying conjectures parallel scientific practice, and PF fulfills the features of authentic learning activities (complex problem, open inquiry, collaboration, independent working). By contrast, DI is characterized as less authentic, promoting a view of scientific inquiry as an application of instructions.
requirements: An initial problem-solving phase before instruction, with collaborative exploration without instructional support
constraints: The empirical test found no effect of PF vs. DI on perceived authenticity or situational interest in this OSL context
target_learners: secondary school students in out-of-school labs
target_learning_goals: understanding scientific practices such as evaluating causal versus correlational evidence
examples: Both conditions used the same violence-in-media problem and published studies as materials; only the sequence of problem solving and instruction differed
key_sources: Valentina Nachtigall, Nikol Rummel. (2021). Investigating students' perceived authenticity of learning activities in an out-of-school lab for social sciences: a replication study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09556-3

article_title: Relevant prior knowledge moderates the effect of elaboration during small group discussion on academic achievement
citation: Floris M. Van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. Van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2013). Relevant prior knowledge moderates the effect of elaboration during small group discussion on academic achievement. Instructional Science, 41, 729-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9252-3
title: Provide students with some relevant prior knowledge before they enter a problem-based discussion, because lacking it may be detrimental for future learning
description: The article's implication for practice is that collaborative problem-based discussions should be matched to students' prior knowledge: "it may be important to provide students with some relevant prior knowledge before they enter the discussion." The experiment showed elaboration helped only when relevant prior knowledge was present and impeded recall when it was absent. The information given beforehand should consist of loose concepts that students connect themselves during the discussion.
requirements: The pre-discussion information should only contain loose concepts, since students need to generate new connections between these concepts themselves during the discussion
constraints: Lacking some basic level of relevant prior knowledge may actually be detrimental for future learning, as the present results indicate
target_learners: undergraduate and secondary students in problem-based or small-group learning
target_learning_goals: recall of information studied after a problem-based discussion
examples: In the experiment, half the participants studied 21 thunder-and-lightning sentences before the discussion while the other half studied seismographic sentences; only the relevant sentences supported later recall
key_sources: Floris M. Van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. Van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2013). Relevant prior knowledge moderates the effect of elaboration during small group discussion on academic achievement. Instructional Science, 41, 729-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9252-3

article_title: Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling
citation: Idit Adler · Saja Rabie. (2026). Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling. Instructional Science (2026) 54:36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09785-4
title: Pragmatic constructionism: an epistemological framework for interdisciplinary understanding with four core cognitive processes
description: Boix Mansilla's pragmatic constructionism, adopted as this study's analytical framework, centers interdisciplinary learning on "purposeful, pluralist, and provisional understandings". It defines interdisciplinary learning as integrating information, data, techniques, tools, perspectives, ideas, concepts and theories from two or more disciplines to create products, explain phenomena, or solve problems in ways unlikely through single-disciplinary means. Learners engage in four dynamically interacting cognitive processes: establishing a purpose; weighing disciplinary insights; building and leveraging integrations; and maintaining a critical stance. The study used this framework to operationalize and code students' discourse.
requirements: Learners bring prior disciplinary knowledge, which informs questions, affords hypotheses, and provides an initial representation of the problem
constraints: The four processes interact dynamically and inform one another as learning progresses iteratively, so they are not sequential stages
target_learners: k-12 learners integrating two or more disciplines
target_learning_goals: interdisciplinary understanding
integration of disciplinary perspectives
examples: The study coded multidisciplinary group discourse against operationalizations of the four processes, e.g., identifying ways to connect the disciplines for establishing purpose and sharing expertise for weighing disciplinary insights
key_sources: Idit Adler · Saja Rabie. (2026). Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling. Instructional Science (2026) 54:36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09785-4

article_title: Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others
citation: Floris M. van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2011). Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others. Instructional Science 39, 189–204. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9124-7
title: Have students actively provide explanations during small-group discussion to support long-term retention
description: When organizing small-group discussion, design activities so that students verbally explain content to others rather than only listening. The article concludes that "providing explanations as well as listening to others during a small group discussion benefit short-term recall, while producing explanations increases retention of knowledge during 1 month". The mechanism proposed is that explaining requires students to structure or restructure their knowledge before verbalizing it, which fosters elaboration and resists forgetting.
requirements: Participants need relevant prior knowledge (gained here from a pre-experiment instruction text) to draw on when explaining
constraints: The long-term advantage of explaining over listening emerged only at the one-month measurement, not immediately; the study used a simulated video discussion, and the authors call for future experiments to minimize discrepancies with real discussions
target_learners: undergraduate students in small-group or problem-based learning
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied subject matter
examples: In the experiment, participants in the explanation condition were instructed to explain as much as possible, answering actors' questions during gaps in the edited video
key_sources: Floris M. van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2011). Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others. Instructional Science 39, 189–204. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9124-7

article_title: Problem based learning: Cognitive and metacognitive processes during problem analysis
citation: de Grave, W. S., Boshuizen, H. & Schmidt, H. (1996). Problem based learning: Cognitive and metacognitive processes during problem analysis. Instructional Science: An International Journal of Learning and Cognition, 24(5), 321–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00118111
title: Problem analysis as a key phase of problem-based learning involving cognitive and metacognitive processes
description: The article frames problem analysis as "an important phase of problem based learning in a tutorial group," during which cognitive and metacognitive processes unfold. These processes are only partially expressed in the group's verbal interaction, which concerns mainly theory building, while stimulated recall exposes hypothesis evaluation, meta-reasoning, and conceptual change when students confront anomalous data.
requirements: A tutorial group setting in which problem analysis is carried out through verbal interaction among group members.
target_learners: students in problem-based learning tutorial groups
target_learning_goals: conceptual change
theory building
metacognitive reasoning
examples: The study investigated whether PBL leads to conceptual change by analysing verbal communication and stimulated recall during problem analysis in a tutorial group.
key_sources: de Grave, W. S., Boshuizen, H. & Schmidt, H. (1996). Problem based learning: Cognitive and metacognitive processes during problem analysis. Instructional Science: An International Journal of Learning and Cognition, 24(5), 321–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00118111

article_title: Designing a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG
citation: Dillenbourg, P. (1989). The design of a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG. Instructional Science, 18(3), 193–216. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00053359
title: PROTO-TEG: a self-improving tutor for geometry
description: PROTO-TEG is a tutoring system for geometry described in this article as "a self-improving tutor in geometry". It holds a set of didactic strategies and maintains a student model; its distinctive feature is a self-improving function that discovers, from its own recorded tutoring episodes, criteria for choosing among those strategies. The system was built to test whether an ITS could acquire its own strategy-selection knowledge rather than having it fully hand-coded.
requirements: A set of didactic strategies available for selection
A student model whose states can be recorded during tutoring episodes
constraints: Domain of application described is geometry
target_learning_goals: geometry learning
examples: The article reports an empirical experiment in which the system's self-improving functions were assessed and conditions were discovered for five of the nine didactic strategies
key_sources: Dillenbourg, P. (1989). The design of a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG. Instructional Science, 18(3), 193–216. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00053359

article_title: Does musical training improve school performance?
citation: Olive Emil Wetter, Fritz Koerner, Adrian Schwaninger. (2009). Does musical training improve school performance? Instr Sci 37:365–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9052-y
title: Promote an early beginning of musical training for children to take advantage of a period of high brain plasticity
description: The authors recommend starting musical training early in childhood, reasoning that musical practice during brain maturation induces structural and functional brain changes with broad implications. They cite evidence that "an introduction to musical training earlier than age 7 is crucial to the development of brain structures" and conclude "it makes sense to take advantage of this period of high brain plasticity". The recommendation extends their finding that continuous musical training accompanies maintained school performance.
requirements: Musical training must be continuous over years to be associated with maintained school performance in this study's data
constraints: The study's retrospective non-randomized design does not allow causal inferences about training effects
target_learners: Children in primary school grades 3–6, with training ideally beginning before age 7
target_learning_goals: General school performance across intellectual subjects
Cognitive and intellectual development
examples: In the study, children with continuous musical training maintained high overall marks from grade 3 to 6 while controls' marks declined significantly
key_sources: Olive Emil Wetter, Fritz Koerner, Adrian Schwaninger. (2009). Does musical training improve school performance? Instr Sci 37:365–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9052-y

article_title: Problem-solving before instruction for learning linear algebra in university mathematics
citation: Baumgartner, V., Daguati, S., Trninic, D., Akveld, M., Caspar, A., Hungerbühler, N., Kapur, M. (2025). Problem-solving before instruction for learning linear algebra in university mathematics. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09709-8
title: Productive failure as a two-phase design with four core learning mechanisms, with PS-I as a subset of preparation for future learning
description: The article describes productive failure (PF) as "a two-phase learning design" comprising a problem-solving phase and an instruction phase, embodying four core learning mechanisms: activation and differentiation of prior knowledge, attention to critical features, explanation and elaboration, and organisation and assembly. It situates PS-I and PF within a family of reversed-order designs in which "PS-I learning designs are a subset of PFL and PF learning designs are in turn a subset of PS-I designs". The CID framework is used to explain how intermediate knowledge from Phase 1 serves as prior knowledge for Phase 2.
requirements: Phase 1 problems must activate and differentiate prior knowledge and allow recognition of critical features so that Phase 2 elaboration and assembly can consolidate discoveries
constraints: If the problem-solving materials fail to trigger activation and critical-feature recognition, the second-phase mechanisms do not have their desired effects
target_learners: university students in introductory mathematics and STEM courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of targeted mathematical concepts
transfer
examples: The study's ten preparatory exercise sheets were designed to trigger activation of prior knowledge and recognition of critical features, e.g. seven contrasting cases of linear systems of equations before instruction on the rank of matrices
key_sources: Baumgartner, V., Daguati, S., Trninic, D., Akveld, M., Caspar, A., Hungerbühler, N., Kapur, M. (2025). Problem-solving before instruction for learning linear algebra in university mathematics. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09709-8

article_title: Effects of a homework implementation method (MITCA) on self-regulation of learning
citation: Tania Vieites, Eleftheria Gonida, Fátima Díaz-Freire, Susana Rodríguez, Antonio Valle. (2024). Effects of a homework implementation method (MITCA) on self-regulation of learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09376-z
title: Prescribe homework following MITCA's premises to support students' self-regulatory skills
description: The article recommends that teachers design homework as varied, specific, worthwhile, weekly and evaluated tasks rather than repetitive traditional assignments. It concludes that "if educators prescribe homework following MITCA's premises and guidelines, students will be better supported to improve their self-regulatory skills, especially those related to environmental management." Diversifying tasks and highlighting their usefulness is said to predispose learners to commit to homework, while weekly assignment with student-set time slots supports time awareness and informative correction dampens procrastination.
requirements: Teachers must be trained to prescribe homework in accordance with the framework of self-regulated learning
constraints: The study was a convenience sample in Galicia with self-report measures only and no follow-up data
target_learners: Primary school students, especially 5th and 6th graders
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation of learning
time and environment management
reduced self-regulatory deficits
examples: Trained experimental-group teachers prescribed MITCA homework weekly for twelve weeks in Spanish language, Galician language and mathematics, with weekly online monitoring of task completion and correction
key_sources: Tania Vieites, Eleftheria Gonida, Fátima Díaz-Freire, Susana Rodríguez, Antonio Valle. (2024). Effects of a homework implementation method (MITCA) on self-regulation of learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09376-z

article_title: The role of metacognition in monitoring performance and regulating learning in early readers
citation: Ioanna Taouki, Marie Lallier, David Soto. (2022). The role of metacognition in monitoring performance and regulating learning in early readers. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09293-1
title: Procedural metacognition as object-level/meta-level monitoring and control
description: The article adopts a procedural metacognition framework in which online task performance is mediated by an interaction between an object-level process (the type-1 task, e.g., reading or perceptual decisions) and a second-order meta-level process (type-2 performance). The meta-level "monitors the first-order process" and, when cognition fails, exerts control processes to promote adaptive behaviour; these are termed metacognitive monitoring and metacognitive control. The study operationalises monitoring via trial-by-trial binary confidence judgments and signal-detection-theory estimates of metacognitive efficiency (meta-d'/d').
requirements: Trial-by-trial confidence ratings collected alongside type-1 responses, with type-1 signal accessible to the child for type-2 judgments
constraints: Metacognitive efficiency estimates can be affected by task difficulty; the M-ratio controls for type-1 performance and difficulty
Young children show overconfidence bias, motivating bias-free SDT measures
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring of task performance
orthographic lexical processing and visual word recognition
examples: Children rated confidence on each trial of VA span, statistical learning, lexical decision and emotion recognition tasks using a two-point scale (doubtful vs sure)
key_sources: Ioanna Taouki, Marie Lallier, David Soto. (2022). The role of metacognition in monitoring performance and regulating learning in early readers. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09292-0

article_title: Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing
citation: Chenghui Chen, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09435-z
title: Attend to monitoring of interactive metadiscourse during writing, since it is the strongest predictor of L2 argumentative writing performance
description: Because monitoring of interactive metadiscourse showed the strongest predictive power for L2 argumentative writing performance, writing instruction should give particular attention to real-time monitoring of metadiscourse use, guiding students to check how interactive metadiscourse devices guide readers through the text while writing. The authors note students "are not fully aware of the importance of pre-writing planning and post-writing revisions/reflection", suggesting instruction should also strengthen planning and evaluating.
requirements: Instruction must address all three regulation strategies, since PIM and EIM were also significant positive predictors
constraints: The predictive hierarchy comes from one regression study with Chinese first-year university students; the authors' explanation for the difference is speculative, drawn from teaching experience
target_learning_goals: L2 argumentative writing performance
examples: The regression showed MIM (β = 0.344) predicting writing performance more strongly than PIM (β = 0.115) and EIM (β = 0.179)
key_sources: Chenghui Chen, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09435-z

article_title: Conditions for Effective Learning from Erroneous Examples: A Systematic Review
citation: Sonja Dieterich, Stefan Rumann, Marc Rodemer. (2025). Conditions for Effective Learning from Erroneous Examples: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10071-x
title: Use contrasting erroneous examples rather than erroneous examples alone when the goal is comparing incorrect and correct solutions
description: The review's synthesis indicates that contrasting erroneous examples, which pair incorrect with correct solutions, were more often the beneficial condition than correct examples or problem-solving, and sometimes equally or more effective than erroneous examples alone. It states that "contrasting erroneous examples are more often effective than correct exam- ples and problem-solving and are sometimes equally or even more effective than erroneous examples". Designers should therefore prefer explicit contrasts when learners are not expected to correct errors unaided.
requirements: Errors must be explicitly paired with correct solutions, either of the same problem or a different one
constraints: Evidence on the comparison between contrasting erroneous examples and erroneous examples is contradictory, especially regarding prior knowledge, cognitive load, and long-term effects
target_learners: school students in grades two to eleven
target_learning_goals: distinguishing correct from incorrect solution approaches
conceptual and procedural knowledge
examples: In Corral and Carpenter (2020), Con-ErrEx learned significantly more than CorrEx and ErrEx for classification questions, while for application questions ErrEx and Con-ErrEx enhanced learning equally
key_sources: Sonja Dieterich, Stefan Rumann, Marc Rodemer. (2025). Conditions for Effective Learning from Erroneous Examples: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10071-x

article_title: Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7
title: Biologically primary versus biologically secondary knowledge distinction in evolutionary educational psychology
description: Evolutionary educational psychology distinguishes two types of human knowledge based on evolutionary origins. Biologically primary knowledge is acquired "early in life, implicitly and unintentionally", requires no working memory resources, and is encoded directly into long-term memory. Biologically secondary knowledge is culture-specific, slow to acquire, heavily dependent on conscious effortful working memory processing, and not naturally motivating. The paper notes that instructional design principles and cognitive load theory recommendations "are mostly related to learning of biologically secondary/explicit types of knowledge".
requirements: Secondary knowledge acquisition requires conscious, explicit, and effortful processes in working memory
constraints: The paper notes primary knowledge and type 1 dual-process mechanisms could not be equated, since reading skills represent type 1 mechanisms for many adults even though they belong to secondary knowledge
target_learning_goals: acquisition of scientific knowledge, literacy and numeracy as biologically secondary knowledge
examples: Listening to and speaking a native language are cited as primary knowledge; writing, reading skills and scientific knowledge as secondary
key_sources: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7

article_title: Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7
title: Design pre-instructional activities that motivate and engage learners before secondary-knowledge instruction
