description: Because formal learning focuses on biologically secondary knowledge requiring conscious working memory processing, the explicit intention to learn principle implies that "every learning task needs to be associated with specific activities aimed at setting the learner's explicit intention to acquire this secondary information". These pre-instructional activities aim to externally motivate and engage learners, trigger curiosity, establish knowledge gaps, or activate relevant knowledge, preparing learners for the following instructional goals.
requirements: Learner activities intentionally designed to get learners motivated for and engaged in learning prior to acquiring the targeted secondary knowledge
constraints: For experts, additional activities designed to foster motivation and engagement could inhibit performance, per the paper's predicted expertise reversal
target_learners: novice learners in formal educational settings
target_learning_goals: preparation and motivation for acquiring biologically secondary knowledge
examples: The paper notes motivating the learner was considered the first step of any instruction by Gagné (1965), and cites productive failure and invention approaches as empirical evidence for exploratory activities achieving pre-instructional goals
key_sources: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7

article_title: A Half Century of Progress in US Student Achievement: Agency and Flynn Effects, Ethnic and SES Differences
citation: M. Danish Shakeel · Paul E. Peterson. (2022). A Half Century of Progress in US Student Achievement: Agency and Flynn Effects, Ethnic and SES Differences. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09657-y
title: Principal-agent framework for interpreting variation in student achievement trend estimates
description: The article applies the principal-agent model from political economy to educational measurement: policymakers (principals) lacking technical expertise delegate trend measurement to survey organizations (agents), risking adverse selection and moral hazard. Because principals hold "ambiguous and not always consistent objectives", agents interpret them distinctively, generating varied trend estimates. The authors use this framework to explain why four agents administering 160 waves of 17 linked surveys produce divergent estimates, and to justify using median rather than mean estimates across surveys.
requirements: Multiple survey agents administering psychometrically linked tests to national probability samples, so medians can be taken across agents
constraints: The framework applies where principals' objectives are unranked or ambiguous, as in a federal system with boundary organizations such as NCES and NAGB
target_learners: US school-age students in cohorts born between 1954 and 2007
target_learning_goals: Tracking cohort progress in mathematics and reading achievement over half a century
examples: The four agents — LTT NAEP, main NAEP, TIMSS-PIRLS, and PISA — each interpret principals' objectives differently: LTT tracks national trends only, NAEP adjusts to changing curricula, TIMSS-PIRLS measures performance against an international curriculum, and PISA measures "preparation for life".
key_sources: M. Danish Shakeel · Paul E. Peterson. (2022). A Half Century of Progress in US Student Achievement: Agency and Flynn Effects, Ethnic and SES Differences. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09657-y

article_title: Evolution of Self-Awareness and the Cultural Emergence of Academic and Non-academic Self-Concepts
citation: Geary, D., Xu, K.M. (2022). Evolution of Self-Awareness and the Cultural Emergence of Academic and Non-academic Self-Concepts. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09669-2
title: Biologically primary versus biologically secondary abilities framework for academic development
description: The article proposes an evolutionary framework distinguishing evolved, biological primary abilities such as spoken language from evolutionarily novel, biologically secondary academic competencies such as reading. Instruction is the mechanism that converts one into the other: "instructional practices modify evolved or biological primary abilities (e.g., spoken language) to create evolutionarily novel or biologically secondary academic competencies (e.g., reading)". The framework grounds the article's account of why academic development requires schooling.
requirements: Formal instruction is needed to build biologically secondary academic competencies from primary abilities
constraints: The framework is a theoretical proposal about evolutionary recency of schooling, not a tested empirical result in this article
target_learning_goals: academic competencies such as reading built from evolved primary abilities
examples: The article contrasts spoken language as a primary ability with reading as a secondary academic competency created by instruction
key_sources: Geary, D., Xu, K.M. (2022). Evolution of Self-Awareness and the Cultural Emergence of Academic and Non-academic Self-Concepts. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09669-2

article_title: Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging
citation: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3
title: Productive disciplinary engagement: a situative framework and four design principles for fostering deep engagement
description: Productive disciplinary engagement (PDE), introduced by Engle and Conant, is both a situative framework for understanding engagement and a set of design principles. Engagement is characterized as "socially rich intellectual discourse, where students make substantive contributions, build on each other's ideas, attend to one another, and work toward advancing shared understanding of disciplinary content." Engagement is productive when students' ideas advance, generate new questions, and reveal confusion. The article treats PDE as central to redefining motivation as socially situated.
requirements: Disciplinary engagement must be both productive (problem-driven inquiry, epistemic agency) and accountable to disciplinary norms
constraints: Few studies have examined these frameworks with systematic attention to motivation
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students in disciplinary classrooms
target_learning_goals: Deep disciplinary engagement and productive discourse
examples: Engle and Conant's analysis of an extended fifth-grade discussion of whether orcas were whales or dolphins, drawn from the Fostering Communities of Learners curriculum
key_sources: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3

article_title: Prediction Versus Explanation in Educational Psychology: a Cross-Theoretical Approach to Using Teacher Behaviour to Predict Student Engagement in Physical Education
citation: Michael Noetel, Philip Parker, Theresa Dicke, Mark R. Beauchamp, Nikos Ntoumanis, Ryan M. Hulteen, et al. (2023). Prediction Versus Explanation in Educational Psychology: a Cross-Theoretical Approach to Using Teacher Behaviour to Predict Student Engagement in Physical Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09786-6
title: Prediction versus explanation as two cultures of statistical modelling in educational psychology
description: The article articulates a framework distinguishing explanatory from predictive statistical modelling. Explanatory approaches build parsimonious, theory-derived models to understand mechanisms, assessing fit on the same data used to build them; by contrast, "the predictive culture does not prioritise explaining the mechanisms underpinning a phenomenon: it instead optimises directly for accuracy on future data". The framework centres on overfitting — where a model predicts training data but fails to generalise — and holds that both approaches are needed, since prediction errors can point to gaps in explanatory models.
requirements: Assessing predictive validity requires data withheld from model building, so studies must reserve held-out test data
constraints: The article notes the approach is arduous if done prospectively, so a pragmatic alternative is quarantining retrospective test data
target_learning_goals: improving the predictive validity of models of student outcomes
examples: The authors applied the framework by training elastic-net models on 70% of their data and testing once on the held-out 30%
key_sources: Michael Noetel, Philip Parker, Theresa Dicke, Mark R. Beauchamp, Nikos Ntoumanis, Ryan M. Hulteen, et al. (2023). Prediction Versus Explanation in Educational Psychology: a Cross-Theoretical Approach to Using Teacher Behaviour to Predict Student Engagement in Physical Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09786-6

article_title: Community, Children, Child: New Directions for Equitable Delivery Of High-Quality Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC)
citation: Bly, S., Houen, S., Staton, S., & Thorpe, K. (2026). Community, Children, Child: New Directions for Equitable Delivery Of High-Quality Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10215-7
title: Proportionate universalism: universal ECEC access with greater intensity of resourcing for services experiencing higher complexity and educator demand
description: The article proposes proportionate universalism (citing Marmot, 2025) as a policy mechanism for equitable ECEC: all children receive access to ECEC services, but services experiencing higher levels of complexity and educator demand receive greater intensity of resourcing. The authors argue that because the distribution of children requiring higher educator support is not equal across communities or levels of disadvantage, moving beyond a single quality standard to equitable resourcing requirements is necessary, and targeted interventions in highly disadvantaged communities provide "strong empirical support for such an approach".
requirements: Measurement to inform resource distribution and placement of targeted programs, such as administrative data on socio-economic distribution or school-entry developmental vulnerability indices
constraints: Geographic-area methods may not capture all children and families who require additional supports, as location of children needing support is not uniformly within low socioeconomic communities
target_learners: Children in ECEC services, especially those in communities experiencing higher levels of complexity and disadvantage
target_learning_goals: Equitable delivery of high-quality, responsive early childhood education that redresses social inequity
examples: The article cites targeted interventions providing intensive supports in ECEC services serving highly disadvantaged communities (e.g., Newman et al., 2022) demonstrating improved equity in child outcomes through provisions and family supports
key_sources: Bly, S., Houen, S., Staton, S., & Thorpe, K. (2026). Community, Children, Child: New Directions for Equitable Delivery Of High-Quality Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10215-7

article_title: Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025)
citation: Eitel, A., Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Schöne, C. (2026). Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025). Educational Psychology Review, 38, 65. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10163-2
title: Assess overall instructional quality at the level of broad predictor constructs rather than individual techniques
description: The predictor-constructs approach evaluates whether instruction is likely 'good enough' by rating overall levels of focus support and reward, rather than tallying individual techniques. The authors argue it is difficult to determine "how many techniques, which combinations, and at what magnitude they need to be applied" because technique effects may interact rather than add up. Experienced researchers, designers, or teachers can expert-rate the two constructs, yielding a testable prediction and a practical heuristic for planning, designing, and evaluating instruction.
requirements: Raters must be familiar with the constructs of focus support and reward and their instantiations such as techniques, effects, and value facets
constraints: The approach complements rather than replaces the technique-focused approach; techniques map to constructs not in a one-to-one fashion
target_learning_goals: overall instructional effectiveness for learning
examples: Expert ratings of instruction with medium-to-high focus support and reward yield the testable prediction of better learning outcomes than instruction rated low on either construct
key_sources: Eitel, A., Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Schöne, C. (2026). Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025). Educational Psychology Review, 38, 65. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10163-2

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: The practicing connections framework: instructional design organized around three connection types and three design principles
description: The practicing connections framework holds that deep understanding in complex domains develops when students repeatedly practice making connections among a domain's contexts and practices, its core concepts, and its key representations. The article states: "we propose three types of connections that should be the focus of instructional design: the world (including practices and contexts); core concepts, which organize the domain; and key representations used for communication and thinking within a domain." It pairs these with three pedagogical principles: making connections explicit, productive struggle, and deliberate practice over time. The framework was developed while designing an online introductory statistics textbook and is offered as a complement to skill-focused frameworks such as 4C/ID.
requirements: Instruction must be designed over long periods such as a semester-long course, since understanding in complex domains develops slowly
A detailed analysis of what expert practice in the domain looks like must precede design decisions
constraints: The authors position the framework as a complement to frameworks such as 4C/ID, which they say apply especially well to complex skills; the framework targets domains requiring reasoning with abstract conceptual structure
target_learners: Novice students in complex academic domains such as statistics, mathematics, and science
target_learning_goals: Deep understanding and transferable knowledge in a complex domain
Adaptive expertise: flexibly applying knowledge in novel contexts
examples: The authors organized their online introductory statistics textbook around three core practices (explore variation, model variation, evaluate and compare models) and three core concepts, repeatedly asking students to translate across five key representations.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: Engage students in productive struggle before presenting explicit connections and solutions
description: The principle holds that connections must be earned through hard work: simply making them explicit is insufficient for deep understanding. The authors design each textbook page with a "struggle first" pedagogy, asking students open-response questions before presenting the information needed for a well-formulated answer. They also remove calculation opportunities, delaying formulas until chapter 5 and using number-free problems so students grapple with concepts rather than rushing to compute, thereby reserving attention for conceptual connections.
requirements: Tasks must be challenging enough that learners work to connect problem features with prior knowledge
Struggle must precede, not follow, the explicit presentation of connections
constraints: The article notes students may resist the sequence, sometimes pointing out that the authors have mistakenly gotten the order wrong
target_learners: US college students in introductory statistics
target_learning_goals: Developing intuitive ideas about models and model comparison
Retaining learning through effortful engagement
examples: Before discussing mean and median, students see a five-point distribution and are asked in what sense each might be the better model; in chapter 4 they compare faceted histograms of restaurant tips across smiley-face conditions without calculating group means.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: Online interactive introductory statistics textbook implementing the practicing connections framework
description: The article's design artifact is an online interactive textbook for introductory statistics developed by the authors, in which the framework's connection types and principles are instantiated. The book is organized around the practice of data analysis (explore variation, model variation, evaluate and compare models), three core concepts, and five key representations, with each page using a "struggle first" pedagogy asking students to answer questions before the relevant information is presented. R is interleaved throughout to reduce extraneous load and free resources for reflecting on connections.
requirements: A description of the world outside the classroom (the practice of data analysis) must be made explicit for textbook authors, students, and instructors
constraints: The article presents the textbook as an illustration of design decisions justified by learning sciences research, not as an evaluated intervention with outcome data
target_learners: College students in introductory statistics courses across multiple academic departments
target_learning_goals: Explaining variation in data through statistical modeling
Developing transferable statistical understanding connected to data science practice
examples: Students are told from the beginning that the goal of statistics is to explain variation in the world, and the textbook continually reminds them where specific skills connect to data scientists' work.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Linguistic Interdependence and the Educational Development of Bilingual Children
citation: Baschek, E. (2022). Using the US standard system for measurement in Germany – Bilingual education in primary school. https://math-primwq-bilingual.sd.uni-frankfurt.de/length-laengen/introduction-einleitung/
title: PrimarWebQuest: an inquiry-oriented, web-based method for using internet sources in bilingual primary lessons
description: PrimarWebQuest is described as "an inquiry-oriented and web-based method for using internet sources" in primary-level lessons. The author positions it as one possible approach for bilingual mathematics classes, noting that "The diversity of the Internet can be a support as there is few materials for many topics". In this project a PrimarWebQuest about lengths was used to familiarise students with the US standard system of measurement, and prior work shows the method can enable dialogues revealing students' understanding of mathematical terms.
requirements: Internet sources and authentic materials on the target topic; the author notes few materials exist for many topics, which the web-based format addresses
constraints: Described for primary level (Primar) use
target_learners: primary school students in bilingual (English-German) mathematics classes
target_learning_goals: mathematical competencies with units of length
linguistic development in the foreign language
intercultural learning about another measurement system
examples: A PrimarWebQuest on lengths (with an online introduction page) was implemented with two small fourth-grade groups to develop ways of converting in and between the metric and US standard systems
key_sources: Baschek, E. (2022). Using the US standard system for measurement in Germany – Bilingual education in primary school. https://math-primwq-bilingual.sd.uni-frankfurt.de/length-laengen/introduction-einleitung/

article_title: Principal Burnout: A Systematic Review
citation: Rogers, L. K., Nguyen, T. D., Timmer, M., & Samson, J. (2025). Principal Burnout: A Systematic Review. Working paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED666666
title: Three-category taxonomy of principal burnout antecedents: environmental, job/organizational, and personal factors
description: The review organizes antecedents of principal burnout into three categories derived from inductive coding of 99 studies: environmental conditions ("pressures and stressors relating to external or societal context, e.g., accountability, the pandemic"), job/organizational conditions (pressures from the particular school, e.g., workload, teacher interactions, parent demands), and personal factors (traits and characteristics such as gender, age, personality, and coping strategies). The authors initially proposed four categories but combined professional and organizational conditions due to difficulty delineating them.
requirements: Studies must empirically examine or hypothesize burnout in relation to at least one antecedent category
constraints: The taxonomy is descriptive and derived from a literature with no causal frameworks; category boundaries between professional and organizational conditions are acknowledged as difficult to delineate
target_learning_goals: understanding causes of principal burnout
informing policies and practices to address principal burnout
examples: The review coded 99 studies and found 67% addressed job/organizational conditions, 12% environmental conditions, and personal factors as the most studied category overall
key_sources: Rogers, L. K., Nguyen, T. D., Timmer, M., & Samson, J. (2025). Principal Burnout: A Systematic Review. Working paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED666666

article_title: The role of social capital for teacher professional learning and student achievement: A systematic literature review
citation: Demir, Ema Kristina. (2021). The Role of Social Capital for Teacher Professional Learning and Student Achievement: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2021.100391
title: PRISMA-guided systematic review corpus of 66 empirical items (2004-2019)
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 66 empirical items on social capital in relation to teachers and teacher professional learning, published between 2004 and 2019. It was "guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Statement, and the Weight of Evidence framework for quality and relevance appraisal." Items entered the final review only after eligibility criteria were applied.
requirements: Eligibility criteria and PRISMA procedures were applied before inclusion; the Weight of Evidence framework was used for quality and relevance appraisal.
target_learning_goals: teacher professional learning
key_sources: Demir, Ema Kristina. (2021). The Role of Social Capital for Teacher Professional Learning and Student Achievement: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2021.100391

article_title: Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review
citation: Boelens, R., De Wever, B., & Voet, M. (2017). Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 22, 1-18. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.06.001
title: Systematic PRISMA-based review corpus of 20 blended learning design studies
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 20 studies on the design of blended learning environments, selected through a staged PRISMA-based procedure. "Starting from 640 sources, 20 studies on the design of blended learning environments were selected through a staged procedure based on the guidelines of the PRISMA statement, using predefined selection criteria." Most studies (n=18) were conducted in higher education contexts, and most (n=15) were intervention studies. Instructional activities were analyzed by two coders, with percent agreement between 74% and 95% across 18 variables.
requirements: Inclusion criteria required blended learning defined as a combination of face-to-face and online interventions, an instructional design point of view at course level, and a detailed description of the design
constraints: Studies focusing on one specific tool, short conference papers, book reviews, and non-English articles were excluded
target_learning_goals: blended course design and development
examples: The Web of Science search in February 2015 with blended/hybrid/flipped learning terms and design-related keywords yielded 496 hits, supplemented by literature suggested in prior reviews
key_sources: Boelens, R., De Wever, B., & Voet, M. (2017). Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 22, 1-18. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.06.001

article_title: Meta-analysis of Interventions for Monitoring Accuracy in Problem Solving
citation: Noortje Janssen · Ard W. Lazonder. (2024). Meta-analysis of Interventions for Monitoring Accuracy in Problem Solving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09936-4
title: For problem-solving tasks, use whole-task, metacognitive knowledge, or external standard interventions and avoid timing interventions
description: This principle guides educators choosing interventions to improve students' monitoring accuracy in problem-solving tasks. The meta-analysis recommends interventions "addressing the whole task, metacognitive knowledge, and external standards" because these significantly improved monitoring accuracy, while advising educators to "refrain from implementing" timing interventions until further research ascertains their effectiveness.
requirements: The intervention must target monitoring accuracy in problem-solving tasks; effectiveness evidence comes from (quasi-)experimental comparisons against untreated or non-monitoring control conditions.
constraints: Timing interventions adversely affected monitoring accuracy in the included studies, though only two studies tested this type.
Caution is needed when generalizing results to educational practice because each study has unique contextual features.
target_learners: Elementary, secondary, and adult students in formal education
target_learning_goals: Accurate monitoring (calibration) of problem-solving performance
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 35 studies in which interventions such as practice problems (whole task), metacognitive questions during the task, and receiving the correct answer after judgment (external standard) were compared with control conditions.
key_sources: Noortje Janssen · Ard W. Lazonder. (2024). Meta-analysis of Interventions for Monitoring Accuracy in Problem Solving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09936-4

article_title: A Systematic Review of Teachers’ Knowledge of Self-Regulated Learning and its Assessment
citation: Yves Karlen · Charlotte Dignath. (2026). A Systematic Review of Teachers' Knowledge of Self-Regulated Learning and its Assessment. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10171-2
title: PRISMA-guided corpus of 33 studies on teachers' knowledge of SRL (1990–2024)
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 33 empirical studies identified through PRISMA-guided searching of nine databases plus citation tracking, from 7,120 initially identified records. Screening was conducted by two independent raters on the Rayyan platform, and coding reached "Cohen's κ = 0.84". Studies span 1990 to 2024, with 28 published after 2014, and cover Europe, North America, Australia, and China, with Germany (n = 9), Switzerland (n = 6), and the United States (n = 5) most frequent.
requirements: Included studies had to report at least one explicit measure of teachers' SRL knowledge with adequate instrument description
Studies had to be set in compulsory education academic subject contexts with pre-service or in-service teachers
constraints: Only peer-reviewed journal articles or doctoral dissertations in English or German were included; the search covers publications up to October 2024
target_learners: pre-service and in-service teachers in compulsory education
target_learning_goals: conceptualization and assessment of teachers' knowledge of self-regulated learning
examples: The PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 2) traces the pathway from 8,207 screened records to 176 full-text assessments and the final 33 included studies
key_sources: Yves Karlen · Charlotte Dignath. (2026). A Systematic Review of Teachers' Knowledge of Self-Regulated Learning and its Assessment. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10171-2

article_title: Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years’ Research
citation: Sébastien Miravete, André Tricot. (2024). Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years' Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09926-6
title: Do not yet integrate general creative skills training into curricula or select for a presumed creative profile
description: Because the evidence for domain-general creativity fails the review's validity conditions — uncontrolled prior knowledge and artificial tasks — the authors advise against, for now, the two educational recommendations they derive from minimalist and maximalist theories: integrating general creativity training into curricula, and selecting students or employees by a general creative profile. They state "it seems premature to recommend the integration of general creative skills into school or training programs, as well as the selection of students or employees with a presumed 'creative profile'".
requirements: Any future adoption of general creativity training or profile-based selection would require studies controlling prior knowledge and using realistic creative tasks
constraints: This is a recommendation against current adoption, not evidence that general creativity training is ineffective; the review's corpus covers only little-c creativity among students
target_learning_goals: creative performance across domains
examples: The review contrasts minimalist educational recommendation 1 (integrate general creativity training) and maximalist recommendation 2 (select by creative profile) and defers both
key_sources: Sébastien Miravete, André Tricot. (2024). Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years' Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09926-6

article_title: Spaced Retrieval Practice Imposes Desirable Difficulty in Calculus Learning
citation: Keith B. Lyle, Campbell R. Bego, Patricia A. S. Ralston, Jason C. Immekus. (2022). Spaced Retrieval Practice Imposes Desirable Difficulty in Calculus Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09677-2
title: Protracted knowledge acquisition account of spacing as desirable difficulty in calculus
description: The authors propose that answering multiple quiz questions gives students opportunities to construct new knowledge, and that spacing "imposed difficulty by protracting the knowledge acquisition process": equivalent knowledge was ultimately acquired in both conditions, as revealed by third-question performance, but the process unfolded over weeks when spaced versus minutes when massed. Drawing on the learning-versus-performance distinction, they suggest spreading acquisition over weeks, while newer objectives were also being learned, offered opportunities to integrate older and newer knowledge into a more cohesive mental model of calculus. This account is distinct from the idea that spacing makes retrieval more effortful.
requirements: The account presupposes practice via multiple quiz questions on the same objective and, in the massed condition, the ability to move back and forth between questions before submitting the quiz
constraints: The authors argue that in this context no amount of retrieval effort would allow students to retrieve knowledge they have not yet acquired, distinguishing the account from retrieval-effort explanations
The account is the authors' interpretation of the practice-phase pattern, not a directly tested mechanism
target_learning_goals: retention of calculus learning objectives such as limits, derivatives, and implicit differentiation
examples: In the spaced condition performance was lowest on the first question, intermediate on the second, and highest on the third, converging with the massed condition once prior practice was equated
key_sources: Keith B. Lyle, Campbell R. Bego, Patricia A. S. Ralston, Jason C. Immekus. (2022). Spaced Retrieval Practice Imposes Desirable Difficulty in Calculus Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09677-2

article_title: Using Primary Knowledge: an Efficient Way To Motivate Students and Promote the Learning of Formal Reasoning
citation: Florence Lespiau, André Tricot. (2019). Using Primary Knowledge: an Efficient Way To Motivate Students and Promote the Learning of Formal Reasoning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09482-4
title: Primary- versus secondary-content syllogism training materials
description: The study's core instructional materials are syllogism training tasks "of unknown content (to reduce the use of prior knowledge)" presented in two framings: primary knowledge ("rules about invented food and animals") and secondary knowledge ("fictitious mathematics and grammar rules"). Students trained with these in order "to best pass a final test", with the training phase either compulsory or left to learners' choice. A third experiment added a priming phase of primary or secondary problems before secondary-only training.
requirements: Content must be unknown to learners to reduce reliance on prior knowledge
constraints: Materials concern formal logical rules (syllogisms) with invented content
target_learning_goals: formal logical reasoning
examples: Two experiments with high school students (n=210) and one with university students (n=227) using these materials across priming, training and final-test phases
key_sources: Florence Lespiau, André Tricot. (2019). Using Primary Knowledge: an Efficient Way To Motivate Students and Promote the Learning of Formal Reasoning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09482-4

article_title: An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load
citation: Joachim Wirth, Ferdinand Stebner, Melanie Trypke, Corinna Schuster, & Detlev Leutner. (2020). An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09568-4
title: Design strategy instruction to move learners from declarative to proceduralized strategy knowledge through repeated practice
description: The article describes how learning strategy interventions typically begin by verbally explaining and demonstrating a strategy, then give learners repeated opportunities to apply it to similar tasks, moving through declarative, knowledge compilation, and procedural phases. As knowledge is proceduralized, conscious interpretation of conceptual and conditional strategy information decreases and the cognitive load of strategy use decreases. This principle follows the article's account of the learning strategy layer.
requirements: Interventions must include phases of skill acquisition as described by Anderson (1982): verbal explanation and demonstration followed by repeated application to different but similar learning tasks
constraints: In the declarative phase, strategy knowledge is conscious and induces cognitive load; the load reduction applies only once knowledge is proceduralized
target_learners: learners acquiring learning strategies across educational levels
target_learning_goals: learning strategy knowledge and use
reducing cognitive load during strategy application
examples: The article describes typical interventions, citing Leopold and Leutner (2015), that start with verbally explaining the strategy and its steps, demonstrating its use, and then giving repeated application opportunities
key_sources: Joachim Wirth, Ferdinand Stebner, Melanie Trypke, Corinna Schuster, & Detlev Leutner. (2020). An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09568-4

article_title: Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: T. Vessonen, M. Dahlberg, H. Hellstrand, A. Widlund, J. Korhonen, P. Aunio, A. Laine. (2024). Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09954-2
title: Design word problem instruction and assessment to be appropriate and progressive based on task demandingness
description: The article recommends that understanding which task characteristics challenge elementary schoolers should shape the design of instruction and assessment. Assessment tools "may be designed to encompass a comprehensive range of different mathematical word problems to understand students' varying performance", and "through understanding how demanding different tasks are, progressive instruction may be designed by simultaneously ensuring that students understand foundational concepts and appropriate strategies for solving more challenging tasks". Instruction should advance in a sequence aligned with students' cognitive capacity.
requirements: Knowledge of the relative demandingness of task characteristics, as provided by the meta-analytic findings
constraints: The article states the findings may guide design and steer future research into interactions among task and individual characteristics; it does not itself test an instructional intervention
target_learners: Elementary school-aged children in Grades 1 to 6
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem-solving
examples: The meta-analysis identified realistic considerations, multiple operations, lexical inconsistency, and first-position unknowns as the characteristics elementary schoolers especially struggle with, informing sequencing decisions
key_sources: T. Vessonen, M. Dahlberg, H. Hellstrand, A. Widlund, J. Korhonen, P. Aunio, A. Laine. (2024). Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09954-2

article_title: Student Teachers’ and Experienced Teachers’ Professional Vision of Students’ Understanding of the Rational Number Concept
citation: Maikki Pouta, Erno Lehtinen & Tuire Palonen. (2020). Student Teachers' and Experienced Teachers' Professional Vision of Students' Understanding of the Rational Number Concept. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09536-y
title: Professional vision as selective attention, knowledge-based reasoning, and decision-making bridging teacher knowledge and practice
description: The article applies a framework in which professional vision in education consists of selective attention and knowledge-based reasoning including "description, explanation and prediction", later expanded to a third interrelated component, decision-making of action. It treats professional vision as "not only an integrated model of a teacher's knowledge but also a system bridging knowledge and practice", developmentally shaped by teachers' knowledge and beliefs and learnable through guided video observation rather than a natural talent.
requirements: Development is strongly guided by teachers' knowledge and beliefs
Execution of decisions demands additional, complex skills beyond noticing
target_learning_goals: noticing and interpreting students' mathematical thinking
instructing students' understanding of fractions
examples: The study coded CRR episodes into descriptive, evaluative and interpretive levels and instruction into supportive versus non-supportive categories to operationalise the framework.
key_sources: Maikki Pouta, Erno Lehtinen & Tuire Palonen. (2020). Student Teachers' and Experienced Teachers' Professional Vision of Students' Understanding of the Rational Number Concept. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09536-y

article_title: Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework
citation: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6
title: Measure utilization of instructional features via process data rather than only comparing learning outcomes
description: The article argues that research focusing only on the direct path—the effect of digital tools on outcomes versus another scenario—allows only limited interpretation. Instead, students' interaction with implemented instructional features (the external behavioral side of learning activities) should be treated as a theoretical and empirical mediator of achievement. The framework treats "process data" as an umbrella term encompassing tool-logged interactions and other process indicators obtained from accompanying assessments during learning.
requirements: A solid theoretical foundation and appropriate indicators inside the process data files to allow differentiated statements about the effects of implemented instructional features
constraints: The article notes the link between behavior and cognition must be established validly; unobtrusive capture of student-tool interactions is named as ongoing future work
target_learners: students in digitally enriched educational settings
target_learning_goals: valid inference about cognitive learning activities from behavioral data
examples: Koedinger et al. (2010) assessed engagement in learning activities by labeling students low or high usage based on items completed in the tool
key_sources: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6

article_title: Does Retrieval Demand Moderate the Effectiveness of Covert Retrieval Practice? Comparing Covert and Overt Retrieval Practice for Learning Key Terms and Definitions
citation: Michelle L. Rivers, Paige E. Northern, Sarah K. Tauber. (2025). Does Retrieval Demand Moderate the Effectiveness of Covert Retrieval Practice? Comparing Covert and Overt Retrieval Practice for Learning Key Terms and Definitions. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10040-4
title: Students should prioritize overt retrieval when mastering complex information such as definitions
description: This principle follows from the article's recommendation that learners who want to maximize performance use overt retrieval (typing or writing responses) rather than covert retrieval for demanding material. The article states: "Until then, we recommend students prioritize overt retrieval when mastering complex information." Overt retrieval consistently produced the best criterion-test performance across both experiments, though it costs more practice time than covert retrieval.
requirements: Learners must be able to produce written or oral responses during practice (e.g., typing into a text field) and receive feedback
constraints: Overt retrieval takes longer per item than covert retrieval; if the objective is efficiency rather than maximum performance, covert retrieval may be preferable.
target_learners: students studying declarative concepts and definitions
target_learning_goals: maximizing delayed recall of complex material such as definitions
examples: In both experiments, undergraduates practiced key-term definitions by typing responses (overt), silently retrieving (covert), or restudying, with a criterion test two days later.
key_sources: Michelle L. Rivers, Paige E. Northern, Sarah K. Tauber. (2025). Does Retrieval Demand Moderate the Effectiveness of Covert Retrieval Practice? Comparing Covert and Overt Retrieval Practice for Learning Key Terms and Definitions. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10040-4

article_title: The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023))
citation: Zitzmann, S., Machts, N., Hübner, N., Schauber, S., Möller, J., & Lindner, C. (2023). The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023)). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09776-8
title: Present responder rates for different subgroups so stakeholders can judge practical significance for their specific target group
description: The article recommends that responder rates be presented for different subgroups of students. It argues "Such a presentation would better reflect that most effects are heterogeneous (Bryan et al., 2021) and would allow stakeholders to judge if findings are of practical significance to their specific target group." This extends the responder-rate communication strategy to heterogeneous effects.
requirements: Responder analysis computed separately for relevant subgroups of students
target_learners: teachers, schools, school authorities, policy makers evaluating findings for their target groups
target_learning_goals: stakeholder judgment of practical significance for specific student subgroups
examples: The article states subgroup presentation of responder rates would reflect effect heterogeneity, citing Bryan et al. (2021)
key_sources: Zitzmann, S., Machts, N., Hübner, N., Schauber, S., Möller, J., & Lindner, C. (2023). The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023)). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09776-8

article_title: Grasping Virtual Objects Benefits Lower Aptitude Learners’ Acquisition of Foreign Language Vocabulary
citation: Manuela Macedonia, Brian Mathias, Astrid E. Lehner, Susanne M. Reiterer, Claudia Repetto. (2023). Grasping Virtual Objects Benefits Lower Aptitude Learners' Acquisition of Foreign Language Vocabulary. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09835-0
title: Procedural–declarative memory account of differential sensorimotor enrichment benefits in L2 vocabulary learning
description: The article interprets its findings via embodied/grounded cognition and the interplay of declarative memory (hippocampal, engaged by reading and listening) and procedural memory (premotor and motor cortices, basal ganglia, cerebellum, engaged by movement-related input). It proposes that high-aptitude learners "may inherently rely on their declarative memory for L2 learning", while low-aptitude learners' word learning "may be supported to a greater extent by the recruitment of procedural memory systems", so sensorimotor enrichment disproportionately helps the latter. Grasping is also framed as cognitive offloading that saves working-memory resources.
requirements: Sensorimotor enrichment must be congruent with the to-be-learned stimuli for actions to enhance task performance, per the article's cited work
constraints: The article states the recruitment of procedural memory in LLA learners "does not occur intentionally" and appears to be an innate strategy
target_learners: Adult foreign-language learners with low or high language aptitude
target_learning_goals: Foreign language vocabulary acquisition and retention
examples: In the VR-cave study, grasping movements during word learning were proposed to have engaged LLA learners' procedural memory, enhancing their vocabulary acquisition relative to HLA learners who benefited from higher declarative memory capacities.
key_sources: Manuela Macedonia, Brian Mathias, Astrid E. Lehner, Susanne M. Reiterer, Claudia Repetto. (2023). Grasping Virtual Objects Benefits Lower Aptitude Learners' Acquisition of Foreign Language Vocabulary. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09835-0

article_title: The Cognitive Architecture of Digital Externalization
citation: Alexander Skulmowski. (2023). The Cognitive Architecture of Digital Externalization. Educational Psychology Review, 35:101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09818-1
title: Design digital learning to rely on biologically primary knowledge instead of technology-related secondary knowledge
description: The principle holds that digital learning tasks should be analyzed for elements requiring biologically secondary knowledge (e.g., learning game rules or unfamiliar interfaces) and replaced with counterparts drawing on biologically primary knowledge such as intuitive gestures. The review reports that "Several studies have utilized biologically primary knowledge in the form of intuitive actions, such as pointing gestures on tablets, with positive effects on learning." Requiring substantial technology-related secondary knowledge before content learning can encumber digital learning.
requirements: An analysis of which task elements rely on biologically secondary versus primary knowledge
Technology-related secondary demands must be minimized before intrinsic content is encountered
constraints: The review notes certain forms of digital learning encumber learning specifically when learners must master substantial technology-related secondary knowledge first
target_learning_goals: reducing extraneous cognitive load in digital learning tasks
examples: Studies using pointing gestures on tablets showed positive learning effects while keeping cognitive load at a minimum
key_sources: Alexander Skulmowski. (2023). The Cognitive Architecture of Digital Externalization. Educational Psychology Review, 35:101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09818-1

article_title: An Evolutionary Upgrade of Cognitive Load Theory: Using the Human Motor System and Collaboration to Support the Learning of Complex Cognitive Tasks
citation: Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2011). An Evolutionary Upgrade of Cognitive Load Theory: Using the Human Motor System and Collaboration to Support the Learning of Complex Cognitive Tasks. Educ Psychol Rev (2012) 24:27–45. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9179-2
title: Use biologically primary skills (communication, gesture, movement, object manipulation) to scaffold acquisition of biologically secondary knowledge
description: The article's central design recommendation: because biologically primary skills make minimal demands on working memory, they can be galvanized to assist acquisition of the high-load secondary content of instruction. As the authors put it, "Organizing general skills to assist in the acquisition of subject matter knowledge may be more productive than attempting to teach skills that we have evolved to acquire automatically." The recommendation is grounded in the collective working memory, human movement, and embodied cognition findings reviewed.
requirements: The communication and coordination costs of the primary activity must be largely biologically primary rather than task-specific secondary processes
constraints: Task-specific communication and coordination costs can be substantial; they may need to be decreased by training or by carefully structured or scripted learning environments
target_learners: learners acquiring biologically secondary school subject matter, including children not yet capable of high-level verbal interaction
target_learning_goals: complex cognitive tasks in domains such as mathematics, science concepts, and reading comprehension
examples: Shoval's (2011) mindful movement study: children using body movements in cooperative geometry learning obtained better results than the conventionally taught control group
key_sources: Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2011). An Evolutionary Upgrade of Cognitive Load Theory: Using the Human Motor System and Collaboration to Support the Learning of Complex Cognitive Tasks. Educ Psychol Rev (2012) 24:27–45. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9179-2

article_title: Interventions and Approaches Targeting Early Self-Regulation or Executive Functioning in Preschools: A Systematic Review
citation: Rosalyn A. Muir · Steven J. Howard · Lisa Kervin. (2023). Interventions and Approaches Targeting Early Self-Regulation or Executive Functioning in Preschools: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09740-6
title: Four-category taxonomy of 12 preschool SR/EF intervention approaches
description: The review organises preschool SR/EF interventions into a taxonomy building on Takacs and Kassai (2019), in which "four higher-order categories comprised of 12 distinct intervention approaches were identified": Play (mediated structured play, semi-structured creative play), Social-Emotional (mindfulness, SEL programs), Curricula and Pedagogy (curricula, multicomponent training, music, mathematics, language training, integrated arts), and Non-routine Activities (task training including digitalised, physical activity). The taxonomy allows results to be synthesised separately for each approach and then reconciled across approaches to identify which content and features yield comparatively more robust child-level effects.
requirements: Studies must target SR and/or EF in typically developing children aged 3–6 in preschool settings with a control group and validated pre/post measures
constraints: Two studies could have been assigned to more than one category; multi-arm interventions were assigned by the stated emphasis and intent of the authors' paper
target_learning_goals: self-regulation
executive function (inhibitory control, working memory, cognitive flexibility)
examples: The review charted 85 studies into the 12 approaches and synthesised results separately for each approach before reconciling them in the Discussion
key_sources: Rosalyn A. Muir · Steven J. Howard · Lisa Kervin. (2023). Interventions and Approaches Targeting Early Self-Regulation or Executive Functioning in Preschools: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09740-6

article_title: The Value of Pretend Play for Social Competence in Early Childhood: A Meta-analysis
citation: Smits-van der Nat, M., van der Wilt, F., Meeter, M., & van der Veen, C. (2024). The Value of Pretend Play for Social Competence in Early Childhood: A Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09884-z
title: Prism model of social competence with three layers and five underlying skills
description: The meta-analysis defines social competence using the prism model developed by Rose-Krasnor (1997) and elaborated by Junge et al. (2020), which consists of three layers: a theoretical layer defining social competence as successful participation in interactions, an indexical layer of behavioral manifestations such as sociometric status and prosocial behavior, and a skills layer of underlying skills. The five identified skills are social encoding, social problem solving, emotion regulation, communicative competence, and empathy. The meta-analysis used this model to categorize the social competence measures of the included studies into underlying skills and indices.
requirements: Measurement of social competence must be mapped onto one of the model's layers, as the meta-analysis did when coding included studies
constraints: The article notes social competence is a complex and multifaceted construct, and that the extensive variety in operationalization across studies made comparing studies difficult
target_learners: Children aged 3–8 years in early childhood education and care
target_learning_goals: Social competence, spanning underlying skills (social encoding, social problem solving, emotion regulation, communicative competence, empathy) and indices (social behavior, sociometric status)
examples: The meta-analysis coded the 34 included studies' social competence outcomes as either underlying skills (21 studies) or indices (23 studies) of the prism model
key_sources: Smits-van der Nat, M., van der Wilt, F., Meeter, M., & van der Veen, C. (2024). The Value of Pretend Play for Social Competence in Early Childhood: A Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09884-z

article_title: Promoting Social Inclusion in Educational Settings: Challenges and Opportunities
citation: Juvonen, J., Lessard, L.M., Rastogi, R., Schacter, H.L., & Smith, D.S. (2019). Promoting social inclusion in educational settings: Challenges and opportunities. Educational Psychologist, 54, 250-270. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2019.1655645
title: Proactive inclusion model: four school-level strategies for promoting social inclusion
description: The article's organizing framework for promoting social inclusion, presented as Figure 1. Rather than reacting to exclusion after it occurs, the model proposes that "students fare best when schools take a proactive approach to maximizing cross-group contact and purposefully facilitating positive peer interactions and relationships across diverse students." It specifies four strategies: "(1) maximizing diversity and ensuring equitable access, (2) increasing teachers' awareness and use of inclusive strategies, (3) promoting shared goals outside of the classroom context, and (4) facilitating cross-group friendships." The model treats inclusive practices as built-in preventions embedded in school organization and instruction.
requirements: School administrators and teachers must be aware of group and interpersonal dynamics that divide and marginalize students
Equitable access and fair distribution of students across classes must be monitored
constraints: The article notes lack of inclusion is likely to arise unless schools disrupt typical social dynamics such as homophily and avoid segregating practices
target_learning_goals: Peer acceptance and cross-group friendships
Engagement and academic performance protected from exclusion
examples: The article cites jigsaw and other group-based cooperative activities, extracurricular activities requiring collaboration, gay-straight alliances, buddy programs, and peer mentoring as practical instantiations of the strategies
key_sources: Juvonen, J., Lessard, L.M., Rastogi, R., Schacter, H.L., & Smith, D.S. (2019). Promoting social inclusion in educational settings: Challenges and opportunities. Educational Psychologist, 54, 250-270. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2019.1655645

article_title: Congruence and friction between learning and teaching
citation: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753
title: Process-oriented teaching promotes congruence and constructive friction while avoiding destructive friction
description: Process-oriented teaching focuses on the processes of knowledge construction and utilization, teaching domain-specific knowledge and learning-and-thinking strategies in coherence. The article states that "Process-oriented teaching tries to promote congruence and constructive friction, and to avoid destructive friction", with "a gradual transfer of learning functions from teachers to students". It aims to stimulate meaning- and application-directed learning styles and discourage undirected and reproduction-directed ways of learning.
requirements: Teachers must diagnose students' learning and thinking strategies to tailor teaching to functions students do not yet master
constraints: The article notes not all parts of the theory can yet be documented equally well with empirical research results
target_learners: upper secondary and higher education students
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge and self-regulated knowledge-construction skills developed in coherence
examples: The article derives four teacher roles from this view: diagnostician, challenger, model learner and activator
key_sources: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753

article_title: Capturing teacher priorities: Using real-world eye-tracking to investigate expert teacher priorities across two cultures
citation: McIntyre, N. A., Jarodzka, H., & Klassen, R. M. (2019). Capturing teacher priorities: Using real-world eye-tracking to investigate expert teacher priorities across two cultures. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.12.003
title: Teachers should prioritise students, as a foundational, culture-transcending element of teacher training curricula
description: Because experts in both cultures directed higher gaze proportions toward students during both attentional and communicative instruction, the article contends that "student-centredness is one aspect of teacher cognition that deserves to be foundational universally, in both Western European and East Asian teacher training curricula." The recommendation rests on the observed expert–novice gaze difference and the absence of cultural differences in student gaze.
requirements: Teacher education programmes willing to treat student-centredness as a foundational component across cultural settings
constraints: The recommendation derives from gaze-proportion evidence in one study of secondary teachers in two cultural settings; the article notes no cultural differences emerged in student prioritisation
target_learning_goals: student-centred teaching
classroom prioritisation of students
examples: Expert teachers in both the UK and Hong Kong samples used higher proportions of student gaze than novices during questioning and lecturing episodes
key_sources: McIntyre, N. A., Jarodzka, H., & Klassen, R. M. (2019). Capturing teacher priorities: Using real-world eye-tracking to investigate expert teacher priorities across two cultures. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.12.003

article_title: General introduction to the special issue on resilience in learning
citation: van Viersen, S., Psyridou, M., & Torppa, M. (2026). General introduction to the special issue on resilience in learning. Learning and Instruction, 101, Article 102254. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102254
title: Promotive, protective, and compensatory effects framework for academic resilience research
description: The special issue's theoretical backbone distinguishes promotive effects (factors benefiting all learners), protective effects (factors offsetting risk), and compensatory mechanisms. Slomowitz et al. introduce "the seesaw metaphor" and provide "definitions and methodological guidelines for analysis and interpretation of promotive and protective effects, as well as compensatory mechanisms in academic resilience research". Appels et al. add guidelines for interpreting main and interaction effects in variable- and person-centered designs.
requirements: Designs and statistical techniques that allow discerning between promotive, protective, and skill-enhancing effects, as the editors state is essential
constraints: The editors note no studies in the issue manipulated protective factors through experiments or interventions, and hypotheses about specific compensatory mechanisms were largely absent
target_learners: At-risk learners, including learners with specific learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Development of foundational academic skills: reading, writing, and mathematics
examples: Slomowitz et al. used examples from the context of learning disabilities, mainly dyslexia, to illustrate the framework
key_sources: van Viersen, S., Psyridou, M., & Torppa, M. (2026). General introduction to the special issue on resilience in learning. Learning and Instruction, 101, Article 102254. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102254

article_title: Designs for learning about climate change as a complex system
citation: Jacobson, Michael, Markauskaite, Lina, Portolese, Alisha, Kapur, Manu, Lai, Polly, & Roberts, Gareth (2017). Designs for learning about climate change as a complex system. Learning and Instruction, 52, pp. 1-14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.007
title: Productive Failure two-phase learning design
description: PF is a learning design approach with two phases: an initial Generation and Exploration phase in which students solve complex problems, activating prior knowledge and generating multiple Representations and Solution Methods (RSMs), followed by a Consolidation and Knowledge Assembly phase in which a teacher helps students compare and contrast their suboptimal RSMs with canonical ones. The article contrasts it with Direct Instruction, where instructional structure is provided initially. Proposed mechanisms include activation and differentiation of prior knowledge and schema abstraction.
requirements: Problems designed to be challenging but not frustrating to students
A teacher-led Consolidation and Knowledge Assembly phase comparing student-generated RSMs with canonical RSMs
constraints: The study was a small-scale quasi-experiment in a single all-girls selective school, so internal validity and generalization are limited
target_learners: ninth-grade (Year Nine) secondary science students, approximately 14 years old
target_learning_goals: explanatory knowledge of climate systems and complex systems ideas such as feedback, emergence, dynamic equilibrium, tipping points, and non-linearity
near and far transfer of complex systems knowledge
examples: In the study, PF pairs worked 15-20 minutes on Challenge Problem 1 with a complexity model and Challenge Problem 2 with a climate model, then received about 15 minutes of teacher instruction, then applied ideas on Challenge Problem 3
key_sources: Jacobson, Michael, Markauskaite, Lina, Portolese, Alisha, Kapur, Manu, Lai, Polly, & Roberts, Gareth (2017). Designs for learning about climate change as a complex system. Learning and Instruction, 52, pp. 1-14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.007

article_title: A digital game-based training improves spelling in German primary school children – A randomized controlled field trial
citation: Holz, H., Ninaus, M., Schwerter, J., Parrisius, C., Beuttler, B., Brandelik, K., & Meurers, D. (2023). A Digital Game-Based Training Improves Spelling in German Primary School Children – A Randomized Controlled Field Trial. Learning and Instruction, 87, 101771. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101771
title: Prosodiya: adaptive digital game-based spelling training for unassisted home use
description: Prosodiya is "an adaptive digital game-based spelling training for mobile touch devices" that systematically teaches orthographic knowledge in combination with syllable stress awareness. It consists of five curriculum units moving from stress-pattern identification and syllable segmentation, through vowel length distinction and open/closed syllables, to orthographic markers, spelling, and consolidation/automation. Game design elements (fantasy-themed setting, points, stars, unlocked levels, tutorials, scaffolding and KCR feedback) support motivation and unassisted use at home.
requirements: Requires mobile touch devices and basic reading skills, since it targets spelling skills covered from second grade onward
constraints: For the field trial, the subchapter on the silent h and capitalization rules was excluded to reduce load; children were asked to train five days per week twenty minutes each following an eight-week plan of 66 levels
target_learners: German second- to fourth-grade primary school children with poor spelling skills, with and without developmental dyslexia
target_learning_goals: Syllable stress awareness
syllable segmentation
vowel length distinction
orthographic marking of long and short vowels
spelling of words
examples: In the field trial, families received Android tablets and children trained at home following a training plan, with new weekly content unlocked on Monday mornings to avoid binge-playing
key_sources: Holz, H., Ninaus, M., Schwerter, J., Parrisius, C., Beuttler, B., Brandelik, K., & Meurers, D. (2023). A Digital Game-Based Training Improves Spelling in German Primary School Children – A Randomized Controlled Field Trial. Learning and Instruction, 87, 101771. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101771

article_title: A digital game-based training improves spelling in German primary school children – A randomized controlled field trial
citation: Holz, H., Ninaus, M., Schwerter, J., Parrisius, C., Beuttler, B., Brandelik, K., & Meurers, D. (2023). A Digital Game-Based Training Improves Spelling in German Primary School Children – A Randomized Controlled Field Trial. Learning and Instruction, 87, 101771. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101771
title: Five-unit curriculum progressing from syllable stress awareness to automation of spelling
description: The training's pedagogical structure is a five-unit progression: "The training consists of five curriculum units" covering syllable stress awareness, syllable structure, orthographic markers, spelling, and consolidation & automation. Each part starts with easy exercises and difficulty continuously increases and adapts individually across units, chapters, subchapters, and levels, so children first attend to stress patterns, then learn vowel-length marking rules, then consolidate and automate their knowledge.
requirements: Difficulty must adapt individually and content must be unlocked progressively to keep children on track
constraints: The acquisition phase covered the first two-thirds of the 66-level schedule, with the last third devoted to training and automation
target_learners: German primary school children in grades 2–4 with poor spelling skills
target_learning_goals: Orthographic knowledge of vowel length marking combined with syllable stress awareness
examples: Unit 1 teaches identifying stress patterns and segmenting words into syllables; unit 3 teaches rules of orthographic marking of long and short vowels; unit 5 practices all games in medium or hard difficulties to automate reading and spelling processes
key_sources: Holz, H., Ninaus, M., Schwerter, J., Parrisius, C., Beuttler, B., Brandelik, K., & Meurers, D. (2023). A Digital Game-Based Training Improves Spelling in German Primary School Children – A Randomized Controlled Field Trial. Learning and Instruction, 87, 101771. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101771

article_title: On the challenges of investigating lasting learning: A commentary
citation: Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Renkl. (2026). On the challenges of investigating lasting learning: A commentary. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102417. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102417
title: Treat prior knowledge as a resource for learning rather than a nuisance variable when evaluating instructional effects
description: The commentary argues that research aiming to inform educational practice should adopt a multidimensional stance on ecological validity, including "treating prior knowledge as a resource for learning rather than a variable to be controlled for when evaluating instructional effects". In real-world scenarios prior knowledge facilitates acquisition of novel content, and instructional techniques activate it, whereas most lab studies minimize or statistically control it. Only two special-issue studies explicitly tested whether instructional approaches had similar effects at different prior-knowledge levels, and both found interactions.
requirements: Studies must measure prior knowledge and analyze its role, e.g., by testing interactions between instructional approach and prior knowledge
constraints: Fully integrating prior knowledge into school-curriculum studies reduces possibilities for far-reaching experimental control
target_learners: school and university students with varying prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: acquisition of novel declarative and procedural knowledge built on existing knowledge
examples: Klimovich and Richter used simple-slope analyses showing interleaving helped high and average prior-knowledge students but not low ones; Ruitenburg et al. tested approach-by-prior-knowledge interactions
key_sources: Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Renkl. (2026). On the challenges of investigating lasting learning: A commentary. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102417. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102417

article_title: Adaptive feedback from artificial neural networks facilitates pre-service teachers’ diagnostic reasoning in simulation-based learning
citation: Sailer, Michael; Bauer, Elisabeth; Hofmann, Riikka; Kiesewetter, Jan; Glas, Julia. (2022). Adaptive Feedback from Artificial Neural Networks Facilitates Pre-Service Teachers' Diagnostic Reasoning in Simulation-based Learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101620
title: Prefer adaptive feedback over static expert-solution feedback when learners collaborate in dyads in simulations
description: Because static expert-solution feedback showed detrimental effects on the learning process in dyads while adaptive feedback facilitated justification quality, collaborative simulation work should be paired with adaptive rather than static feedback. The article reports that "static feedback even had detrimental effects on the learning process in dyads", motivating this design choice for collaborative settings.
requirements: Learners working collaboratively (dyads) on simulations; availability of adaptive feedback
constraints: The detrimental effect of static feedback was reported for dyads specifically
target_learning_goals: Diagnostic reasoning in simulation-based learning
examples: In the experiment, dyads and individuals worked on computer lab-based simulations under adaptive or static feedback conditions
key_sources: Sailer, Michael; Bauer, Elisabeth; Hofmann, Riikka; Kiesewetter, Jan; Glas, Julia. (2022). Adaptive Feedback from Artificial Neural Networks Facilitates Pre-Service Teachers' Diagnostic Reasoning in Simulation-based Learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101620

article_title: Timing matters! Explaining between study phases enhances students’ learning.
citation: Lachner, A., Backfisch, I., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Renkl, A. (2020). Timing matters! Explaining between study phases enhances students' learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 112(4), 841–853. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000396
title: Prepone explaining to between study phases when designing learning environments
description: The principle holds that the instructional timing of explaining matters: placing an explanation activity between study phases, rather than only at the end of the study phase, fosters learning because it raises learners' awareness of knowledge gaps early, which they can remedy during further studying. The authors state that "preponing explaining between study phases enhances learning more than explaining at the end of the entire study phase" and that "the timing of explaining is crucial, and should be considered during designing learning environments".
requirements: Learners must get the opportunity to repair detected knowledge gaps during subsequent study phases after the in-between explaining activity.
constraints: The benefit was demonstrated with university students learning from an expository text on combustion engines; transfer performance was very low and not improved in either experiment.
target_learners: university students in self-study with expository texts
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of expository text content
examples: In Experiment 1, students in the in-between explaining condition recorded a video explanation for a fictitious fellow student after studying the first of two text units, before studying the second.
key_sources: Lachner, A., Backfisch, I., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Renkl, A. (2020). Timing matters! Explaining between study phases enhances students' learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 112(4), 841–853. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000396

article_title: Supplemental Material for A Growth-Theory-of-Interest Intervention Increases Interest in Math and Science Coursework Among Liberal Arts Undergraduates
