citation: Paul A. O'Keefe, E. J. Horberg, Carol S. Dweck and Gregory M. Walton. (2024). A Growth Theory of Interest Intervention Increases Interest in Math and Science Coursework Among Liberal Arts Undergraduates. https://tinyurl.com/2yjm7rf9
title: Preregistered pilot and main studies with pre-matriculation and semester follow-up registrations
description: The article's open-practices disclosure documents preregistrations for both a pilot study and a main study, each with a pre-matriculation registration and follow-up registrations (pilot follow-up, Semester 1 follow-up, and Semester 2 follow-up for the main study). The authors state they "pre-registered hypotheses but not specific analyses", and that all pre-registered hypotheses were reported. Time-stamped registrations are hosted in public repositories via the listed links.
requirements: Registrations must be time-stamped and immutable in a public, open-access repository to qualify for the preregistered badge
constraints: The analysis plan itself was not registered prior to examining the data; only hypotheses were pre-registered
Two pilot-study semester-one survey registrations were not reported because no math/science coursework was completed during that semester
target_learning_goals: interest in math and science coursework
math/science course grades
examples: Main Study registrations: pre-matriculation, Semester 1 follow-up, and Semester 2 follow-up, each at a listed tinyurl.com OSF link
key_sources: Paul A. O'Keefe, E. J. Horberg, Carol S. Dweck and Gregory M. Walton. (2024). A Growth Theory of Interest Intervention Increases Interest in Math and Science Coursework Among Liberal Arts Undergraduates. https://tinyurl.com/2yjm7rf9

article_title: Mental adaptation during the school day as measured by arithmetical reasoning - Part I.
citation: Winch, W. H. (1911). Mental adaptation during the school day as measured by arithmetical reasoning.—Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Mental+adaptation+during+the+school+day%22+Winch+1911
title: Problematic arithmetic tests scored for rational steps toward solution
description: The measuring instrument in both experiment series: cyclostyled sets of multi-step problematic arithmetic questions, with marking that ignores the numerical answer. The marker asked "Was the problem done the right way!" and scored by "allowing one mark for every rational'' step'' which wa& on the way to a correct solution, even though no solution was actually ar- rived at", with figures chosen so mechanical computation difficulties were avoided and a fixed maximum mark per set (12 in the first series, 23 in the second).
requirements: Tests of the right pitch of difficulty and practice tests before scoring counts, since first-test results were discarded and preliminary sets established steadiness.
constraints: In the first series the order of problems was kept constant across sets, while in the second series both wording and problem order varied from set to set.
target_learners: elementary school children in Standards III to VII
target_learning_goals: problematic arithmetical reasoning, marked for rational method rather than numerical correctness
examples: Sample problems include one-step, two-step, three-step and four-step questions such as combining pole lengths or computing a profit per pound of bacon.
key_sources: Winch, W. H. (1911). Mental adaptation during the school day as measured by arithmetical reasoning.—Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Mental+adaptation+during+the+school+day%22+Winch+1911

article_title: Latent profiles as predictors of response to instruction for students with reading difficulties.
citation: Kulesz, P. A., Roberts, G. J., Francis, D. J., Cirino, P., Walczak, M., & Vaughn, S. (2024). Latent profiles as predictors of response to instruction for students with reading difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(3). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000832
title: Match reading intervention design to students' cognitive-language profiles: students with lower basic language but stronger attention may succeed with a non-customized multi-component intervention, while students with better language but weaker attention may need attention supports and more linguistic-comprehension focus
description: The article argues that latent cognitive-language profiles can guide customization of reading interventions. It reports that "Profile 1 students could benefit from a more customized intervention targeting attention and linguistic comprehension, while Profile 2 students may benefit from a non-customized (but evidence-based) multi-component reading intervention." Tailoring to a group profile rather than one-on-one customization may also yield cost savings, since customized one-on-one instruction is costly and time consuming.
requirements: Latent profile classification of students on basic language, cognitive, and attention measures to identify profile membership before assigning intervention components
constraints: The authors state it is conceivable but remains to be further examined that customized intervention based on cognitive-language profiles improves outcomes; profiles are sample specific and generalizability is unknown
target_learners: Upper elementary students with reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
examples: In the study, Profile 2 students (lower basic language, higher attention) in the intervention condition outperformed controls on the Gates post-test, while Profile 1 students did not, prompting the recommendation that Profile 1 students need attention supports plus linguistic-comprehension instruction.
key_sources: Kulesz, P. A., Roberts, G. J., Francis, D. J., Cirino, P., Walczak, M., & Vaughn, S. (2024). Latent profiles as predictors of response to instruction for students with reading difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(3). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000832

article_title: In-class attention, spatial ability, and mathematics anxiety predict across-grade gains in adolescents’ mathematics achievement.
citation: Geary, D. C., Hoard, M. K., Nugent, L., & Scofield, J. E. (2021). In-Class Attention, Spatial Ability, and Mathematics Anxiety Predict Across-Grade Gains in Adolescents' Mathematics Achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(4), 754-769. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000487
title: When targeting mathematics interventions for at-risk middle schoolers, prioritize in-class attention and spatial ability alongside prior knowledge
description: The article argues that because many factors have been proposed as contributing to mathematics growth, interventions risk being unfocused; its broad assessment identified the most plausible contributors for middle school students. The results "have implications for how to best target interventions for students at risk for long-term difficulties with mathematics," pointing to in-class attention, spatial ability, and prior competence as the factors to prioritize. This is a targeting principle grounded in the study's Bayesian and multilevel findings, not a tested intervention.
requirements: Assessment battery covering prior mathematical competence, teacher-rated in-class attention, and a complex spatial ability measure to identify students at risk
constraints: The data are correlational and preclude strong causal statements; the authors state findings may not generalize to earlier or later grades or to other populations
target_learners: middle school students at risk for long-term difficulties with mathematics
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement growth across grades
examples: The study assessed 317 seventh-graders on memory, spatial, intelligence, attitude, anxiety, and attention measures and used Bayesian selection to identify the best predictor set
key_sources: Geary, D. C., Hoard, M. K., Nugent, L., & Scofield, J. E. (2021). In-Class Attention, Spatial Ability, and Mathematics Anxiety Predict Across-Grade Gains in Adolescents' Mathematics Achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(4), 754-769. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000487

article_title: Verbal and abstract elements in intelligence examinations.
citation: Herring, J. P. (1923). Verbal and Abstract Elements in Intelligence Examinations. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Prefer abstract and verbal test content when selecting material for intelligence examinations
description: For prediction and control, the article recommends building intelligence examinations chiefly from abstract and verbal content, because such tests "afford better means for the prediction of human intelligence" than concrete and non-verbal tests, and because they also "have higher coefficients of reliability." The middle portions of both scales are distinguishably better material than the extreme concrete and non-verbal ends but inferior to the abstract extremes.
requirements: A validated composite criterion of intelligence against which candidate test content can be correlated
constraints: The data do not permit the conclusion that concrete and non-verbal tests may not properly supplement the others in a battery of tests; there are circumstances in which they are the feasible form of procedure
target_learners: School-age children in grades IV–VII and age groups of ten to twelve year olds
target_learning_goals: Prediction of general intelligence and selection of examination content
examples: The study correlated segments of the Dearborn, Army Beta, Pressey Primer, Indiana Cross-cut and Thorndike Visual Vocabulary examinations, classified by judges, against a seven-part weighted composite criterion.
key_sources: Herring, J. P. (1923). Verbal and Abstract Elements in Intelligence Examinations. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org

article_title: The correlation of general intelligence tests and school standing.
citation: E. B. Skaggs. (1918). The Correlation of General Intelligence Tests and School Standing. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Pressey's new silent-reading test: children cross out the wrong word in paragraphs
description: A new form of silent reading test devised at Indiana University by Mrs. S. L. Pressey. It "consists of paragraphs in each of which there is a word which spoils the meaning of the paragraph or makes a false statement," and children are told to cross out the wrong word in each paragraph. The test is being validated against pooled teacher ratings of reading ability.
requirements: Validation against an independent statement of reading ability based on pooled ratings from four teachers for each child in a large junior high school.
target_learning_goals: silent reading ability, including rate and comprehension
examples: The article gives the sample item about men in shoe factories striking for shorter hours, lower wages, and recognition of their union.
key_sources: E. B. Skaggs. (1918). The Correlation of General Intelligence Tests and School Standing. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: Explanatory models in the processing of science text: The role of prior knowledge activation through small-group discussion.
citation: Schmidt, H. G., De Volder, M. L., De Grave, W. S., Moust, J. H. C., & Patel, V. L. (1989). Explanatory Models in the Processing of Science Text: The Role of Prior Knowledge Activation Through Small-Group Discussion. Journal of Educational Psychology, 81(4), 610-619. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.81.4.610
title: Activation hypothesis: problem analysis packages activated prior knowledge into explanatory models that speed access and integration of new text information
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that discussing a problem mobilizes relevant prior knowledge, which is "packaged" in a problem-specific explanatory model. Because the task demands explanation, the activated knowledge tends to be explanatory in nature and is therefore more easily accessed when the text is processed, enabling integration of new concepts into existing cognitive structures. The theory explains both greater overall recall and the specific advantage for explanatory information, since causally linked propositions are more coherent and easier to retrieve.
requirements: Learners must possess some prior knowledge, however imprecise, that can be activated by the problem description
constraints: If subjects' knowledge is insufficient to make any sense of a problem, facilitative effects of problem analysis are not expected, per the article's own analysis
target_learners: secondary school and college science students, novices and experts alike
target_learning_goals: comprehension and integration of causal, explanatory concepts from expository science text
examples: In Experiment 2, subjects analyzing the blood cell problem before reading a text on osmosis and diffusion recalled significantly more explanatory propositions than controls
key_sources: Schmidt, H. G., De Volder, M. L., De Grave, W. S., Moust, J. H. C., & Patel, V. L. (1989). Explanatory Models in the Processing of Science Text: The Role of Prior Knowledge Activation Through Small-Group Discussion. Journal of Educational Psychology, 81(4), 610-619. https://doi.org/10.1037//0022-0663.81.4.610

article_title: Measurement of some abilities in scientific thinking.
citation: Herring, J. P. (1918). Measurements of some abilities in scientific thinking. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IX(10), 535-558.
title: Base school conclusions on primary data from immediate experience rather than on secondary data alone
description: The article distinguishes primary data, "selected by the individual from immediate experience," from secondary data, selected from representations of others' experience, arguing primary data are more educative and that secondary data are subject to prejudice, carelessness, and greed. It urges schools to train children to rely much upon the testimony of their own senses and to seek primary data rather than habitually accept conclusions of others.
requirements: Instruction must give central importance to when to investigate, when to recognize authority, and how to combine the two
constraints: The distinction is stated to form no defined part of the measurements themselves
target_learning_goals: scientific method
judging when to trust authority versus personal investigation
examples: The author contrasts seeing James board a street-car (primary datum) with being told that James boarded it (secondary datum).
key_sources: Herring, J. P. (1918). Measurements of some abilities in scientific thinking. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IX(10), 535-558. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0075736

article_title: Needed research in method.
citation: Clayton C. Kohl. (1911). Needed Research in Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Needed+Research+in+Method%22+Kohl
title: The true province of method is the scientific study of the child's mind acquiring a given piece of subject-matter
description: The article proposes that method should be redefined as a branch of educational psychology that psychologizes definite subject-matter from the child's viewpoint. In the author's words, "The true province of method would seem to lie right here: it is the scientific study of the child's (not the adult's) mind as it acquires a given experience involved in a given piece of subject-matter." Under this view all method becomes essentially special, general method being elaborated, modified and corrected rather than ignored. The article argues this is the only way to remove adult faculty psychology from method.
requirements: Educational psychology standing as an independent science rather than trailing behind general psychology
Research that considers general psychology, the particular psychology of the subject taught, and the child being instructed
constraints: The article presents this as the author's argued position, not a tested result
target_learning_goals: defining the scope of method as a field of study
key_sources: Clayton C. Kohl. (1911). Needed Research in Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Needed+Research+in+Method%22+Kohl

article_title: Research versus Propaganda in Visual Education.
citation: Frank N. Freeman. (1922). Research Versus Propaganda in Visual Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XI, No. 5. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/13/5/
title: Treat each presentation problem as a special case decided on its merits rather than applying a wholesale sensory doctrine
description: Freeman's thesis is that choices among modes of presentation cannot be settled by any general principle about the supremacy of a sense. While certain senses have advantages in particular cases and some experiences can only be initiated by particular sensations, "It is necessary rather that each case be examined for itself, in order that it may be determined what the most advantageous type of sensory stimulus may be."
requirements: Each presentation problem must be examined individually, and analysis should be supplemented and verified by careful scientific procedure
constraints: Freeman regards his own psychological analysis as somewhat tentative, pointing out only the most probable lines of development
target_learning_goals: selecting the most advantageous mode of presentation for given content
examples: Freeman grants special cases such as music depending on hearing and appreciation of painting on sight, but denies wholesale arguments can be based on them
key_sources: Frank N. Freeman. (1922). Research Versus Propaganda in Visual Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XI, No. 5. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/13/5/

article_title: Associations between teacher and student mathematics, science, and literacy anxiety in fourth grade.
citation: McLean, L., Janssen, J., Espinoza, P., Lindstrom Johnson, S., & Jimenez, M. (2023). Associations Between Teacher and Student Mathematics, Science, and Literacy Anxiety in Fourth Grade. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000790
title: Prioritize low-SES students and their teachers for added support to improve STEM teaching and learning experiences
description: Because teachers' mathematics and science anxiety were most strongly related to the anxiety of their low-SES students, the article recommends that low-SES students and the teachers who serve them be prioritized for added support. The authors state that "low-SES students (and more broadly, students from underrepresented communities) and the teachers who serve these students should be prioritized for added support to improve their STEM teaching and learning experiences," naming three contexts: schools and districts of practicing teachers, teacher preparation programs, and community settings via educational and social policy.
requirements: School and district leaders able to direct targeted professional development and mental health consultation toward high-STEM-anxiety teachers.
constraints: The supporting evidence is correlational and exploratory; the article frames the study as an exploratory first step and calls for replication with larger samples.
target_learning_goals: Reducing students' mathematics and science anxiety
Fostering low-SES students' interest and engagement in STEM
examples: The article recommends school and district leaders prioritize targeted support of high-STEM-anxiety teachers via additional training and professional development that builds self-efficacy and positive emotions, plus mental health consultation services addressing the emotional aspects of teaching low-income students in STEM.
key_sources: McLean, L., Janssen, J., Espinoza, P., Lindstrom Johnson, S., & Jimenez, M. (2023). Associations Between Teacher and Student Mathematics, Science, and Literacy Anxiety in Fourth Grade. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000790

article_title: The meetings at Mobile, Alabama, February 22-25, 1911.
citation: The Meetings at Mobile, Alabama, February 22-25, 1911. (1911). The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Preprint meeting papers beforehand and concentrate discussion on a few dominant topics rather than relying on extemporaneous remarks
description: The article argues that conference quality improves when principal contributions are printed beforehand, which eliminates papers prepared merely to make a good impression when read. It warns that "purely extemporaneous discussion encourages loose thinking and discourages concentration upon a few dominant topics," and that in reacting against set papers the societies had gone to the other extreme.
requirements: Papers must be printed and distributed to members before the meetings; the article notes the 1911 year books arrived too late to reach a majority of members beforehand.
constraints: The article states this in the context of the Mobile meetings of the Department of Superintendence and affiliated societies.
target_learning_goals: productive professional discussion and interpretation of educational data
examples: At Mobile, the societies printed principal contributions beforehand, yet year books still arrived too late for most members.
key_sources: The Meetings at Mobile, Alabama, February 22-25, 1911. (1911). The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: Criteria to Employ in Choice of Tests.
citation: Franzen, R., & Knight, F. B. (1921). Criteria to Employ in Choice of Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Decide primary psychological and statistical values of a test first; consider price, time and convenience only in ratio to benefits derived
description: The article holds that administrative exigencies (price, administration time, scoring convenience) are secondary criteria, admissible only after establishing how much service each candidate test performs. An administrator should 'decide primary values first; then let him consider price, time and convenience in ratio to the benefits derived', because often the only affordable test is the one that does not perform the needed service.
requirements: The administrator must first know how much service can be expected from each of a group of tests before weighing cost, time and scoring convenience
constraints: Cost, time and convenience remain legitimate factors once all considered tests perform the needed service
target_learners: school students measured by district testing programs
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of abilities such as reading for school decision-making
examples: The authors argue that if a test does not really measure reading, it would pay an administrator to use the test that did the service even though it cost more, took longer, and was scored with great time and energy
key_sources: Franzen, R., & Knight, F. B. (1921). Criteria to Employ in Choice of Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0075312

article_title: Solution of Problems in Geometry.
citation: Wood, B. D., & Bell, J. C. (1914). Solution of problems in geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Wood+Bell+Solution+of+Problems+in+Geometry
title: Prerequisite life habits of attention, precise language, and conscious motor control should precede instruction aimed at developing skilled geometry problem solvers
description: The study's authors argue that success in geometry problem solving rests on "neural organization" — readiness to grasp significant features and reject irrelevant ones — built from life habits of noting and recalling details, precise language use, and conscious motor control. They warn that "unless these life habits are already well formed, the prospect of developing a good geometer is not a very favorable one." Design of geometry instruction should therefore attend to these habits as prerequisites.
requirements: Learners must already have well-formed habits of accurately noting and recalling details, care and precision in language use, and conscious control of motor activities for such readiness to be present.
constraints: The authors state that the extent to which these life habits are developed by the study of formal geometry remains an open question for experimental investigation.
target_learners: secondary and teacher-training students studying plane geometry
target_learning_goals: geometry problem solving
locus reasoning
geometrical construction
examples: The six good students showed faultless verbal description and inhibited motor activity, while poor students like PD produced unstable, incorrect figures and uncontrollable pencil use.

article_title: A Book Describing An Elementary School Curriculum Based on Year-Long Series of Projects.
citation: Rugg, E. U. (1921). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology
title: Project curriculum theory: each phase of school work should be as far as possible a replica of a life activity
description: The organizing theory of Wells' project curriculum holds that "each phase of school work shall be so far as posible a replica of a life activity". Children are organized as families, the year's work is dramatized, and doll families provide motivation even for arithmetic. Proponents extend this to seeking life activities through which all skills, information, problem-solving training, and attitudes are developed.
requirements: Requires school work to be organized as life activities such as families, in which children take assigned roles across a full school year
constraints: As reviewed, the theory was implemented only in grades 1-3 of one Trenton, N. J. school; the grades 4-6 course remained theoretical
target_learners: children in the first six grades of elementary school
target_learning_goals: school skills
information
problem solving
fundamental attitudes
examples: First grade project Playing Families; second grade Playing Store; third grade Playing City, taught in Trenton, N. J.
key_sources: Rugg, E. U. (1921). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology

article_title: A stitch in time: Strategic self-control in high school and college students.
citation: Duckworth Angela L., White Rachel E., Matteucci Alyssa J., Shearer Annie, Gross James J. (2016). A Stitch in Time: Strategic Self-Control in High School and College Students. Journal of educational psychology, 108(3), 329-341. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000062
title: The process model of self-control organizes strategies into five categories corresponding to stages of impulse generation
description: The process model of self-control organizes self-control strategies by their underlying mechanism and the stage at which they are employed during impulse generation. Impulses develop through a recursive "situation-attention-appraisal-response sequence," yielding "five categories of self-control strategies can be identified, corresponding to distinct stages of impulse generation": situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change, and response modulation. Its central prediction is that "intervening earlier in the cycle of impulse generation, when impulses are still developing, is more effective than intervening later." The article uses it as a coding taxonomy and as the framework for the interventions.
requirements: Strategies are classifiable by mechanism and by the stage of impulse generation at which they operate
constraints: Direct empirical evidence on situation selection in adolescent students is lacking, per the article
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
self-control in everyday academic and interpersonal dilemmas
key_sources: Duckworth Angela L., White Rachel E., Matteucci Alyssa J., Shearer Annie, Gross James J. (2016). A Stitch in Time: Strategic Self-Control in High School and College Students. Journal of educational psychology, 108(3), 329-341. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000062

article_title: Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence.
citation: De Sanctis, S. (1911). Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 498-507.
title: Graded-question scale: questions of progressive difficulty grouped into levels to classify subjects by degree
description: A general psychological method in which a list of questions of increasing difficulty is used to grade the level of intelligence: with forty questions of progressive difficulty, some subjects master the first ten, others reach the first thirty-five, and a small minority answer all forty. Grouping the questions (four groups of ten, or ten groups of ten from one hundred questions) yields classification into as many degrees. De Sanctis reports using this method with great success on mental defectives ten years old and over, and identifies it as the principle underlying the Binet-Simon scale.
requirements: A pool of questions ordered by increasing difficulty, grouped into equal-sized sets so that the group reached indexes the subject's level
constraints: The Binet-Simon version adds the assumption that each stage corresponds to the intellectual development characteristic of a given age, an assumption the author says must be verified before judging the scale's applicability
target_learners: mental defectives ten years old and over
target_learning_goals: grading and classifying the level of intelligence
examples: De Sanctis describes dividing one hundred questions of increasing difficulty into ten groups of ten to classify subjects into ten different grades
key_sources: De Sanctis, S. (1911). Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 498-507. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0069835

article_title: Explanatory models in the processing of science text: The role of prior knowledge activation through small-group discussion.
citation: Schmidt, H. G., De Volder, M. L., De Grave, W. S., Moust, J. H. C., & Patel, V. L. (1989). Explanatory Models in the Processing of Science Text: The Role of Prior Knowledge Activation Through Small-Group Discussion. Journal of Educational Psychology, 81(4), 610-619. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.81.4.610
title: Prior-knowledge activation through problem analysis: explanatory models as vehicles for text comprehension
description: The article proposes that discussing a problem mobilizes relevant prior knowledge, which is packaged in a problem-specific explanatory model—a set of concepts connected by causal links interpreting phenomena in terms of their underlying structure. This model, constructed before reading, facilitates comprehension of a relevant text because activated explanatory knowledge is more easily accessed and causally linked propositions are more coherent. The account explains why problem analysis aids recall of explanatory but not descriptive information.
requirements: Learners must analyze a problem describing natural phenomena and generate explanations in terms of underlying processes, principles, or mechanisms before encountering the relevant text
constraints: The effect was demonstrated for recall of explanatory propositions; retention of descriptive facts was not specifically supported by the procedure
target_learners: secondary-school and college science students, both novices and experts
target_learning_goals: acquisition of causal, explanatory concepts from expository science text
examples: Small groups discussed why a red blood cell swells and bursts in pure water but shrinks in salt solution, then read a text on osmosis and diffusion
key_sources: Schmidt, H. G., De Volder, M. L., De Grave, W. S., Moust, J. H. C., & Patel, V. L. (1989). Explanatory Models in the Processing of Science Text: The Role of Prior Knowledge Activation Through Small-Group Discussion. Journal of Educational Psychology, 81(4), 610-619. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.81.4.610

article_title: A brief scale of intelligence for use in school surveys.
citation: Pressey, S. L. (1920). A Brief Group Scale of Intelligence for Use in School Surveys. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: The Pressey 'Cross-out' brief group intelligence scale for grades 4-8
description: A four-test group scale of general intelligence printed as a four-page 9-inch by 12-inch folder, with "four tests each of twenty-five items (a total of 100 'points')": verbal ingenuity, logical judgment, arithmetical ingenuity, and moral judgment, all using a cross-out response. It was intended (a) for survey comparisons between sections, schools, or systems and (b) as an aid in individual diagnosis.
requirements: Administered by teachers or field workers without special training in mental tests, with directions read verbatim from a one-page script and blanks scored by crossing out one word or number per line
constraints: "Sufficient accuracy for the final diagnosis of any individual case can, of course, not be expected from such a brief scale"; it is for preliminary selection of individuals deserving further study
target_learning_goals: measurement of level and distribution of general ability in groups and preliminary individual diagnosis
examples: Given to all children from the third grade through high school in three Indiana city surveys, with the final form based on item analysis by P.E. deviations against a sixth-grade base
key_sources: Pressey, S. L. (1920). A Brief Group Scale of Intelligence for Use in School Surveys. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: The Correlations of Achievement in School Subjects with Intelligence Tests and Other Variables (Continued).
citation: Arthur I. Gates. (1923). The correlations of achievement in school subjects with intelligence tests and other variables (Continued). The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1923-02675-001
title: For predicting school achievement, choose a very verbal test over a very long test when both cannot be had
description: The article derives a practical selection rule from its partial and multiple correlations: when a test battery cannot be both verbal and long, verbalness should be weighted over length because "verbalness alone yields a higher correlation with achievement than time alone." The best option remains a long verbal test, whose combined multiple correlation reaches 0.73.
requirements: Applies to predicting achievement in largely verbal school subjects in grades IV-VIII
constraints: The author notes the ideal is a long verbal test; the rule concerns choosing when only one property can be had
target_learning_goals: Prediction of achievement in school subjects such as arithmetic, spelling, and reading
examples: The author states: "for purposes of predicting school achievement it is better to have a very verbal test than a very long test, if one cannot have both."
