article_title: Beneficial for some or for everyone? Exploring the effects of an autonomy-supportive intervention in the real-life classroom.
citation: Flunger, B., Mayer, A., & Umbach, N. (2019). Beneficial for Some or for Everyone? Exploring the Effects of an Autonomy-Supportive Intervention in the Real-Life Classroom. Journal of Educational Psychology, vol. 111, no. 2, pp. 210-234. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000284
title: Provide autonomy support in physics instruction because it benefits students' motivation and learning behaviors
description: The article concludes that physics instruction should incorporate autonomy support, implemented through provision of choices, rationales, and informational language. The authors state "These findings point to the benefits of providing autonomy support in physics". The recommendation rests on randomized classroom evidence showing positive average effects on need satisfaction, emotions, and learning behaviors, while acknowledging that effects may differ across student characteristics.
requirements: Teachers need training or support to deliver choices, rationales, and informational language within subject-matter lessons
constraints: Differential effects were observed: higher prior-grade students reported greater optional choices, joy and effort
target_learning_goals: Motivation, need satisfaction, achievement emotions, and self-regulated learning
examples: The intervention operationalized autonomy support via provision of choices, provision of rationales, and informational language in a heat-transfer unit.
key_sources: Flunger, B., Mayer, A., & Umbach, N. (2019). Beneficial for Some or for Everyone? Exploring the Effects of an Autonomy-Supportive Intervention in the Real-Life Classroom. Journal of Educational Psychology, vol. 111, no. 2, pp. 210-234. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000284

article_title: Optimizing practice scheduling requires quantitative tracking of individual item performance
citation: Luke G. Eglington and Philip I. Pavlik Jr. (2020). Optimizing practice scheduling requires quantitative tracking of individual item performance. npj Science of Learning 5:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00074-4
title: Value practice decisions by learning gain per unit of time (efficiency), not by gain alone
description: The article argues that practice scheduling is fundamentally an economic problem: gains in learning should be valued relative to their time cost. Efficiency is "the gain in retrievability at some ﬁnal test divided by the time cost of the current practice". Considering time cost led to different conclusions than prior recommendations, because difficult items take longer and fail more often, reducing learning per second. This principle motivated the OET scheduling approach and its simulations and experiment.
requirements: A way to quantify both learning gain and time cost per trial (e.g., a model estimating recall probability and response latency)
constraints: If failures provide larger or faster learning gains, lower difficulty thresholds may be preferable; efficiency is relevant unless the gains and time costs of successes and failures are equal
target_learners: students practicing factual material in online educational systems
target_learning_goals: efficient allocation of limited practice time to maximize retention
examples: Simulations comparing schedules that valued efficiency against conventional schedules ignoring time cost; an experiment testing OET 0.40 (discrepancy reduction) against higher OETs
key_sources: Luke G. Eglington and Philip I. Pavlik Jr. (2020). Optimizing practice scheduling requires quantitative tracking of individual item performance. npj Science of Learning 5:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00074-4

article_title: The representational instability in the generalization of fear learning
citation: Kenny Yu, Wolf Vanpaemel, Francis Tuerlinckx & Jonas Zaman. (2024). The representational instability in the generalization of fear learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00287-x
title: Probabilistic dynamic framework of stimulus representation in fear generalization
description: The article proposes that behavior transfer must consider internal representational variability as well as external environmental variability, challenging static stimulus representation assumptions in generalization research. It formulates "a comprehensive system for perceptual fear generalization, which integrates error-driven learning and similarity-based generalization processes", treating perception as a dynamic, probabilistic process and perceptual memory as a separate, stable component whose mapping may shift over time.
requirements: Simultaneous measurement of perception (size estimation) and perceptual memory (size reproduction) during learning and generalization tasks
constraints: Investigated under fear contexts in a differential conditioning paradigm with size stimuli; the authors note the dynamic interplay between perceptual and memory systems remains largely unexplored beyond this setting
target_learning_goals: understanding how stimulus representations shape generalization of learned threat and safety associations
examples: A differential conditioning experiment (N = 80) with size estimation, US expectancy, and size reproduction tasks, analyzed with Bayesian state-space and mixture models
key_sources: Kenny Yu, Wolf Vanpaemel, Francis Tuerlinckx & Jonas Zaman. (2024). The representational instability in the generalization of fear learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00287-x

article_title: Seeking the neural representation of statistical properties in print during implicit processing of visual words
citation: Jianyi Liu, Tengwen Fan, Yan Chen and Jingjing Zhao. (2023). Seeking the neural representation of statistical properties in print during implicit processing of visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00209-3
title: Predictive coding with precision modulation explains how long-term statistical knowledge and short-term predictions interact in word processing
description: The article uses predictive coding, in which learning is "a continuous optimization of a generative model" achieved through continuous interaction between top-down predictions and bottom-up prediction errors. The system assigns different weights to real-time prediction errors according to environmental variability (prediction precision), a mechanism the authors call conceptually "a form of meta-learning". In the experiment, low-precision equal probability sequences revealed only lexical frequency representations, while high-precision oddball sequences caused inconsistent information to be evaluated as worthy of learning, yielding stronger sub-lexical consistency representations and vMMN responses.
requirements: Short-term predictions with built-in high precision (e.g., repeated standard stimuli) for sub-lexical consistency representations to become detectable
constraints: The study did not consider participants' hearing characteristics, a stated limitation for generalizability
The assumption of no long-term prediction differences between stimulus types lacks direct proof, a stated limit on explanatory power
target_learning_goals: implicit neural processing of statistical regularities in print
visual word recognition
examples: Equal probability sequences with low built-in prediction precision and three oddball sequences with high precision were used; consistent characters appeared with p = 0.75 and inconsistent deviants with p = 0.25
key_sources: Jianyi Liu, Tengwen Fan, Yan Chen and Jingjing Zhao. (2023). Seeking the neural representation of statistical properties in print during implicit processing of visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00209-3

article_title: Commensality and academic performance: measuring peer acceptance among college students
citation: Jinxi Wen, Wenjing Lyu, Jin Liu & Li Yang. (2025). Commensality and academic performance: measuring peer acceptance among college students. npj Science of Learning 10:69. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00357-8
title: Universities should explore promoting environments that encourage peer commensality
description: The article suggests that "promoting environments that encourage peer commensality could be a valuable strategy for universities to explore." Because commensality values were positively correlated with academic outcomes across multiple metrics, campus dining arrangements and residential design that create opportunities for shared mealtimes — including with classmates beyond one's own dormitory — merit consideration. The authors frame this as exploratory, given that their findings are correlational rather than causal.
requirements: Institutional infrastructure the article names: a high-density residential campus, a centralized payment system, and a cultural norm of on-campus dining
constraints: The approach may not be directly transferable to non-residential or commuter models common in many Western countries; the authors note their findings are not causal due to potential self-selection bias
target_learning_goals: academic performance and peer integration
examples: The article's measurement used campus card swipe data: two students swiping in the same canteen within a 2-min interval during the same meal period counted as sharing a meal
key_sources: Jinxi Wen, Wenjing Lyu, Jin Liu & Li Yang. (2025). Commensality and academic performance: measuring peer acceptance among college students. npj Science of Learning 10:69. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00357-8

article_title: Social learning through prediction error in the brain
citation: Jessica Joiner, Matthew Piva, Courtney Turrin and Steve W. C. Chang. (2017). Social learning through prediction error in the brain. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0009-2
title: Table 1: taxonomy of prediction-error types and correlated brain areas
description: The review provides a representative table mapping prediction-error types to brain areas from primate electrophysiology or human neuroimaging, organized along an egocentric/allocentric axis. Egocentric rows cover self action, self reward outcome, self reward value, and self reward timing errors (e.g., VTA, SN, striatum, OFC); allocentric rows cover other action, other reward outcome, and other motivation errors (e.g., ACCg, dmPFC, dlPFC, TPJ, MTG, STS). It is explicitly "not a comprehensive list but rather a list to highlight the presence of predictive coding in the brain".
requirements: Evidence from primate electrophysiology or human neuroimaging to assign an area to a prediction-error type
constraints: Not comprehensive; distributions of areas are naturally constrained by the amount of research examining different types of prediction errors
target_learners: researchers studying neural mechanisms of learning
target_learning_goals: mapping prediction-error computations to brain structures
key_sources: Jessica Joiner, Matthew Piva, Courtney Turrin and Steve W. C. Chang. (2017). Social learning through prediction error in the brain. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0009-2

article_title: Improvements in naturalistic speech-in-noise comprehension in middle-aged and older adults after 3 weeks of computer-based speechreading training
citation: Raffael Schmitt, Martin Meyer and Nathalie Giroud. (2023). Improvements in naturalistic speech-in-noise comprehension in middle-aged and older adults after 3 weeks of computer-based speechreading training. npj Science of Learning 8:32. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00179-6
title: Pro audito computer-based speechreading training (lippenlesen.ch)
description: A freely accessible computer-based speechreading training by pro audito Schweiz (www.lippenlesen.ch), used by the speechreading training group in this study. The training "contains eight lessons structured in the same way": an introductory video, flashcards, and exercises, covering vowel and consonant mouth forms, contextual information, numbers and names, and speech perception in noise. Participants trained 20 minutes on each of five days per week over three weeks, with log files recording training time.
requirements: Requires participants to practise 20 minutes on each of five days per week over a three-week period, keeping a learning diary of exercises solved and time spent
constraints: The article notes lessons using sentences as training material create potential lexical overlap with similar sentence-based tests, though follow-up analyses suggested this was not a relevant confound in this study
target_learners: middle-aged and older adults with normal to moderately impaired hearing (PTA 10–83 dB HL)
target_learning_goals: using visual speech cues to improve audiovisual speech comprehension in noise
examples: In this study, 32 adults aged 50–83 completed the training and improved significantly in the audiovisual speech-in-noise task relative to an active foreign-language learning control group
key_sources: Raffael Schmitt, Martin Meyer and Nathalie Giroud. (2023). Improvements in naturalistic speech-in-noise comprehension in middle-aged and older adults after 3 weeks of computer-based speechreading training. npj Science of Learning 8:32. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00179-6

article_title: Morphology in children’s books, and what it means for learning
citation: Korochkina, M. & Rastle, K. (2025). Morphology in children's books, and what it means for learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00313-6
title: Print-exposure account of derivational affix learning through naturalistic reading of children's books
description: This theoretical account describes how children may learn derivational affix morphemes through real-life reading experience rather than explicit instruction. The article offers "the first concrete description of how readers may learn afﬁx morphemes through real-life text input", grounded in quantification of the CYP-LEX corpus. The account "considers the realities of morpheme presentation in natural language", including the low number of distinct words carrying each affix, the need for specialised linguistic knowledge to identify many morphemes, and misleading spelling patterns such as pseudo-affixed words.
requirements: Children must encounter affixes with a large number of distinct stems and predictable meaning shifts for learning without instruction to be feasible, as the article states as a prerequisite for affix learning in the absence of instruction.
constraints: The account is largely confined to English and its writing system; the article states its conclusions about what children may learn through reading experience are largely confined to English.
target_learners: British children aged 7–16 reading for pleasure
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of derivational morpheme knowledge supporting vocabulary growth and rapid word recognition
examples: The authors quantified type frequency, token frequency, cross-book distribution, and orthographic detectability of 48 common affixes in 1200 popular children's books to characterise the learning input.
key_sources: Korochkina, M. & Rastle, K. (2025). Morphology in children's books, and what it means for learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00313-6

article_title: Executive functions as mediators of early educational disparities by SES, gender and birth month
citation: Rémeau, M., Schmitt, P., & Borst, G. (2026). Executive functions as mediators of early educational disparities by SES, gender and birth month. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00422-w
title: Promote executive function development early (e.g., through enriched structured play or targeted support) to reduce multiple forms of early academic disadvantage
description: The article proposes that because EFs mediate SES-, gender- and birth-month-related disparities, supporting EF growth from an early age is a promising equity lever. It states that "promoting EF development from an early age, through enriched structured play or targeted support, may represent a promising pathway for reducing disparities" rooted in socioeconomic disadvantage, age differences and gender-based self-regulation challenges.
requirements: EFs are characterized as a common, malleable mechanism underlying early inequalities, so interventions must target EFs specifically rather than demographic factors that cannot be changed
constraints: The article calls for future research to examine the effectiveness of such interventions; effectiveness has not been demonstrated in this study
The study is cross-sectional, limiting causal inference about EF as mechanism
target_learners: preschool children in their first year of formal schooling (age 3 in France)
target_learning_goals: early oral language and early numeracy (pre-academic) abilities; school readiness
examples: The study's own mediation modeling showed EFs accounted for 23–51% of the total effects of SES, gender and birth month on pre-academic scores, motivating the recommendation
key_sources: Rémeau, M., Schmitt, P., & Borst, G. (2026). Executive functions as mediators of early educational disparities by SES, gender and birth month. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00422-w

article_title: Learning reduces ingroup bias more with perceived losses than gains across cultures
citation: Yuqing Zhou, Björn Lindström, Alexander Soutschek, Pyungwon Kang, Shihui Han, Philippe N. Tobler & Grit Hein. (2025). Learning reduces ingroup bias more with perceived losses than gains across cultures. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00362-x
title: Prediction-error learning account of intergroup impression updating
description: The article frames impression formation as continuous reinforcement learning: impressions and closeness are updated trial by trial through prediction errors. "These updates are driven by prediction errors — discrepancies between expected and actual outcomes." The rate of updating is modulated by prior uncertainty, with strong priors slowing updating. Rescorla-Wagner models with separate learning rates for positive and negative prediction errors best fit expectancy ratings, and a closeness model driven by time-discounted sums of positive and negative prediction errors best fit closeness ratings in both cultures. Negative ingroup prediction errors in the Loss frame carry the weight (Wneg_in) that links learning to bias reduction.
requirements: Formal testing requires computational reinforcement learning modeling with parameters estimated from trial-by-trial expectancy and closeness ratings.
constraints: The account was tested with all-male samples in two cultures and specific group inductions (Swiss-Middle East; Chinese-German), which the authors note may introduce context-specific confounding factors.
target_learning_goals: Formation and updating of intergroup impressions and social closeness
examples: The winning Learning Model 3 fit expectancy ratings with r2 = 0.33 ± 0.26 (Loss) and r2 = 0.38 ± 0.30 (Gain) in the Western sample, with good parameter recovery (rs > 0.88).
key_sources: Yuqing Zhou, Björn Lindström, Alexander Soutschek, Pyungwon Kang, Shihui Han, Philippe N. Tobler & Grit Hein. (2025). Learning reduces ingroup bias more with perceived losses than gains across cultures. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00362-x

article_title: How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain
citation: van Kesteren, M. T. R. & Meeter, M. (2020). How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain. npj Science of Learning 5:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0064-y
title: Predictive coding account: the brain builds a world model that generates prediction errors, and very strong schemas resist change
description: The review presents predictive coding as a general theory of brain function explaining why information is organized into schemas: "our brains evolved to predict what will happen next", requiring a clear and consistent world model similar to semantic memory or schema. This model generates prediction errors when inconsistent information is encountered and supports prospection recruiting the mPFC. The review notes a drawback: "when it becomes very strong it will be resistant to change; many and large prediction errors are needed to adapt it."
requirements: A not-yet-fully-developed model for prediction errors to drive adaptation
constraints: Once the model becomes very strong, many and large prediction errors are needed to adapt it
target_learning_goals: schema-based prediction
memory generalization
key_sources: van Kesteren, M. T. R. & Meeter, M. (2020). How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain. npj Science of Learning 5:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0064-y

article_title: Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure
citation: Manu Kapur, Janan Saba and Ido Roll. (2023). Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure. npj Science of Learning 8:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00165-y
title: Productive Failure: problem-solving before instruction as a subset of PS-I designs
description: Productive Failure is an instructional sequence in which "students generate representations and solutions to a novel problem that targets a concept they have not learned yet prior to receiving instruction on the same topic." It comprises a generation and exploration phase, where students in groups generate multiple Representations and Solution Methods (RSMs) without scaffolds, followed by a consolidation and knowledge assembly phase in which the teacher compares student-generated RSMs with canonical solutions. PF is "a subset of the PS-I design" and is "intentionally designed to result in failure in problem-solving" so that failure prepares students to learn the target concepts.
requirements: A generation and exploration phase in which students generate multiple RSMs in groups before instruction
A consolidation phase where the teacher contrasts student-generated RSMs with canonical solutions
constraints: Most student-generated solutions are not complete in mathematical validity, efficiency, or generalizability; failure is expected by design
target_learning_goals: Deep conceptual understanding of challenging math concepts such as average speed and standard deviation
examples: In both studies, students worked in triads on a complex problem for two periods with no scaffolds, then received whole-class consolidation instruction and practiced isomorphic problems.
key_sources: Manu Kapur, Janan Saba and Ido Roll. (2023). Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure. npj Science of Learning 8:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00165-y

article_title: The precision of attention selection during reward learning influences the mechanisms of value-driven attention
citation: Oudeng Jia, Qingsong Tan, Sihan Zhang, Ke Jia & Mengyuan Gong. (2025). The precision of attention selection during reward learning influences the mechanisms of value-driven attention. npj Science of Learning 10:49. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00342-1
title: Precision-of-selection account of value-driven relational attention
description: This account holds that how reward-associated stimuli are represented during learning depends on the precision of attentional selection the training task demands. The article states that "when the learning task required only coarse selection (e.g., singleton search or feature search among dissimilar items), a relational code for reward-associated feature was formed. However, whenﬁne selection was necessary (e.g., feature search among similar items), a more precise feature code was utilized." Search mode and stimulus similarity jointly determine selection precision, so neither alone explains whether learned value generalizes via feature relationships or exact feature values. The account links value-driven attention theories with visual search theories in which relational coding is a typical guidance format.
requirements: A training task whose selection demands (search mode plus target-distractor similarity) determine whether coarse or fine selection is required
A subsequent test task able to dissociate feature-value matching from feature-relationship matching of distractors
constraints: Findings were obtained in simplified visual search contexts; the authors state generalizability to naturalistic viewing conditions requires further investigation
No direct, continuous measure of attentional precision was used; the article calls for future work employing such measures
The specific neural mechanisms by which reward modulates relation-based attention remain unclear
target_learners: Adult participants in visual search and reward-learning experiments
target_learning_goals: Value-driven attentional priority for reward-associated stimuli and generalization of learned reward contingencies to novel stimuli
examples: Experiments 1a and 1b (singleton search) and Experiment 2a (feature search among dissimilar items) showed relational reward effects, while Experiment 2c (feature search among similar items) did not
key_sources: Oudeng Jia, Qingsong Tan, Sihan Zhang, Ke Jia & Mengyuan Gong. (2025). The precision of attention selection during reward learning influences the mechanisms of value-driven attention. npj Science of Learning 10:49. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00342-1

article_title: Psychological proximity improves reasoning in academic aptitude tests
citation: Britt Hadar, Maayan Katzir, Sephi Pumpian, Tzur Karelitz and Nira Liberman. (2023). Psychological proximity improves reasoning in academic aptitude tests. npj Science of Learning 8:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00158-x
title: Test developers should pre-test question materials so content is not psychologically closer to some examinees than to others
description: The article recommends that cognitive-test developers treat the psychological distance of question content as a designable property rather than a neutral one. It argues that "some differences in a person 's distance to test items may also depend on social group", since culture-specific entities feel close to some examinees and alien to others. Developers should therefore "take into account the demographic and socioeconomic characteristics of examinees" and "try to construct questions that do not create or amplify differences in level of achievement that are based on these differences", via pre-testing and tailoring content.
requirements: Access to examinee demographics or pre-test panels to judge whether items invoke proximal or distal content for the target population
constraints: Psychological distance to test items is idiosyncratic, depending on familiarity, knowledge and exposure, so calibration is population-specific
target_learners: Examinees taking high-stakes academic aptitude and cognitive assessment tests
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of verbal reasoning ability without distance-based cultural bias
examples: The authors propose pre-testing materials and tailoring content to avoid making it psychologically closer to some examinees than to others, noting the bias would impact low-scoring examinees in particular.
key_sources: Britt Hadar, Maayan Katzir, Sephi Pumpian, Tzur Karelitz and Nira Liberman. (2023). Psychological proximity improves reasoning in academic aptitude tests. npj Science of Learning 8:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00158-x

article_title: Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far
citation: Genevieve McArthur and Anne Castles. (2017). Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far. npj Science of Learning (2017) 2:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0008-3
title: Proximal and distal causal schema for reading difficulties
description: The article proposes organising the causes of reading difficulties along a proximal/distal axis. A proximal cause is "a component of the cognitive system that directly and immediately produces that reading behaviour", while "a distal cause has a distant (i.e., an indirect or delayed) impact on a reading behaviour". The schema is used to categorise comorbidities as proximal or distal, to clarify reciprocal causal relationships between reading and self-concept, and to divide interventions into proximal (e.g., phonics, vocabulary training) and distal (e.g., coloured lenses) types.
requirements: Causal hypotheses generated by the schema must ultimately be tested through experimental training studies, as the authors state.
constraints: The authors present the schema as a simplifying tool for "almost overwhelming complexity", not as established causal knowledge.
target_learning_goals: word reading accuracy
reading fluency
reading comprehension
examples: The article uses the schema to explain how a history of poor vocabulary understanding may reduce motivation to read (distal), impairing letter-sound learning (proximal) and word reading.
key_sources: Genevieve McArthur and Anne Castles. (2017). Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far. npj Science of Learning (2017) 2:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0008-3

article_title: Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue
citation: Long, Y., Luo, H. & Zhang, Y. (2024). Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue. npj Science of Learning 9:60. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00273-3
title: Productive classroom dialogue framework: Alexander's five characteristics, exploratory talk, and accountable talk
description: The article organises classroom dialogue research around socio-cultural views of learning as socially mediated, and identifies consensus features of productive dialogue. Alexander's characteristics hold that classroom dialogue should be "collective, with participants reaching a shared understanding", "reciprocal", "supportive", "cumulative" and "purposeful". Littleton and Mercer distinguish disputational, cumulative and exploratory student–student talk, with exploratory talk regarded as most educationally effective, and accountable talk encompasses accountability to the learning community, standards of reasoning, and knowledge.
requirements: A generally participative ethos with participants respecting and listening to all ideas, making discourse norms accessible to all
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking, reasoning, collaborative problem-solving through dialogic pedagogy
examples: The authors drew on these frameworks, especially Hennessy et al.'s coding scheme, when constructing their revised 15-category coding scheme
key_sources: Long, Y., Luo, H. & Zhang, Y. (2024). Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue. npj Science of Learning 9:60. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00273-3

article_title: The Evolution of Research on Digital Education
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z
title: Probabilistic approaches to pedagogical decision-making replace declarative tutoring knowledge
description: Tutoring knowledge, once stored in declarative formats such as production rules, evolved towards probabilistic approaches that represent what the system needs to choose between learning activities, following Self's slogan 'do not diagnose what you cannot treat'. The article notes these approaches take advantage of MOOC participant numbers and that Markov models capture learning-process dynamics. It asks whether empirically acquired pedagogical expertise is more effective than symbolically elicited laws such as aptitude-treatment interactions.
requirements: A sufficient number of learners must have used the system for the algorithms to become reliable
constraints: The cold start problem: these algorithms only become reliable when a sufficient number of learners have used the system
Whether probabilistic expertise is more effective than elicited pedagogical knowledge is posed as an open question
target_learning_goals: adaptive instructional decisions at run time
examples: Bayesian networks for learner modelling appeared in the early nineties and continued to grow
key_sources: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z

article_title: How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences
citation: Eglington, L.G., Pavlik, P.I. (2022). How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00296-0
title: Prior Error Valence (PEV) feature for learner models
description: PEV is a model feature the authors introduce for adaptive instructional systems: "PEV is a recency-weighted cumulative moving average of the signed model error on all prior trials for the student". Signed error is the model's predicted correctness probability minus the student's binary response, and errors are downweighted with an exponential smoothing kernel using a decay parameter. Unlike the proportional-decay feature it adapts from Galyardt and Goldin, PEV takes model error rather than binary correctness as input and does not require ghost attempts.
requirements: Requires prior correctness outcomes and prior learner model predictions, data the authors note is frequently available in AIS already
constraints: PEV tracks systematic error from any source, including possible model misspecification, which the authors say makes its effects differ from proportional decay
target_learners: students in adaptive instructional systems without prior individual parameter estimates
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of student knowledge and mastery for practice sequencing
examples: Implemented as EPFA, a PFA model plus PEV, and evaluated on six datasets with student-stratified 10-fold cross-validation
key_sources: Eglington, L.G., Pavlik, P.I. (2022). How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00296-0

article_title: Care - Making the Affective Leap: More Than a Concerned Interest in a Learner's Cognitive Abilities
citation: Bridget Cooper. (2003). Care - Making the Affective Leap: More Than a Concerned Interest in a Learner's Cognitive Abilities. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.3-9. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197311
title: Profound empathy as the affective core of care in learning systems
description: The article proposes profound empathy as the construct through which care should be understood in intelligent learning systems. It 'reflects on the association of profound empathy with care and in what ways the systems described in this issue illustrate features of profound empathy'. The construct functions as a benchmark: systems can be examined for whether they exhibit the features of profound empathy that caring human educators display, and the article uses it to diagnose what the issue's systems achieve and what they lack.
requirements: Assessment of a system's care requires examining it against the features of profound empathy
constraints: The systems reviewed only partially instantiate the construct, showing 'some features of profound empathy'
target_learners: learners interacting with intelligent tutoring and learning systems
target_learning_goals: affective engagement and caring relationships in learning
examples: The commentary reviews the intelligent learning systems in the same journal issue for features of profound empathy
key_sources: Bridget Cooper. (2003). Care - Making the Affective Leap: More Than a Concerned Interest in a Learner's Cognitive Abilities. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.3-9. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197311

article_title: Teaching a Conversational Agent using Natural Language: Effect on Learning and Engagement
citation: Rachel Love, Edith Law, Philip R. Cohen, Dana Kulić. (2025). Teaching a Conversational Agent using Natural Language: Effect on Learning and Engagement. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00461-1
title: Protégé Effect framing for teachable agents
description: The Protégé Effect is "a pedagogical phenomenon in which the student is likely to invest more in learning the material when it is for the beneﬁt of the agent". When a teachable agent occupies the novice role, students synthesise information better and adapt teaching based on the tutee's performance, which may lead to positive cognitive outcomes. Teachable agents additionally offer unlimited attention and tolerate incorrect teaching without harm to their own outcomes.
requirements: An agent framed as a novice learner for the student to teach
target_learners: students in classroom or remote settings
target_learning_goals: increased engagement and investment in learning material through teaching
examples: The Curiosity Notebook study framed teaching as helping agents Alpha and Gamma prepare for a test to establish motivation to teach well
key_sources: Rachel Love, Edith Law, Philip R. Cohen, Dana Kulić. (2025). Teaching a Conversational Agent using Natural Language: Effect on Learning and Engagement. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00461-1

article_title: Automated Gaze-Based Identification of Students’ Strategies in Histogram Tasks through an Interpretable Mathematical Model and a Machine Learning Algorithm
citation: Boels, L., Garcia Moreno-Esteva, E., Bakker, A., & Drijvers, P. (2024). Automated Gaze-Based Identification of Students' Strategies in Histogram Tasks through an Interpretable Mathematical Model and a Machine Learning Algorithm. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 931-973. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00368-9
title: Prefer interpretable models over black-box machine learning when strategy identification must be transparent to educational researchers
description: The article argues that when automated classification must be understood by educational researchers, an interpretable model built directly from the data is preferable to a black-box MLA. The authors note that "the disadvantage of many MLAs is that they are effectively like black boxes that do not reveal how they identify the results from the data," whereas an interpretable model "captures the most important characteristics of the strategy, in a way that can be understood by human beings and that is transparent." They used the MLA only as a baseline for the IMM.
requirements: Prior qualitative or theoretical insight into the task-specific strategies to guide model construction
Sufficient data quality for the model to classify strategies from raw gaze data
constraints: A white-box model built a priori risks relevant information in the eye-movement data being overlooked because it is based on human assumptions, not on data
target_learning_goals: Automated identification of students' task-specific strategies for estimating the mean from histograms
examples: The authors compared a random forest MLA baseline with their interpretable mathematical model and reported the IMM was transparent, performed well, and was theoretically meaningful
key_sources: Boels, L., Garcia Moreno-Esteva, E., Bakker, A., & Drijvers, P. (2024). Automated Gaze-Based Identification of Students' Strategies in Histogram Tasks through an Interpretable Mathematical Model and a Machine Learning Algorithm. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 931-973. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00368-9

article_title: BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics
citation: Dzikovska, M., Steinhauser, N., Farrow, E., Moore, J., & Campbell, G. (2014). BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24, 284–332. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0017-9
title: Predict-Verify-Evaluate (PVE) cycle combining prediction, simulation testing, and reflective explanation
description: PVE is the lesson-level instructional pattern used across most of the BEETLE II curriculum. Students predict a circuit's behavior and explain the prediction, test it in the simulator, compare outcome to prediction, and when predictions fail they are "asked to try and generate an explanation for the behavior of the circuit that they just observed" — a flow the authors call the "“Predict-Verify-Evaluate” strategy (PVE)". It is designed to encourage deep thinking about observed phenomena and inference of underlying explanatory principles, rather than misconception-specific remediation dialogues.
requirements: A simulation environment in which students can build circuits and observe behavior
Tutorial dialogue support for the prediction and reflection steps
constraints: Most, not all, of the curriculum is set up in this manner
target_learners: students learning basic electricity and electronics concepts
target_learning_goals: self-explanation of observed phenomena
conceptual change away from naïve circuit misconceptions
examples: For each topic students predict, build and observe circuits in the simulator, evaluate whether results matched predictions, and complete a reflection dialogue when predictions were not realized
key_sources: Dzikovska, M., Steinhauser, N., Farrow, E., Moore, J., & Campbell, G. (2014). BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24, 284–332. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0017-9

article_title: Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times
citation: Pelánek, R., & Jarušek, P. (2015). Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0048-x
title: Problem Solving Tutor — web-based adaptive practice system recommending problems by predicted solving time
description: A free web-based tutoring system (tutor.fi.muni.cz) providing computerized adaptive practice focused on the outer loop of tutoring. "The tutor contains 30 types of problems (more than 1400 specific problem instances) mainly from areas of programming, mathematics, and logic puzzles." It estimates each student's skill from past attempts, predicts solving times, and recommends two problems per step — one harder, one easier — using a linear scoring function over expected time, randomness, and prior attempts. Students see personalized time predictions and post-solution comparisons with peers, adding a game-like competitive element. The system is used in more than 20 schools with more than 10 000 registered users and data from more than 400 000 solved problems.
requirements: A gradual-start approach with initial difficulty estimates added as artificial users to handle the cold start problem, running a simplified model until richer models predict better
constraints: The system focuses solely on the outer loop of tutoring (problem ordering), not on within-problem hints or step-level tutoring
target_learners: university and high school students in more than 20 schools
target_learning_goals: problem solving practice in programming, mathematics, and logic puzzles at suitable difficulty
examples: Problem types include graphs and functions, linear transformations, robot programming, standard programming, finite automata, and logic puzzles such as Sudoku and Sokoban
key_sources: Pelánek, R., & Jarušek, P. (2015). Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0048-x

article_title: Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement
citation: Bhimdiwala, A., Neri, R. C., & Gomez, L. M. (2022). Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00278-8
title: Embed practical measures into daily practice to assess AIEd adaptations
description: The article recommends practical measures—"metrics of process data about what happens in a classroom" (e.g., transitions, instructional shifts, class discussion)—aligned to a driver diagram, to indicate whether changes and adaptations are driving the improvement aim. Because teachers are overburdened, "practical measures are interwoven into daily practice to support teachers' efforts to assess if and how adaptations to the system result in improvement," opening the black box of AIEd systems for users.
requirements: Alignment with a working theory of practice improvement (driver diagram)
Measures that do not overburden teachers, since they "rarely have the time needed" for extra measurement work
constraints: The article notes measurement has too often been used to forge inequality; in an improvement context it becomes a tool for iterative progress
target_learning_goals: Assessing whether AIEd adaptations improve instruction
key_sources: Bhimdiwala, A., Neri, R. C., & Gomez, L. M. (2022). Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00278-8

article_title: Looking Ahead to Select Tutorial Actions: A Decision-Theoretic Approach
citation: R. Charles Murray, Kurt Vanlehn, Jack Mostow. (2004). Looking Ahead to Select Tutorial Actions: A Decision-Theoretic Approach. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197308
title: Prototype action selection engines for calculus and elementary reading
description: The article built "prototype action selection engines for diverse domains – calculus and elementary reading" to illustrate its decision-theoretic approach. The two engines span very different learner populations and subject matters, showing the approach's intended breadth. Each engine uses the article's rich tutorial state model and was evaluated with simulated students rather than in a complete tutoring system.
requirements: Domain-specific models of the tutorial state for each subject area
constraints: Neither engine had been integrated into a complete ITS at the time of the study
target_learning_goals: tutorial action selection in mathematics and reading
examples: The engines employ a rich model of the tutorial state including knowledge, attention, affect, next actions, task progress and discourse state
key_sources: R. Charles Murray, Kurt Vanlehn, Jack Mostow. (2004). Looking Ahead to Select Tutorial Actions: A Decision-Theoretic Approach. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197308

article_title: Complexity and Difficulty of Items in Learning Systems
citation: Pelánek, R., Effenberger, T., & Čechák, J. (2022). Complexity and Difficulty of Items in Learning Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00252-4
title: Pragmatic distinction between complexity and difficulty measures based on data source
description: The article proposes a pragmatic distinction between complexity and difficulty measures for well-structured problems in learning systems: "a complexity measure is based only on the item description, it does not use any data about student performance; a difficulty measure is based only on data about student performance". Complexity is "an intrinsic item characteristic" concerned with the structure of the item, while difficulty describes how hard the item is for students. The authors acknowledge that context, biases, and scaffoldings make the distinction "more convoluted", so measures "end up lying on a spectrum rather than at two clear poles".
requirements: Items must be well-structured problems with clear instructions and an objective solution that can be checked algorithmically
constraints: The distinction is a pragmatic simplification; aspects like the role of context, biases, and scaffoldings make the distinction between complexity and difficulty more convoluted
target_learning_goals: Appropriate sequencing of learning items
Accurate student modeling
key_sources: Pelánek, R., Effenberger, T., & Čechák, J. (2022). Complexity and Difficulty of Items in Learning Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00252-4

article_title: Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age
citation: Ken Koedinger. (2024). Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00350-5
title: From prediction to causal models: AIED research should move from diagnosis to remedy rather than stopping at prediction
description: This account explains a perceived failure mode of current AIED research and prescribes its remedy. Its core claim is that "Real problems bring up causal inference which none of these machine learning systems do, they just do correlation." The framework holds that biases inherent in data sets processed in a correlational way get reflected in system decisions, and that opening up the black box to build better causal models lets research move from diagnosis to remedy — from identifying injustices and inequities to moving forward toward justices. The article uses it to argue that papers stopping at prediction mean the field has lost its way.
requirements: New research on causal inference and attention to bias in a deep way
Community support for work that takes the next steps beyond prediction
constraints: The author acknowledges some progress has been made on building systems that make inferences about cause, but says there is still much to be found in that area
target_learners: Students and schools meant to benefit from AIED research moving to remedies
target_learning_goals: Improving education by moving from diagnosing learner states to selecting and acting on remedies
examples: The author cites John Self's statement that a key theme of AI in education is to build systems that care, and recalls 1990s work in highly diverse urban schools motivated by social justice concerns
key_sources: Ken Koedinger. (2024). Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00350-5

article_title: Implementation and use of Simulated Students for Test and Validation of new Adaptive Educational Systems: a Practical Insight
citation: Fabiano Dorça. (2015). Implementation and use of Simulated Students for Test and Validation of new Adaptive Educational Systems: a Practical Insight. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0037-0
title: Probabilistic learning styles model based on FSLSM dimensions
description: The article treats FSLSM learning-style tendencies as probabilities, called student's probabilistic learning styles (LSp), representing "the probability of preference for each learning style by a specific student." Each of the four FSLSM dimensions (processing, perception, input, understanding) holds a probability pair summing to 1; learning style combinations are stochastically selected per session via roulette wheel selection, and LSp is updated by reinforcement learning as the process evolves. The model can be initialized by cold start (0.50) or from Index of Learning Styles Questionnaire results divided by 11.
requirements: LSp values must maintain consistent probability distributions within each dimension when updated
constraints: The student model is restricted to learning styles and based on FSLSM, though the article notes it could have been realized with other learning styles theories
target_learning_goals: content personalization through learning-style adaptation
examples: Table 1 shows an example LSp with values such as 0.35 Active / 0.65 Reflective
key_sources: Fabiano Dorça. (2015). Implementation and use of Simulated Students for Test and Validation of new Adaptive Educational Systems: a Practical Insight. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0037-0

article_title: Discovering technology-aided possibilities for automatic analysis of science teacher questions
citation: Lehesvuori, S., Urrutia, F., Heilala, V., Araya, R., & Hämäläinen, R. (2026). Discovering technology-aided possibilities for automatic analysis of science teacher questions. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10545-3
title: Prompt engineering techniques for LLM-based classroom discourse analysis
description: The article describes a framework of prompting techniques — Vanilla, Chain of Thought, and Self-Ask — applied with zero-shot and few-shot strategies to detect teacher questions from ASR outputs. "Recent advancements have introduced techniques to enhance response quality, such as Chain of Thought (CoT) (Lee et al., 2024) and Self-Ask (SA) (Press et al., 2023)." Self-Ask "explicitly introduces intermediate sub-questions that guide the model through each reasoning step." The framework frames prompt engineering as "designing effective prompts to elicit desired responses from LLMs, crucial for instructing models in specific tasks."
requirements: Carefully crafted prompts paired with human validation
constraints: The number of shots was set to five, as research suggests that using more examples leads to only limited improvements in performance
target_learning_goals: Automatic detection of teacher questions in classroom discourse
examples: Vanilla zero-shot and Self-Ask prompts tested on Finnish ASR outputs with context sentences before and after the target sentence
key_sources: Lehesvuori, S., Urrutia, F., Heilala, V., Araya, R., & Hämäläinen, R. (2026). Discovering technology-aided possibilities for automatic analysis of science teacher questions. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10545-3

article_title: Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education
citation: Sun, C., Major, L., Daltry, R., Obradovic, L., & Friedberg, A. (2026). Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10703-1
title: Prescriptive grouped dashboard design with action-oriented category labels
description: The Grouped Dashboard categorised learners into three groups based on the same ranking calculation as the List Dashboard, using labels designed to adopt 'prescriptive' language which prompts specific pedagogical action: 'practised enough', 'keep going' and 'need more practice'. The category labels echoed categorisations made by teachers themselves, identified in prior design-based research as 'fast learners', 'time-takers' and those in between. Both dashboard designs featured brief explanatory text and a clean user interface following guidelines for low visualisation-literate users.
requirements: Dashboard design should strike an effective balance between supporting teachers' awareness in their classroom and informing their decision-making more directly.
constraints: The pedagogical purpose of the dashboard was limited to the digital learning environment, specifically supporting teachers' distribution of the DPL tool amongst learners rather than directly informing classroom teaching practices.
target_learners: Teachers of early-years learners in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: Supporting teachers' pedagogical decision-making in distributing DPL tools
key_sources: Sun, C., Major, L., Daltry, R., Obradovic, L., & Friedberg, A. (2026). Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10703-1

article_title: Promoting preservice teachers’ multiperspective professional vision in virtual learning environments – On the effects of modeling videos and prompts during video-based lesson analysis
citation: Janeczko, J. M., Lehmkuhl, A., Junker, R., Zucker, V., Meschede, N., & Holodynski, M. (2026). Promoting preservice teachers' multiperspective professional vision in virtual learning environments – On the effects of modeling videos and prompts during video-based lesson analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10546-2
title: Professional vision as a situation-specific skill mediating between professional knowledge and teaching actions
description: The article defines professional vision (PV) as teachers' ability to notice and reason about relevant classroom events based on their professional knowledge. According to the model of competence as a continuum, PV is a situation-specific skill that mediates between teachers' professional knowledge and their teaching actions. The article identifies four facets of PV: description, interpretation, evaluation, and generation of alternative teaching actions.
requirements: PV development requires structured opportunities to apply professional knowledge to authentic classroom situations, such as through video-based analysis.
target_learning_goals: noticing and reasoning about relevant classroom events
key_sources: Janeczko, J. M., Lehmkuhl, A., Junker, R., Zucker, V., Meschede, N., & Holodynski, M. (2026). Promoting preservice teachers' multiperspective professional vision in virtual learning environments – On the effects of modeling videos and prompts during video-based lesson analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10546-2

article_title: Use of graphs in air force teaching materials
citation: Research Abstracts. (1953). https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Match chart type to the graphic problem: preferred charts for common graphic problems
description: The monograph gives design guidance pairing graph types with the kind of comparison a chart must show. The abstract reports: "The preferred charts for several of the common graphic problems are given: (a) Simple comparisons---multiple bars and pictograph. (b) A whole and its parts--divided bar, divided circle, cosmograph, and pictograph." Similar pairings are given for multiple comparisons, loss and gain comparisons, and frequency.
requirements: The designer must first identify which of the common graphic problems (simple comparison, whole and parts, multiple comparison, loss and gain, frequency, narrative) the chart addresses.
target_learning_goals: choosing effective graph formats for instructional displays
examples: For frequency problems the preferred charts are multiple bars and line graph; for loss and gain comparisons, multiple bars, line graph, composite bars, and pictograph.
key_sources: Research Abstracts. (1953). https://eric.ed.gov/

article_title: Contextualized-OLPC education project in rural India: measuring learning impact and mediation of computer self-efficacy
citation: Ale, K., Loh, Y. A.-C., & Chib, A. (2017). Contextualized-OLPC education project in rural India: measuring learning impact and mediation of computer self-efficacy. Education Tech Research Dev, 65, 769–794. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9517-2
title: Prioritize local contexts during technology implementation design to attain educational impact
description: The article recommends that implementers "prioritize local contexts during technology implementation design in order to attain educational impact in terms of improved learning outcomes for students." This principle directs attention away from affordable hardware provision alone and toward deeply contextualized implementation design that considers user-level psychological mechanisms.
requirements: Implementation design must attend to contextually germane factors such as teacher training, unbiased gender access, and local language use.
constraints: The article argues this applies where mere deployment of laptops has limited relevance to children in use and outcome.
target_learners: primary school students in rural developing-country contexts
target_learning_goals: improved learning outcomes
functional literacy
examples: The Contextualized-OLPC project addressed teacher training, unbiased gender access, and local language use in nine rural Indian primary schools.
key_sources: Ale, K., Loh, Y. A.-C., & Chib, A. (2017). Contextualized-OLPC education project in rural India: measuring learning impact and mediation of computer self-efficacy. Education Tech Research Dev, 65, 769–794. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9517-2

article_title: The relative effectiveness of differing commentaries in an animated film on elementary meteorology
citation: Nelson, H. E. and Vandermeer, A. W. (1955). The Relative Effectiveness of Differing Commentaries in an Animated Film on Elementary Meteorology. Technical Report SDC 269-7-43. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED016911
title: Present new or difficult terminology in both pictorial and sound elements
description: The article recommends that, based on slight differences favoring modified commentaries, it may be desirable to "present new or difficult terminology in both pictorial and sound elements". This principle directs instructional film designers to reinforce unfamiliar terms through both the visual track and the narration simultaneously.
requirements: The film must contain both pictorial and sound elements capable of carrying the same terminology.
constraints: Based on slight differences that were not statistically significant at a high level of confidence.
target_learning_goals: elementary meteorology terminology
examples: Version 4 of the film attempted to emphasize the visual element by reducing the number of words and making direct references to the visuals.
key_sources: Nelson, H. E. and Vandermeer, A. W. (1955). The Relative Effectiveness of Differing Commentaries in an Animated Film on Elementary Meteorology. Technical Report SDC 269-7-43. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED016911

article_title: Profile analysis and its effect on learning when used to shorten recorded film commentaries
citation: Fletcher, Richard M. (1955). Profile Analysis and Its Effect on Learning When Used To Shorten Recorded Film Commentaries. Technical Report SDC Z69-7-55, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Fletcher+profile+analysis+film+commentaries
title: Employ profile analysis before production to eliminate commentary material that does not contribute to learning
description: The report recommends that writers of film commentaries use profile analysis of viewer learning reports to identify and remove material that does not support learning before production, freeing time for material that does. As the report states, "profile analysis be employed by writers of film commentaries to eliminate material prior to production that does not contribute to learning so that it can be replaced with material that does." It rests on the finding that learning was equal for a much shorter profile version.
requirements: Four groups of about 32 recruits each providing continuous learning profiles by turning a knob during the commentary
constraints: Demonstrated at the commentary stage of instructional films; the report notes "It is at the commentary stage that it is most feasible to make any desired modification."
target_learners: military recruits in instructional film training
target_learning_goals: learning of information presented in instructional film commentaries
examples: The Human Reproduction commentary was shortened by judges with profiles and by judges without profiles, and the shortened versions were tested on each bit of information contained in the commentaries.
key_sources: Fletcher, Richard M. (1955). Profile Analysis and Its Effect on Learning When Used To Shorten Recorded Film Commentaries. Technical Report SDC Z69-7-55, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Fletcher+profile+analysis+film+commentaries

article_title: Profile analysis and its effect on learning when used to shorten recorded film commentaries
citation: Fletcher, Richard M. (1955). Profile Analysis and Its Effect on Learning When Used To Shorten Recorded Film Commentaries. Technical Report SDC Z69-7-55, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Fletcher+profile+analysis+film+commentaries
title: Profile technique with knob-response learning reports for shortening instructional material
description: The profile technique, developed by Twyford, collects moment-by-moment learning judgments from a viewing audience: "Each recruit turned a knob to indicate whether he was learning nothing, little, average, much, or the most he could." These profiles, obtained from four groups of 32 recruits each, guide judges in shortening film commentaries, and the report describes the technique as "much simpler and quicker to use in making an evaluation than the established method of measuring learnings with tests."
requirements: A recorded instructional material whose commentary can be modified, and a group of audience members providing knob-based learning ratings during presentation
constraints: Report notes the commentary stage is where modification is most feasible
target_learners: military recruits (profile providers); learners of instructional films
target_learning_goals: identifying which instructional material contributes to learning
examples: Four profiles were obtained from four groups of 32 recruits each for the commentaries of The Weather and Human Reproduction.

Technical Report SDC Z69-7-55, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Fletcher+profile+analysis+film+commentaries
