article_title: Introduction
citation: A Bibliography of Teaching Machines. (1960). Audiovisual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=A+Bibliography+of+Teaching+Machines
title: Success of teaching machines depends primarily on program quality, since building a device is easier than writing its program
description: The authors argue that the decisive factor in automated instruction is the instructional material, not the hardware: "The success or failure of teaching machines surely will depend upon the programs produced for them." They observe that "It obviously is easier to build a gadget than it is to write a program for it." They also note that although commercial devices are becoming more sophisticated, "all these devices are merely implementations of methods or principles," which motivates the catalogs of devices and machines included in the bibliography.
requirements: Substantial effort must go into writing carefully worked programs of items on which students succeed a high percentage of the time
constraints: The authors state program effort is expanding rapidly, so any catalog of programs is necessarily incomplete
target_learners: students using teaching machines from elementary grades through adult education
target_learning_goals: subject-matter learning delivered through programmed instruction
examples: Table 1 lists older experimental programs by investigator and subject; Table 2 lists program development in progress in early 1960
key_sources: A Bibliography of Teaching Machines. (1960). Audiovisual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=A+Bibliography+of+Teaching+Machines

article_title: Generative AI as a cognitive partner: personalised GPTs and differentiated learning in undergraduate teacher education
citation: Jason Zagami. (2026). Generative AI as a cognitive partner: personalised GPTs and differentiated learning in undergraduate teacher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10746-4
title: Prompt–Reflect–Refine cycle as a model for AI-mediated dialogic learning
description: The Prompt–Reflect–Refine cycle is the study's structured pedagogical routine for AI-mediated learning: students formulate a prompt, evaluate the AI response against pedagogical frameworks (TPACK and AITSL Standards), then modify their artefact or prompt and document reasoning. The article states "the prompt initiates cognitive activation, reflection triggers evaluation, and refinement consolidates learning". It operationalises dialogic metacognition, constrains interaction away from one-shot querying, and creates analysable traces of metacognitive regulation across successive prompts and artefacts.
requirements: Students must explicitly evaluate AI outputs against nominated pedagogical frameworks rather than accept them
Weekly tasks structured around the three-cycle steps with documented reasoning
constraints: Replication should focus on reproducing the pedagogical workflow rather than an immutable underlying language model, since OpenAI periodically updates foundation models
target_learners: pre-service secondary teachers in Initial Teacher Education
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of Digital Technologies curriculum
pedagogical reasoning and lesson design
metacognitive regulation
critical AI literacy
examples: Students completed weekly Prompt–Reflect–Refine tasks within the Canvas LMS, with reflection prompts requiring evaluation against TPACK and AITSL Standards
key_sources: Jason Zagami. (2026). Generative AI as a cognitive partner: personalised GPTs and differentiated learning in undergraduate teacher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10746-4

article_title: Analyzing properties of success for assessment development in maker-based learning
citation: Kailea Saplan · Sam Abramovich · Peter Wardrip. (2024). Analyzing properties of success for assessment development in maker-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10286-1
title: The five Properties of Success framework for unpacking definitions of success in maker-based learning
description: The Properties of Success framework decomposes any definition of success in maker-based learning into five underlying properties: Subject of Success, Guiding Metaphor of Success, Timescale for Success, Data for Success, and Audience for Success. It emerged when the authors realized their five interview themes were "not an exhaustive list of overarching categories of success, but rather underlying features within a definition of success." Each property carries design assertions, such as that many different stakeholders can be the subject of success, not just the participating patron.
requirements: Educators articulate a definition of success for their program before selecting or designing an assessment
constraints: Derived from a small qualitative sample of 17 staff and educators in two public library systems; the tools built on it have not undergone extensive testing
target_learners: library staff and maker educators in public library makerspaces
target_learning_goals: assessment design and evaluation of maker-based learning programs
examples: The framework's properties structure the petal diagram at the center of the Properties of Success Analysis Tool
key_sources: Kailea Saplan · Sam Abramovich · Peter Wardrip. (2024). Analyzing properties of success for assessment development in maker-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10286-1

article_title: Addressing students’ emotional needs during the COVID-19 pandemic: a perspective on text versus video feedback in online environments
citation: Regina Kaplan-Rakowski. (2021). Addressing students' emotional needs during the COVID-19 pandemic: a perspective on text versus video feedback in online environments. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09897-9
title: During times of crisis, educators should prioritize emotional support and wellness over instructional efficiency, shifting to a more affective approach such as video for communication and feedback
description: The article argues that although teaching and learning efficiency should always be a concern, the pandemic increased the importance of emotional learning, mental health, and wellness, so instructors should reevaluate priorities. Its key message is that "educators should shift to a more affective approach during times of crisis, and one way to do this is by implementing video for communication and feedback". This may come at the expense of instructional efficiency.
requirements: Instructors must recognize crisis conditions such as social isolation and mental stress that accompany a pandemic
constraints: The article states video feedback is not a panacea for any learning scenario and feedback type should be selected with respect to situational principles
target_learning_goals: emotional support and mental wellness
social presence in online learning
examples: The article recommends implementing synchronous and asynchronous video for communication and feedback, noting asynchronous video allows flexibility in timing and longer reflection on assignments
key_sources: Regina Kaplan-Rakowski. (2021). Addressing students' emotional needs during the COVID-19 pandemic: a perspective on text versus video feedback in online environments. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09897-9

article_title: Reflective comments on shifting to digital
citation: J. Michael Spector, Phil Harris. (2021). Reflective comments on shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09961-y
title: Use prior published research, rather than a particular pedagogical or technological approach, to inform responses to rapid shifts to digitally intensive learning
description: The article describes a deliberate, well-reasoned editorial process in which scholars examined recently published research from multiple perspectives and contexts to identify what might be applied when educators must make a sudden shift to digitally-based learning. Its focus was "on what has been established by prior research that can help in this situation and similar situations that might arise in the future", rather than on COVID-19 or any single approach. The article uses this principle to organize a special issue of reflective commentaries on flexible learning.
requirements: Identify and examine recently published research applicable to the shift situation, gathered from multiple countries, cultures, perspectives, and situations
constraints: The article states the focus was not on COVID-19 and not on a particular pedagogical or technological approach
target_learners: educators required to make a sudden shift to digitally-based learning and instruction
target_learning_goals: informing practice and improving instruction during rapid shifts to digitally-based learning
examples: The editors and editorial boards of a special issue on flexible learning asked a group of scholars to examine selected recently published papers from various points of view to identify what might be applied in the current situation and what might inform future research.
key_sources: J. Michael Spector, Phil Harris. (2021). Reflective comments on shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09961-y

article_title: The iBuddy experience: A digital simulation-based approach to enhance secondary school students’ privacy awareness
citation: Luca Botturi, Tiffany Fioroni, Chiara Beretta, Davide Andreoletti, Alessandro Ferrari, Felipe Cardoso, Anna Picco-Schwendener, Suzanna Marazza, Silvia Giordano. (2024). The iBuddy experience: A digital simulation-based approach to enhance secondary school students' privacy awareness. Education Tech Research Dev 72. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10309-x
title: Three interpretations of the privacy paradox guiding instructional design
description: Drawing on Kokolakis (2017), the article organizes the privacy paradox—the inconsistency between stated privacy concerns and observed behavior—into three interpretations: (1) surveys are the wrong methodology and most people have only vague concerns, so behavior should be monitored; (2) users lack information about how their data are captured, stored and used, so invisible data flows should be made visible; (3) the paradox exists as a positive privacy vs. utility trade-off. The authors used these interpretations to determine their instructional approach, translating them into letting participants experience first-hand the exposure of data they were unaware of having exposed.
requirements: Awareness interventions should address factual knowledge of how technologies operate, not only lists of do's and don'ts
Relevance must be tied to personal situations where sensitivity and visibility of data are at stake
constraints: The theoretical debate on the existence of the privacy paradox is still open; different interpretations may explain different users
Conceptualizing privacy risks is inherently challenging, depending on technical, cultural and subjective factors
target_learning_goals: privacy awareness
informed decisions about personal data disclosure
examples: The iBuddy wow effect was designed by provoking students with data that are highly sensitive, difficult to extract, and not frequently exposed
key_sources: Luca Botturi, Tiffany Fioroni, Chiara Beretta, Davide Andreoletti, Alessandro Ferrari, Felipe Cardoso, Anna Picco-Schwendener, Suzanna Marazza, Silvia Giordano. (2024). The iBuddy experience: A digital simulation-based approach to enhance secondary school students' privacy awareness. Education Tech Research Dev 72. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10309-x

article_title: Understanding students’ game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game
citation: Phuong Bui, Gabriela Rodríguez-Aflecht, Boglárka Brezovszky, Minna M. Hannula-Sormunen, Samuli Laato, Erno Lehtinen. (2020). Understanding students' game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09755-8
title: Serious game designers should prioritize usability and interface clarity, and design reward systems so players can see and own their transformations
description: Based on the NNG developmental evidence, the article recommends that designers focus effort on usability and clarity of the user interface in addition to educational content, and that reward mechanisms be designed so players visibly construct and own their game world. The article concludes that "improvement in game's usability and clarity in the user interface were effective in providing more positive, smooth and immersive game experiences for players". It also stresses paying attention to "the integration of meaningful use of extrinsic game elements" to maintain players' interest and motivation.
requirements: Designers must attend to how reward systems and motivating mechanisms are designed, since the same functional rewards produced different experiences depending on whether players could see and take part in the transformation
constraints: The article notes that not all motivating elements have the intended impacts on students' gaming experiences, and that further work is needed to investigate the exact value extrinsic elements add
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement and motivation in mathematics game-based learning
examples: NNG 2 added a number pad, visual cues, a materials bar and per-material saving, which improved game experience; NNG 4's Lighthouse Island let students construct buildings and buy ships with earned materials and coins, which students described as owning something
key_sources: Phuong Bui, Gabriela Rodríguez-Aflecht, Boglárka Brezovszky, Minna M. Hannula-Sormunen, Samuli Laato, Erno Lehtinen. (2020). Understanding students' game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09755-8

article_title: Prioritizing teacher emotions: shifting teacher training to a digital environment
citation: Owens, J.K., Hudson, A.K. (2021). Prioritizing teacher emotions: shifting teacher training to a digital environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09921-y
title: Prioritize teachers' emotional well-being and provide intervention support to increase teacher self-efficacy during the shift to digital learning
description: The commentary argues that Jarrell et al.'s findings could be "a starting place for educational stakeholders to prioritize teachers' emotional well-being and offer an opportunity to provide intervention support in order to increase teacher self-efficacy in the shift to digital and possibly reduce teacher burnout." The principle holds that emotional well-being should be treated as a priority during technology-driven changes in teaching, with intervention support offered proactively rather than after burnout or attrition occurs.
requirements: Educational stakeholders must treat teachers' emotional well-being as a priority during the digital shift
Intervention support must be available to increase teacher self-efficacy
constraints: The commentary states the reduction in burnout is possible rather than demonstrated, using the hedge "possibly reduce teacher burnout"
target_learning_goals: teacher self-efficacy
teacher emotional well-being
reduced teacher burnout
examples: The commentary frames Jarrell et al.'s findings as a starting place for stakeholders to prioritize teacher emotional well-being and offer intervention support during the shift to digital learning.
key_sources: Owens, J.K., Hudson, A.K. (2021). Prioritizing teacher emotions: shifting teacher training to a digital environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09921-y

article_title: Online professional development to support K-12 teachers’ computer science integration
citation: Lauren E. Margulieux · Brendan D. Calandra · Bryan Cox. (2026). Online professional development to support K‑12 teachers' computer science integration. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10640-z
title: Project MICRO micro-courses and ISTE integrated-CT micro-credential badges
description: Project MICRO (Micro-credentials for Integrating Computing Responsibly into Other Domains) is a set of three free, online, self-paced micro-courses of about one college credit hour each, co-created by Georgia State University, the Georgia Department of Education, and ISTE. Courses cover everyday computing, information literacy, cybersecurity, data, CT concepts (abstraction, algorithms, automation, decomposition, debugging), block-based programming, and teaching methods. Teachers can submit assignments, including lesson plans, to earn ISTE badges aligned to the Integrated CT Endorsement: "CT learner", "CT designer", and "CT facilitator".
requirements: Courses were adapted from a 3-credit-hour digital literacy and CT course in a CS endorsement program and aligned to ISTE's CT Competencies and CSTA standards, with instructions added to highlight activities that satisfy badge requirements.
constraints: Personalized support of participants was not feasible at this scale, and teachers engaged independently, potentially without social or intellectual support from peers.
target_learners: preservice and in-service K-12 teachers outside of computer science
target_learning_goals: integrating computational thinking and CS concepts into non-CS content-area instruction
examples: 215 teachers completed pre- and post-surveys; a subset of 15 teachers submitted 17 lesson plans, which were scored with a 0–3 rubric for CT and CS concepts.
key_sources: Lauren E. Margulieux · Brendan D. Calandra · Bryan Cox. (2026). Online professional development to support K‑12 teachers' computer science integration. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10640-z

article_title: Experiences of using a public key infrastructure for the preparation of examination papers
citation: David W Chadwick, Rana Tassabehji and Andrew Young. (1999). Experiences of Using a Public Key Infrastructure for the Preparation of Examination Papers. IT Institute, University of Salford. http://www.salford.ac.uk/its024/X500.htm
title: Before introducing an electronic process, profile user types and design a tailored implementation with training and education
description: The article recommends that organisational change begins with user profiling: "Before any kind of change can take place, a full assessment of the types of user in an organisation must be made." By identifying types and profiles, an implementation process can be tailored to differing needs, and stakeholders can be educated in a way that builds commitment, without which no project can succeed. Users need both software training and an appreciation of how the encryption works to avoid mistakes.
requirements: A consultative stage involving all parties, since views of the existing process differed (50% of CMS staff found it satisfactory while others found it inconvenient, slow and antiquated)
constraints: Derived from a small pilot in two computer-literate departments; results may differ in computer-naïve departments
target_learners: university staff adopting new administrative technology
target_learning_goals: commitment to and effective use of a new electronic process
examples: The pilot used in-depth interviews, questionnaires at start and end, and semi-structured observations during training to profile participants before and during rollout
key_sources: David W Chadwick, Rana Tassabehji and Andrew Young. (1999). Experiences of Using a Public Key Infrastructure for the Preparation of Examination Papers. IT Institute, University of Salford. http://www.salford.ac.uk/its024/X500.htm

article_title: The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic
citation: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University.
title: Pair practice with constant, consistent, specific and immediate feedback so that practice makes correct learning permanent
description: The dissertation argues that practice alone does not guarantee learning: "Practice does not make perfect. Practice makes permanent" (Sousa, 2006). For practice to improve learning, learners must analyse results and know what to change, so "Practice should thus be accompanied by feedback that is constant, consistent, and specific" and the effect of feedback "is also amplified if it is immediate". This principle directly shaped the intervention's interactive feedback design.
requirements: Feedback must be constant, consistent and specific to the learner's performance; immediacy amplifies its effect
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of algorithm and problem-solving skills
examples: The intervention included an "Example of immediate interactive feedback during fizzbuzz task" (Figure 3.6)
key_sources: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.09.008

article_title: Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal
citation: Pynoo, B., Tondeur, J., Van Braak, J., Duyck, W., Sijnave, B. & Duyck, P. (2012). Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1308-1317. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.026
title: Provide training, resources and safeguard ease of use to support perceived behavioral control and ease of use
description: The article recommends that policymakers and school boards introducing a voluntary educational technology address perceived behavioral control by providing training and support, and by safeguarding ease of use. It states that "Skills and knowledge can be addressed by providing training and support, but also by safeguarding the ease of use of the portal". Resources such as sufficient internet-connected computers at school and home access initiatives are also recommended.
requirements: Training and support provision to build skills and knowledge
Sufficient internet-connected computers at school
constraints: Applies to voluntary technologies that cannot be imposed on users
target_learners: Teachers in primary and secondary education
target_learning_goals: Effective use of educational technology portals for professional development
examples: The Belgian federal government's "Internet for all" and "Start to surf" initiatives providing discounted computers and internet connections
key_sources: Pynoo, B., Tondeur, J., Van Braak, J., Duyck, W., Sijnave, B. & Duyck, P. (2012). Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1308-1317. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.026

article_title: Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal
citation: Pynoo, B., Tondeur, J., Van Braak, J., Duyck, W., Sijnave, B. & Duyck, P. (2012). Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1308-1317. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.026
title: Provide content and stimulate contribution to sustain perceived usefulness
description: Because most teachers use the portal to search and download, the article recommends that policymakers and school boards provide interesting content through the portal and stimulate teachers to contribute. It notes that "policymakers/school boards could stimulate teachers to contribute, or could even provide additional interesting (yet non-essential as long as use of the portal is not mandatory) information themselves exclusively through the portal".
requirements: A critical mass of useful, relevant content available through the portal
constraints: Content should remain non-essential as long as use of the portal is not mandatory
target_learners: Teachers in primary and secondary education
target_learning_goals: Access to quality teaching materials and professional knowledge sharing
examples: KlasCement's resource-based model where members gain download points by uploading information
key_sources: Pynoo, B., Tondeur, J., Van Braak, J., Duyck, W., Sijnave, B. & Duyck, P. (2012). Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1308-1317. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.026

article_title: Analysis and discovery of procrastination patterns in a language learning MOOC
citation: Vázquez Mendoza, J. A., Ferri Ramírez, C., & Monserrat Aranda, C. (2024). Analysis and discovery of procrastination patterns in a language learning MOOC. Computers & Education, 223, 105154. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105154
title: Process mining methodology (adapted PM2) applied to MOOC event logs for discovering procrastination patterns.
description: The study employs an adapted version of the Process Mining Methodology (PM2) with seven steps, from definition of objectives to evaluation of process models, using the Disco Fluxicon software tool with an adapted Fuzzy Minner algorithm. Process mining is described as "a family of techniques based on the areas of data science and process management that provide tools to support the analysis of operational processes based on event logs." The authors note it has advantages including real-time modelling of events, modelling without a base model, easy comparison of process models, and clear visualization of behaviour.
requirements: Event logs generated by the learning platform
Software tool such as Disco Fluxicon for process model discovery
constraints: The authors note that process mining techniques remain conspicuously underutilised within the education domain despite their advantages.
target_learners: Researchers and instructors analysing MOOC user behaviour
target_learning_goals: Identifying behavioural patterns associated with course success or failure
examples: The methodology was applied to event logs from the 'Basic Spanish 1' MOOC with 96,815 active users.
key_sources: Vázquez Mendoza, J. A., Ferri Ramírez, C., & Monserrat Aranda, C. (2024). Analysis and discovery of procrastination patterns in a language learning MOOC. Computers & Education, 223, 105154. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105154

article_title: Unplugged or plugged-in programming learning: A comparative experimental study
citation: Sigayret, K., Tricot, A., & Blanc, N. (2022). Unplugged or plugged-in programming learning: A comparative experimental study. Computers and Education, 184, 104505. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104505
title: Use educational programming software such as Scratch rather than unplugged activities when teaching programming to end-of-primary students
description: The article recommends a plugged-in approach for introducing programming at the end of primary school, reporting "a positive impact of the Scratch software on learning performances that may help to convince some teachers of the need and interest to provide a plugged-in approach to programming". The ten-session sequence and assessment tests were designed so teachers can adopt either mode, but the evidence favours the software-based one.
requirements: Access to computers with Scratch 3.0 (one computer for 3–4 students in the study)
constraints: Results are specific to one audience, one school system, and sessions and tests specific to the experimental protocol; the authors note other studies with younger students or mixed approaches found different results
target_learners: Grade 5 primary school students (end of primary)
target_learning_goals: Mastery of computational concepts (algorithms, instructions, loops, conditionals, variables)
Ability to solve algorithmic problems
examples: Ten 45-minute sessions introducing algorithms, instructions, loops, conditionals and variables, with a creative project in the last four sessions
key_sources: Sigayret, K., Tricot, A., & Blanc, N. (2022). Unplugged or plugged-in programming learning: A comparative experimental study. Computers and Education, 184, 104505. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104505

article_title: Investigating the Acceptance of Mobile Library Applications with an Extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM)
citation: Rafique, H., Almagrabi, A. O., Shamim, A., Anwar, F., & Bashir, A. K. (2020). Investigating the acceptance of mobile library applications with an extended technology acceptance model (TAM). Heliyon, 6(6), e03733. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2020.e03733
title: Designers and developers of mobile library applications must prioritize habit, system quality, perceived ease of use, and perceived usefulness
description: The article recommends that developers of mobile library applications should prioritize the factors found to be significant predictors of usage intention. The authors state that "habit; system quality and perceived ease of use must be considered while promoting MLA usage" and that "developers must keep these factors and core construct of TAM (i.e. PEOU and PU) in priority for developing the application".
requirements: Understanding of the target user population's habits and system quality expectations
constraints: The recommendation is based on a study conducted in a developing country context with a specific MLA
target_learners: University students using mobile library applications
target_learning_goals: Improving user acceptance and usage of mobile library applications
key_sources: Rafique, H., Almagrabi, A. O., Shamim, A., Anwar, F., & Bashir, A. K. (2020). Investigating the acceptance of mobile library applications with an extended technology acceptance model (TAM). Heliyon, 6(6), e03733. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103732

article_title: Can teaching simulations in a virtual classroom help trainee teachers to develop oral communication skills and self-efficacy? A randomized controlled trial.
citation: Angélique Remacle, Stéphane Bouchard, Dominique Morsomme. (2023). Can teaching simulations in a virtual classroom help trainee teachers to develop oral communication skills and self-efficacy? A randomized controlled trial. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104808
title: Train oral communication skills in situations as close as possible to professional reality using VR
description: The article's findings suggest that "practicing oral communication skills in situations as close as possible to their professional reality – by using VR – can improve (trainee) teachers' belief in their ability to implement these skills in real-life situations". A virtual classroom constitutes a safe environment to practice communication skills by controlling task complexity, with stepwise training that could begin with restless pupils and progressively increase their agitation level to replicate the complexity of real school situations. This principle supports designing training that embeds skill practice in representative environmental and communicative conditions rather than decontextualized exercises.
requirements: A virtual environment representative of the professional setting, with adjustable noise and pupil agitation levels
constraints: Training in actual school situations is challenging for ethical and logistical reasons, which motivates the VR-based alternative
target_learning_goals: oral communication skills in noise
transfer of trained skills to real-life teaching situations
examples: The VirtuVox program immersed trainee teachers in a virtual classroom with 16 pupils, with noise set at 70 dBA and pupils' agitation increasing from 30% to 70% across the three sessions.
key_sources: Angélique Remacle, Stéphane Bouchard, Dominique Morsomme. (2023). Can teaching simulations in a virtual classroom help trainee teachers to develop oral communication skills and self-efficacy? A randomized controlled trial. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104808

article_title: Enhancing goal attainment in higher education with a scripted conversational agent: Effects of monitoring and reflection support in digital learning
citation: Martins van Jaarsveld, G., Wong, J., Baars, M., Specht, M., & Paas, F. (2025). Enhancing goal attainment in higher education with a scripted conversational agent: Effects of monitoring and reflection support in digital learning. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105441
title: Prioritize goal-monitoring activities in SRL interventions to support the transition from goal setting to goal striving
description: The article recommends that educators developing SRL supports prioritize goal-monitoring activities, because monitoring resulted in significant improvements in goal attainment while reflection alone did not. Implementing regular progress monitoring mechanisms is presented as an effective means of helping students remain engaged with their learning goals and supporting the transition to goal striving behaviours.
requirements: Requires a mechanism for regular progress-monitoring prompts, such as weekly check-in sessions
constraints: Reflection alone showed no immediate benefit in the short five-week intervention and may require longer periods
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
goal attainment
examples: Participants in the MO and MO+RF conditions received weekly Thursday/Friday check-in prompts asking them to discuss their progress on the goal they set earlier that week
key_sources: Martins van Jaarsveld, G., Wong, J., Baars, M., Specht, M., & Paas, F. (2025). Enhancing goal attainment in higher education with a scripted conversational agent: Effects of monitoring and reflection support in digital learning. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105441

article_title: The use of video technology for providing feedback to students: Can it enhance the feedback experience for staff and students?
citation: Crook, A., Mauchline, A., Maw, S., Lawson, C., Drinkwater, R., Lundqvist, K., Orsmond, P., Gomez, S., and Park, J. (2012). The use of video technology for providing feedback to students: can it enhance the feedback experience for staff and students? Computers & Education, 58(1), 386-396. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.08.025
title: Deliver generic video feedback promptly so students can act on it before starting their next assignment.
description: The article recommends that staff provide a rapid, generic response to all students, for example in a brief video, so students can use the information before completing their next assignment. This 'enough for now' feedback summarises what was done well and badly across the cohort while staff undertake the more time-consuming task of individual feedback. The approach addresses staff concerns about engagement, efficiency, timeliness, and quality identified in the pre-use survey.
requirements: Staff need to quickly skim-read the cohort's work to identify key points done well or badly before recording.
constraints: Generic feedback does not replace the need for individual, tailored feedback, which remains more time-consuming.
target_learning_goals: Improving future performance on subsequent assignments
Providing feed-forward information in a timely manner
examples: In the ASSET pilot, staff uploaded brief 2-3 minute generic feedback videos that students could access as soon as they were uploaded.

The use of video technology for providing feedback to students: can it enhance the feedback experience for staff and students? Computers & Education, 58(1), 386-396. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.08.025

article_title: Effectiveness of Computer-Assisted Mathematics Education (CAME) over Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Demir, S., & Başol, G. (2014). Effectiveness of Computer-Assisted Mathematics Education (CAME) over Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis Study. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 14(5), 2026-2035. http://www.edam.com.tr/estp
title: Use computer-assisted education in mathematics at every level of the education system, given the pooled positive effect
description: The authors draw a design recommendation from their meta-analytic finding that CAME has a large positive effect on mathematics achievement. They write that because "The usage of specialized software increased the positive effect of CAE on mathematics achievements", "it is possible to propose the usage of CAE in every level of the education system". The recommendation is grounded in the pooled ES = .8999 result from 40 Turkish studies.
requirements: Studies included should be experimental or quasi-experimental and contain sufficient data (means, standard deviations, group sizes) for effect size calculation
constraints: The recommendation rests on studies mostly sampled from large cities, which the authors note may limit generalizability
Some included studies reported no significant effect of CAME on academic achievement
target_learners: preschool, primary, secondary, high-school, and college students in Turkey
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
geometry achievement
examples: The meta-analysis combined 40 studies (4 PhD theses, 16 master's theses, 17 articles, and 3 technical/congressional/symposium reports) with a total sample of 5623 students, 3002 experimental and 2621 control.
key_sources: Demir, S., & Başol, G. (2014). Effectiveness of Computer-Assisted Mathematics Education (CAME) over Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis Study. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 14(5), 2026-2035. http://www.edam.com.tr/estp

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Relationship between E-Learning and Students' Academic Achievement in Higher Education
citation: Gloria Mothibi. (2015). A Meta-Analysis of the Relationship between E-Learning and Students' Academic Achievement in Higher Education. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.9. https://www.iiste.org
title: Provide adequate ICT infrastructure to facilitate e-learning in higher education, because the meta-analytic effect size indicates this can substantially improve learning and achievement
description: The article argues that because e-learning's success depends on the quality of ICT, higher education institutions should invest in adequate, well-managed ICT facilities. It states that "Considering the effect size of 0.712, it can statis tically be inferred that provision of adequate ICT infrastructure towards facilitating use of e-learning can substant ially lead improved learning and students' academic achievement." It also identifies adequate provision and better management of available ICT facilities as means to improve utilization.
requirements: Adequate supply of computer hardware and software, reliable power, teacher training opportunities, and funding and maintenance, which the article identifies as constraints on ICT utilization
constraints: The article notes many colleges lack well-equipped computer laboratories and are constrained by inadequate ICT facilities
target_learning_goals: overall academic achievement across disciplines
examples: The meta-analysis of 15 studies reported a mean effect size of 0.712 for e-learning's impact on academic achievement, which the article uses to ground the infrastructure recommendation.
key_sources: Gloria Mothibi. (2015). A Meta-Analysis of the Relationship between E-Learning and Students' Academic Achievement in Higher Education. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.9. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1082408

article_title: Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review
citation: Philominraj, A., Ranjan, R., Ubilla Rosales, L., Cocio, A., & Brauchy Castillo, J. G. (2023). Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review. MEXTESOL Journal, 47(2). https://www.mextesol.net/journal/
title: PRISMA-screened corpus of 40 Chilean EFL methodology studies (2011–2021) from Web of Science, SCOPUS and SCIELO
description: The review's empirical corpus consists of 40 research studies retrieved from three databases and screened following PRISMA guidelines, with thematic analysis and snowball sampling. The authors state that "40 articles (Web of Science=05, SCOPUS = 16, SCIELO= 19)met the criteria for this systematic review" after screening 80 titles and checking 73 usable articles for duplicity against inclusion criteria (methodology, approach, strategies, EFL, Chile, teaching, English language) and exclusion criteria (students' perspective, teacher-centered, other subjects, other languages).
requirements: Inclusion criteria: studies on methodology, approach, strategies, EFL, Chile, and teaching, written in English, published 2011–2021 in the three named databases
constraints: The restriction to Web of Science, SCOPUS and SCIELO limited the search to published studies, excluding doctoral dissertations and master's theses
target_learners: Chilean primary, secondary and tertiary EFL learners and teacher-education populations covered by the reviewed studies
target_learning_goals: EFL communicative competence and teaching methodology in the Chilean context
examples: A PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1) presents the search and inclusion/exclusion process from 80 initial titles to 40 final articles

article_title: Learning How to Use Input-Based and Output-Based Form-Focused Instruction: A Meta-Analytic Comparison of Persian EFL Learners
citation: Schenck, A. (2024). Learning How to Use Input-Based and Output-Based Form-Focused Instruction: A Meta-Analytic Comparison of Persian EFL Learners. Journal of Second Language Acquisition and Teaching, 30.
title: Processability Theory's three-level morphosyntactic complexity taxonomy (intra-phrasal, inter-phrasal, clausal)
description: The article uses Processability Theory (Pienemann & Lenzing, 2015) to organize grammatical features into three complexity levels: intra-phrasal features modifying one phrase (e.g., past -ed, plural -s), inter-phrasal features requiring manipulation of multiple phrases (e.g., subject-auxiliary inversion, third person -s), and clausal features including subordinate clauses (e.g., conditionals, relative clauses). The theory holds that "specific target features are, in fact, teachable when grammatical complexity is just above a learner's English proficiency level", so timing of instruction matters. The article categorizes the 41 treatment groups by these levels.
requirements: Target features must be classifiable into intra-phrasal, inter-phrasal, or clausal categories
constraints: The article notes prior Processability Theory research examined only a limited number of grammatical features
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of English grammatical features of varying morphosyntactic complexity
examples: The meta-analysis categorized 41 treatment groups from 18 studies as 11 intra-phrasal, 21 inter-phrasal, and 9 clausal
key_sources: Schenck, A. (2024). Learning How to Use Input-Based and Output-Based Form-Focused Instruction: A Meta-Analytic Comparison of Persian EFL Learners. Journal of Second Language Acquisition and Teaching, 30. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1457419

article_title: Integrated Education Models for Addressing Substance Use Among Schoolchildren: A Scoping Review of School-Based Educational Interventions.
citation: Bajpai Tewari, D., Gautam, U., Jaiswal, V., Pooja, Mishra, A., & Das, P. (2026). Integrated Education Models for Addressing Substance Use Among Schoolchildren: A Scoping Review of School-Based Educational Interventions. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph23081073
title: Preventive, protective, and corrective classification of school-based substance use intervention models
description: The review organises school-based substance use intervention models along an approach axis with three branches: "preventive models are defined as those delivered to substance-naive populations before any use has occurred; protective models as those that build resilience or resistance skills in general or identified at-risk populations without requiring prior use; and corrective models as those explicitly designed to intervene with students who have already initiated substance use." This taxonomy frames the review's mapping, its synthesis via a socio-ecological framework, and its finding that the corrective branch is empty in the current evidence base.
requirements: Interventions must be evaluated in school settings with school administration involvement, per the review's eligibility criteria.
constraints: The review found all 43 examined models fell only into the preventive or protective branches; no corrective model was identified.
target_learners: School-going children and adolescents, including substance-naive, at-risk, and substance-using students
target_learning_goals: Preventing substance use initiation, building resilience and resistance skills, and intervening after initiation
examples: The review applies the classification across 33 distinct intervention models in Table 3, tagging each as preventive and protective or preventive.
key_sources: Bajpai Tewari, D., Gautam, U., Jaiswal, V., Pooja, Mishra, A., & Das, P. (2026). Integrated Education Models for Addressing Substance Use Among Schoolchildren: A Scoping Review of School-Based Educational Interventions. article_title: Preparedness of Dental Hygiene Students for Clinical Practice: A Scoping Review.
citation: Asraf Suadah Ismail, Sethi Ahsan, Ali Kamran. (2026). Preparedness of Dental Hygiene Students for Clinical Practice: A Scoping Review. International Journal of Dental Hygiene. https://doi.org/10.1111/idh.70076
title: Preparedness for practice as a construct encompassing professional competence plus readiness to function independently across diverse work environments
description: The review frames preparedness for practice in the health professions as extending beyond clinical competence. It states that "The concept of 'preparedness for practice' in the health professions encompasses not only professional competence but also readiness to function independently across diverse work environments." Accordingly, being prepared "encompasses a wide range of cognitive and behavioural attributes to ensure a smooth transition" from university into the work environment, which the review operationalises through attributes such as clinical skills, communication, cultural competence, adaptability, and resilience.
requirements: Education must develop cognitive and behavioural attributes alongside clinical competence to support the transition into practice
constraints: The review's synthesis focuses on general clinical readiness; only two included studies addressed alternative settings or independent roles
target_learning_goals: Clinical competence
Independent functioning across diverse work environments
Professional behaviours
examples: The review maps ten studies against this construct using Tables 2 and 3 of core attributes and gaps

article_title: Occupational Therapists' Psychotherapy Competence: A Scoping Review of Secondary Data.
citation: Mandzuk Andrea, Wener Pamela. (2025). Occupational Therapists’ Psychotherapy Competence: A Scoping Review of Secondary Data. Canadian Journal of Occupational Therapy. https://doi.org/10.1177/00084174251319768
title: Professional Identity as the overarching theme of psychotherapy competence literature in occupational therapy
description: The review's narrative synthesis identified one overall theme, Professional Identity, further explained by three subthemes: Competence, Attaining and Maintaining Competence, and The Great Debate. The authors state that "The three subthemes are dynamic and continually influence each other while contributing to an evolving professional identity." This framework organizes the 104 included articles and frames psychotherapy competence as reciprocally related to occupational therapists' sense of belonging to their profession.
requirements: Articles included in the synthesis pertain to psychotherapy competence within occupational therapy literature or practice
constraints: Synthesis is based on a secondary analysis of articles from a prior scoping review (Marshall et al., 2022), not on newly collected primary data

understanding professional identity in mental health practice

description: The review concludes that future educational programmes should adopt proficiency-based training: "Training should be proficiency-based, requiring all trainees to continue practising until skills are ensured using an assessment tool with solid evidence of validity." This accommodates individual learning curves better than time- or procedure-based approaches.

article_title: The Effectiveness of Community Nurse Training Programs to Improve Nurses' Competency in Community Settings: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Pumsopa, N., Jirapongsuwan, A., Kalampakorn, S., Siri, S., and Klainin‐Yobas, P. (2025). The Effectiveness of Community Nurse Training Programs to Improve Nurses' Competency in Community Settings: a Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis. International Journal of Nursing Practice. https://doi.org/10.1111/ijn.70090
title: Integrate hybrid or blended training into community nurse education because it sustains knowledge and skill gains better than onsite‐only formats
description: The review concludes that "CNTPs could be offered to community nurses through hybrid pedagogical methods, given their effectiveness." Hybrid learning lets nurses apply newly acquired knowledge in practice, leading to sustained improvements, and offers flexibility for nurses with high workloads and time constraints that make face‐to‐face attendance challenging. Discussions and case study analyses can be integrated using tools such as chats or social networks to leverage peer interaction.

constraints: The review found considerable heterogeneity across studies and a small number of eligible online and traits studies, so findings should be interpreted with caution
target_learning_goals: knowledge retention
skill application in practice
continuing professional development
examples: Hybrid program components in included studies included e‐learning, group discussions online and onsite, education videos, case studies, demonstrations, practice, web‐based learning and social networking services

article_title: Impact of different teaching modes on medical students' performance under the scoring criteria for multiple-choice questions: A meta-analysis.

title: Prioritize flipped classroom and simulation teaching for improving medical students' knowledge assessment performance
description: The authors recommend that "high-quality flipped classroom teaching and simulation teaching should continue to be developed to address the challenges in medical education reform." This recommendation is grounded in the meta-analytic finding that these two modes produced significantly higher multiple-choice question scores than traditional teaching, while team-based learning and blended teaching did not.
requirements: Instructional contexts where multiple-choice question performance is a primary outcome measure
constraints: Effect sizes are small to moderate, suggesting limited improvement or moderating factors
Findings are specific to medical students and multiple-choice question assessment

article_title: The effect of experiential learning interventions on physical activity outcomes in children: A systematic review.
citation: Varman Sumantla D., Jones Rachel A., Kelly Bridget, Hammersley Megan L., Parrish Anne-Maree, Stanley Rebecca, Cliff Dylan P. (2023). The effect of experiential learning interventions on physical activity outcomes in children: A systematic review. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294987
title: Experiential learning physical activity interventions structured as practical components plus theory components
description: The review categorises experiential learning physical activity interventions into practical components — outdoor and adventure activities, fitness activities and challenges, rhythmic and expressive movement activities, modified sports and games, and active play and tummy time — and theory components: "behaviour change and motivational strategies" and "information and education strategies". Most included studies (n = 8) used approaches from both theory categories, and the review considered both component types when interpreting intervention effects.
requirements: A practical component and a theory-based component, coordinated by a facilitator such as a teacher, educator or parent who provides structure such as basic instruction or questions invoking problem-solving or reflection
constraints: One study added environmental/organisational change strategies on top of both theory categories; the pattern as categorised covers only practical and theory components

target_learning_goals: physical activity behaviour change
physical activity knowledge
physical activity attitudes and self-efficacy
examples: Eather et al. combined fitness activities and challenges with modified sports and games, plus behaviour change/motivational and information/education strategies, over 8 weeks in primary schools

article_title: The impact of project ECHO on physician preparedness to treat opioid use disorder: a systematic review.
citation: Puckett, H. M., Bossaller, J. S., & Sheets, L. R. (2021). The impact of project ECHO on physician preparedness to treat opioid use disorder: a systematic review. Addiction Science & Clinical Practice, 16, 6. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13722-021-00215-z
title: Project ECHO as a case-based tele-mentoring model for extending specialist capacity to community providers
description: Project ECHO (Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes) is described as "a collaborative tele-mentoring program in which specialists train health-care workers to treat medical conditions". It is explicitly distinguished from telemedicine: rather than a physician treating a patient remotely, it "connects learners with experienced specialists in order to improve services", so learners can implement new services after participation. Sessions are case-based, multi-disciplinary, and aimed at community and rural providers treating conditions such as OUD.
requirements: Requires specialists willing to facilitate case-based sessions and community providers (typically primary care) who attend and present cases
constraints: The review states the model is not traditional telemedicine and that a study by the Rand Corporation found building capacity to evaluate ECHO outcomes is a critical unmet need
target_learners: Primary care physicians and cross-disciplinary health care teams, especially in rural and underserved locations
target_learning_goals: Knowledge and self-efficacy for treating opioid use disorder, including buprenorphine prescribing
examples: The University of New Mexico OUD ECHO runs 2-hour case presentations facilitated by a physician specializing in OUD, a psychiatrist, a social worker, a psychiatric nurse, and a community health worker

article_title: Educational outcomes of children in contact with social care in England: a systematic review.
citation: Jay Matthew A., Mc Grath-Lone Louise. (2019). Educational outcomes of children in contact with social care in England: a systematic review. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-019-1071-z
title: Prioritise population-level longitudinal research on the educational prospects of children in contact with CSC services, viewed from the child's journey through the system
description: The review concludes that the scarcity and crudeness of existing evidence creates an urgent need for more population-level research into the educational prospects of children in contact with CSC services. It states the review "throws into sharp relief the urgent need to conduct more population-level research into the educational prospects of children in contact with CSC services, especially from the perspective of the child's journey through CSC services", which it found was the weakest point of the existing evidence base. Addressing this knowledge gap is framed as the first step to helping vulnerable children and young people.
requirements: Administrative data linked over time, since data on all children can be linked to fully examine their careers in the care system and through school
constraints: Studying children and families in contact with CSC is difficult, and paucity of research generation and use within the family legal system and CSC has been identified as a key barrier
target_learners: Children in need and children looked after under the Children Act 1989 in the UK
target_learning_goals: Improving educational outcomes and narrowing gaps in attainment, absence and exclusion relative to the general population
examples: The review searched 16 databases plus snowball, Google Scholar and grey-literature searches and still found only seven eligible studies, six of which were published very recently (2015, 2016 and 2018)

article_title: Acute surgical wound-dressing procedure: Description of the steps involved in the development and validation of an observational metric.
citation: Hegarty Josephine, Howson Victoria, Wills Teresa, Creedon Sile A., Mc Cluskey Pat, Lane Aoife, Connolly Aine, Walshe Nuala, Noonan Brendan, Guidera Fiona, Gallagher Anthony G, Murphy Siobhan. (2019). Acute surgical wound‐dressing procedure: Description of the steps involved in the development and validation of an observational metric. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.13072
title: Proficiency-based progression training (PBPT): trainees practice until an unambiguously demonstrated quantitative performance benchmark is reached, with metric-based feedback
description: PBPT is a training approach for high-volume, high-risk technical and non-technical skills in which trainees receive precise feedback proximate to performance and "a quantitative performance benchmark to work towards" that "should be a valid representation of the procedure". It requires learners to practice until the benchmark is unambiguously demonstrated, relying on a comprehensive quantitative characterisation of the skill. In this study PBPT principles underpinned the six-stage development of the ANTT wound-dressing observational metric, whose metrics and operational definitions offer specific goals for a training curriculum.
requirements: A valid observational metric that quantitatively characterises the procedure, with operationally defined steps and errors, so feedback can delineate deviation from optimal performance
target_learners: trainee health care professionals learning acute surgical wound-dressing procedures
target_learning_goals: proficient performance of aseptic non-touch technique during acute surgical wound dressings
examples: The study's metric development process followed PBPT steps: literature scoping, video-based task analysis, stress testing for reliability, and Delphi validation of the resulting metric.

article_title: Academic Outcomes of School-Aged Children Born Preterm: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
citation: McBryde M, Fitzallen GC, Liley HG, Taylor HG, Bora S. (2020). Academic Outcomes of School-Aged Children Born Preterm: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Network Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2020.2027
title: Subskill taxonomy of reading and mathematics achievement used to profile preterm academic outcomes
description: The article demarcates reading and mathematics into higher- and lower-order subskills by investigating the content and structure of psychoeducational measures. Reading is categorized into "overall reading, decoding (lower-order skill), and reading comprehension (higher-order skill)", with decoding further split into word identification and pseudoword decoding. Mathematics is categorized into overall mathematics, mathematical knowledge, calculation, mathematical fluency, and applied problems, with applied problems defined as the highest-order skill requiring interpretation, approach selection, and accurate answers.
requirements: Academic outcomes assessed by validated, standardized tests reporting mean (SD) scores, normed to a mean (SD) of 100 (15) for comparability across measures
constraints: The demarcation of subskills came from the authors' own investigation of the psychoeducational measures' content and structure, not from an independently validated taxonomy
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
decoding and word identification
mathematical knowledge, calculation, fluency, and applied problem solving
examples: All assessment measures were normed to a mean (SD) of 100 (15) and compared in this metric across the 33 included studies

article_title: Common Elements of Practice, Process and Implementation in Out-of-School-Time Academic Interventions for At-risk Children: a Systematic Review.
citation: Engell, T., Kirkøen, B., Hammerstrøm, K. T., Kornør, H., Ludvigsen, K. H., & Hagen, K. A. (2020). Common Elements of Practice, Process and Implementation in Out-of-School-Time Academic Interventions for At-risk Children: a Systematic Review. Prevention Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-020-01091-w
title: Three-part taxonomy of intervention elements: practice, process, and implementation elements
description: The review distinguishes three discrete element types in interventions for children at risk. Practice elements are "specific activities or actions used to evoke or influence an outcome (e.g., positive reinforcement)"; process elements cover delivery forms and contexts such as home visitation; implementation elements are "discrete strategies to facilitate or enable the delivery of practice and process elements" such as ongoing training. The taxonomy organizes the review's coding matrices and frequency analyses of 147 identified elements.
requirements: Interventions must be described in enough detail (articles, manuals, or appendices) for coders to identify discrete elements
constraints: Frequency analyses do not merit conclusions about the effectiveness of elements; FVs are likely skewed by publication bias

target_learning_goals: academic achievement in reading, math, and grade point average
examples: Coders used consensus mapping with a priori listed elements plus discovery of 11 unanticipated elements, achieving 90.4% total coding agreement

article_title: Towards Enhanced Learning through Presence: A Systematic Review of Presence in Virtual Reality Across Tasks and Disciplines
citation: Zheng Wei, Junxiang Liao, Lik-Hang Lee, Huamin Qu, and Xian Xu. (2025). Towards Enhanced Learning through Presence: A Systematic Review of Presence in Virtual Reality Across Tasks and Disciplines. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13845
title: PRISMA-based systematic review corpus of 78 VR presence studies (2020-2024)
description: A curated corpus of 78 studies on presence in VR learning and collaborative environments, assembled through the PRISMA framework. The review reports screening 2,793 articles, removing 301 duplicates, excluding 2,329 by title and abstract, and excluding 84 more after full-text evaluation, ultimately retaining 78 studies. Data extraction covered twelve items (DE1-DE12) including presence type, task type, presence combination, evaluation method, VR environment design, collaboration type, learning outcomes, participant numbers, and domain. Two extraction rounds occurred in August 2024 and December 2024.
requirements: Included studies must manipulate a presence type, contain a self-reported presence measure, allow determination of condition immediacy, be published within five years, and address design effects on learning outcomes
constraints: Corpus limited to studies published 2020-2024 in VR education and collaboration venues
target_learning_goals: Understanding presence-learning outcome relationships
examples: The review's Table 1 presents the twelve-item data extraction rubric applied to all 78 articles

article_title: Effects of Physics Teaching Materials on Student Critical Thinking and Creative Thinking Skills: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Serli Ahzari, Asrizal, Usmeldi. (2024). Effects of Physics Teaching Materials on Student' Critical Thinking and Creative Thinking Skills: A Meta-Analysis. Jurnal Penelitian Pembelajaran Fisika (JPPF). https://jppf.ppj.unp.ac.id/index.php/jppf/article/view/129627
title: Use modules and student worksheets as the physics teaching material formats most strongly associated with critical and creative thinking gains
description: The article recommends that physics educators and curriculum developers favor modules and student worksheets when designing materials for 21st-century thinking skills, because these formats showed the highest average effect sizes in its meta-analysis. It states "the use of modules and student worksheets in physics learning can make a significant contribution to improving students' critical skills and creative thinking skills." The recommendation rests on the stratified comparison of material types in Table 3.
requirements: Materials must be designed for high school physics learning contexts as in the sampled articles
constraints: Based on only 20 national-journal articles from 2019-2023, a scope the authors themselves flag as limited
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
creative thinking skills
examples: The meta-analysis coded 22 effect sizes across four material types and found modules (3.93) and student worksheets (3.97) in the high category while general teaching materials (0.23) were medium

article_title: Process oriented guided inquiry learning (POGIL®) marginally effects student achievement measures but substantially increases the odds of passing a course.
citation: Walker L, Warfa A-R M. (2017). Process oriented guided inquiry learning (POGIL®) marginally effects student achievement measures but substantially increases the odds of passing a course. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0186203
title: Coupling process skills to content instruction does not inhibit content learning and improves success measures
description: The article addresses the fear that developing process skills comes at the cost of content coverage. Its meta-analytic results suggest that "providing opportunities to improve process skills during class instruction does not inhibit content learning but enhances conventional success measures". Instructors concerned about coverage trade-offs can therefore adopt pedagogies like POGIL that embed process skills within content learning without sacrificing achievement or pass rates.
requirements: Instructional activities that deliberately target process skills alongside content, as in well-designed POGIL activities
constraints: Evidence comes from studies where content coverage was reported as similar between POGIL and lecture conditions; the analyzed studies did not directly measure process-skill gains
target_learners: high school and college/university STEM students
target_learning_goals: content mastery
process and transferable skills
course persistence
examples: The meta-analysis found POGIL students scored about 0.3 standard deviations higher on exams and concept inventories and had roughly double the odds of passing than lecture students

article_title: Effect of Strategy Teaching for the Solution of Ratio Problems on Students' Proportional Reasoning Skills
citation: Şen, C., & Güler, G. (2017). Effect of Strategy Teaching For the Solution of Ratio Problems on Students' Proportional Reasoning Skills. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Sciences, 5(2). https://www.moj-es.net
title: Proportional Reasoning Test (PRT)
description: The Proportional Reasoning Test is a researcher-developed instrument used as pretest and posttest in this study. It "included 6 ratio problem states including one question of finding a value which is not given, two questions of quantitative comparison, two questions of qualitative comparison and one question of inverse proportion", drawable within a 40-minute course hour. It was piloted with 10 sixth-grade students, refined with expert opinion, and scored 0-20 according to Langrall and Swafford's proportional reasoning levels. Sample items include diet weight comparisons, basketball shooting percentages, lemonade concentration, balloon pricing, flower growth, and pine-tree planting.
requirements: Questions of each Lamon (1993) problem type and completion within one 40-minute course hour
constraints: Developed for and piloted with sixth-grade students; scored against Langrall and Swafford (2000) levels
target_learning_goals: proportional reasoning
solving ratio problems
examples: Appendix A prints the six items, including a missing-value balloon problem (2 liras for 3 balloons, cost for 24 balloons) and a pine-tree planting table.

constraints: The article ties the recommendation to K12 and first-tier university contexts and cites prior literature on complicated syntax hindering concept grasp

article_title: Teaching Vocabulary with Graphic Novels
citation: Ahmet Başal, Talat Aytan & İbrahim Demir. (2016). Teaching Vocabulary with Graphic Novels. English Language Teaching, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n9p95

target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning
idiomatic expression learning
examples: The experimental group read a weekly ten-idiom section of the graphic novel, guessed meanings, and received teacher-checked meanings and extra example sentences
key_sources: Ahmet Başal, Talat Aytan & İbrahim Demir. (2016). Teaching Vocabulary with Graphic Novels. English Language Teaching, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n9p95

article_title: Scaffolding in a Medicine Education Intervention for Student Teachers Based on the PROFILES Three Stage Model
citation: Sirpa Kärkkäinen, Jari Kukkonen and Tuula Keinonen. (2014). Scaffolding in a Medicine Education Intervention for Student Teachers Based on the PROFILES Three Stage Model. ceps Journal, Vol. 4, No. 1. https://journals.cepsj.si
title: PROFILES Three Stage Model (Scenario, Inquiry, Decision-making)
description: The PROFILES Three Stage Model is a science-education approach that organises learning in three phases: "the Scenario Stage", "the Inquiry Stage", and "the Decision-making Stage". It "aims to arouse students’ intrinsic motivation through a student-familiar, socio-scientific context (the Scenario Stage), to offer a meaningful inquiry-based learning environment (the Inquiry Stage), and to use science learning in deciding on socio-scientific issues (the Decision-making Stage)". In this study it structures a medicine education environment ('Flu') emphasising critical thinking, with the three phases kept interconnected rather than handled separately.
requirements: The three phases should not be handled separately; continuous professional development should strengthen the interconnectedness of the Model components
constraints: Applied here to a six-hour medicine education module for primary school teacher students in biology education
target_learners: primary school students in grades 4-6 (original module design)
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
problem solving and decision-making
argumentation and reasoning skills
inquiry skills
examples: The 'Flu' module used a scenario about Veijo's sore throat and sneezing, an Inquiry Stage using three given websites, and a Decision-making Stage in which groups suggested treatment and prevention recommendations justified by reliable sources
key_sources: Sirpa Kärkkäinen, Jari Kukkonen and Tuula Keinonen. (2014). Scaffolding in a Medicine Education Intervention for Student Teachers Based on the PROFILES Three Stage Model. ceps Journal, Vol. 4, No. 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1129505

article_title: Influence of Prior Knowledge Questions on Pupils' Performance in Reading Comprehension in Primary Schools in Kaduna, Nigeria
citation: Hanna Onyi Yusuf & Sadiq Mohammed. (2013). Influence of Prior Knowledge Questions on Pupils' Performance in Reading Comprehension in Primary Schools in Kaduna, Nigeria. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 4(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.4n.1p.134
title: Learning as conceptual change: prior knowledge actively shapes how learners interpret instruction
description: The article's literature review frames learning not as absorption of transmitted information but as conceptual change, in which new ideas can only be interpreted against existing knowledge. It states that "learning proceeds primarily from prior knowledge, and only secondarily from the presented materials," and that neglected prior knowledge can lead learners to distort material or learn something opposed to the educator's intentions. Prior knowledge operates at levels from perception and procedural skill to beliefs about knowledge itself, across ages and ability levels. The study applies this account by activating pupils' relevant schemata through questions before, during and after reading.
requirements: Educators must understand how prior knowledge affects learning in order to help learners make the most of a new experience
constraints: Prior knowledge can be at odds with presented material, causing learners to distort it; the article notes effects may take weeks or years to resolve in some domains
target_learners: primary school pupils learning in a second language
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
connecting new information to background knowledge
examples: The experimental treatment began reading activities with what pupils already knew from home, community and school, using questions such as what the passage title suggests or reminds them of
key_sources: Hanna Onyi Yusuf & Sadiq Mohammed. (2013). Influence of Prior Knowledge Questions on Pupils' Performance in Reading Comprehension in Primary Schools in Kaduna, Nigeria. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 4(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.4n.1p.134

article_title: The Effect of Practical Presentations' Strategy on the Achievement of the Ninth Graders Students of the Pre-Vocational Education Subject in Shobak District Schools
citation: Haroon M. Al Tawarah, Omar M. Mahasneh & Nourah A. Al-Hawartheh. (2017). The Effect of Practical Presentations' Strategy on the Achievement of the Ninth Graders Students of the Pre-Vocational Education Subject in Shobak District Schools. International Education Studies, 10(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n5p109
title: Practical presentation strategy as purposeful demonstration combining teacher performance with dialogue and illustration means
description: The practical presentation strategy is defined as "a purposeful educational activity, combining teacher performance of practical presentation with investigative represented in intellectual dialogue and questions", using illustration means such as samples, drawings, or practical experience so learners can carry out and apply skills. Presentations may be given by the teacher alone, with student help, by students on a rotational basis, or by a visiting guest. The study operationalized it with samples, items, models, movies, and experiments in two pre-vocational units.
requirements: A hall for the educational operator was prepared, in addition to preparing all the needed equipments
teacher meetings to explain the strategy, program skills, purposes and contents, classroom activities, and evaluating methods
constraints: studied only in two units (sanitation and environment waste recycling) of ninth-grade pre-vocational education in Shobak district schools
target_learning_goals: pre-vocational education knowledge and skills in sanitation and environment waste recycling
examples: The experimental group studied the sanitation and environment waste recycling units using samples, items, models, movies, and experiments, while the control group received lecturing

article_title: Activating Junior Secondary School Students' Prior Knowledge for the Development of Vocabulary, Concepts and Mathematics through Instructional Strategies
citation: Olu Oyinloye, Abiodun.A. Popoola. (2013). Activating Junior Secondary School Students' Prior Knowledge for the Development of Vocabulary, Concepts and Mathematics through Instructional Strategies. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 1(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.1n.2p.1
title: Preview, view and review: a lesson structure for second-language learners that activates first-language background knowledge
description: A three-stage lesson pattern for English and Mathematics learners who are second-language speakers. In the preview stage the teacher helps pupils preview the lesson in the child's first language to activate first-language background knowledge; the view stage is the main lesson taught in English; the review stage revisits the key concept in the pupils' first language, with pupils working in groups and reporting to the teacher for correction.
requirements: Pupils can discuss the topic with others who speak the same language
Review is followed by group reporting to the teacher for necessary correction
constraints: Designed for learners whose prior knowledge base has not been developed around English and its cultural traditions
target_learning_goals: comprehension in English
Mathematics concept understanding
examples: The article attributes this structure to Freeman and Freeman (1997) and lists it among techniques for accessing prior knowledge in English language and Mathematics.

Activating Junior Secondary School Students' Prior Knowledge for the Development of Vocabulary, Concepts and Mathematics through Instructional Strategies.
