article_title: Assessment of the Effects of Problem Solving Instructional Strategies on Students' Achievement and Retention in Chemistry with Respect to Location in Rivers State
citation: Jacobson Barineka Nbina & Obomanu, B. Joseph. (2011). Assessment of the Effects of Problem Solving Instructional Strategies On Students' Achievement and Retention in Chemistry With Respect to Location in Rivers State. World Journal of Education, 1(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n2p74
title: Chemistry teachers in both rural and urban schools should use problem solving strategies, particularly model use supplemented with feedback-correctives
description: Based on the finding that the PF strategy produced the highest achievement and retention means, the article recommends "that both rural and urban Chemistry teachers use problem solving instructional strategies, particularly that in which use of a model is supplemented with feedback-correctives in teaching". It further recommends that "teachers should as much as possible, use activity based methods as instructional strategies, so as to improve cognitive development, acquisiti on of skills and retention of subject matter amongst students", and that the chemistry curriculum be restructured to aid teaching through problem solving.
requirements: Teachers trained in the treatment techniques and validated lesson plans reflecting the instructional pattern
constraints: The recommendation rests on a single quasi-experimental study with no randomization of subjects; location made no significant difference, so the recommendation is not location-specific
target_learners: Senior secondary (SS II) chemistry students in urban and rural schools
target_learning_goals: Cognitive achievement, retention of subject matter, and acquisition of skills in chemistry
examples: The study assigned intact classes to PF (model plus feedback-correctives), PM (model only) and PC (conventional method) over eight weeks and found PF highest on both outcomes
key_sources: Jacobson Barineka Nbina & Obomanu, B. Joseph. (2011). Assessment of the Effects of Problem Solving Instructional Strategies On Students' Achievement and Retention in Chemistry With Respect to Location in Rivers State. World Journal of Education, 1(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n2p74

article_title: Learning Physics through Project-Based Learning Game Techniques
citation: Baran, M., Maskan, A., & Yaşar, Ş. (2018). Learning Physics through Project-Based Learning Game Techniques. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 221-234. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11215a
title: Provide the needed materials and technical infrastructure before implementing project-based learning with game techniques
description: The article concludes that project-based learning with game techniques requires equipment to be in place beforehand, because students reported difficulty obtaining materials during the application. It states that "in order to achieve positive results, the implementation of project based learning method should be initiated after providing the needed equipment and the appropriate infrastructure," and that "the necessary technical equipment should be in place" for science/physics classes.
requirements: Needed equipment and appropriate infrastructure provided before the application begins
Technical equipment in place in science/physics classes
constraints: The recommendation arises from students' reported difficulty in finding materials in this single 9th-grade vocational school setting
target_learning_goals: Physics concept achievement through project-based game activities
examples: In the study's self-evaluation forms, difficulty in finding the materials was coded 3 times as a challenge faced during the activity, and students stated they had difficulties finding the necessary materials during the application process.
key_sources: Baran, M., Maskan, A., & Yaşar, Ş. (2018). Learning Physics through Project-Based Learning Game Techniques. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 221-234. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11215a

article_title: Effects of Semantic Web Based Learning on Pre-Service Teachers' ICT Learning Achievement and Satisfaction
citation: Karalar, H., & Korucu, A. T. (2016). Effects of Semantic Web Based Learning on Pre-service Teachers' ICT Learning Achievement and Satisfaction. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 4(8). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i8.1676
title: Prerequisite-first navigation pattern: agent lists prerequisite objectives and learning objects before the selected objective
description: In the SWBL environment, when a learner selects an objective, the pedagogical agent first lists related prerequisite objectives and their learning objects, then the learning objects for the selected objective, and finally states which future objectives would become difficult unless the chosen objectives are learned. This sequencing operationalizes prerequisite analysis so learners make up for educational shortcomings before new content.
requirements: an ontology encoding prerequisite relations between objectives
learning objects attached to each objective in a repository
target_learning_goals: learning objectives with explicit prerequisite dependencies
examples: Table 1 shows the agent's lettered panels: prerequisite learning questions, learning objects related to the prerequisite objective, learning objects for the chosen objective, and future objectives that would become difficult
key_sources: Karalar, H., & Korucu, A. T. (2016). Effects of Semantic Web Based Learning on Pre-service Teachers' ICT Learning Achievement and Satisfaction. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 4(8). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i8.1676

article_title: The Effect of Various Media Scaffolding on Increasing Understanding of Students' Geometry Concepts
citation: Sutiarso, S., Coesamin, M., & Nurhanurawati. (2018). The effect of various media scaffolding on increasing understanding of students' geometry concepts. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 95-102. https://ejournal.unsri.ac.id/index.php/jme
title: Teachers should prepare a variety of media scaffolding, attending to students' ability level and gender
description: The article concludes that teacher-prepared media scaffolding is important for students with learning difficulties and that teachers should offer several media forms rather than one. As the conclusion states, "Teachers should be able to prepare various media scaffolding with attention level of ability and gender, such as charts, props and visual." The study observed that students differentially chose charts, props, and visual, supporting variety with attention to learner characteristics.
requirements: Media scaffolding is provided by the teacher as a learning aid for students who have difficulty learning geometry
constraints: Evidence comes from one quasi-experiment with 40 fifth-grade students in a single Indonesian school
target_learners: fifth-grade elementary students with geometry learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: understanding of geometry concepts, including properties of shapes and area of trapezoid and kite
examples: The experimental class was offered charts, props, and visual media; observation showed male students mostly used props (70%) and female students mostly used charts (60%).
key_sources: Sutiarso, S., Coesamin, M., & Nurhanurawati. (2018). The effect of various media scaffolding on increasing understanding of students' geometry concepts. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 95-102. https://ejournal.unsri.ac.id/index.php/jme

article_title: Reading Skill Transfer across Languages: Outcomes from Longitudinal Bilingual Randomized Control Trials in Kenya and Haiti
citation: Piper, B., Bulat, J., & Johnston, A. (2015). Reading Skill Transfer Across Languages: Outcomes from Longitudinal Bilingual Randomized Control Trials in Kenya and Haiti. SREE Spring 2015 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: PRIMR and ToTAL structured bilingual literacy programs (150 structured lessons per language, aligned student books, teachers' guides, and coaching)
description: PRIMR (Kenya) and ToTAL (Haiti) were instructional interventions centered on improving teacher practices for literacy acquisition, moving teachers beyond whole-class oral repetition toward research-supported strategies for bilingual literacy. Each included "150 structured lessons" in each target language, low-cost student books aligned to scripted lessons (with a 1:1 student-to-textbook ratio in PRIMR rather than the mandated 3:1), teachers' guides, pocket charts and flashcards, controlled-text and read-aloud stories, ongoing trainings, and regular pedagogical coaching, focusing on letters, phonological awareness, decoding, and comprehension strategies.
requirements: student books aligned with the scripted lessons
ongoing teacher trainings and regular pedagogical coaching
constraints: the ToTAL French curriculum focused on oral language development rather than full literacy instruction
target_learners: Grade 1 and 2 students in government and nonformal schools in Kenya and Haiti
target_learning_goals: letter knowledge, phonological awareness, decoding, oral reading fluency, and reading comprehension
examples: PRIMR classrooms moved from the national 3:1 student-to-textbook ratio to a 1:1 ratio; lessons were intended to move children with little alphabet exposure to full fluency and comprehension within one school year.
key_sources: Piper, B., Bulat, J., & Johnston, A. (2015). Reading Skill Transfer Across Languages: Outcomes from Longitudinal Bilingual Randomized Control Trials in Kenya and Haiti. SREE Spring 2015 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562423

article_title: The Use of Program Theory in Mathematics Education Evaluation Research
citation: Charles Munter, Paul Cobb, and Calli Shekell. (2014). The Use of Program Theory in Mathematics Education Evaluation Research. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Framework for analyzing evaluators' articulation and use of program theory in three dimensions: type, quality, and use
description: A coding framework, summarized in Figure 1 and drawing on theory-based evaluation principles and the National Research Council committee's mathematics-specific criteria, that "combined perspectives from both “method-oriented” evaluation (as emphasized by WWC) and “theory-driven” evaluation." It codes each evaluation report on three dimensions: the type of program theory articulated (none, sub-theoretical implementation description, or theoretical programmatic causal-chain mapping), the quality of articulation (entirely implicit, limited sources, or multiple resources including research literature), and how theory is used in research questions, construct measurement (outcomes and fidelity), and analysis (whether mechanisms are explained). The review applied it to 36 WWC-qualified mathematics program evaluation reports.
requirements: Coding is limited to what is described in evaluation reports, not inferences about evaluators' understanding
At least two individuals score every report, with discrepancies resolved
constraints: Applied to K-12 general education mathematics program evaluations meeting WWC evidence standards from 1993 onward
target_learning_goals: Evaluation of mathematics program effectiveness and the mechanisms by which programs support mathematics learning
examples: The framework's theoretical category requires mapping the causal chain including mechanisms and moderator and mediator variables, and relating program theory to implementation resources
key_sources: Charles Munter, Paul Cobb, and Calli Shekell. (2014). The Use of Program Theory in Mathematics Education Evaluation Research. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563007

article_title: Effects of Behavioural Objectives-Based Instructional Strategy on Senior School Students' Academic Performance in Mathematics in Omu-Aran, Nigeria
citation: M. F. Salman, L. A. Yahaya, A. Yusuf, M. A. Ahmed & J. O. Ayinla. (2012). Effects of Behavioural Objectives-based Instructional Strategy on Senior School Students’ Academic Performance in Mathematics in Omu-Aran, Nigeria. Journal of Education and Learning, 1(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v1n2p121
title: Present the set behavioural objectives to students prior to the lesson to enhance participation and performance
description: The article recommends that mathematics teachers make lesson objectives visible to students before instruction begins, rather than keeping them in lesson notes. It argues that "Presenting students therefore with the behavioural objectives of the lesson topic at the beginning of instruction can alert their sensitivity to the learning situation", and that referring to objectives during teaching serves an evaluating role for teachers and students. The recommendation is grounded in the study's finding that the objectives-presented group significantly outperformed the control group.
requirements: Objectives must be properly formulated and communicated to students, and if possible given in written form, since objectives "would certainly make no difference if the students pay no attention to them in the learning situations"
constraints: The article notes prior studies in which availability of behavioural objectives did not help learning, so the result on efficacy of prior objectives is non conclusive
target_learning_goals: Academic performance in mathematics (set theory)
examples: In the study, experimental-group students had access to the teacher's set behavioural objectives before the lesson commenced, while control students did not, across two weeks of set theory instruction
key_sources: M. F. Salman, L. A. Yahaya, A. Yusuf, M. A. Ahmed & J. O. Ayinla. (2012). Effects of Behavioural Objectives-based Instructional Strategy on Senior School Students’ Academic Performance in Mathematics in Omu-Aran, Nigeria. Journal of Education and Learning, 1(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v1n2p121

article_title: Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues
citation: Elif Ozata Yucel, Muhlis Ozkan. (2015). Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.4.2579
title: Use process-oriented assessment activities that turn assessment into a learning process
description: Assessment activities were planned to determine the degree to which objectives were achieved, letting students notice and immediately eliminate deficiencies and achieve deep learning. Process assessments replaced result-oriented assessment. The article states that "assessments throughout the process were made to replace result-oriented assessment, and an attempt was made to turn the assessment process into a learning process".
requirements: Assessment activities designed to show students' environmental attitudes, behaviors, feelings, and thoughts as well as conceptual understanding
target_learning_goals: Deep learning of ecosystem, biodiversity, and environmental issues
Noticing and eliminating deficiencies during instruction
examples: Assessment activity titles included "Let's Pose a Question," "Let's Create Our Own Ecosystem," and "If We Were in Charge"
key_sources: Elif Ozata Yucel, Muhlis Ozkan. (2015). Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.4.2579

article_title: Comparative Effects of Concept Mapping and Cooperative Learning Strategies on Senior Secondary School Students' Achievement in Mathematics-Trigonometry in Kano State, Nigeria
citation: T. D. Bot & John E. Eze. (2016). Effects of concept mapping and cooperative learning strategies on senior secondary school students' achievement in trigonometry in Kano state, Nigeria. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 4(1), 56-66. https://www.ejmste.com
title: Pre-/Post-Trigonometry Achievement Test (PRE-TAT / POST-TAT)
description: The study's instrument was a "Pre‐Trigonometry Achievement Test (PRE‐TAT) which also served as Post‐Trigonometry Achievement Test (POST‐TAT)", made of 10 essay questions on sine and cosine rules and their practical applications. It was developed by the researchers, validated by mathematics education and test-and-measurement experts, and pilot-tested with a Cronbach Alpha internal consistency coefficient of 0.78.
requirements: Validated by mathematics education and test and measurement experts before use
target_learners: SSII senior secondary school students in Nigeria
target_learning_goals: Trigonometry achievement: sine and cosine rules and their applications
examples: Used as both pre-test and post-test across the control and two experimental groups in the four-week Kano study
key_sources: T. D. Bot & John E. Eze. (2016). Effects of concept mapping and cooperative learning strategies on senior secondary school students' achievement in trigonometry in Kano state, Nigeria. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 4(1), 56-66. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1107765

article_title: Teaching Probability to Pre-Service Teachers with Argumentation Based Science Learning Approach
citation: Ömer Sinan Can, Tevfik İşleyen. (2016). Teaching Probability to Pre-Service Teachers with Argumentation Based Science Learning Approach. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.33. https://www.iiste.org
title: Probability Achievement Test (PAT)
description: The Probability Achievement Test is a 15-question open-ended instrument prepared by the researcher with input from a faculty member who lectured in the Probability and Statistics course. Questions were distributed across probability sub-topics: determination of sample space, counting methods, permutation, combination, and probability. It was piloted with 87 fourth-grade pre-service teachers who had taken and passed the probability course, yielding a Cronbach's alpha of 0.724, and a sixty-minute period was found sufficient for implementation. It served as both pre-test and post-test in the quasi-experimental design.
requirements: A sixty minute period was found to be sufficient time for the implementation of the test
constraints: The test was developed for and piloted with pre-service teachers in one Turkish public university context
target_learning_goals: probability achievement across sample space, counting, permutation, combination, and probability topics
examples: Applied as pre-test and post-test to both experimental and control groups in the 2014-2015 study
key_sources: Ömer Sinan Can, Tevfik İşleyen. (2016). Teaching Probability to Pre-Service Teachers with Argumentation Based Science Learning Approach. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.33. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1122873

article_title: The Impact of Watching Subtitled Animated Cartoons on Incidental Vocabulary Learning of ELT Students
citation: Ali Karakaş and Arif Sariçoban. (2011). The Impact of Watching Subtitled Animated Cartoons on Incidental Vocabulary Learning of ELT Students. Teaching English with Technology, 12(4), 3-15. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: Present new vocabulary items in context rather than in isolation
description: The article concludes that vocabulary development needs contextual support because guessing meaning from context is more likely, while isolated words give no clues. It draws the teaching implication that "the new vocabulary items should be presented in context rather than in isolation", grounded in its finding that both groups gained vocabulary from words embedded in cartoon contexts.
requirements: Target words must be embedded in meaningful context (e.g., video material) so learners can infer meanings
constraints: The article notes this conclusion would need to be verified by a longitudinal study, since the interval between tests was too short
target_learning_goals: incidental foreign-language vocabulary learning
examples: Both experimental groups watched Family Guy episodes with 18 target verbs embedded and gained significantly on the VKS without being told the study purpose or allowed dictionaries
key_sources: Ali Karakaş and Arif Sariçoban. (2011). The Impact of Watching Subtitled Animated Cartoons on Incidental Vocabulary Learning of ELT Students. Teaching English with Technology, 12(4), 3-15. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1144953

article_title: Integrating Cognitive Linguistics Insights into Data-Driven Learning: Teaching Vertical Prepositions
citation: Kilimci, A. (2017). Integrating cognitive linguistics insights into data-driven learning: teaching vertical prepositions. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 13(2), 681-719. https://www.jlls.org
title: Principled Polysemy model of preposition semantics
description: The Principled Polysemy (PP) model, proposed by Tyler and Evans, holds that the senses of a spatial preposition form a motivated network radiating from a central prototypical sense rather than an arbitrary list. In the study's instruction, students were told that "the senses regarding over and above are not unrelated, or arbitrary, but in fact motivated and extend from one prototypical sense", and PP semantic networks were used as visual rubrics during corpus activities. The article credits the model with reducing arbitrariness and learners' need for rote learning.
requirements: Instruction using the model presents extended senses as systematically connected to a proto-scene, drawing on comparatively few principles
constraints: The article notes the earlier full-specification approach was criticized for lacking a principle and yielding a redundant number of senses, motivating the PP model
target_learners: second-year Turkish university students of English
target_learning_goals: acquiring the polysemous senses of English spatial prepositions
examples: The experimental instruction used PP polysemy networks for over/above and under/below alongside BNCweb concordance activities over two three-hour weekly sessions
key_sources: Kilimci, A. (2017). Integrating cognitive linguistics insights into data-driven learning: teaching vertical prepositions. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 13(2), 681-719. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1159243

article_title: Improving Young English Learners' Language and Literacy Skills through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized Controlled Trial
citation: Leslie M. Babinski, Steven J. Amendum, Steven E. Knotek, Marta Sánchez, Patrick Malone. (2018). Improving Young English Learners’ Language and Literacy Skills Through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized Controlled Trial. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217732335
title: Prioritize unconstrained literacy skills such as vocabulary and comprehension when instructing English learners
description: The article argues that while PD should address both constrained skills (phonemic awareness, phonics) and unconstrained skills (vocabulary, comprehension), instruction for English learners should give much greater emphasis to unconstrained skills, which continue developing over time, given persistent comprehension achievement gaps. The article states the PD "addresses both constrained and unconstrained skills but provides much greater emphasis on unconstrained skills, such as vocabulary and comprehension."
requirements: Teachers need strategies targeting vocabulary and comprehension, such as Modified DRA, language frames, and Vocabulary Text Talk
constraints: Based on NAEP gap data and Paris's constrained/unconstrained skills distinction as applied to ELs
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
vocabulary development
oral language development
examples: The PD's Table 1 lists unconstrained strategies including Teaching Cognates, Vocabulary Text Talk, Frayer Model, Modified DRA, and oral and written sentence frames
key_sources: Leslie M. Babinski, Steven J. Amendum, Steven E. Knotek, Marta Sánchez, Patrick Malone. (2018). Improving Young English Learners’ Language and Literacy Skills Through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized Controlled Trial. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217732335

article_title: PRWR: Evidence of Its Effectiveness in Teaching Academic Content-Area Reading across English Proficiency
citation: Azhar Aziz Lubis; Gunadi Harry Sulistyo. (2018). PRWR: Evidence of Its Effectiveness in Teaching Academic Content-Area Reading across English Proficiency. Dinamika Ilmu, Vol. 18 No. 1. http://dx.doi.org/10.21093/di.v18i1.1070
title: PRWR: a four-phase preview-read-write-recite pattern embedded in a three-phase teaching framework with scaffolding questions
description: PRWR organizes academic reading into four phases — preview, read, write, and recite — delivered through a pre, whilst, and post teaching framework in which "several questions or questioning were deployed" in each phase to scaffold comprehension. Preview activates content and formal schemata via title, headings, and visuals; reading focuses on micro skills such as context clues, main ideas, and factual information with underlining and marking; writing produces a summary of key points; reciting restates the summary using recall words. The article presents detailed syntax tables of activities and guide-questions for each phase.
requirements: Teacher-deployed questions in each phase to scaffold comprehension of academic texts
Guide-questions targeting micro reading skills (context clues, denotation and connotation, topic, main idea and supporting details, factual information)
constraints: Studied at the tertiary level with non-English department students; the article notes limited prior PRWR research at this level
target_learning_goals: academic content-area reading comprehension in terms of word attack skills and text attack skills
examples: In the study, the experimental class was taught with the full PRWR syntax while the control class read passages aloud, translated difficult words to Bahasa Indonesia, and had errors corrected orally
key_sources: Azhar Aziz Lubis; Gunadi Harry Sulistyo. (2018). PRWR: Evidence of Its Effectiveness in Teaching Academic Content-Area Reading across English Proficiency. Dinamika Ilmu, Vol. 18 No. 1. http://dx.doi.org/10.21093/di.v18i1.1070

article_title: PRWR: Evidence of Its Effectiveness in Teaching Academic Content-Area Reading across English Proficiency
citation: Azhar Aziz Lubis; Gunadi Harry Sulistyo. (2018). PRWR: Evidence of Its Effectiveness in Teaching Academic Content-Area Reading across English Proficiency. Dinamika Ilmu, Vol. 18 No. 1. http://dx.doi.org/10.21093/di.v18i1.1070
title: 30-item posttest of micro reading skills (word attack and text attack skills) with expert validation and tryout
description: The study measured academic content-area reading comprehension with a reading comprehension test developed by the authors, expert validated and tried out before administration. "There were 30 items in the posttest measuring students' reading comprehension in terms of word attack skills and text attack skills", operationalizing comprehension as decoding meaning through context clues, denotation and connotation, topic of a paragraph, main idea and supporting details, and factual information. English proficiency was measured separately via a TOEFL PBT Equivalent test administered by an English institute in Malang.
requirements: Expert validation and tryout prior to administration
constraints: Confined to micro reading skills as defined by Sulistyo (2011)
target_learning_goals: academic content-area reading comprehension (word attack and text attack skills)
examples: Posttest scores from this instrument were analyzed with Mann-Whitney U tests and two-way ANOVA

article_title: Learning from Errors: Effects of Teachers Training on Students' Attitudes towards and Their Individual Use of Errors
citation: Rach, S., Ufer, S., & Heinze, A. (2013). Learning from errors: effects of teachers’ training on students’ attitudes towards and their individual use of errors. PNA, 8(1), 21-30. http://hdl.handle.net/10481/27879
title: Process model of learning in error situations with a pragmatic and an analytic path
description: The article proposes a process model describing two different ways of dealing with errors: a pragmatic, outcome-oriented path and an analytic, process-oriented path. As the article states, "the former proceeds directly from error detection to error correction, the latter path includes a closer analysis of the error and the generation of error prevention strategies." The analytic path is expected to be more beneficial for generating negative knowledge, and the strategy materials in the second experimental condition were based on this model.
requirements: Individual experiences in error situations are considered necessary to acquire negative knowledge, since individuals are not usually taught about incorrect facts or processes
constraints: It is questionable whether all error situations are fruitful learning opportunities
target_learning_goals: Learning from errors in mathematics
Acquisition of negative knowledge and error prevention strategies
examples: The strategy materials for the second experimental group encouraged learners to reflect on errors made in homework or exercises and were based on the right part of the process model
key_sources: Rach, S., Ufer, S., & Heinze, A. (2013). Learning from errors: effects of teachers’ training on students’ attitudes towards and their individual use of errors. PNA, 8(1), 21-30. http://hdl.handle.net/10481/27879

article_title: The Influence of Process Approach on English as Second Language Students' Performances in Essay Writing
citation: Akinwamide, T. K. (2012). The Influence of Process Approach on English as Second Language Students' Performances in Essay Writing. English Language Teaching, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n3p16
title: The Process Approach model of writing as a non-linear, recursive, three-stage process
description: The article presents writing as "a non-linear, recursive and generative process" comprising pre-writing, composing/writing and re-writing stages, with editing occurring at the end of each basic stage. Its Figure 1 model organizes pre-writing activities (reminiscing, brainstorming, researching, observing, imagining), composing around audience, intention and time-and-tense relations, and final writing with proofreading, polishing and peer-editing. The author uses this model as the treatment delivered to the Experimental group. Errors are expected and are terminated through recursive editing rather than prevented in advance.
requirements: Students receive procedural information from the teacher before the final writing is done
Editing is systematically carried out at every stage of the work
constraints: The article reports the approach tested only with senior secondary ESL students in two Nigerian state-capital schools
target_learning_goals: essay writing: content, organization, expression, mechanical accuracy
examples: The Experimental group was taught for six weeks using this staged process model before the post-test
key_sources: Akinwamide, T. K. (2012). The Influence of Process Approach on English as Second Language Students' Performances in Essay Writing. English Language Teaching, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n3p16

article_title: The Influence of Process Approach on English as Second Language Students' Performances in Essay Writing
citation: Akinwamide, T. K. (2012). The Influence of Process Approach on English as Second Language Students' Performances in Essay Writing. English Language Teaching, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n3p16
title: Pre-writing task repertoire for generating and ordering ideas before composing
description: The article enumerates pre-writing tasks that expose students to self-assessment, observation and exploration of the subject matter: "a. Observation b. Imagining c. Clustering d. Outlining e. Interviewing f. Brainstorming". These tasks help students assess the dimensions of a rhetorical problem, recall experiences, examine relationships between ideas and find an implicit order in their subject matter. The focus at this stage is developing and ordering relevant facts before drafting begins.
requirements: Pre-writing precedes composing, whose data serve as the springboard for the draft
target_learning_goals: idea generation and organization in essay writing
examples: The Experimental group carried out these pre-writing tasks during the six-week treatment

article_title: Outcomes of the Best in Class Intervention on Teachers' Use of Effective Practices, Self-Efficacy, and Classroom Quality
citation: Maureen A. Conroy, Kevin S. Sutherland, James Algina, Crystal Ladwig, Brittany Werch, Jose Martinez, Gabriel Jessee, Maria Gyure. (2019). Outcomes of the BEST in CLASS Intervention on Teachers' Use of Effective Practices, Self-Efficacy, and Classroom Quality. School Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.17105/SPR-2018-0003.V48-1
title: Cyclical weekly practice-based coaching cycle of goal setting, focused observation, and reflection with performance feedback
description: The article's coaching model is a recurring weekly cycle in which coach and teacher set measurable goals, the coach observes practice, and they meet to review data and plan next steps. The article states coaching "included three key components: (a) goal setting and action planning, (b) focused observations, and (c) reflection and performance feedback." Observations were video-recorded, coaches collected data on teachers' use of the practices, and meetings reviewed progress toward weekly goals and collaboratively planned goals for the following week.
requirements: Coaches trained to mastery via a six-step checkout process before coaching
Weekly coaching meetings with data collected during observations
constraints: Implemented over 14 weeks, two weeks per manual module, in early childhood classrooms
target_learners: early childhood teachers implementing a targeted intervention
target_learning_goals: high-fidelity implementation of instructional practices with focal children
examples: Coaches observed teachers for approximately 45 min per week and held a coaching meeting the same day, reviewing progress toward weekly goals
key_sources: Maureen A. Conroy, Kevin S. Sutherland, James Algina, Crystal Ladwig, Brittany Werch, Jose Martinez, Gabriel Jessee, Maria Gyure. (2019). Outcomes of the BEST in CLASS Intervention on Teachers' Use of Effective Practices, Self-Efficacy, and Classroom Quality. School Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.17105/SPR-2018-0003.V48-1

article_title: Site Selection in Experiments: A Follow-Up Evaluation of Site Recruitment in Two Scale-Up Studies
citation: Tipton, E., Fellers, L., Caverly, S., Vaden-Kiernan, M., Borman, G., Sullivan, K., & Ruiz de Castillo, V. (2015). Site selection in experiments: A follow-up evaluation of site recruitment in two scale-up studies. SREE Spring 2015 Conference Abstract. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs
title: Propensity-score stratified site-selection method for improving generalization from experiments
description: A multistep design-based method for selecting experiment sites so the sample resembles a defined inference population. It uses propensity score methodology to compare the population to eligible sites and create strata for site selection, so that, when perfectly implemented, the sample is "like a miniature of the inference population of interest". The method calls for defining the inference population, eligibility requirements, treatment-effect-relevant covariates, proportional strata allocation, and recruiting at least some eligible sites in each stratum.
requirements: An inference population must be defined with data on covariates related to treatment-effect variability
Not all units in the population may be eligible for the experiment; otherwise an alternative cluster-analysis stratification applies
constraints: When perfectly implemented is seen as likely not to occur, the goal shifts to reducing under-coverage problems that limit post-hoc statistical adjustments
target_learners: Elementary schools and districts in scale-up evaluations
target_learning_goals: Generalizable estimation of average treatment effects of curricular interventions
examples: Applied in the Open Court Reading and Everyday Math scale-up studies, which began recruitment in fall 2011, with twelve covariates from the Common Core of Data and three-by-three combined strata
key_sources: Tipton, E., Fellers, L., Caverly, S., Vaden-Kiernan, M., Borman, G., Sullivan, K., & Ruiz de Castillo, V. (2015). Site selection in experiments: A follow-up evaluation of site recruitment in two scale-up studies. SREE Spring 2015 Conference Abstract. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs

article_title: Improving Reading Outcomes in Kenya: First-Year Effects of the PRIMR Initiative
citation: Stephanie Simmons Zuilkowski & Benjamin Piper. (2014). Improving Reading Outcomes in Kenya: First-Year Effects of the PRIMR Initiative. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org/
title: PRIMR literacy intervention: 150 structured bilingual lessons with aligned low-cost books and modest instructional aids
description: The PRIMR literacy arm is a structured instructional package for early-grade bilingual reading. "The literacy arm of the program included 150 structured lessons in both Kiswahili and English." Teachers received pocket charts and letter flashcards, and students received low-cost books aligned to the scripted lessons, moving the student-to-textbook ratio to 1:1 from the standard 3:1. The books targeted letters, phonological awareness, and decoding, plus controlled-text stories and teacher read-alouds with "a heavy emphasis on comprehension strategies."
requirements: Teachers and head teachers receive 10 days of training in the first year, with TAC tutors and instructional coaches receiving 15 days and providing follow-up support
constraints: Intended for children who had not attended preschool and had little exposure to the alphabet, moving them from basic letter knowledge toward fluency and comprehension within one school year
target_learners: Grade 1 and 2 pupils in Kenyan government and nonformal slum schools learning to read in English and Kiswahili
target_learning_goals: Oral reading fluency
Reading comprehension
Letter knowledge and decoding in English and Kiswahili
examples: In PRIMR classrooms the student-to-textbook ratio was 1:1 rather than the standard 3:1 mandated by national textbook policy and found at baseline
key_sources: Stephanie Simmons Zuilkowski & Benjamin Piper. (2014). Improving Reading Outcomes in Kenya: First-Year Effects of the PRIMR Initiative. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562806

article_title: The Use of Pre-Recorded Lectures on Student Performance in Physiology
citation: Rim Mekonnen Hadgu, Sophia Hoang-Vy Huynh, & Chaya Gopalan. (2016). The Use of Pre-recorded Lectures on Student Performance in Physiology. Journal of Curriculum and Teaching, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/jct.v5n1p105
title: Use pre-recorded lectures as a supplement to live lecture rather than a full replacement
description: The article concludes that pre-recorded lectures effectively support mastery of basic factual details but not complex conceptual processing, so instructors should treat them as "additional, supplementary options of study methods for students" rather than substitutes for live lecture. It warns that replacing live lecture may hinder students from conceptualizing complex information and deprive them of social aspects of the classroom. The conclusion states that "learning is more comprehe nsive when students are in a classroom setting rather than learning from a recorded video".
requirements: Live lecture must remain available for content requiring higher-order comprehension and conceptual processing
constraints: The finding comes from one introductory physiology course with a small sample of 60 students and only two replaced lectures, and students self-selected into PRL use
target_learners: undergraduate introductory physiology students in higher education
target_learning_goals: mastering factual details
processing and comprehending complex conceptual information
examples: Two live lectures (blood coagulation and the role of the liver, gallbladder and pancreas in digestion) were replaced by approximately 40-minute pre-recorded lectures recorded with Camtasia and posted on Moodle, while two other live lectures served as controls
key_sources: Rim Mekonnen Hadgu, Sophia Hoang-Vy Huynh, & Chaya Gopalan. (2016). The Use of Pre-recorded Lectures on Student Performance in Physiology. Journal of Curriculum and Teaching, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/jct.v5n1p105

article_title: Enhancing Academic Achievement and Retention in Senior Secondary School Chemistry through Discussion and Lecture Methods: A Case Study of Some Selected Secondary Schools in Gboko, Benue State, Nigeria
citation: Efe M.Omwirhiren, Esq. [Ph.D]. (2015). Enhancing Academic Achievement And Retention In Senior Secondary School Chemistry Through Discussion And Lecture Methods: A Case Study Of Some Selected Secondary Schools In Gboko, Benue State, Nigeria. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.21. https://www.iiste.org
title: Use discussion method rather than lecture to teach organic chemistry in senior secondary schools
description: The article recommends that Nigerian secondary school teachers replace lecture with discussion method, a step-by-step procedure of teaching that utilizes guided interaction in groups with the teacher acting as facilitator. It concludes that "discussion enhanced better achievement and productivity than the lecture method" and that discussion gives learners room to develop communicating, critical thinking and reflective thinking skills.
requirements: Topics suitable for guided group interaction; the article notes the method is time consuming and suits debatable and problematic topics
constraints: Evidence base is one quasi-experiment in intact classes in Gboko, Benue State, on the topic of nomenclature of compounds in organic chemistry
target_learners: SSII senior secondary science students, ages 16-17
target_learning_goals: Achievement and retention in organic chemistry nomenclature
examples: The experimental group was taught using the discussion method that created maximum room for interaction in groups, while the control group was taught using traditional lecture, over an 8-week treatment

Enhancing Academic Achievement And Retention In Senior Secondary School Chemistry Through Discussion And Lecture Methods: A Case Study Of Some Selected Secondary Schools In Gboko, Benue State, Nigeria. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.21. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1079117

article_title: The Effects of Processing Instruction and Traditional Instruction on Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Ability
citation: Hossein Hashemnezhad & Sanaz Khalili Zangalani. (2012). The Effects of Processing Instruction and Traditional Instruction on Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Ability. English Language Teaching, 5(11). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n11p125
title: Processing Instruction: an input-processing model of explicit grammar instruction
description: Processing Instruction (PI), developed by VanPatten, is an explicit form-focused instruction model that targets how learners process input rather than output. Wong and VanPatten's three basic features are that "Learners are given information about a linguistic structure or form", learners are informed about a processing strategy that may negatively affect pickup of the form, and learners are pushed to process the form during structured input activities without producing it. The article applies this model by building a PI treatment package of explicit information plus structured input activities for six English tenses.
requirements: PI requires a structural syllabus taught by means of structured input activities, with explicit information on the target forms and activities manipulated so learners depend on form to get meaning
constraints: Learners do not produce the target structure during structured input activities; the article notes PI's ultimate scope is not raising consciousness about grammatical form but making learners appreciate the form's communicative function
target_learning_goals: grammatical accuracy in L2 writing
acquisition of target grammatical structures (English tenses)
examples: The study's PI package gave explicit information on six tenses, then three structured input activities per tense: two referential and one affective, all with written stimuli and no production of the target structures.
key_sources: Hossein Hashemnezhad & Sanaz Khalili Zangalani. (2012). The Effects of Processing Instruction and Traditional Instruction on Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Ability. English Language Teaching, 5(11). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n11p125

article_title: Improving First Computer Programming Experiences: The Case of Adapting a Web-Supported and Well-Structured Problem-Solving Method to a Traditional Course
citation: Murat Pasa Uysal. (2014). Improving First Computer Programming Experiences: The Case of Adapting a Web-Supported and Well-Structured Problem-Solving Method to a Traditional Course. Contemporary Educational Technology, 5(3), 198-217. https://www.cedtech.net
title: Well-structured PS course design pattern: problem-led lectures integrated with guided practice labs
description: The experimental course design pattern organizes each weekly unit around a well-defined programming problem: lectures open with the problem, review prerequisite knowledge, present conceptual models (flowcharts plus pseudo codes) and worked examples, while labs provide varied practice problems, support for searching different solutions (analogical problems, recalling prior programs, breaking problems into sub-problems), and reflection on effective solutions. This integrated lectures and labs "to model CP as a form of well -structured PS process with its required activities".
requirements: Instructors trained to guide PS activities and provide just-in-time support
A web-based tool presenting practice problems, worked examples and conceptual models
constraints: Effects were observed with military undergraduate novices on campus; the authors state the findings "may not be widely generalized"
target_learners: first-year undergraduate novice programmers in engineering disciplines
target_learning_goals: well-structured problem-solving skills
C programming performance
examples: Practice problems were made more realistic by withholding programming elements or including irrelevant variables so learners identified critical missing information
key_sources: Murat Pasa Uysal. (2014). Improving First Computer Programming Experiences: The Case of Adapting a Web-Supported and Well-Structured Problem-Solving Method to a Traditional Course. Contemporary Educational Technology, 5(3), 198-217. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105559

article_title: Compared to What? Estimating Causal Effects for Latent Subgroups to Understand Variation in the Impacts of Head Start by Alternate Child Care Setting
citation: Avi Feller, Todd Grindal, Luke Miratrix, Lindsay C. Page. (2014). Compared to what? Estimating Causal Effects for Latent Subgroups to Understand Variation in the Impacts of Head Start by Alternate Child Care Setting. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Principal stratification with hierarchical random effects and Bayesian estimation for latent care-setting subgroups
description: The article develops a framework that models students as a mixture of latent subgroups, each defined by the pair of care types a child would receive with and without a Head Start offer (e.g., "Center Compliers" and "Always Head Start"). It combines a principal stratification framework with a hierarchical random effects model, jointly fitting a choice sub-model and an outcome sub-model via Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in Stan. The classic IV model is described as a special case.
requirements: Baseline covariates sufficient to predict each child's care choice under treatment and control in the choice sub-model
Random effects for the center groups of random assignment to account for the clustered design
constraints: Group membership is not fully observed because it depends on counterfactual care choices
Generating results required careful modeling and extensive sensitivity checks
target_learners: low-income preschool children in Head Start programs
target_learning_goals: estimating causal effects of an educational offer within subgroups defined by counterfactual care setting
examples: The framework was applied to the HSIS, with 4,440 children in 202 center groups, jointly imputing missing data and modeling differential attrition as part of the model
key_sources: Avi Feller, Todd Grindal, Luke Miratrix, Lindsay C. Page. (2014). Compared to what? Estimating Causal Effects for Latent Subgroups to Understand Variation in the Impacts of Head Start by Alternate Child Care Setting. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562722

article_title: Changing the Developmental Trajectory in Early Math through a Two-Year Preschool Math Intervention
citation: Prentice Starkey, Alice Klein, & Lydia DeFlorio. (2013). Changing the Developmental Trajectory in Early Math Through a Two-Year Preschool Math Intervention. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Pre-Pre-K Mathematics and Pre-K Mathematics curricula with home activities and professional development
description: Two paired early-math curricula: Pre-Pre-K Mathematics for 3-year-olds with 13 classroom math activities, and Pre-K Mathematics for 4-year-olds with 24 classroom math activities. Activities in both curricula "were implemented with concrete manipulatives and employed rich mathematical language", delivered in small groups with teacher scaffolding, and paired with home math activities in English or Spanish sent to parents. Teachers received intensive workshops distributed across the year plus on-site facilitation with formative evaluation visits and corrective feedback.
requirements: Professional development including intensive workshops distributed across the year of implementation and on-site facilitation by project staff
Each teacher received a math curriculum book and manipulative materials to accompany small-group classroom activities
constraints: Pre-Pre-K Mathematics had not been previously evaluated for effectiveness prior to this study
target_learners: low-income 3- and 4-year-old Head Start preschool children
target_learning_goals: informal mathematical knowledge and school readiness in mathematics
examples: Fidelity observations were made of each teacher 6 times during the year, with fidelity scores of I-2 and I-1 teachers above .9 of 1.0; time was built in for make-ups and review based on a progress-monitoring instrument.
key_sources: Prentice Starkey, Alice Klein, & Lydia DeFlorio. (2013). Changing the Developmental Trajectory in Early Math Through a Two-Year Preschool Math Intervention. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563068

article_title: Lagging behind Writing Pedagogical Developments: The Impact of Implementing Process-Based Approach on Learners' Writing in a Vietnamese Secondary Education Context
citation: Ngo, C. M. & Trinh, L. Q. (2011). Lagging Behind Writing Pedagogical Developments: The Impact of Implementing Process-Based Approach on Learners' Writing in a Vietnamese Secondary Education Context. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, 1(3), July-September 2011. https://www.imanagerpublications.com
title: The process approach to writing instruction: recursive composing through pre-writing, drafting, peer-evaluating and revising
description: The process approach treats composing as "a recursive, exploratory and generative process wherein ideas are discovered and meaning made", in contrast to product approaches centered on imitating model texts. The study operationalized it through lesson plans adapted from Seow's (2002) process model, moving students from modeling to collaborative practice to individual practice, with teacher help gradually withdrawn. It calls for "a positive, encouraging and collaborative workshop environment" in which students act as both writer and reader.
requirements: Time for writing and revising in a supported learning environment, as the article's recommendations state
constraints: The article notes it does not deny grammatical knowledge matters, but holds grammatical knowledge alone is no guarantee of good writing
target_learning_goals: English writing performance and positive perceptions toward writing activities
examples: Eight lesson plans adapted from Seow's process model were implemented in the experimental group using the Grade-10 textbook topics

article_title: Effectiveness of Proactive Intensive FFI in Cultivating Grammatical Knowledge of Iranian EFL Learners at Different Proficiency Levels
citation: Amir Rooholamin, Reza Biria & Hamid Reza Haghverdi. (2016). Effectiveness of Proactive Intensive FFI in Cultivating Grammatical Knowledge of Iranian EFL Learners at Different Proficiency Levels. English Language Teaching, 9(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n3p197
title: Proactive intensive form-focused instruction (FFI)
description: Proactive intensive FFI is a type of form-focused instruction in which the teacher selects demanding target forms before instruction and treats a limited number of features in depth. In this study it comprised three components: "metalinguistic explanations, i.e. explicit explanations of the grammar", "repeated form-focused tasks", and "explicit corrective feedback on form", delivered within free discussion classes over nine sessions targeting nine verb tenses.
requirements: Instruction must be embedded in meaning-focused communicative classes, integrating form with meaning as the article's FFI framework prescribes.
A limited set of target forms must be selected prior to instruction and treated intensively across repeated tasks.
constraints: The study tested it only with intermediate and advanced adult Persian-speaking EFL learners in a four-week free discussion program.
target_learners: Intermediate and advanced adult EFL learners
target_learning_goals: Grammatical knowledge of English verb tenses
examples: Experimental groups received metalinguistic explanations, repeated form-focused tasks, and explicit corrective feedback during nine free discussion sessions, one verb tense per session.
key_sources: Amir Rooholamin, Reza Biria & Hamid Reza Haghverdi. (2016). Effectiveness of Proactive Intensive FFI in Cultivating Grammatical Knowledge of Iranian EFL Learners at Different Proficiency Levels. English Language Teaching, 9(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n3p197

article_title: The Influence of the Project Method on the Achievement of Young Learners in the Field Science and Social Studies
citation: Prtljaga, S. & Veselinov, D. (2017). The influence of the project method on the achievement of young learners in the field science and social studies. Research in Pedagogy, 7(2), 254-264. https://doi.org/10.17810/2015.63
title: The project method as a constructivist, integrative learning approach
description: The article presents the project method as an innovative approach to learning in which children are active, constructive participants rather than recipients of transmitted knowledge. It defines project activity as a "constructive activity with a goal" and describes its didactic apparatus as workshop cooperative work, interactive strategies, research tasks, learning through discovery and problem solving. It is grounded in the constructivist educational paradigm whose foundation is independent activity of the individual.
requirements: Learners work on projects with didactic instructions such as research and try out, modify, change, combine
Cooperative group work and research tasks are incorporated
constraints: The article states it should not be placed above all other teaching methods, but given the opportunity to contribute
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition in science and social studies
independent learning skills
examples: In the experimental program learners worked on individual and group research tasks, learning through discovery, problem solving and computers, covering the topic A look back – the past.
key_sources: Prtljaga, S. & Veselinov, D. (2017). The influence of the project method on the achievement of young learners in the field science and social studies. Research in Pedagogy, 7(2), 254-264. https://doi.org/10.17810/2015.63

article_title: The Impact of Out-of-School Learning Environments on 6th Grade Secondary School Students Attitude towards Science Course
citation: Halil Ibrahim Yildirim. (2018). The Impact of Out-of-School Learning Environments on 6th Grade Secondary School Students Attitude Towards Science Course. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 6(12). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i12.3624
title: Three-phase structure for out-of-school learning trips: pre-trip preparation, guided participation during the visit, and post-trip classroom follow-up
description: The article organizes out-of-school learning activities into three phases with distinct requirements: before the trip, educational preparations such as "planning trips and activities in line with the learning outcomes in the curriculum, preparing worksheets" plus logistics and permissions; during the trip, guidance, participation and questions; after the trip, classroom activities to share observations. This structure was implemented across the 18-week experimental process.
requirements: Pre-trip educational preparation linked to learning outcomes, logistics planning, permissions, and informing parents and students
During-trip guidance service, student participation, questioning, and planned leisure activities
Post-trip classroom activities for sharing observations to support the out-of-school teaching
target_learning_goals: Attitude toward science course
Curriculum learning outcomes in science
examples: In the study, worksheets and visit plans were prepared in advance, guidance was provided during visits, and students' observations were shared in class afterward

article_title: Early Intervention for Preschoolers at Risk for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: Preschool First Step to Success
citation: Feil, E. G., Small, J. W., Seeley, J. R., Walker, H. M., Golly, A., Frey, A., & Forness, S. R. (2016). Early intervention for preschoolers at risk for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: Preschool First Step to Success. Behavioral Disorders, 41(2), 95-106. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Preschool First Step to Success: a targeted tier-two behavioral intervention combining a classroom component and a home component
description: Preschool First Step to Success is a secondary-tier intervention for children 3-5 years old with externalizing behavior problems that forges a home-school partnership among teacher, parents, and a behavioral coach. The classroom component "had three phases of 10 days each: (a) the coach phase, (b) the teacher phase, and (c) maintenance", using green and red cards, points and praise, group dependent contingencies, and a home-school reward system. In the home component, "caregivers meet for six home visitation sessions with the First Step coach to learn how to teach school success skills via reading, discussion, role play, and demonstrations", covering communication and sharing, cooperation, limit setting, problem solving, friendship making, and self-confidence.
requirements: A trained behavioral coach assigned to each participating teacher, with teachers receiving 4 hours of PFS training plus 4 hours in general classroom management and positive behavior support
Parent participation across six home visitation sessions supported by a manual containing all information and accompanying materials
constraints: Although not specifically designed for preschoolers at risk for comorbid ADHD, it was evaluated with that population via a retrospective subgroup analysis
target_learners: preschool children aged 3-5 with elevated externalizing behavior, including those at risk for comorbid ADHD
target_learning_goals: school success skills
social skills
reduction of externalizing and ADHD-related problem behaviors
examples: In the trial, teachers received training and ongoing one-on-one coach consultation; coaches attended a 2-day intensive training session and were monitored via frequent fidelity checks
key_sources: Feil, E. G., Small, J. W., Seeley, J. R., Walker, H. M., Golly, A., Frey, A., & Forness, S. R. (2016). article_title: A Comparison of Heritage Learners and L2 Learners of Spanish: A Study on Compliment Sequences in the Classroom
citation: Bachelor, J. W., & Barros García, M. J. (2019). A comparison of heritage learners and L2 learners of Spanish: A study on compliment sequences in the classroom. Journal of Foreign Language Education and Technology, 4(1). http://jflet.com/jflet/
title: Do not assume heritage learners need explicit instruction in pragmatic norms they already command; reserve explicit pragmatic lessons for beginning L2 learners
description: The article concludes that pragmatic instruction should be differentiated by learner background: heritage learners of Spanish already display high pragmatic competence in compliment recognition, so "it may not be necessary to teach pragmatic norms to heritage language learners," while beginner L2 students "greatly benefited from the interventions" with statistically significant growth. Teachers should therefore target explicit pragmatic lessons at L2 beginners rather than heritage learners.
requirements: Assessment of learners' existing pragmatic competence before deciding to intervene
Pragmatic lessons targeting speech acts not already mastered by the learner group
constraints: The conclusion is hesitantly drawn and limited to SHL enrolled in Spanish 200-level courses or above
The study assessed recognition only, not pragmatic production
target_learning_goals: pragmatic recognition of Spanish compliments and compliment responses
examples: The study gave three pragmatic lessons to heritage and L2 experimental groups and compared their pre and post MCDCT scores against matched control groups
key_sources: Bachelor, J. W., & Barros García, M. J. (2019). A comparison of heritage learners and L2 learners of Spanish: A study on compliment sequences in the classroom. Journal of Foreign Language Education and Technology, 4(1). http://jflet.com/jflet/

article_title: How Much Videos Win over Audios in Listening Instruction for EFL Learners
citation: Yasin, B., Mustafa, F., & Permatasari, R. (2018). How Much Videos Win Over Audios in Listening Instruction for EFL Learners. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://tojet.net/
title: Use video rather than audio materials for teaching listening skills
description: Based on its experimental comparison, the article recommends that teachers choose video materials over audio-only recordings for listening instruction, because video was more effective in both outcome (larger, criterion-meeting score gains) and process (higher motivation, response, teamwork and participation). As the authors conclude, "teachers are recommended to use video materials instead of their audio counterparts for teaching listening skills". The recommendation rests on the reported 2.5-times-larger improvement and the observation means favouring video.
requirements: Playback equipment (projector, computer, sound system) or student devices able to play videos, plus adequate teacher computer skills, as the article notes
constraints: Videos are more expensive than audio and less feasible in remote or less developed areas, which the article flags as a concern for teachers in remote Indonesia
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension
learning motivation
examples: In the experiment, both groups received identical materials over four 90-minute meetings, but the video group watched a video while the audio group only listened to a recording

article_title: The Impact of Project GLAD on Students' Literacy and Science Learning: Year 1 Results from a Cluster-Randomized Trial of Sheltered Instruction
citation: Theresa Deussen, Elizabeth Autio, Angela Roccograndi, Makoto Hanita. (2014). The Impact of Project GLAD on Students' Literacy and Science Learning: Year 1 Results from a Cluster-Randomized Trial of Sheltered Instruction. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Project GLAD: a multi-component K-12 sheltered instruction model of 35 strategies in four components
description: Project GLAD (Guided Language Acquisition Design) is described as "a multi-component K-12 instructional model designed to build academic English and grade-level content knowledge for students at varying levels of English language proficiency." Its "35 individual instructional strategies ... fall into four broad components": motivation strategies that set behavior expectations and build interest, input strategies presenting information in multiple formats, guided oral practice strategies scaffolding vocabulary through cooperative learning, and reading and writing strategies scaffolding academic literacy. The strategies intentionally build in differentiated instruction for varying English proficiency.
requirements: Teachers learn the approach through a highly structured seven-day training sequence with follow-up coaching
constraints: Before this study Project GLAD had not undergone a rigorous evaluation; a recent review found limited evidence of effectiveness for sheltered instruction
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly English learners, at varying levels of English language proficiency
target_learning_goals: Academic English development
Grade-level content knowledge in mainstream classrooms
examples: In the trial, all 42 treatment teachers attended all seven training days and all used at least some Project GLAD strategies, though frequency and quality varied substantially

article_title: Impacts of the CARE for Teachers Program on Teachers' Social and Emotional Competence and Classroom Interactions
citation: Jennings, P. A., Brown, J. L., Frank, J. L., Doyle, S., Oh, Y., Davis, R., Rasheed, D., DeWeese, A., DeMauro, A. A., Cham, H., & Greenberg, M. T. (2017). Impacts of the CARE for Teachers Program on Teachers' Social and Emotional Competence and Classroom Interactions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000187
title: Prosocial classroom model: teacher social and emotional competences sustain classroom climate and prevent burnout
description: The prosocial classroom theoretical model proposes that teachers' social and emotional competences support coping with teaching demands and prevent burnout. The article states these competencies "include self-awareness of emotional states and cognitions and the ability to effectively regulate their emotions while teaching". When competences are lacking, well-being erodes, classroom climate deteriorates, and a "burnout cascade" is triggered; when high, teachers maintain positive climate and supportive student relationships. CARE for Teachers was designed to target these competences.
requirements: Teachers must develop self-awareness of emotional states and the ability to regulate emotions while teaching for the model's protective pathway to operate
target_learners: K-5 elementary school teachers in high-poverty urban schools
target_learning_goals: teacher social and emotional competence
stress management and burnout prevention
quality of classroom interactions
examples: The CARE for Teachers logic model operationalizes the prosocial classroom model by targeting emotion skills instruction, mindful awareness practices, and caring and listening practices

Impacts of the CARE for Teachers Program on Teachers' Social and Emotional Competence and Classroom Interactions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000187

article_title: Pragmatic Comprehension Development through Telecollaboration
citation: Vahid Rafieyan, Maryam Sharafi-Nejad, Zahra Khavari, Lin Siew Eng & Abdul Rashid Mohamed. (2014). Pragmatic Comprehension Development through Telecollaboration. English Language Teaching, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n2p11
title: Pragmatic comprehension as two-level understanding of sense and speaker intention
description: The article's framing account of pragmatic comprehension, attributed to Thomas (1995) and Holtgraves and Kashima (2008): understanding an expression requires both "assigning sense to the words uttered and the speaker's intention behind the words". Because intended meanings differ considerably from culture to culture, the semantic aspect (what is communicated) must be complemented by the pragmatic aspect (what is meant), which the study operationalizes as comprehension of implied opinions.
requirements: Exposure to target language culture and contact with target language speakers to develop the pragmatic aspect
constraints: Sociolinguistic perspectives of source and target languages differ significantly, so interpretations of the same utterance vary across cultures
target_learning_goals: Interpreting implied meanings and speaker intention in the target language
examples: The study measured this construct with implied-opinion items in a listening comprehension test following an 18-week intervention.
key_sources: Vahid Rafieyan, Maryam Sharafi-Nejad, Zahra Khavari, Lin Siew Eng & Abdul Rashid Mohamed. (2014). Pragmatic Comprehension Development through Telecollaboration. English Language Teaching, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n2p11

article_title: Implementation of Cooperative Learning Model in Preschool
citation: Nilüfer Okur Akçay. (2016). Implementation of Cooperative Learning Model in Preschool. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n3p83
title: Preschool teachers should use varied, active methods and be trained to organize cooperative learning
description: Drawing on the study's findings and cited literature, the article recommends that "the preschool teachers should use different methods and techniques in their classes" and that teachers "should be informed of organizing and implementing" cooperative learning, in which the teacher creates the learning environment and both teacher and students act as learning sources. It also cites the recommendation that teachers determine and list the social skills (respect, adopting the task, participating, encouraging friends, staying within the group, talking undertone) to teach and use in evaluation.
requirements: Teachers should know methods and techniques that help understand students' cognitive structures
Preparations before implementation are as important as the implementation; criteria and social skills should be determined in advance
constraints: Recommendation grounded in a single small quasi-experiment and cited literature, not tested directly in this study
target_learning_goals: non-memorization-based science concept learning and social skill development
examples: In this study the teacher presented rules, guided groups, supplied materials, and led experiments such as blindfolded smelling and listening to music with one ear closed

article_title: The Acquisition of French Vocabulary in an Interactive Digital Gaming Context
citation: Rueb, A., Cardoso, W., & Grimshaw, J. (2018). The acquisition of French vocabulary in an interactive digital gaming context. In P. Taalas, J. Jalkanen, L. Bradley & S. title: Prêt à Négocier (PàN): a digital information gap game for French oral interaction and vocabulary
description: Prêt à Négocier is an interactive digital information gap game in which students have three minutes to exchange information about a product they are buying or selling and agree on a final price. It runs on computers, tablets, and smartphones, playable face-to-face in class or remotely via a built-in audio chat feature. In this study it was played twice weekly for 25 minutes across four themed weeks (apartment rentals, cars, apartments, pirate ships).
requirements: Pairs of learners must negotiate orally and synchronously, using oral interaction skills and appropriate vocabulary persuasively to win the negotiation
constraints: In this study it was compared against paper-based gamified information gap activities emulating the same oral interactions, and showed limited pedagogical value for vocabulary acquisition overall
target_learners: intermediate-level post-secondary French as second language learners
target_learning_goals: L2 French vocabulary acquisition
oral interaction skills
examples: Students negotiated purchases or rentals of items like cars, houses, and trips to the moon, with vocabulary used meaningfully and connected to personal experiences

article_title: On the Effects of Focus on Form, Focus on Meaning, and Focus on Forms on Learners' Vocabulary Learning in ESP Context
citation: Mahnaz Saeidi, Elaheh Zaferanieh & Hafez Shatery. (2012). On the Effects of Focus on Form, Focus on Meaning, and Focus on Forms on Learners' Vocabulary Learning in ESP Context. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p72
title: ESP vocabulary teaching should favor Focus on Form tasks such as dictogloss over word-list memorization
description: Based on the finding that the dictogloss-based FoF group significantly outperformed both the FoM and FoFs groups on productive vocabulary, the article recommends that teachers learn "which kinds of instruction (focus on form, focus on forms or focus on meaning) would be more effective in vocabulary learning in ESP context" and apply FoF techniques in the classroom. Material developers are likewise advised to design tasks that provide opportunities for the most effective approach.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of different techniques for applying FoF instruction in classroom contexts
constraints: The study is limited to beginning proficiency level, to dictogloss as the single FoF technique, and to Iranian participants, so the authors state results cannot be generalized to learners of other nationalities
target_learning_goals: Productive L2 vocabulary knowledge
examples: The study assigned 70 Iranian architecture-engineering students to dictogloss, discussion, or word-list conditions and compared posttest scores

article_title: The Impact of Using Authentic Videos on Prosodic Ability among Foreign Language Learners
citation: Namaziandost, E., Esfahani, F. R., & Hashemifarnia, A. (2018). The Impact of Using Authentic Videos on Prosodic Ability among Foreign Language Learners. International Journal of Instruction, 11(4), 375-390. https://www.e-iji.net
title: Researcher-designed 0-100 prosody rating scale with weighted prosodic components
description: The researchers built an oral-interview rating scale for general prosodic ability, scored out of 100 and distributed across prosodic components: "30 scores for intonation, 30 for pronunciation,  20 for stress, 10 for pause, and 10 for juncture". Four expert raters each assessed one prosodic dimension individually to prevent subjectivity, produced detailed written reports, and the total score was computed out of 100 for each student in both groups at pre- and post-test. Face validity was checked by three TEFL experts.
requirements: Administered as oral interviews conducted by well-experienced English experts
Four raters, each responsible for one prosodic dimension, to prevent subjectivity
constraints: Scores were dispersed only across the five prosodic components the researchers named
target_learning_goals: Prosodic ability: intonation, pronunciation, stress, pause, and juncture
examples: Pre- and post-test oral interviews scored with this scale produced the totals analysed in Tables 1-10

article_title: The Effectiveness of the Problem Solving Strategy and the Scientific Approach to Students' Mathematical Capabilities in High Order Thinking Skills
citation: Hardi Tambunan. (2019). The Effectiveness of the Problem Solving Strategy and the Scientific Approach to Students' Mathematical Capabilities in High Order Thinking Skills. International Electronic Journal of Mathematics Education, 14(2), 293-302. https://doi.org/10.29333/iejme/5715
title: Prefer problem solving strategy over the scientific approach when the goal is students' higher order thinking skills in mathematics
description: Based on its hypothesis tests, the article recommends that "so that students' mathematical abilities are better in HOTS, then problem solving strategy are better used compared to scientific approaches." The recommendation rests on the quasi-experimental finding that the problem solving group scored significantly higher on communication, creativity, problem solving, and reasoning. It applies to mathematics teaching aimed at higher order thinking outcomes.
requirements: Teachers trained to implement Polya's four-stage problem solving strategy
constraints: Evidence base is a non-randomized quasi-experiment in 10th-grade classes in Medan, Indonesia, on system of linear equations material
target_learning_goals: higher order thinking skills: communication, creativity, problem solving, mathematical reasoning
examples: The study assigned four classes (two public, two private schools) to problem solving strategy or scientific approach conditions and compared posttest scores

article_title: The Efficacy of a Home-School Intervention for Preschoolers with Challenging Behaviors: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Preschool First Step to Success
citation: Feil, E. G., Frey, A., Walker, H. M., Small, J. W., Seeley, J. R., Golly, A., & Forness, S. R. (2014). The Efficacy of a Home-School Intervention for Preschoolers With Challenging Behaviors: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Preschool First Step to Success. Journal of Early Intervention. https://doi.org/10.1177/1053815114566090
title: Preschool First Step to Success (PFS) intervention
description: PFS is a secondary-tier, home-school collaborative intervention for behaviorally at-risk preschoolers. It combines a 30-day classroom component with a green/red card feedback and group-dependent reward system, coach and teacher phases, and a 6-8 week homeBase parent component teaching six skills including "communication and sharing, cooperation, limits setting, problem solving, friendship making, and self-confidence." A behavioral coach consults with teachers throughout.
requirements: Trained behavioral coach with bachelor's degree or higher
Daylong teacher workshop training
Parent participation in weekly homeBase sessions
constraints: Coach phase extended up to 10 days for preschoolers versus 5 in elementary version
Parent meetings conducted with child present
Home component begins after Day 2 rather than Day 10
target_learners: Preschool children with challenging behaviors at risk for EBD
target_learning_goals: Prosocial behavior and social skills
Reduction of externalizing problem behaviors
