article_title: The Probability Approach to English If-Conditional Sentences
citation: Mei Wu. (2012). The Probability Approach to English If-conditional Sentences. English Language Teaching, 5(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n5p37
title: The Probability Approach: classifying English conditionals into four types by likelihood of the result-clause event
description: The Probability Approach is a framework for teaching English if-conditional sentences in which learners "firstly judge how likely (i.e. the probability) the event in the result-clause will take place when the condition in the if-clause is met, then chose the corresponding conditional sentence type based on the probability." It classifies conditionals into four types ordered by probability: factual (100%), predictive (~50%), hypothetical (~10%), and counterfactual (0%). The approach was tested in a controlled experiment with Chinese freshman English majors.
requirements: Learners must be able to judge the probability of the result-clause event given the if-clause condition
constraints: The four basic types are a simplified representation; mixed conditionals and colloquial or sub-standard expressions fall outside them
The article recommends it for beginner learners of English conditionals
target_learning_goals: distinguishing factual, predictive, hypothetical and counterfactual conditionals
choosing correct conditional sentence type
examples: A 30-minute lecture taught students to decide conditional type by judging probability of the result-clause event
key_sources: Mei Wu. (2012). The Probability Approach to English If-conditional Sentences. English Language Teaching, 5(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n5p37

article_title: Self-Regulated Strategy Instruction for Developing Speaking Proficiency and Reducing Speaking Anxiety of Egyptian University Students
citation: El-Sakka, S. M. F. (2016). Self-Regulated Strategy Instruction for Developing Speaking Proficiency and Reducing Speaking Anxiety of Egyptian University Students. English Language Teaching, 9(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n12p22
title: Three-stage lesson structure of preparation, performance, and reflection for self-regulated speaking practice
description: Each intervention lesson was divided into three main stages — "Preparation, Performance, reflection" — each with an explanation sub-stage where the instructor explicitly teaches and models strategies, and an application sub-stage where students practice them. In preparation, students set goals, generate and organize ideas, and seek help; in performance, small groups of five discuss the topic while the instructor circulates; in reflection, students use reflective journals and evaluation checklists. The pattern embeds self-regulated strategy training directly into content-based speaking lessons.
requirements: Explicit teaching and modeling of strategies in each explanation sub-stage
Small-group application with instructor guidance and support
constraints: Developed and evaluated for ELT Methodology Course speaking classes with third-year EFL university students
target_learning_goals: speaking proficiency
reducing speaking anxiety
examples: Students reflected on their own and peers' speaking using reflective journals and researcher-made evaluation checklists
key_sources: El-Sakka, S. M. F. (2016). Self-Regulated Strategy Instruction for Developing Speaking Proficiency and Reducing Speaking Anxiety of Egyptian University Students. English Language Teaching, 9(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n12p22

article_title: Can a Multimedia Tool Help Students' Learning Performance in Complex Biology Subjects?
citation: Koseoglu, P., & Efendioglu, A. (2015). Can a Multimedia Tool Help Students' Learning Performance in Complex Biology Subjects? South African Journal of Education, 35(4). https://doi.org/10.15700/saje.v35n4a1169
title: Use dynamic visualisation (simulation/animation) rather than static visuals when designing multimedia science-teaching tools
description: The article's implication section advises that, in designing multimedia teaching and learning tools, "designers ought to prefer dynamic visualisation techniques (simulation /animation) rather than static visualization." Dynamic visuals are credited with helping students concretise abstract biology content and sustain attention. The recommendation rests on the study's achievement and interview findings for the multimedia tool.
requirements: Multimedia design principles such as modality, multiple representation, coherence, contiguity and redundancy should be observed, as the article states these were taken into consideration during tool development.
constraints: The recommendation derives from a single five-week study with 48 Grade 12 students on nervous-system content; the article calls for larger-sample replication.
target_learners: Grade 12 secondary school students studying biology
target_learning_goals: Understanding abstract biology concepts such as the nervous system
examples: The Mbio tool embedded simulations and audio-visual animations controlled by the teacher, and students reported that visuality helped concretise abstract subjects.

article_title: First Step to Success: Applications to Preschoolers at Risk of Developing Autism Spectrum Disorders
citation: Frey, A. J., Small, J. W., Feil, E. G., Seeley, J. R., Walker, H. M., & Forness, S. (2015). First Step to Success: Applications to Preschoolers at Risk of Developing Autism Spectrum Disorders. Education and Training in Autism and Developmental Disabilities, 50(4), 397-407. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=First+Step+to+Success+Applications+to+Preschoolers+at+Risk+of+Developing+Autism+Spectrum+Disorders
title: Preschool First Step to Success: a manualized collaborative home-and-school tier-two intervention
description: First Step to Success is "a collaborative home and school intervention to help at risk children in getting off to a good start in school", targeting children who have difficulty adjusting to routine school demands. A teacher, parent, and coach triad teaches generic school success skills such as following directions, doing one's work, and getting along with peers. The program has three modular components — screening, classroom, and home. The classroom component is a red/green feedback-card game with points awarded in 30-second intervals and a child-selected rewarding activity when the daily criterion is met, plus a daily note home; the home component consists of six coach-led home-visitation sessions covering communication, cooperation, limit setting, problem solving, friendship-making, and confidence building. The coach implements the school component for 10 days, hands it to the teacher for 10 days, then feedback and reinforcements are phased out over 10 days.
requirements: A trained behavioral coach who implements the program first and supports the teacher and parents
One target child per classroom, since the intervention can only be administered to one student at a time
constraints: The article states it was not designed to target specific disorders such as ASD and is not proposed as a comprehensive or specific treatment for young children with ASD
target_learners: preschool children with externalizing behavior problems at risk for ASD
target_learning_goals: prosocial academic behaviors
school success skills such as following directions, doing one's work, and getting along with peers
examples: In the trial, coaches met weekly for 6 to 8 weeks with parents on promoting school success skills via reading, discussion, role-plays, and demonstrations, and the preschool version was modified for younger children and teachers with less classroom-management training.

article_title: Effects of an Informational Text Reading Comprehension Intervention for Fifth-Grade Students
citation: Kristen D. Ritchey, Kimberly Palombo, Rebecca D. Silverman, and Deborah L. Speece. (2017). Effects of an Informational Text Reading Comprehension Intervention for Fifth-Grade Students. Learning Disability Quarterly, 40(2). https://doi.org/10.1177/0731948716682689
title: Screening measures used in RTI may not serve as progress-monitoring tools for informational-text comprehension interventions
description: The article argues that validated screening measures may be inadequate for monitoring response to short-term comprehension interventions. The fluency and TOSREC screening measures used in this study "would not be useful for progress monitoring" because fluency probes do not assess informational text comprehension and TOSREC is not designed for brief-interval monitoring. The authors call for prioritizing development and validation of progress-monitoring assessments for informational text.
requirements: Progress-monitoring probes must address text reading level, informational text structure, and the role of topical background knowledge
constraints: TOSREC has only three alternate forms designed for fall, winter, and spring plus one additional form
target_learners: Upper elementary students receiving tiered comprehension interventions
target_learning_goals: Accurate monitoring of responsiveness to comprehension instruction
examples: The study selected Passage Reading Fluency and TOSREC as validated screening measures, yet neither could monitor progress across brief intervals.
key_sources: Kristen D. Ritchey, Kimberly Palombo, Rebecca D. Silverman, and Deborah L. Speece. (2017). Effects of an Informational Text Reading Comprehension Intervention for Fifth-Grade Students. Learning Disability Quarterly, 40(2). https://doi.org/10.1177/0731948716682689

article_title: The Effect of Implementation of TBLT in Reading Comprehension Classes of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Mozhgan Madhkhan & Seyed Mojtaba Mousavi. (2017). The Effect of Implimentation of TBLT in Reading Comprehension Classes of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p119
title: Replace traditional post-reading comprehension questions with pre-planned task-based reading activities
description: Based on the study's results, the authors recommend that reading instruction use pre-planned tasks instead of traditional post-reading activities such as comprehension questions, true/false and open-ended items, arguing this "could provide more competent learners". The recommendation rests on the experimental group's significantly higher post-test scores and is framed as especially valuable where evaluation systems are traditional and exams are knowledge-oriented.
requirements: Tasks should be pre-planned and based on the reading texts being taught
Teachers should choose tasks for their educational potential and capacity to convey the content to learners
constraints: Supported here by one study with intermediate Iranian EFL learners; the authors note results of prior TBLT reading research do not agree in all cases
target_learning_goals: L2 reading comprehension
examples: The experimental group worked on tasks such as reading and discussing visuals, note-taking with product creation, and summary writing, while the control group answered open-ended, true/false and matching comprehension questions
key_sources: Mozhgan Madhkhan & Seyed Mojtaba Mousavi. (2017). The Effect of Implimentation of TBLT in Reading Comprehension Classes of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p119

article_title: Management of Development of Creative Civil Activity of Student's Youth
citation: Belentsov S.I., Gribanova V.A., Brasnik O.U., Pozdniakov A.V. (2018). Management of Development of Creative Civil Activity of Student's Youth. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(2): 257-264. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.2.257
title: Project work with master classes producing socially significant student projects
description: Within the interiorization stage, master classes in creation and presentation of projects were organized for the experimental group, ending with discussion of present problems and ways of their decision. The article reports that "28 socially significant proj ects were developed by students" addressing Russian culture and traditions, promotion of a healthy lifestyle, design of the inclusive educational environment, and creation of space promoting formation of civil activity; the prepared projects were submitted to a competition of city youth self-government. More than 50 people from 84 students who passed a master class became active participants of forums, student's self-government, moderators of projects (6 in student council, 16 forum organizers, 34 volunteers).
requirements: Master classes in creation and presentation of projects, plus collaboration with teachers, curators and self-government institutions
constraints: Activity took place within one institute and city (Taganrog) context during the experiment
target_learning_goals: practical experience of civil action
promotion of civil activity of student's audience
examples: 16 student volunteers used created media materials and video records distributed via social networks to promote an active civic stand among school students of Taganrog

article_title: The Effect of Using Prezi on Al Zaytoonah University Students' Performance in French Language Reading Skills
citation: Samer Al-Hammouri. (2019). The Effect of Using Prezi on Al Zaytoonah University Students' Performance in French Language Reading Skills. International Education Studies, 12(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v12n1p128
title: Prezi web-based zoomable presentation tool as used for French reading instruction
description: Prezi is a web-based presentation application that uses one canvas instead of sequential slides, letting users place text, images and video in frames and define paths between them. The article defines it as "a presentation that displays information in an optical map, in which text, video and graphics can be rendered dynamically to zoom in and out within content". In this study it was the instructional medium for the experimental group's French reading lessons, and the article credits it with supporting conceptual mapping and non-linear presentation of relationships between concepts.
requirements: Internet connection for rendering when used online; users must be able to operate its applications and templates
constraints: The site does not support Arabic language input; offline viewing requires the paid professional version; limited font types; notes cannot be added for viewing
target_learners: middle school students in the reviewed prior studies
target_learning_goals: Presenting lesson content visually and non-linearly; supporting reading and concept understanding
examples: The experimental group's French reading lessons were taught using Prezi while the control group was taught the traditional way.
key_sources: Samer Al-Hammouri. (2019). The Effect of Using Prezi on Al Zaytoonah University Students' Performance in French Language Reading Skills. International Education Studies, 12(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v12n1p128

article_title: Determination Instructions Efficiency of Teaching Methods in Teaching Physics in the Case of Teaching Unit "Viscosity. Newtonian and Stokes Law"
citation: Branka Radulović, Maja Stojanović. (2015). Determination Instructions Efficiency of Teaching Methods in Teaching Physics in the Case of Teaching Unit „Viscosity. Newtonian and Stokes law“. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 8, Number 2. https://adn.teaching.ro
title: Prefer teaching methods that yield positive instructional efficiency — higher standardized achievement with lower cognitive load
description: The article recommends that teachers select methods by their measured instructional efficiency, computed from standardized cognitive load and standardized achievement. "Positive values instructional efficiency mean that the application of these teaching methods achieved higher standardized achievement and a small er load." Therefore "teachers should use different teaching methods that will result in a positive instructional effectiveness."
requirements: Measurement of both student achievement (pre/post tests) and perceived cognitive load to compute standardized efficiency values
constraints: Efficiency values depend on the kind of tasks involved, as the authors note that how schema quality is measured may depend on the tasks
target_learning_goals: physics concept understanding
examples: In this study the experiment method produced EE = 0.37 (high-efficiency quadrant) and the traditional method EC = -0.37 (low-efficiency quadrant) for the viscosity unit
key_sources: Branka Radulović, Maja Stojanović. (2015). Determination Instructions Efficiency of Teaching Methods in Teaching Physics in the Case of Teaching Unit „Viscosity. Newtonian and Stokes law“. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 8, Number 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1073276

article_title: The Effect of Using Mind Maps on the Development of Maths and Science Skills
citation: Polat, O., Yavuz, E., A. & Tunc, A., B., O. (2017). The effect of using mind maps on the development of mathematics and science skills. Cypriot Journal of Educational Science. 12(5), 32-45. https://www.cjes.eu
title: Mind map evaluation system for pre-school children
description: A researcher-developed scoring rubric, modelled on the Evrekli, Inel and Balim (2010) system but adapted because writings are scored in the original, for evaluating pre-school children's mind maps. It scores "First-Level sub-branches: 2 Points" up to fourth-level branches at 8 points, cross links at 10 points, relationships at 2 points and each example at 1 point. Two reviewers coded the water and clothes maps and the cohesion co-efficiency between reviewers was .93, which the authors took as evidence the system was valid and reliable for this study.
requirements: Themes chosen should be topics thought to be known by children
Two independent reviewers code the maps to establish inter-rater cohesion
constraints: Developed and validated only on the water and clothes theme maps in this study
Adapted from a system designed for older learners because the original scores writing
target_learning_goals: maths skills
science skills
mind map structure (sub-branches, relationships, cross links, examples)
examples: The water and clothes theme mind maps were coded by two separate reviewers using a statistics program, yielding a cohesion co-efficiency of .93.
key_sources: Polat, O., Yavuz, E., A. & Tunc, A., B., O. (2017). The effect of using mind maps on the development of mathematics and science skills. Cypriot Journal of Educational Science. 12(5), 32-45. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1140786

article_title: Effects of Audiovisual Media on L2 Listening Comprehension: A Preliminary Study in French
citation: Shannon R. Becker and Jessica L. Sturm. (2017). Effects of Audiovisual Media on L2 Listening Comprehension: A Preliminary Study in French. CALICO Journal. https://doi.org/10.1558/cj.26754
title: Audiovisual listening activities structured as prelistening, listening, and postlistening phases
description: The article describes a three-phase structure for activities built around audiovisual materials, in which "activities can be divided into prelistening, listening, and postlistening categories" to help students derive maximum benefit from the materials. Preliminary activities activate schemata to reduce cognitive load, the listening phase applies metacognitive strategies guided by the instructor, and postlistening activities require application of newly acquired knowledge rather than mere comprehension questions. The study's treatment group used this structure daily during its four-week learning phase.
requirements: Audiovisual materials must be incorporated into well-structured, pedagogically sound activities rather than used on their own
target_learners: foreign language learners in instructed SLA contexts
target_learning_goals: L2 listening comprehension
listening strategies and metacognitive regulation
examples: In the study's treatment group, students brainstormed possible causes of stains before watching laundry-tips video clips, listened to prove or disprove their ideas, then discussed comprehension questions and completed a partner activity on the video content
key_sources: Shannon R. Becker and Jessica L. Sturm. (2017). Effects of Audiovisual Media on L2 Listening Comprehension: A Preliminary Study in French. CALICO Journal. https://doi.org/10.1558/cj.26754

article_title: Using a New Schema Approach with Primary at Risk Students in Word Problem Solving
citation: Amiripour, P., Dossey, J.A., & Shahvarani, A. (2017). Using a new schema approach with primary at-risk students in word problem solving. REDIMAT, 6(3), 228-255. http://dx.doi.org/10.17583/redimat.2017.2612
title: Problem Patterns (PP) approach: a schema-based word-problem-solving model using colored circles, operators, and paths
description: The Problem Patterns approach is a schema-based instructional model in which students represent word problems as diagrams of circles holding data points and operator circles, connected by colored lines showing the solution path. Students were "taught to break problems into data, units, and desired solution, removing irrelevant information, and make a solution model with manipulatives." The model distinguishes linear PPs, nonlinear PPs built from embedded linear sub-paths, and open versus closed forms, with irrelevant information appearing as unconnected circles.
requirements: Students first identify main information, then relate known data and unknowns, then attach an operation to form the main path
Different colors distinguish data circles, operator circles, and connecting lines so the main path can be found
constraints: Closed nonlinear PPs were very difficult for at-risk students, particularly second graders
Nonlinear problems with more than one operation created greater information-processing load
target_learners: at-risk grade 2 and 3 students with mathematical difficulties retained in grade at least once
target_learning_goals: solving whole-number contextual word problems using addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division
examples: Students first built linear PP models with colored clay and pipe cleaners in small groups, then moved to nonlinear PPs in the second month and closed nonlinear PPs in the third month
key_sources: Amiripour, P., Dossey, J.A., & Shahvarani, A. (2017). Using a new schema approach with primary at-risk students in word problem solving. REDIMAT, 6(3), 228-255. http://dx.doi.org/10.17583/redimat.2017.2612

article_title: Evaluating the Effects of Input-Based Approaches to the Teaching of Pragmalinguistics and Sociopragmatics in Second Language Pragmatics: A Case of English Request Hedges
citation: Takimoto, M. (2014). Evaluating the Effects of Input-based Approaches to the Teaching of Pragmalinguistics and Sociopragmatics in Second Language Pragmatics: A Case of English Request Hedges. The IAFOR Journal of Language Learning, I(I). https://iafor.org/journal-of-language-learning
title: Depth-of-processing account: CI-formed explicit knowledge is procedural, SI-formed explicit knowledge is declarative
description: The article explains its asymmetric results with Craik's levels-of-processing claim that memory-trace quality depends on depth of perceptual and mental processing where meanings and forms are linked. Because CI participants worked on pragmalinguistics-sociopragmatics connection activities requiring them to access and integrate both kinds of meaning, the article surmises that "explicit knowledge formed through the CI treatment is procedural, whereas explicit knowledge established through the SI treatment is declarative," drawing on Ellis's (2008) distinction between rapidly accessible procedural and more slowly accessed declarative explicit knowledge.
requirements: Learners must process both pragmalinguistic and sociopragmatic meaning connections for explicit knowledge to become procedural and rapidly accessible in production
constraints: The article states that no information regarding the psycholinguistic processing involved in the treatments or tests is available, so explanations must be speculative and explanatory in nature
target_learning_goals: recognizing and producing contextually appropriate English request hedges
examples: CI participants rated politeness and listed ways requests could be made more polite, connecting pragmalinguistic and sociopragmatic factors; SI participants only rated closeness and request difficulty
key_sources: Takimoto, M. (2014). Evaluating the Effects of Input-based Approaches to the Teaching of Pragmalinguistics and Sociopragmatics in Second Language Pragmatics: A Case of English Request Hedges. The IAFOR Journal of Language Learning, I(I). https://iafor.org/journal-of-language-learning

article_title: Evaluating the Effects of Input-Based Approaches to the Teaching of Pragmalinguistics and Sociopragmatics in Second Language Pragmatics: A Case of English Request Hedges
citation: Takimoto, M. (2014). Evaluating the Effects of Input-based Approaches to the Teaching of Pragmalinguistics and Sociopragmatics in Second Language Pragmatics: A Case of English Request Hedges. The IAFOR Journal of Language Learning, I(I). https://iafor.org/journal-of-language-learning
title: Design input-based pragmatics tasks so learners process both pragmalinguistic and sociopragmatic features, and repeat the tasks
description: The article's pedagogical implication is that effective input-based instruction occurs "when the tasks provide learners with opportunities for processing both pragmalinguistic and sociopragmatic features of the target structures." It further advises that "it is advisable for the task to be repeated so that the connections between pragmalinguistic-sociopragmatic factors of target features are significantly reinforced," citing Sharwood Smith's (1993) suggestion that repeated exposure guides learners to analyze discrete features and derive rules.
requirements: Tasks must give learners opportunities to process both pragmalinguistic and sociopragmatic features of the target structures
Tasks should be repeated across sessions to reinforce pragmalinguistic-sociopragmatic connections
constraints: The recommendation rests on one study with 45 learners and a non-interactive DCT instrument; the article calls for more research to confirm the outcome
target_learning_goals: L2 pragmatic competence in producing and recognizing request hedges
examples: The CI treatment combined pragmalinguistics-focused activities, sociopragmatics-focused rating activities, and a pragmalinguistics-sociopragmatics connection activity across four weekly 20-minute sessions
key_sources: Takimoto, M. (2014). Evaluating the Effects of Input-based Approaches to the Teaching of Pragmalinguistics and Sociopragmatics in Second Language Pragmatics: A Case of English Request Hedges. The IAFOR Journal of Language Learning, I(I). https://iafor.org/journal-of-language-learning

article_title: Pragmatic Instruction May Not Be Necessary among Heritage Speakers of Spanish: A Study on Requests
citation: Barros García, M. J., & Bachelor, J. W. (2018). Pragmatic Instruction May Not Be Necessary Among Heritage Learners of Spanish: A Study on Requests. Journal of Foreign Language Education and Technology, 3(1). https://jflet.com/jflet/
title: Reserve explicit pragmatic instruction on requests for beginner L2 learners rather than advanced heritage learners
description: The article recommends tailoring pragmatic instruction to learner profile: lessons on Spanish request strategies may help beginner L2 learners, who depend on classroom input, while heritage learners with advanced proficiency already maintain the pragmatic norms of their family and community. The authors state the lessons "may be especially useful for beginner L2 learners but unnecessary for SHL learners with a more advanced level of proficiency," and question prior recommendations to teach pragmatics in heritage courses.
requirements: Learner proficiency and background must be assessed before deciding whether to include pragmatic lessons, as the SHL participants had all placed at intermediate-high per the ACTFL guidelines before the course.
constraints: The article cautions that the pragmatic lessons may actually confuse students and result in poorer pragmatic competence, and that one study cannot make a declarative statement; the recommendation is limited to request strategies and awaits replication with other proficiency levels.
target_learners: U.S. heritage learners of Spanish at intermediate-high proficiency
beginner L2 learners of Spanish in U.S. higher education
target_learning_goals: pragmatically appropriate production of requests in Spanish, including hearer-oriented and conventionally indirect strategies
examples: Three 20-minute pragmatic lessons (about 60 minutes total) were delivered to the SHL and L2 experimental groups during the spring 2017 semester, based on activities from Langer (2013), CARLA (2006), and Martín Ruiz (2011).
key_sources: Barros García, M. J., & Bachelor, J. W. (2018). Pragmatic Instruction May Not Be Necessary Among Heritage Learners of Spanish: A Study on Requests. Journal of Foreign Language Education and Technology, 3(1). https://jflet.com/jflet/

article_title: Effects of Hierarchy Vocabulary Exercises on English Vocabulary Acquisition
citation: Lin, Ching-Ying & Hsu, Wei Shu. (2013). Effects of Hierarchy Vocabulary Exercises on English Vocabulary Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 6(9). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n9p110
title: Use hierarchy vocabulary exercises rather than copying exercises after explicit vocabulary instruction
description: The article concludes that "hierarchy vocabulary exercise was a more effective exercise type for vocabulary acquisition and reading comprehension". After explicit instruction of target words, teachers should assign exercises that require progressively deeper mental processing (attention, recognition, manipulation, interpretation, production) instead of copying drills, because copying involves rote repetition without deeper and more detailed thinking and may not require learners to actually produce language.
requirements: Exercises follow explicit instruction of target words, as in the study where both groups received the same vocabulary instruction and differed only in exercise type
constraints: The evidence comes from a single quasi-experiment with 56 Grade 5 EFL students in Taiwan using sixteen target words; the article notes previous research offered mixed perceptions about the effect of copying exercises
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary gains, short-term and long-term word retention, and reading comprehension
examples: In the study, both groups received the same explicit target-word instruction and differed only in the exercise type performed in class afterwards; the hierarchy group then scored higher on immediate, delayed, and reading comprehension measures.
key_sources: Lin, Ching-Ying & Hsu, Wei Shu. (2013). Effects of Hierarchy Vocabulary Exercises on English Vocabulary Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 6(9). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n9p110

article_title: Problem Based Learning in Cooperative Situation (PBLCS) and Its Impact on Development of Personal Intelligence
citation: Ahmad Talib, Ismail Bin Kailani. (2014). Problem Based Learning in Cooperative Situation (PBLCS) and Its Impact on Development of Personal Intelligence. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), 3(4). http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE
title: Replace traditional lecture-style teaching with student-centered problem-based cooperative learning to develop personal intelligences
description: The article recommends that mathematics teachers adopt learning models that develop interpersonal and intrapersonal intelligences rather than traditional strategies. It argues teachers "need to leave the traditional strategies implemented, which do not only fail to improve academic achievement, but do not develop multiple intelligences of learners", and are "encouraged to take initiatives to adopt the learning models that can develop interpersonal and intrapersonal intelligences of students". The quasi-experiment's MANOVA results support the recommendation in this setting.
requirements: Teachers select and use appropriate learning models actively and wisely
Problems that students solve individually or in teams with teacher guidance
constraints: Evidence comes from a quasi-experiment in Makassar senior high schools with intact classes
target_learning_goals: personal intelligence development alongside mathematics learning
examples: The study assigned intact classes to PBLCS (103 students) or traditional strategies (103 students) and compared development scores
key_sources: Ahmad Talib, Ismail Bin Kailani. (2014). Problem Based Learning in Cooperative Situation (PBLCS) and Its Impact on Development of Personal Intelligence. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), 3(4). http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE

article_title: The Effect of Project Based Learning in "Ratio, Proportion and Percentage" Unit on Mathematics Success and Attitude
citation: Ahmet Şükrü Özdemir, Filiz Yıldız and Sevda Göktepe Yıldız. (2015). The effect of project based learning in “ratio, proportion and percentage” unit on mathematics success and attitude. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, Vol. 3, No. 1. https://ojs.uef.fi/ejsme
title: Project pre-study files guiding weekly group inquiry in the ratio, proportion and percentage unit
description: The researchers prepared five project pre-study files, one for each sub-issue of the unit, containing research questions and thought-provoking router questions. Each file opened with the research issue of the week and closed with an individual 'What I have learned?' section, with group tasks, debate questions and everyday-life connections between. Groups of 4 or 5 students worked through one file per week over 7 weeks, presented projects in the final week, and the teacher guided groups and canalized them to proper resources.
requirements: Groups of 4 or 5 students with a named group leader
Teacher guidance and access to resources such as the library and ICT laboratory
Class time allocated for completing the files
constraints: The study is limited to the ratio, proportion and percentage unit in 7th grade
Some files needed more than one week because of content density
target_learning_goals: ratio, proportion and percentage concepts and problem solving
collaboration and learning-to-learn skills
examples: Eight heterogeneous groups studied the files for 7 weeks and submitted weekly project progress reports, ending in 10-15 minute computer-based presentations
key_sources: Ahmet Şükrü Özdemir, Filiz Yıldız and Sevda Göktepe Yıldız. (2015). The effect of project based learning in “ratio, proportion and percentage” unit on mathematics success and attitude. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, Vol. 3, No. 1. https://ojs.uef.fi/ejsme

article_title: Exploring the Impact of Parallel Teaching on General Language Proficiency of EFL Learners
citation: Aliakbari, M. & Bazyar, A. (2012). Exploring the Impact of Parallel Teaching on General Language Proficiency of EFL Learners. Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 16(1), 55-71. https://www.paaljapan.org
title: Prepare learners educationally and culturally before implementing co-teaching approaches
description: Based on the null result and participant feedback, the article concludes that learners must be readied before co-teaching is introduced: "before any attempt in its implementation, learners need to be educated and culturally prepared to benefit from such an approach". The study's students were unaccustomed to two instructors, felt shy, and found simultaneous teaching distracting, which the authors treat as causes of the treatment failure.
requirements: Learners educated and culturally prepared for co-teaching before implementation
constraints: The finding comes from one small, non-representative sample of Iranian junior-high learners in a public governmental context; the authors call for replication in other contexts, populations, and private language institutes
target_learners: EFL learners in junior high school in contexts unfamiliar with co-teaching
target_learning_goals: general language proficiency
examples: The experimental group received parallel teaching for 16 sessions over two months without prior learner preparation, and post-test gains did not exceed the control group's
key_sources: Aliakbari, M. & Bazyar, A. (2012). Exploring the Impact of Parallel Teaching on General Language Proficiency of EFL Learners. Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 16(1), 55-71. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ979922

article_title: Developing Written Text Production Competence Using the Reader-Response Method
citation: Paraschiva Demény. (2012). Developing Written Text Production Competence Using the Reader-Response Method. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 5, Number 3. https://add.econ.ubbcluj.ro
title: Process reading: staged, discussion-based text interpretation in small groups or pairs
description: Process reading is a text interpretation method traced to reader-response, in which pupils are presented with a text fragment, formulate hypotheses and predictions, then debate and discuss, triggering complex cognitive processes. The article lists its stages: predictions based on text fragments, "problem solving process, debate, discussion", evaluation of the literary work, recreation through another method such as visualizing or staging, and self-evaluation. It is described as most efficient in small groups or pairs and as complementing traditional analysis-synthesis processing.
requirements: Small groups or pairs for efficiency
a suitable learning environment based on communication between pupils and educator
constraints: Such processing can leave unresolved issues behind, which the article says are dealt with through traditional, more in-depth analysis-synthesis methods
target_learners: primary school pupils (third graders in the study)
target_learning_goals: text interpretation and understanding
critical reading skills
written text production
examples: The development program asked children to work in groups, pairs and individually on age-adapted literary texts over five months
key_sources: Paraschiva Demény. (2012). Developing Written Text Production Competence Using the Reader-Response Method. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 5, Number 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1054357

article_title: Drug Prevention by Increasing Self-Esteem: Influence of Teaching Approaches and Gender on Different Consumption Groups
citation: Heyne Thomas & Bogner Franz X. (2013). Drug Prevention by Increasing Self-Esteem: Influence of Teaching Approaches and Gender on Different Consumption Groups. World Journal of Education, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v3n1p1
title: Link self-esteem promotion with basic drug instruction and resistance self-efficacy training, delivered jointly by teachers and external experts
description: The article recommends structuring school drug prevention so that self-esteem promotion is combined with substance-specific content and resistance self-efficacy training, and that delivery is shared between classroom teachers and external experts. It states that "teachers and external experts should work together in drug prevention programs", with teachers providing didactical know-how in open learning environments and external experts ensuring objectivity. The recommendation rests on the study's finding that the PC cluster gained self-esteem across all teaching implementations.
requirements: Self-esteem promotion should be linked with basic instruction about drugs and resistance self-efficacy training, as the conclusion states
constraints: An increase in individual self-esteem requires a continuous educational process involving repeated instruction during a school year
target_learning_goals: self-esteem
resistance self-efficacy
drug prevention knowledge
examples: The nine-lesson unit combined a three-lesson cannabis module taught via three different approaches with six student-centered lessons strengthening self-esteem and resistance self-efficacy, conducted by a male external educator in all classes.
key_sources: Heyne Thomas & Bogner Franz X. (2013). Drug Prevention by Increasing Self-Esteem: Influence of Teaching Approaches and Gender on Different Consumption Groups. World Journal of Education, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v3n1p1

article_title: Designing, Implementing and Evaluating Preclinical Simulation Lab for Maternity Nursing Course
citation: Haya ALFozan, Yousria El Sayed, Farida Habib. (2015). Designing, Implementing and Evaluating Preclinical Simulation Lab for Maternity Nursing Course. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.12. https://www.iiste.org/journals/
title: Three-week preclinical simulation lab structured as briefing, recorded practice, and 20-minute debriefing every 40 minutes of practice
description: The article's simulation lab ran over three weeks (one day per week per section of 8-10 students, 8 am to 4 pm) before clinical placement, week by week covering antenatal, labor and delivery, and postpartum skills. Each session begins with a patient report and a work-allocation meeting, and "The student's practice was recorded and used for debriefing and evaluation. Debriefing was done every 40 minutes of practice for 20 minutes." This mirrors the briefing-participation-debriefing structure the article attributes to Cant & Cooper (2009) and the Jeffries framework.
requirements: Instructors received about 2 weeks of specialist simulation training, mandatory for all course instructors, before conducting sessions
constraints: Sessions were limited to the first 3 weeks of a 16-week semester prior to clinical placement
target_learners: undergraduate female nursing students in a maternity course
target_learning_goals: basic maternity skills: history taking, physical examination, antepartum, labor and delivery, and postpartum care
examples: Ten clinical scenarios covering antenatal, natal, and postnatal care were developed by instructors, with Mosby maternity skills learning guides and checklists adopted as learning resources
key_sources: Haya ALFozan, Yousria El Sayed, Farida Habib. (2015). Designing, Implementing and Evaluating Preclinical Simulation Lab for Maternity Nursing Course. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.12. https://www.iiste.org/journals/

article_title: Strategies Training in the Teaching of Reading Comprehension for EFL Learners in Indonesia
citation: Junaidi Mistar, Alfan Zuhairi & Nofita Yanti. (2016). Strategies Training in the Teaching of Reading Comprehension for EFL Learners in Indonesia. English Language Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n2p49
title: Twelve-session reading-strategies training cycle: predict, read and check, map, summarize, share
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern adapted from Brown and Palincsar (1984) in which each 90-minute session works through one ~300-word text: the teacher activates background knowledge, models prediction from the title, students read silently and check predictions, identify text elements, draw a text map of main ideas and supporting details, write a summary from the map, and share summaries before answering comprehension questions. The article reports that "the teacher asked them to make text mapping of the main ideas and supporting details, here they could use colo ur pencils to clear their ma pping". It was applied over twelve sessions with descriptive, procedure, and report texts.
requirements: One reading text of about 300 words per session
Explicit teacher explanation of the strategies and their benefits before training
Pre-reading activities to activate students' background knowledge
constraints: Evaluated only with grade-ten Indonesian EFL students of elementary proficiency in a vocational school
target_learning_goals: literal reading comprehension
inferential reading comprehension
examples: Two intact classes (36 experimental, 35 control) studied twelve passages over twelve 90-minute sessions; the control group received translation- and dictionary-based conventional instruction
key_sources: Junaidi Mistar, Alfan Zuhairi & Nofita Yanti. (2016). Strategies Training in the Teaching of Reading Comprehension for EFL Learners in Indonesia. English Language Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n2p49

article_title: The Impact of Teaching EFL Medical Vocabulary through Collocations on Vocabulary Retention of EFL Medical Students
citation: Maryam Najafi, Mohammad Reza Talebinezhad. (2018). The Impact of Teaching EFL Medical Vocabulary Through Collocations on Vocabulary Retention of EFL Medical Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 9(5). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.9n.5p.24
title: Prefabricated units (collocations) serve four functions in language: learning, fluency, comprehension, and group membership
description: The article presents collocations as one type of prefabricated unit (also called chunks or formulaic sequences) and identifies four functions: supporting language learning, supporting fluency by reducing processing effort, supporting comprehension, and indicating membership of a linguistic group. It cites psycholinguistic evidence that "the human brain is much better equipped for memorizing than for processing", so a large repertoire of prefabricated units makes fluent language possible. For adult non-native speakers, fluency and comprehension functions are emphasized.
requirements: Learners must acquire a repertoire of prefabricated units, since non-native-like prefabs can irritate recipients and draw attention from the message
constraints: The article states prefabricated language is not regularly used as a basis for creative language in adult L2 acquisition, so the learning function may not play a major role for adult learners
target_learning_goals: Fluent and accurate spoken and written production
Comprehension of medical texts
examples: The article gives medical collocation examples such as prescribe treatment, adjust the dosage, and have an operation, and notes some collocations are fixed (strip to the waist) while others are more open (take the temperature/check the temperature)
key_sources: Maryam Najafi, Mohammad Reza Talebinezhad. (2018). The Impact of Teaching EFL Medical Vocabulary Through Collocations on Vocabulary Retention of EFL Medical Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 9(5). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.9n.5p.24

article_title: Evaluating the Impact of Virtual Exchange on Initial Teacher Education: A European Policy Experiment
citation: The EVALUATE Group. (2019). Evaluating the impact of virtual exchange on initial teacher education: a European policy experiment. Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2019.29.9782490057337
title: Progressive exchange model: three-stage telecollaborative task sequence
description: The virtual exchange model used in EVALUATE was based on the Progressive Exchange Model, which "involves 'three interrelated tasks which move from information exchange to comparing and analysing cultural practices and finally to working on a collaborative product'". This staged structure scaffolds online intercultural collaboration by progressively deepening the level of engagement between partner classes.
requirements: Teacher trainers from partner institutions co-design a joint curriculum integrated into their respective courses.
constraints: Tasks must be matched to the key competences and themes identified by public authorities or course objectives.
target_learners: Student teachers in initial teacher education
target_learning_goals: Intercultural competence
Digital-pedagogical competence
Collaborative online learning
examples: 25 virtual exchanges were run using this model across 34 institutions in 16 countries.
key_sources: The EVALUATE Group. (2019). Evaluating the impact of virtual exchange on initial teacher education: a European policy experiment. Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2019.29.9782490057337

article_title: Impact of Electronic Teaching Materials on Process of Education--Results of an Experiment
citation: Záhorec, J., Hašková, A., & Munk, M. (2010). Impact of Electronic Teaching Materials on Process of Education – Results of an Experiment. Informatics in Education, 9(2), 261–281. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ894821
title: Principles of Geometry Optics – interactive multimedia teaching material for secondary physics
description: An electronic teaching material with flash animations and interactive simulations of optical phenomena, developed by the authors for teaching geometry optics at higher secondary level. Its "main attention was paid to visualisation of the presented physical concepts (notions) and relations" through "a big number of (flash) animations and interactive simulations". It was used hands-on by experimental group A and won first place in the Assistance materials for on-line education category at the E-learning in practice competition at ICETA 2007.
requirements: Designed for selected topics of higher secondary school geometry optics curricula; usable at school or at home for self study
constraints: Created for a specific research purpose; authors note it can be used generally without specific oriented purpose
target_learners: 17–19 year old higher secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Basic topics from geometry optics
examples: Used in experimental group A during regular physics lessons and seminars over a 3-month pedagogical experiment
key_sources: Záhorec, J., Hašková, A., & Munk, M. (2010). Impact of Electronic Teaching Materials on Process of Education – Results of an Experiment. Informatics in Education, 9(2), 261–281. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1064255

article_title: The Impact of Multiple Intelligences-Based Instruction on Developing Speaking Skills of the Pre-Service Teachers of English
citation: Salem, A. A. M. S. (2013). The Impact of Multiple Intelligences-Based Instruction on Developing Speaking Skills of the Pre-Service Teachers of English. English Language Teaching, 6(9), 53-66. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n9p53
title: Profile learners' intelligence preferences before designing MI-based language activities
description: The study suggests that MI-based instruction should begin by diagnosing learners' preferred intelligences and then designing activities accordingly. The researcher administered the McKenzie (1999) inventory so that "the students were given some feedback so as to be aware of their preferred intelligences," and used the resulting profile as the basis on which activities and tasks were designed in accordance with students' preferred intelligences. This diagnostic-first step supports attending to individual differences within a learner-centered program.
requirements: A validated MI inventory appropriate to the learners (here, McKenzie's 1999 inventory for EFL young adults)
Time and procedure to give learners feedback on their profiles
constraints: The profile reflects self-reported preferences at one point in time and was used for one cohort of fourth-year EFL pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: Speaking skills development through activities matched to intelligence preferences
examples: The dominant intelligences in the participant profile were interpersonal (M = 16.17), verbal-linguistic (M = 15.533), and intrapersonal (M = 15.167).

article_title: Learning and Retaining Technical Vocabulary with Enhancement Activities in an ESP Course
citation: Liju Xu. (2018). Learning and Retaining Technical Vocabulary with Enhancement Activities in an ESP Course. English Language Teaching, 11(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n10p145
title: Use discipline-specific productive activities (like journal entry practice) rather than decontextualized vocabulary exercises to teach ESP technical terms
description: The article recommends that deliberate learning of technical terms should stem from the aim of the ESP course, "to provide conditions for the acquisition of language necessary for the successful implementation of the students' professional tasks". Journal entry practice required students to analyze business events with accounting concepts and explain treatments in English. The authors link this productive, discipline-specific activity to better post-test outcomes than general vocabulary exercises.
requirements: Activities must be designed around the characteristics of the ESP course and learners' subject matter knowledge level
constraints: Evidence comes from one quasi-experimental study with accounting juniors at a single Chinese university
target_learning_goals: learning and retaining technical vocabulary
using terms accurately in professional tasks
examples: Group B students worked in groups of three on sets of 10-15 business transactions for 15-20 minutes, then gave oral reports
key_sources: Liju Xu. (2018). Learning and Retaining Technical Vocabulary with Enhancement Activities in an ESP Course. English Language Teaching, 11(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n10p145

article_title: When Creative Problem Solving Strategy Meets Web-Based Cooperative Learning Environment in Accounting Education
citation: CHENG Kai Wen. (2011). When Creative Problem Solving Strategy Meets Web-Based Cooperative Learning Environment in Accounting Education. New Horizons in Education, 59(1), 106-118.
title: Problem-solving attitudes as three constructs: problem-solving confidence, approach-avoidance style, and personal control
description: Following Heppner & Peterson (1982), the article defines problem-solving attitudes as involving three constructs: (1) problem-solving confidence — 'whether one has confidence in face of a problem'; (2) approach-avoidance style — 'whether one will directly cope with a problem or choose to avoid it'; and (3) personal control — 'whether one can execute a decision after making a thorough plan.' The study measured these constructs using a 31-item problem-solving scale modified from the Problem-Solving Inventory, rated on a 6-point Likert scale.
requirements: Measured via the problem-solving scale developed by Lee et al. (1998), a modification of the Problem-Solving Inventory (PSI)
target_learning_goals: problem-solving attitudes
examples: The formal scale consisted of 31 items in three constructs with Cronbach's α of .92 for the overall scale.
key_sources: CHENG Kai Wen. (2011). When Creative Problem Solving Strategy Meets Web-Based Cooperative Learning Environment in Accounting Education. New Horizons in Education, 59(1), 106-118. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ955493

article_title: Fostering Ethnic and Religious Harmony through Classroom Language Experiences
citation: Eucharia Obiageli Obiekezie & Alexander Essien Timothy. (2015). Fostering Ethnic and Religious Harmony through Classroom Language Experiences. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.25. https://www.iiste.org
title: Prejudice Sustenance Mechanism (PSM) and Prejudice Reversal Mechanism (PRM)
description: The article proposes two complementary frameworks. The Prejudice Sustenance Mechanism (Fig. 1) holds that ignorance, myths, misinformation and fallacy are mutually dependent: "ignorance sustains myths; myths are sustained by misinformation and fallacy which, in turn, fuel ignorance", providing "the strong pillars for prejudice". The Prejudice Reversal Mechanism (Fig. 2) holds that accurate knowledge, accurate information, accurate facts and critical thinking are pillars on which tolerance might rest, reversing prejudice.
requirements: Reversal requires accurate knowledge, accurate information and facts, and engagement in critical thinking, per the article's conclusion
constraints: The mechanisms are the authors' conceptual illustrations (Figures 1 and 2), not tested components in isolation
target_learning_goals: ethnic and religious tolerance
critical appraisal of generalisations and stereotypes
examples: The GAG game was designed to break the chain of mechanisms sustaining prejudice by having students query whether statements are always, sometimes, never or rarely true
key_sources: Eucharia Obiageli Obiekezie & Alexander Essien Timothy. (2015). Fostering Ethnic and Religious Harmony through Classroom Language Experiences. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.25. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1078506

article_title: The Project-Based Flipped Learning Model in Business English Translation Course: Learning, Teaching and Assessment
citation: Lijun Deng. (2018). The Project-Based Flipped Learning Model in Business English Translation Course: Learning, Teaching and Assessment. English Language Teaching, 11(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n9p118
title: Project-based flipped learning pattern with client and translator groups rotating across business translation units
description: A lesson/unit-level design in which each business translation unit is run as a real translation project: pre-class video and checklist study on Blackboard, a client group selecting a theme-related source text and setting standards, three translator groups producing and revising drafts with translation logs and peer review forms, and client evaluation plus teacher summary in class. The article states that "The 32 students of the experimental class were divided into one client group and three translator groups" and that students "switched their roles as clients and translators in each theme unit". It integrates learning, teaching and assessment activities before, in and out of class.
requirements: Access to an online platform (Blackboard) for uploading video clips and checklist exercises
Business theme units providing authentic source texts for translation projects
constraints: Tested only in a Business English Translation course for third-year English majors over one 16-week semester with two classes (65 students)
target_learning_goals: English-Chinese business translation competence
translation process awareness and self-reflection
examples: In the English Contract Translation unit, the client group presented a contract source text, three translator groups produced revised drafts with logs and peer review forms, and the client group announced the best translation in the second session
key_sources: Lijun Deng. (2018). The Project-Based Flipped Learning Model in Business English Translation Course: Learning, Teaching and Assessment. English Language Teaching, 11(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n9p118

article_title: The Project-Based Flipped Learning Model in Business English Translation Course: Learning, Teaching and Assessment
citation: Lijun Deng. (2018). The Project-Based Flipped Learning Model in Business English Translation Course: Learning, Teaching and Assessment. English Language Teaching, 11(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n9p118
title: Process-oriented assessment model for the flipped Business English Translation classroom
description: The article proposes replacing test-oriented summative assessment with a process-oriented assessment model that draws on artifacts the flipped model already generates. It lists as assessment components "The on-line study checklists before class, the translation logs, the peer review forms, the translated versions, the teacher's observation of the translator groups' discussion and performance and the feedbacks and comments from the client group". The teacher takes a new identity as observer of the translation process, and the model is presented as the assessment component of an integrated flipped classroom pedagogy in which learning, teaching and assessment mutually reinforce each other.
requirements: The project-based flipped learning activities (checklists, logs, peer review forms, translated versions, client feedback) that supply the assessment evidence
constraints: The model is explicitly tentative: the article states it "is still in its tentative stage and leaves much to be improved and tested", with efficacy to be tested in follow-up research
target_learners: third-year English-major university students in Business English Translation
target_learning_goals: translation competence assessed across the translation process rather than by product alone
examples: Diagram 2 of the article lists the assessment elements to be included before, in and after class in a flipped Business English Translation classroom
key_sources: Lijun Deng. (2018). The Project-Based Flipped Learning Model in Business English Translation Course: Learning, Teaching and Assessment. English Language Teaching, 11(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n9p118

article_title: Measuring Teacher Implementation of the "BEST in CLASS" Intervention Program and Corollary Child Outcomes
citation: Conroy, M. A., Sutherland, K. S., Algina, J. J., Wilson, R. E., Martinez, J. R., & Whalon, K. J. (2014). Measuring Teacher Implementation of the BEST in CLASS Intervention Program and Corollary Child Outcomes. Journal of Emotional and Behavioral Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/1063426614532949
title: Pair one-time training with sustained practice-based coaching and performance feedback to change and maintain teacher practice
description: BEST in CLASS pairs a 6-hr workshop with 14 weeks of practice-based coaching in which coaches provide modeling, focused observation, and weekly data-based feedback. The article argues this matters because professional development in the form of one-time training does not result in proficient delivery of practices in authentic settings. The study's results support the coaching model as the active ingredient sustaining teacher behavior change.
requirements: A trained coach spending approximately 2 hr per week in each teacher's classroom
Weekly data-based feedback on teachers' implementation of each practice
constraints: The expert coaching model with comprehensive data collection can be costly and time-intensive, making widespread implementation difficult
target_learners: Early childhood teachers of children at risk for emotional/behavioral disorders
target_learning_goals: Use of evidence-based instructional practices with fidelity
examples: Coaches videotaped teachers, shared video clips, and provided graphs depicting the percentage of intervals during which they used the strategy

article_title: A Daily Dose of CALM: Supporting Middle School Educators' Wellbeing and Classroom Functioning through a Brief Stress Reduction Intervention
citation: Harris, A.R., Jennings, P.A., Abenavoli, R.M., Katz, D.A., Greenberg, M.T., & Schussler, D. (2014). A daily dose of CALM: Supporting middle school educators' wellbeing and classroom functioning through a brief stress reduction intervention. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Prosocial Classroom model as theoretical basis for educator contemplative interventions
description: The article situates contemplative teacher interventions within the Prosocial Classroom model (Jennings and Greenberg, 2009), which the CARE intervention "draws from," and which links teacher social-emotional competence to child and classroom outcomes. CALM extends this line by combining "emotion skills instruction with mindfulness and stress reduction practices" and compassion practices to promote empathy and compassion in the classroom. The model frames educator wellbeing as a lever for improving the social-emotional climate of learning environments.
requirements: Teacher-focused interventions targeting social-emotional competence
target_learning_goals: teacher social-emotional competence
classroom social-emotional climate

citation: Fahrutdinova, R. A., Yarmakeev, I. E., & Fakhrutdinov, R. R. (2014). The Formation of Students’ Foreign Language Communicative Competence during the Learning Process of the English Language through Interactive Learning Technologies (The Study on the Basis of Kazan Federal University). English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p36
title: Professionally-communicative orientation with substantial and procedural components
description: The article states that using interactive learning technologies to develop foreign language communicative competence should include two components of professionally-communicative orientation: a substantial component — "the orientation of the linguistic material used in class: special vocabulary, texts (including audio and videotext) associated with the profession" — and a procedural component of games, situations and discussions close to realistic action, associated with future teachers revealing their professional communicative competence.
requirements: Linguistic material must connect to the students' future profession

target_learning_goals: Professional communicative competence in English
examples: Class materials included special vocabulary and audio/videotexts associated with the teaching profession

article_title: The Effects of Vocabulary Instructions on Students' Reading Comprehension across Cognitive Styles in ESP
citation: Kusumawati, E., & Widiati, U. (2017). The Effects of Vocabulary Instructions on Students’ Reading Comprehension across Cognitive Styles in ESP. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(2). https://journals.iiste.org/index.php/JEP/article/view/2894
title: Prefer explicit vocabulary instruction over implicit instruction to promote ESP reading comprehension
description: The article concludes that explicit vocabulary instruction is more effective than implicit instruction for promoting ESP reading comprehension, and recommends that language practitioners “take it into account in teaching reading, especially in ESP context.” Explicit instruction is characterized as teacher-centered, with clear behavioral and cognitive goals made transparent to learners, involving setting a purpose, telling students what to do, showing them how, and guiding hands-on application. The principle directs ESP teachers toward structured, teacher-led vocabulary presentation rather than relying on incidental learning.
requirements: Teacher-delivered structured instruction with clear goals and procedures, supported by lesson plans
constraints: Evidence comes from a single quasi-experimental study of 54 polytechnic students in Indonesia; the article does not claim generalizability beyond ESP reading contexts
target_learning_goals: ESP reading comprehension
Vocabulary development
examples: In this study, the explicit group received PANORAMA-structured instruction and outperformed the implicit group on ESP reading comprehension posttests
key_sources: Kusumawati, E., & Widiati, U. (2017). The Effects of Vocabulary Instructions on Students’ Reading Comprehension across Cognitive Styles in ESP. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(2). https://journals.iiste.org/index.php/JEP/article/view/2894

article_title: Mindfulness Promotes Educators' Efficacy in the Classroom
citation: Abenavoli, R. M., Harris, A. R., Katz, D. A., Jennings, P. A., & Greenberg, M. T. (2014). Mindfulness promotes educators’ efficacy in the classroom. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://sree.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/02/Abenavoli-et-al-SREE-2014.pdf
title: Prosocial Classroom Model: mindfulness as a component of social-emotional competence protecting against burnout cascade
description: The Prosocial Classroom Model (Jennings & Greenberg, 2009) proposes that mindfulness and other aspects of social-emotional competence lead to more effective classroom management and protect educators from a "burnout cascade" of deteriorating classroom climate, student misbehavior, and emotional exhaustion. This study tested and demonstrated some support for the hypothesis that mindfulness is one aspect of social-emotional competence predicting effective classroom performance.
requirements: Mindfulness is conceptualized as one aspect of educators' broader social-emotional competence.
constraints: The study is non-experimental, limiting the strength of causal conclusions about the model.
target_learning_goals: Supporting educator wellbeing and classroom effectiveness
key_sources: Abenavoli, R. M., Harris, A. R., Katz, D. A., Jennings, P. A., & Greenberg, M. T. (2014). Mindfulness promotes educators’ efficacy in the classroom. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://sree.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/02/Abenavoli-et-al-SREE-2014.pdf

article_title: Effects of Practical Activities and Manual on Science Students' Academic Performance on Solubility in Uruan Local Education Authority of Akwa Ibom State
citation: Rebecca, Ufonabasi Etiubon & Nsimeneabasi Michael Udoh. (2017). Effects of Practical Activities and Manual on Science Students’ Academic Performance on Solubility in Uruan Local Education Authority of Akwa Ibom State. title: Use practical activities and practical manuals to teach abstract science concepts like solubility
description: The article recommends that "science teachers should make effective use of practical activities and manual in teaching abstract concepts like solubility". Its study found both approaches produced equal, improved performance, and the conclusion attributes gains to students having "direct access and adequate instructional materials to work with".
requirements: Adequate facilities and materials, including supportive science practical manuals
constraints: Findings are from senior secondary two students in two public schools in Uruan Local Education Authority, Nigeria, on the concept of solubility
target_learning_goals: understanding the concept of solubility
acquiring laboratory and practical science skills
examples: Two intact SS2 classes were taught for three weeks, one with practical activities and one with a practical manual, then assessed with a reshuffled 20-item Science Performance Test

description: The study used a "non- randomized pretest – posttest experimental design in two in tact classes" with two experimental groups, one taught with practical activities and one with practical manual. constraints: Non-randomized design with intact classes; hypotheses tested at .05 alpha level

article_title: Potential Effects of Teaching Strategies on Students' Academic Performance under a Trump Administration
citation: Guirguis, R., & Pankowski, J. (2017). Potential Effects of Teaching Strategies on Students’ Academic Performance under a Trump Administration. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 5(4). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i4.2263
title: Privatization policies may reduce opportunities to practice differentiation and individualized goal setting
description: The article argues that a movement toward privatized education in New York State could reduce educators' opportunities to practice differentiation, accommodation, and modification of instruction. Charter schools enroll a smaller percentage of English Language learners, special education students, and other categories of needy students than local public schools, creating more homogeneous student bodies. The authors warn that "Goals, as a strategy will most likely not be as effective when teachers will have fewer opportunities to individualize learning."
requirements: A diverse, heterogeneous student population across public schools for differentiation and individualized goal setting to be practiced
constraints: The article frames this as a potential effect of proposed policy changes under a specific administration, not an empirically tested outcome
target_learners: Pre-K-12 students in New York State public schools
target_learning_goals: Academic performance across subject areas
Individualized learning goals
Differentiated instruction
examples: The article cites a 2015 UFT research report indicating that the charter school sector in New York City has enrolled a smaller percentage of high-need students than local public schools.
key_sources: Guirguis, R., & Pankowski, J. (2017). Potential Effects of Teaching Strategies on Students’ Academic Performance under a Trump Administration. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 5(4). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i4.2263

article_title: Applying Cognitive Linguistics to Teaching English Prepositions: A Quasi-Experimental Study
citation: Hung, B. P., Vien, T., & Vu, N. N. (2018). Applying Cognitive Linguistics to Teaching English Prepositions: A Quasi-Experimental Study. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 327-346. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11323a
title: Add productive tasks after CL-based instruction to boost retention of target items
description: The article recommends delivering productive tasks after instruction and forced-choice written exercise, citing assertions that "these post-teaching activities could contribute to learners' retention of the target items". The authors suggest their gains exceeded those of Song et al. (2015) "probably because of the application of productive tasks after instruction". This study added a speaking and a writing task after the instruction.
requirements: Productive tasks follow the instruction and forced-choice written exercise
constraints: The comparison with Song et al. (2015) is the authors' explanation; there was no direct test of the tasks' contribution
target_learning_goals: retention of English preposition semantics
examples: Two tasks for productive skills were delivered after the instruction and forced-choice written exercise
key_sources: Hung, B. P., Vien, T., & Vu, N. N. (2018). Applying Cognitive Linguistics to Teaching English Prepositions: A Quasi-Experimental Study. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 327-346. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11323a

article_title: Formation of the Professional and Didactic Culture of the Future Teacher
citation: Mirzagitova, A. L. & Akhmetov, L. G. (2016). Formation of the Professional and Didactic Culture of the Future Teacher. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(14), 6675-6689. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1118411
title: Professional and didactic culture of the future teacher: five features of formation
description: The article defines professional and didactic culture as a prerequisite for pedagogical activity that contributes to the self-development of the teacher's professional and personal qualities. It formulates five features of its formation in future history teachers: constant actualization of a valuable attitude towards pedagogical activity, formation of self-improvement skills, the ability to find innovative solutions to pedagogical situations, intellectually and creatively productive cooperation under a cultural approach, and a holistic person-centered process with individual professional growth trajectories. The framework was taken into account in Stage 3 of the study.
requirements: The article states the formation process depends on constant actualization of the valuable attitude towards pedagogical activity and a conscious attitude towards the chosen profession.
constraints: The article states that so far there are no works devoted to the complex research of the formation of professional and didactic culture of the future teacher.
target_learning_goals: formation of professional and didactic culture
professional development of teachers
examples: Stage 3 taught the experimental group of 23 students on the basis of the research findings during the 2014/15 academic year.
key_sources: Mirzagitova, A. L. & Akhmetov, L. G. (2016). Formation of the Professional and Didactic Culture of the Future Teacher. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(14), 6675-6689. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1115889

article_title: Project Based-Content Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) at Mathematics Department Universitas Lampung
citation: Yufrizal, H., Huzairin, & Hasan, B. (2017). Project Based - Content Language Integrated Learning (Clil) at Mathematics Department Universitas Lampung. English Language Teaching, 10(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n9p131
title: Project-based CLIL model integrating language form practice with subject-matter projects
description: The article applies content and language integrated learning combined with project-based learning, in which students "explore their field of study using English as a medium of communication" and "Language form practice was done integratedly within the subject study." Groups of 4-5 students complete mathematics, physics, biology, or chemistry projects culminating in English oral presentations. The model draws on immersion and ESP arguments that combining language with other subjects benefits learning.
requirements: Groups of 4-5 students assigned projects in their field of science
Presentations conducted entirely in English
One week of group preparation time
constraints: Tested only in a mathematics study program at one Indonesian university over a single semester
target_learning_goals: English oral proficiency
academic communication in science fields
examples: Groups prepared papers and PowerPoint presentations on mathematics, physics, biology, and chemistry topics and presented them in English with question-and-answer sessions
