article_title: Effects of Phonological Input as a Pre-Listening Activity on Vocabulary Learning and L2 Listening Comprehension Test Performance
citation: Mihara, K. (2015). Effects of Phonological Input as a Pre-Listening Activity on Vocabulary Learning and L2 Listening Comprehension Test Performance. TESL-EJ 19(2). https://tesl-ej.org/pdf/ej74/a1.pdf
title: Pre-teaching vocabulary should give students a chance to hear target words in connected speech rather than in isolation
description: The article concludes that phonological input has no effect if target vocabulary items are pronounced in isolation, and suggests that "pre-teaching of vocabulary should be conducted in such a way as to give students a chance to hear the target word in the context of a string of sounds linked together." This is because focusing on individual words does not reflect the radical phonological changes that words undergo in connected speech.
requirements: Vocabulary pre-teaching activities should present target words within connected speech rather than as isolated items.
constraints: This recommendation is based on a study with homogeneous Japanese participants at the same proficiency level, and a different result might emerge with different cultural or language backgrounds.
target_learners: First-year Japanese university students learning English as a foreign language
target_learning_goals: L2 listening comprehension
vocabulary learning
examples: The study's phonological input condition involved listening to each target word pronounced twice in isolation, which showed no benefit over silent reading.
key_sources: Mihara, K. (2015). Effects of Phonological Input as a Pre-Listening Activity on Vocabulary Learning and L2 Listening Comprehension Test Performance. TESL-EJ 19(2). https://tesl-ej.org/pdf/ej74/a1.pdf

article_title: The Efficacy of Written Corrective Feedback and Language Analytic Ability on Chinese Learners' Explicit and Implicit Knowledge of English Articles
citation: Lin Jiang & Hailing Xiao. (2014). The Efficacy of Written Corrective Feedback and Language Analytic Ability on Chinese Learners’ Explicit and Implicit Knowledge of English Articles. English Language Teaching, 7(10). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n10p22
title: Teachers should not hesitate to provide written corrective feedback in English writing teaching.
description: The provision of written corrective feedback in reviewing learners' texts is necessary and effective. Teachers should not hesitate to provide written CF in English (writing) teaching so as to draw learners' attention to the gaps between their interlanguage and the target language, which may promote language acquisition. For the effect of written CF to be maximized, teachers should pay attention to individual differences and select CF strategies based on learners' level of development.
requirements: Teachers review learners' texts and provide written corrective feedback on linguistic errors
constraints: For the effect of written CF to be maximized, teachers need to pay more attention to individual differences and select CF strategies based on learners' level of development
target_learning_goals: explicit and implicit knowledge of English articles
linguistic accuracy in new pieces of writing
examples: An 8-week study with 92 low-intermediate Chinese EFL learners found both DOC and DMC benefited explicit and implicit knowledge of English articles compared to a no-feedback control group
key_sources: Lin Jiang & Hailing Xiao. (2014). The Efficacy of Written Corrective Feedback and Language Analytic Ability on Chinese Learners’ Explicit and Implicit Knowledge of English Articles. English Language Teaching, 7(10). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n10p22

article_title: Using Anticipatory Reading Guides to Improve Elementary Students' Comprehension
citation: Ortlieb, E. (2013). Using Anticipatory Reading Guides to Improve Elementary Students' Comprehension. International Journal of Instruction, 6(2), 145-162. https://www.e-iji.net
title: Teach struggling readers to preview questions before reading to direct attention and set a purpose.
description: Anticipatory reading guides direct learners' attention toward specific goals within upcoming text by having them examine questions, titles, and text features before reading. The article states that "Assigning a purpose for the reading has long been known to be effective at directing the learner's attention towards particular goals and in turn, results in increases in comprehension of content." This principle was implemented through a three-column guide directing students to specific paragraphs and look-fors.
requirements: Teacher modeling of the strategy through a gradual release of responsibility model before independent student use
constraints: Requires sufficient practice time; the author notes 30 minutes daily may have limited mastery in this study
target_learners: Elementary struggling readers, particularly grade three
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension across fiction and nonfiction content-area texts
examples: Students used a three-column spreadsheet guide specifying which paragraph to read, what to look for, and space to record responses
key_sources: Ortlieb, E. (2013). Using Anticipatory Reading Guides to Improve Elementary Students' Comprehension. International Journal of Instruction, 6(2), 145-162. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085407

article_title: Practitioner Inquiry with Early Program Teacher Candidates
citation: Michele Hollingsworth Koomen. (2016). Practitioner Inquiry with Early Program Teacher Candidates. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i11.1915
title: Use practitioner inquiry with video review to help novice teachers study their own teaching
description: The article recommends engaging early program teacher candidates in practitioner inquiry of their own teaching through a Study of Teaching project. Candidates videotape lessons, analyze them, conduct a modified literature review, and synthesize findings in a written paper and class symposium. This process provides explicit opportunities to focus on the tasks and activities of teaching and fosters learning from practice in practice.
requirements: Candidates need access to video technology, a short field practicum placement, and mentored guidance through the inquiry process.
constraints: Evidence for cognitive load theory was retrospective, analyzed after the moments of teaching rather than in real time.
target_learning_goals: learning from practice in practice
developing knowledge of teaching practice
examples: Forty-two student pairs and twelve trios completed the Study of Teaching, videotaping five lessons and presenting findings in a class symposium.

article_title: Blended learning in laboratory science education: comparison of flipped classroom and traditional lectures in immunohematology training.
citation: Saniee Nadia, Seidi Masoumeh, Amiri Fatemeh. (2026). Blended learning in laboratory science education: comparison of flipped classroom and traditional lectures in immunohematology training. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09985-z
title: Shifting theoretical content to the pre-class phase frees in-class time for skill practice, feedback, and interactive learning in laboratory courses
description: The blended learning model frontloads declarative knowledge outside class via the flipped classroom, allowing in-class sessions to focus entirely on skill execution. By moving theoretical content to the pre-class phase, students arrive better prepared for hands-on laboratory sessions, allowing in-class time to focus on skill practice, guided demonstrations, and interactive learning. This sequential two-stage mechanism is theorized to reduce intrinsic cognitive load during in-class sessions, freeing working memory resources for skill-focused activities.
requirements: Structured blended learning approach integrating a virtual flipped classroom with in-person demonstration-based teaching
Educational materials (online videos, podcasts, narrated PowerPoints, and text-based resources) provided via LMS or university platform
Structured communication channels and virtual student groups for announcements
constraints: Implemented at a single institution in one laboratory science course, which may restrict external validity
Full blinding of participants and instructors was not possible due to the nature of the educational intervention
target_learning_goals: psychomotor laboratory skills
immunohematology knowledge acquisition
practical competency
examples: The intervention group received the same core curriculum via a structured blended learning approach integrating a virtual flipped classroom with in-person demonstration-based teaching over five fall semesters

description: The article frames procedural competency as combining technical and cognitive elements requiring alignment with self-confidence, and notes "The optimal approach for assessment of competence is open to debate, with arguments for a minimum number of procedures performed versus an observed assessment of performance". ACEM currently uses Direct Observation of Procedural Skills (DOPS) for 12 core procedures, with no indication of how many procedures are needed to achieve competency. The authors argue low exposure undermines either approach and should inform curriculum updates.

constraints: DOPS opportunities decrease when procedure exposure is low, limiting the current ACEM assessment approach

title: Direct assessment design effort toward high-stakes assessments where AI poses the greatest validity risk, preserving flexibility where AI use aligns with practice

constraints: A low likelihood of AI use does not mean an assessment is appropriate for evaluating clinical competency or progression

examples: The guide pairs total scores with a targeted improvement guide making recommendations based on the individual scores of the 2 parts, the criteria scoring, and the assessment type

article_title: Why Controlling Teaching Persists in Medical Education: A Self-Determination Theory Perspective.
citation: Neufeld A. (2026). Why Controlling Teaching Persists in Medical Education: A Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2417
title: Pressure-travels-downward framework: controlling teaching as a downstream expression of system pressure
description: The article proposes a framework in which psychologically controlling teaching is conceptualized not as individual pedagogical failure but as "a downstream behavioural expression of pressure travelling through educational systems." Institutional demands shape educators' motivational experiences, cultural norms legitimize controlling responses, and educational structures transmit those responses to learners. Control is framed as an emergent property of interactions among educators, learners, professional cultures, and educational systems, drawing on SDT, psychological reactance, and stress and coping theory.
requirements: Educators, learners, professional cultures, and educational systems must all be considered when analyzing why control persists
constraints: The framework is a conceptual analysis, not an empirically tested model in this article
target_learning_goals: Sustaining learner autonomy, motivation, and well-being in clinical education

title: Professional learning episode (PLE) as the basic unit of creditable learning
description: The PLE is CLICS's fundamental unit of creditable learning: "a coherent, AI-mediated interaction demonstrating (1) a clinically meaningful problem, (2) reasoning development through iterative inquiry, (3) integration of contextual or evidentiary information, and (4) reflective synthesis." description: The article frames premature closure as the early acceptance of a diagnostic hypothesis followed by curtailed consideration of alternatives, operationalised here as a decreased investment of processing time. The authors state the study is "the first in which premature closure is measured directly, namely, as a decreased investment of time to process a clinical case in response to an early wrong but salient diagnostic hypothesis". They also argue premature closure is a consequence of physicians' confidence in an early biased hypothesis rather than a cognitive bias itself.

constraints: Reduced processing time does not uniquely identify premature closure; confirmation bias offers an alternative account

title: Three-component simulation design: prebriefing, immersive scenario, and structured debriefing aligned with Healthcare Simulation Standards of Best Practice
description: A simulation-based educational design comprising 3 structured components aligned with best practices for simulation-based education: prebriefing, immersive simulation, and debriefing. Prebriefing was an asynchronous session establishing psychological safety, reviewing learning objectives, and outlining expectations. The immersive scenario involved a high-fidelity manikin reproducing respiratory mechanics, hemodynamic variability, and physiological responses. Debriefing was a structured 30-minute session emphasizing reflective practice, emotional processing, recognition of performance gaps, and reinforcement of effective clinical judgment.

Faculty facilitators conducting a structured debriefing designed to meet the Healthcare Simulation Standards of Best Practice.
constraints: Participation in the simulation was a required component of the course curriculum; completion of the SET-M evaluation was voluntary.
target_learning_goals: Structured handoff communication
Clinical decision-making in high-acuity scenarios
Interprofessional collaboration and leadership
examples: The scenario followed a 28-year-old male patient status post gunshot wound who underwent an exploratory laparotomy and required return to the OR for re-exploration and washout, with embedded clinical data including ventilator settings, hemodynamic parameters, laboratory results, and medications.

resilience

The authors note this supports a focused, learner-adapted program while cautioning that learning is nonlinear, so subskills should also be varied rather than drilled one at a time.

article_title: Supporting comprehension: The advantages of multiple-choice over true-false practice tests.
citation: Hildenbrand Lena; Wiley Jennifer. (2025). Supporting comprehension: The advantages of multiple–choice over true—false practice tests. Memory & Cognition. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-025-01726-9
title: When using closed-ended practice tests to build comprehension, prefer multiple-choice inference questions over matched true—false items
description: For self-guided reading tasks aimed at comprehension, the article's evidence favors multiple-choice over true—false practice: multiple-choice answer options provide scaffolding that supports comparing and contrasting choices and active reasoning even with limited knowledge, whereas true—false statements offer no additional information to support a validity judgment early in learning. The principle is limited to closed-ended inference questions used as practice; true—false practice may need added support such as feedback or text access to benefit learning.
requirements: Practice items must be inference questions that test connections between ideas beyond explicitly stated text content, with matched content across formats.
constraints: True—false practice did not significantly outperform rereading on short-answer tests; feedback alone did not rescue the true—false format in Experiment 3.
target_learning_goals: comprehension and transfer of text-based understanding
examples: Experiments 2-4 used matched five-question multiple-choice and twenty-item true—false practice tests built from the same inference content, and multiple-choice practice repeatedly produced better short-answer outcomes.

citation: Frampton, S. E., Vesely, S. E., & Jackson, K. (2025). Teaching undergraduates to solve equivalence problems by using cover, copy, and compare: A translational study. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 58(4), 805–820. https://doi.org/10.1002/jaba.70026
title: Skinner's precurrent behavior framework conceptualizes problem solving as mediating responses that modify the environment to occasion solution responses
description: The article frames CCC-produced graphic organizers as overt mediating behavior within Skinner's (1953, 1984) account of problem solving. When encountering a problem, "solvers engage in precurrent behavior that modifies the environment," producing response products that "change the situation" and eventually give rise to the solution response. In equivalence testing, unprogrammed precurrent behavior may produce supplementary sources of stimulus control that mediate correct selection responses. The study evaluates whether CCC note taking functions as such mediation.
requirements: Mediating responses are predicted to occur under conditions in which the sample and comparison stimuli fail to occasion a selection response
constraints: The relatively low incidence of graphic organizer construction during testing suggests the CCC package established strong conditional control, limiting the need for mediation during tests

problem solving

title: Process-oriented approach to procedural training: process mining analysis of executions against a normative reference model to produce objective feedback
description: The process-oriented approach treats a bedside procedure as a process with steps in a predetermined sequence, analysed with process mining. The article states that process mining "allows for the analysis of procedural executions performed in a training context, providing objective information about adherence with a normative procedural model (similarity), the number of repetitions of steps (reworks), and performance metrics." Feedback is derived from event logs capturing rework, activities executed in incorrect order, and durations of activities and transitions, enabling objective comparison of each execution with a reference model. The approach makes explicit activities that are omitted, repeated, or executed in unexpected order, which classic assessment tools do not address.
requirements: A reference process model of the procedure (here defined by expert Delphi consensus)

A discovery algorithm to obtain a process model representing each executed procedure
constraints: In this study the approach was applied and evaluated only in a simulated environment
The rework and similarity effects are secondary outcomes for which statistical power was not calculated
target_learners: Residents and trainees learning multi-step medical procedures
target_learning_goals: Procedural proficiency, particularly correct control flow (sequence, omissions, repetitions) of procedure execution
examples: The POG's training supplemented a three-stage simulation program with process-oriented teaching, self-labelling, and individual process mining feedback reports

description: The article's implication and conclusion recommend that nursing curricula replace predominantly lecture-based delivery with active, student-centered methods. The authors state "educators should prioritize active learning interventions in both classroom and clinical education", and conclude that the results "support the integration of structured role play and collaborative group activities into nursing curricula". The recommendation rests on the study's three-arm comparison in which both active methods significantly outperformed traditional teaching.
requirements: Structured clinical scenarios with defined roles and a facilitator, as used in the intervention sessions
Supplementary practice sessions of the kind delivered here (six 60-minute sessions reinforcing previously taught theoretical content)
constraints: Findings come from a single university in Iran, which the authors state may limit generalizability to other cultural, educational, or resource settings
The authors note some prior studies, such as Alamrani et al., found no significant superiority over traditional teaching, so implementation context matters
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing students (fifth-semester pediatric nursing students in this study)
target_learning_goals: Clinical self-efficacy
Professional confidence and readiness for professional practice
examples: In the study, the role-playing arm used groups of four with nurse, parent, child, and observer roles enacting structured clinical scenarios, while the group discussion arm used facilitated subgroups of six working through clinical scenarios.

description: Because the primary barrier to arthroscopic simulation training is financial, the article recommends low-cost, 3D-printed anatomic simulators deployable worldwide through common fused deposition modeling. The authors "developed a three-dimensional (3D) printed anatomic shoulder simulator that is low cost" with a total material cost of 48 USD, in contrast to commercial simulators the article cites costing $3500 to $114,000.

Shoulder anatomy knowledge
examples: The study developed and tested a 48 USD 3D-printed shoulder simulator against a commercial simulator in a randomized controlled trial with medical students and expert surgeons

article_title: A competency-based instructional design: A progressive blended case-based teaching method.
citation: Zhu P, Jiang B, Lu R, Wang B, He Y, Yang K, Zhang Q, Zhao P, Huang B. (2025). A competency-based instructional design: A progressive blended case-based teaching method. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000043920
title: Progressive blended case-based teaching pattern: pre-class preparation, stepwise in-class case discussions, and post-class consolidation via a digital platform
description: A three-tier instructional pattern combining online pre-class materials, in-class interactive case discussion, and post-class personalized review, delivered through the Rain Classroom platform. The in-class discussions progress through "Keyword extraction", "Standardized cases", and "Inquiry-based thinking", moving students from first exposure to real clinical scenarios toward student-to-student and teacher-to-student debate. The article implements it in an integrated urology module for fifth-year medical students.
requirements: Instructors prepare pre-class lecture videos, reference papers, and guidelines distributed via the platform
A digital platform that supports in-class questioning, answer aggregation, and automated post-class review推送 such as Rain Classroom
Instructors of similar experience across comparison groups and equivalent instructional time
constraints: Evaluated over a 4-week single-institution module; the authors note instructor styles, classroom dynamics, and peer interactions were not fully standardized
target_learning_goals: clinical knowledge application and diagnostic reasoning
communication, teamwork, and other CanMEDS-based clinical competencies
examples: Students received about 30 minutes of video, 3 reference papers, and diagnostic-treatment guidelines before class; in-class case discussions progressed from keyword extraction to standardized cases to inquiry-based debates; the platform pushed personalized review materials after class

article_title: Assessment of simulation training efficacy in improving microsurgical skills: a retrospective analysis.
citation: He Xuecheng MD, Gao Tao MD, Tang Jianfei MD, Jiang Zengxin MD, PhD, Zhang Zeng MD, PhD, Lin E. MD, Yuan Hengfeng MD, PhD. (2025). Assessment of simulation training efficacy in improving microsurgical skills: a retrospective analysis. International Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/JS9.0000000000002259
title: Progressively graded simulation practice with spaced repetition for surgical skill acquisition
description: The rat tail program structures practice as short, recurring sessions sequenced from easier to harder material: training "started with larger vessels at the proximal end of the rat tail and moved toward the finer vessels at the distal end". The twice-weekly schedule over one month was chosen, the authors state, to encourage "spaced repetition—a strategy proven to improve memory retention and skill acquisition". Repetition and categorization of essential skills (coordination, visual adaptation, positioning, dissection, suturing) are emphasized throughout.
requirements: A simulation model offering vessels of graded diameter so difficulty can increase progressively
Supervised practice sessions schedulable at regular intervals alongside clinical duties
constraints: The article states the schedule suited its clinical setting (two classes per week for a month, 16 hours total); it did not experimentally compare scheduling variants
target_learning_goals: microsurgical technique proficiency
skill retention and mastery through repetitive graded practice
examples: Participants engaged in 2-hour training sessions, held twice weekly for 1 month before their clinical operations, totaling 16 hours

article_title: Planting the seed: how parental negative conditional regard boosts vulnerability to excessive study behaviour and burnout.
citation: Brueckmann M, Wild E, Wolff F. (2025). Planting the seed: how parental negative conditional regard boosts vulnerability to excessive study behaviour and burnout. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03354-z
title: Burnout prevention should address students' self-evaluation of failure, not only behavioural time-management
description: The article argues that preventing excessive study behaviour and academic burnout requires more than behavioural resource activation. Students "need to reflect on how they evaluate their own failures and what such evaluation means for their own self-esteem", question internalised demands, and learn to deal with shame and guilt when prioritising non-academic activities, so they can regain freedom to plan leisure, friends and self-care.
requirements: Interventions must work at the level of self-esteem contingency and internalised demands, not only at the behavioural level of activating resources and planning breaks
constraints: The article notes interventions must counteract the chronification of an unhealthy work and lifestyle, implying prevention is needed before behaviour becomes entrenched
target_learners: university students with high academic self-esteem contingency
target_learning_goals: healthy study engagement and prevention of academic burnout
examples: The authors' practical implications section recommends psychoeducation-style reflection on failure evaluation, internalised demands, and feelings of shame and guilt, combined with actively planning time for leisure, friends, and self-care.

article_title: A comparison of objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs) for medical students, modified during the COVID-19 pandemic.
citation: O'Malley A, Fitzgerald N, Moylett E, Gaffney G, McCarthy G, Murphy A.W., Geoghegan R, Hallahan B. (2025). A comparison of objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs) for medical students, modified during the COVID-19 pandemic. Irish Journal of Medical Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11845-025-03976-7
title: When shortening a high-stakes OSCE, preserve sufficient station count and blueprint breadth to maintain comparability with the original examination
description: This principle holds that pandemic-driven or other compression of an OSCE should cut examination time but retain enough stations and learning outcomes to keep results comparable with the unmodified format. The article found the 96-min, 8-station 2021 OSCE (37 learning outcomes) produced results similar to the 128-min 2019 OSCE, whereas the 56-min, 4-station 2020 OSCE (18 learning outcomes) yielded inflated marks. As the authors put it, the shortened format risked "some clinical knowledge being assessed in less detail than with previous examinations".
requirements: Sufficient stations and learning outcomes to cover core features such as risk and communication across all disciplines examined
constraints: The 70–160 min duration range suggested for adequate OSCE reliability is described as quite broad; the reduced 2020 blueprint was associated with reduced discriminative power across grading categories
target_learning_goals: assessment of advanced clinical skills in psychiatry, general practice, obstetrics and gynaecology, and paediatrics, including history taking, communication and safe practice
examples: The 2021 ACS OSCE used eight stations of 12 minutes each (two per discipline) with all core features examined, and matched the pre-pandemic 2019 results, whereas the 2020 four-station format produced potentially inflated marks
key_sources: O'Malley A, Fitzgerald N, Moylett E, Gaffney G, McCarthy G, Murphy A.W., Geoghegan R, Hallahan B. (2025). A comparison of objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs) for medical students, modified during the COVID-19 pandemic. Irish Journal of Medical Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11845-025-03976-7

article_title: Assessing healthcare simulation facilitation using a competency-based tool derived from practice in low-resource settings.
citation: Mossenson Adam I., Brown Janie A., Tuyishime Eugene, Rubio Martinez Rodrigo, Khalid Karima, Livingston Patricia. (2025). Assessing healthcare simulation facilitation using a competency‐based tool derived from practice in low‐resource settings. Anaesthesia. https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.16621
title: Three-category organisation of facilitation competencies applying the Practice Development Triangle framework: techniques, artistry and values
description: The competency set underpinning the tool is arranged thematically into three performance categories applying the Practice Development Triangle framework for expert debriefing practice. As the article defines them: "techniques (the practical approach and micro‐skills of facilitation); artistry (the dynamic, creative and individualised nature of facilitation); and values (the fundamental principles that form the foundation of facilitation practice)". These three categories serve as the items for internal consistency scoring.
requirements: Derived from a rigorous, international modified Delphi study establishing the 32 core facilitation competencies
constraints: Framework delineates competencies specifically for effective facilitation practice in low-resource settings
target_learners: Simulation facilitators and faculty in low-resource settings
target_learning_goals: Understanding and assessing the dimensions of effective simulation facilitation practice
examples: The tool's internal consistency analysis used techniques, artistry and values as its three items

article_title: Students Don't Learn the Way They Think They Do in a Large, Active-Learning Genetics Course.
citation: Walck-Shannon, E. M., Barton, H. D., Rowell, S. F., Chalker, D. L., & Fink, A. (2025). Students Don't Learn the Way They Think They Do in a Large, Active-Learning Genetics Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-10-0251
title: Loibl et al.'s four-step mechanism account of why prediction activities before instruction are effective
description: The article attributes to Loibl and colleagues a theorized sequence explaining why problem solving followed by instruction works. "these activities activate students' prior knowledge"; students then "identify their own knowledge gaps"; through contrasting cases or comparing solutions they "identify deep features in the problem"; finally, "students receive direct, explicit instruction, which fills in their knowledge gaps", yielding organized and well-connected knowledge that prepares for future learning.
requirements: Prediction activities must be followed by direct, explicit instruction that fills the identified knowledge gaps
constraints: The article presents this as a theorized account attributed to Loibl et al., not as a mechanism tested in this study
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory biology courses
target_learning_goals: constructing deep, principled knowledge
transfer of knowledge to superficially different problems
examples: The article cites contrasting cases in which students compare scenarios sharing surface features but differing in deep features to recognize the deep features that need addressing

article_title: Faculty development for undergraduate student programmatic assessment: a Brazilian multi-centered longitudinal study.
citation: Flauzino Rodrigo Humberto, Panúncio-Pinto Maria Paula, Bollela Valdes Roberto, de Almeida Troncon Luiz Ernesto. (2025). Faculty development for undergraduate student programmatic assessment: a Brazilian multi-centered longitudinal study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07337-x
title: Programmatic assessment as a centrally coordinated, feedback-centred assessment system
description: The article describes programmatic assessment as an innovative approach that applies current assessment principles so that assessment maximizes learning while supporting robust progress decisions. It features centralized institutional coordination, emphasis on formative assessment, individual events that "are not intended for decision making for approval or failure purposes", portfolio-based aggregation of predominantly formative data, periodic review for summative decisions, remediation plans, and continuous student–mentor dialogue. Quality criteria include validity, reliability, acceptability and positive educational effects.
requirements: Considerable investments in material, human and time resources
Changes in the mind-set of those involved with teaching and evaluation processes
Consistent faculty development for teachers and managers
constraints: Implementation depends heavily on local contexts — the article quotes that "one size does not fit all programmes"
A "gatekeeper" attitude among faculty can be a non-negligible barrier
target_learning_goals: Clinical skills
Professionalism
Comprehensive competence development with feedback for learning
examples: The article's FD project prepared teachers across nine Brazilian institutions to develop future programmatic assessment systems emphasizing formative assessment of clinical skills and professionalism
key_sources: Flauzino Rodrigo Humberto, Panúncio-Pinto Maria Paula, Bollela Valdes Roberto, de Almeida Troncon Luiz Ernesto. (2025). academic achievement (CGPA)

description: The simulator structures practice as progressive difficulty: training begins with basic target practice and advances to complete procedure simulation with placental models, with five target boards that increase in difficulty. Each level measures accuracy and time to produce an overall score and grade, and a persistent leaderboard "records and displays top scores across users, introducing an element of competitive motivation within the educational framework". an educator to interpret performance data for competency determination
constraints: the automated assessment of definitive procedural competency is not yet fully integrated

procedural timing
technical skill in fetoscopic laser surgery

article_title: The impact of the flipped classroom on the motivation and academic performance of Chinese college English learners.
citation: Wang Zhonger, Lu Jin, Yu Shenchen. (2025). The impact of the flipped classroom on the motivation and academic performance of Chinese college English learners. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0322094
title: In flipped college English teaching, prioritize cultivating students' autonomous learning motivation and intrinsic learning motivation
description: Because autonomous learning motivation and intrinsic motivation were the motivation factors that significantly predicted English scores, the article recommends that teaching focus on them: "it is recommended to focus on cultivating students' autonomous learning motivation and intrinsic learning motivation in the teaching process." The flipped classroom design supports this by letting students independently schedule learning progress and by making learning enjoyable through varied online resources.
requirements: Requires a flipped classroom or comparable arrangement in which students can independently manage learning time and progress and find learning intrinsically enjoyable.
constraints: The article warns that students without good self-management skills may procrastinate on preview tasks, and heavy academic burden can make added preview demands feel overburdening, weakening motivation.
target_learning_goals: Sustained English learning motivation
improved English academic performance
examples: The study's regression analysis showed autonomous learning motivation (P = 0.022) and intrinsic motivation (P = 0.001) significantly predicted English scores, which the authors use to ground this recommendation.

article_title: Application of practical training scenario simulation teaching method oriented to strengthen clinical skills in the clinical internship stage of medical students.
citation: Fang Xiang, Jin Shan, Sun Zhengzhe. (2025). Application of practical training scenario simulation teaching method oriented to strengthen clinical skills in the clinical internship stage of medical students. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2025.2500557
title: Practical training scenario simulation teaching method oriented to strengthen clinical skills
description: A teaching method in which interns prepare a typical neurological case beforehand, form groups of five with four groups per cohort, role-play physician, patient, and family, then perform simulated operations in a simulation ward while the teacher supervises, poses potential problems and emergencies, and leads a closing discussion of theory and skill points. The article describes it as enabling students "to carry out safe and efficient clinical skills operations in an autonomous and interactive simulated clinical environment". Cases cover cerebral hemorrhage, cerebral infarction, migraine, epilepsy, sleep disorders, and Parkinson's disease.
requirements: An instructor who selects a typical clinical case, assigns diagnostic and treatment problems beforehand, supervises role-playing throughout, and sets up potential problems and emergencies during the simulation
constraints: In the reported implementation the simulation phase ran for only 3 weeks (weeks 2–4 of the placement) due to the neurology placement syllabus and policy
target_learners: 5-year clinical medicine interns in a neurology department
target_learning_goals: Clinical skills including neurological physical examination, doctor-patient communication, humanistic care, organizational skills, and clinical thinking
examples: Interns searched medical websites for references, discussed issues, agreed a diagnosis and treatment plan, then role-played and performed simulated operations in a simulation ward with teacher supervision

title: Ten-criterion formative assessment rubric for practical radiology sessions

article_title: Study on the application of progressive training method combined with imagery training method in laparoscopic suturing skills training for resident physicians.
citation: Lin Wenxue, Yu Jian, Peng Xiaoping, Xia Jianfu, Huang Bingchen, Li Rizeng. (2025). Study on the application of progressive training method combined with imagery training method in laparoscopic suturing skills training for resident physicians. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06928-y
title: Progressive-plus-imagery laparoscopic suturing training pattern: six decomposed steps practiced sequentially with brief guided imagery before each step and before continuous practice
description: A lesson-level training pattern in which the complete intracorporeal suturing process is decomposed and practiced step by step, with short instructor-guided motor imagery sessions before practice. The article states "The complete suturing process is broken down into six steps: needle positioning, needle handling, needle entry and exit, knot tying 1 (looping the thread), knot tying 2 (tightening the knot), and cutting the thread." constraints: The article notes the inability to independently quantify the effects of each method, so the pattern's two components have not been separately validated

target_learning_goals: intracorporeal laparoscopic suturing and knot-tying skill, accuracy, and suturing quality
examples: In the trial, trainees practiced each decomposed step during weeks 1–2, performed 2 min of imagery before each of the six steps, then entered continuous suturing training in week 3, completing an average of 8.7 continuous sessions

article_title: Teaching Self-efficacy and Teaching Methods in the Aquatic Environment.
citation: Fonseca-Pinto R and Moreno-Murcia JA (2024). Teaching Self-efficacy and Teaching Methods in the Aquatic Environment. F1000Research 13: 1363. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.150535.1

title: Proctor's three-domain model of clinical supervision (normative, formative, restorative)
description: The article adopts Proctor's model as its framing account of what clinical supervision does. It describes "health professional support in normative, formative and restorative domains of practice": the normative supports organisational policy and procedure compliance, the formative supports professional skill development, and the restorative supports the emotional burden of professional practice. constraints: Does not inform the components or content of clinical supervision, only its functions
target_learners: Physiotherapists and allied health professionals at varied career stages
target_learning_goals: Professional skill development and safe, quality clinical practice
examples: The study evaluates a supervisor-led aquatic physiotherapy group supervision program against the formative domain, the domain the article says effective physiotherapy supervision focusses on.

article_title: Generating learning guides for medical education with LLMs and statistical analysis of test results.
citation: Roselló Atanet Iván, Tomova Mihaela, Sieg Miriam, Sehy Victoria, Mäder Patrick, März Maren. (2025). Generating learning guides for medical education with LLMs and statistical analysis of test results. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06978-2
title: Precursor questions: a non-symmetric, non-transitive relative-risk-based relation between test items indicating prerequisite-like empirical relationships
description: The precursor question relation is the article's formal account of empirical relationships between test items: question A is a precursor of B when f(A,B)=P(B=1|A=0)/P(B=1|A=1) falls below a threshold, an "adaptation of the relative risk index to the context of a multiple-choice test" with Cohen's d gauging strength. The threshold was derived from Sawilowsky's effect-size categories, with f(A,B) <0.485 chosen, corresponding to a large effect size. Unlike local dependence, the relation is not symmetric, and unlike Doignon and Falmagne's surmise relations it is not transitive; the authors position it as a concrete implementation of surmise relations "based primarily on operational needs rather than on theoretical considerations".
requirements: A sample of questions spanning a wide range of difficulty levels; the authors state the idea of precursor questions "would not be meaningful for a sample of questions having similar difficulty".
constraints: The relation is not transitive and is binary only by a 0/1 convention on f(A,B).
Empirically connected questions should also be topically connected to be relevant for learning guides, per the authors' two-dimension framework.
target_learners: medical students taking the Progress Test Medizin
target_learning_goals: identifying prerequisite-like relationships between test topics to sequence learning advice
examples: Applied to PT46 answer patterns to sequence questions within MeSH-term-based paths ordered from easiest to most difficult.

description: The article concludes that yoga providers could play a key role in arthritis treatment in the UK only if enabling conditions are met: yoga should be "adequately promoted and made accessible to people with arthritis, yoga delivery is regulated", and providers should have access to arthritis-specific training based on the best available scientific evidence. It frames these as system-level prerequisites for safe, credible yoga delivery in arthritis care.

constraints: Providers' concern that unregulated delivery may allow undertrained individuals to deliver contraindicated practices, risking injury

citation: Minouei Marzieh Sadat, Omid Athar, Yamani Nikoo Nikooyamani, Nasri Peiman, Ahmady Soleiman. (2025). Enhancing clinical faculties’ knowledge, attitudes, and performance in clinical supervision: a workplace-based faculty development program using proctor’s model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06769-9
title: Proctor's model of clinical supervision: formative, restorative, and normative supervisor functions
description: Proctor's model is a framework that organizes a clinical supervisor's responsibilities into three functions. The article describes it as "a thorough framework that categorizes the responsibilities of a clinical supervisor into three functions: formative, restorative, and normative". The formative function covers formative assessment and feedback to improve learning; the restorative function provides support to learners facing challenges; the normative function sets standards, guidelines, and ethical principles for professional conduct. The study used the model both to structure the faculty development curriculum and to build its attitude questionnaire and observation checklist.
requirements: Supervisors must understand all three functions to identify areas in which students need improvement and target instructional interventions
constraints: The article notes the restorative function may be minimized when supervisors face heavy workload and competing demands

target_learning_goals: effective clinical supervision of trainees
formative feedback and assessment
professional conduct and standards in clinical education
examples: The program's objectives, media, and evaluation instruments (attitude questionnaire and 26-item observation checklist) were all structured around the formative, restorative, and normative functions

citation: Neubauer R, Recker F, Weimer J, Jenssen C, Nürnberg D, Karlas T, Westerway SC, Ruppert JP, Daum N, Gschmack A, Dong Y, Möller K, Nourkami-Tutdibi N, Barth G, Şirli R, Lucius C, Prats M, Sänger SL, Keil M, Zervides C, Hoffmann B, Dietrich CF. (2025). Verifying learning success: assessment and certification of student ultrasound education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07469-0
title: Use pre-testing and differentiated feedback to measure teaching effectiveness and support learning
description: The review distinguishes measuring student competence from measuring didactic effectiveness: when evaluating a training intervention, a baseline test of pre-existing skills should precede teaching and be compared with post-training scores, since evaluation forms capture only subjective parameters. It also cites Hattie's meta-analysis that feedback and self-assessment have high effect sizes promoting learning, while noting "undifferentiated grading is probably the least effective option of different feedback methods as it provides minimal guidance for improvement".

Provide differentiated feedback rather than undifferentiated grading
constraints: Evaluation forms provide only subjective parameters and cannot independently prove teaching effectiveness

title: Future palliative care education for heart failure nurses should prioritize symptom management and palliative care perceptions
description: Based on the observed knowledge gains and remaining gaps, the article recommends that "future education should emphasize improving PC perceptions and symptom management", particularly appropriate medication use for pain management in heart failure. Perception of PC as end-of-life care is identified as a significant obstacle addressable through professional training. The article also calls for further research with a larger sample, longer implementation time, ongoing evaluation, and nurses of diverse ages and experiences.

article_title: European expert consensus on a structured approach to circular stapling anastomosis in minimally invasive left-sided colorectal resection.
citation: Tou S, Gallagher AG, Bislenghi G, Farinha R, Wolthuis A. (2025). European expert consensus on a structured approach to circular stapling anastomosis in minimally invasive left‐sided colorectal resection. Colorectal Disease. https://doi.org/10.1111/codi.70037
title: Proficiency-based progression (PBP) training methodology
description: Proficiency‐based progression is a scientific approach to surgical skill acquisition in which a procedure is first deconstructed into explicitly defined, binary performance metrics that are then validated. The article states that "PBP begins by deconstructing the procedure or skill being focused on into explicitly defined (binary) performance metrics, which are then validated". During training, trainees receive metric‐based feedback described as "explicit, constructive and formative", which the authors say makes skill acquisition more objective, transparent and fair. This article applies PBP by developing and validating metrics for circular stapling anastomosis as the first stage of a structured training programme.
requirements: Metrics must be explicitly defined and binary so that steps either occurred or did not occur and can be scored reliably by an external reviewer
constraints: The article cites a systematic review reporting a 60% reduction in performance errors for PBP‐trained surgeons, attributed to that review rather than tested here
target_learners: surgical trainees learning circular stapling anastomosis in minimally invasive left‐sided colorectal resection
target_learning_goals: safe and optimal performance of circular stapling anastomosis
reduction of procedural errors and critical errors
examples: The Metrics Group scored five unedited anonymized anastomosis videos with the metrics, iterating until inter‐rater reliability exceeded 0.8.

article_title: "MORAD ESCAPE", a novel research-based escape room approach for evaluating research competencies of health professions students.
citation: Mirshahi Arvin, Khanipour-Kencha Ali, Keyvanpour Sogol, Motlagh Maryam Karbasi. (2025). “MORAD ESCAPE”, a novel research-based escape room approach for evaluating research competencies of health professions students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06781-z
title: Progressive puzzle difficulty aligned to flow to sustain engagement in educational escape rooms
description: The escape room was designed to start with simpler puzzles and gradually increase in complexity, aligning with the flow concept in game theory. The article explains that "overly simple puzzles may lead to disengagement, while overly complex puzzles may cause frustration and fatigue"; progressively increasing difficulty maintained participant motivation and engagement throughout the experience. Puzzles served as interactive mechanisms for accessing research data rather than as standalone educational tools.
requirements: Puzzle difficulty calibrated through expert feedback and pilot trials to complement educational goals
constraints: The subjective experience of challenge may vary among individuals, an area the authors say warrants continuous refinement
target_learners: health professions students in team-based games
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement and motivation during competency assessment
examples: The game's five stations followed a linear plot with each completed puzzle unlocking new clues, and difficulty was balanced through iterative expert feedback

article_title: Comparing the impact of online and in-person active learning in preclinical medical education.
citation: Malta Kiana, Glickman Cynthia, Hunter Krystal, McBride Amanda. (2025). Comparing the impact of online and in-person active learning in preclinical medical education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06846-z
title: Deliver case-based active learning groups in a primarily in-person hybrid format, reserving virtual sessions for flexibility
description: The article concludes that students prefer in-person ALG for interpersonal learning and education but value virtual delivery for work-life balance, so a blended curriculum could combine the strengths of both. Students' own suggested model was "ALG primarily being in person, but able to switch to virtual before exams or busy time periods". The authors state that "students do not widely prefer a completely in-person or virtual format and could benefit from a blended ALG curriculum".
requirements: Requires institutional capacity to deliver the same case-based ALG in both in-person and synchronous virtual formats.
constraints: Evidence comes from a single-institution retrospective survey with recall and voluntary response bias; the article states generalizability may be limited compared to other institutions with different resources and class sizes.
target_learning_goals: collaborative case-based clinical reasoning
peer and faculty relationships
time management and work-life balance
examples: Among hybrid-preferring students, 47.3% wanted a quarter of the curriculum virtual and 40.0% wanted half virtual.

article_title: Investigation and implementation of case-based learning in the sino-foreign joint program of preventive medicine.
citation: Liu Zhipeng, Na Guanqiong, Liu Lihua, Tian Sicong, Shan Yujuan. (2024). Investigation and implementation of case-based learning in the sino-foreign joint program of preventive medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06372-4
title: Promote case-based learning in medical education reform to enhance students' comprehensive quality and classroom participation
description: The article's conclusion recommends active promotion of CBL in medical education reform because, in its words, "case-based learning can enhance students' comprehensive quality and classroom participation." The recommendation rests on the study's exam-score comparison and subjective evaluations showing improved performance, competence self-ratings, and course satisfaction. The authors explicitly withhold a stronger recommendation: "Further research is required to ascertain whether it can replace traditional teaching methods."
requirements: Cases must be designed around clinically relevant public health topics, delivered in a blended online/offline format, and supported by student-led discussion roles and instructor guidance.
constraints: The evidence comes from one cohort of 79 Sino-foreign joint-program students at a single institution; the authors state outcomes "might vary for students from different schools or pursuing different majors" and replacement of traditional teaching remains untested.
target_learning_goals: Preventive medicine knowledge, learning enthusiasm, teamwork, interpersonal communication, and knowledge application abilities
examples: The implementation combined online micro-lesson videos with offline case analysis, group discussion, and teacher-guided appraisal of discussion content.

article_title: 3D monitors improve performance on the HUGO™ RAS system: a randomised trial.
citation: Østdal TB, Tang DHY, Olsen RG, Olsen LM, Konge L, Bjerrum F. (2024). 3D monitors improve performance on the HUGO™ RAS system: a randomised trial. Surgical Endoscopy. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11615040/
title: Use 3D monitors for open-console robotic surgery training, as they improve speed and efficiency without added side effects
description: The article recommends adopting 3D monitors on open-console robotic systems for training, because the randomised trial found the 3D group operated more swiftly and precisely while 3D "does not induce more 'visual and physical discomfort' than 2D". The only reported drawback, difficulty focusing, was confined to the first session, supporting implementation of 3D vision in simulated robotic training with articulated instruments.
requirements: Surgeons or trainees must have adequate stereopsis; the trial stratified participants by stereo blindness measured with the TNO test before randomisation
constraints: Evidence is from surgical novices on a virtual reality simulator; the authors cannot exclude different results with experienced surgeons or on a real robotic system, and no proficiency-based intervention was used

target_learning_goals: efficiency and precision in robot-assisted surgical tasks
examples: In the trial, one investigator turned the 3D effect on or off before participants entered the simulator room, and both groups wore 3D glasses throughout to preserve blinding

title: prEPAred mobile application for near real-time workplace-based assessment of EPAs
description: The prEPAred app (precisionED Ltd, Wollerau, Switzerland) is a mobile application that lets trainees and supervisors record workplace-based assessments of EPAs in daily clinical routine. "The trainee initiates the process by selecting the EPA performed", after which both parties independently rate task complexity and the recommended level of supervision; comparing the two assessments "a feedback conversation is stimulated which is optionally guided by the app using structured feedback instructions". Each datapoint is stored in the trainee's ePortfolio. In this study it was used to record 3936 assessments across 28 Swiss anesthesia residency programs.

stimulating feedback conversations and documentation of learning goals

title: Nurse educators should promote HRQoL, reduce academic burnout, and increase motivation to improve nursing students' academic success
description: The article's stated design recommendation: because HRQoL influenced success only through burnout and motivation pathways, educators should act on all three determinants together rather than on GPA directly. The article recommends that "nurse educators develop and implement appropriate interventions to promote HRQoL, reduce AB, and increase both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, thereby improving AS." It grounds the recommendation in the finding that HRQoL "did not have a direct effect on academic success" but shaped "motivational dynamics". This principle applies to undergraduate nursing and other health-professions students.

citation: Park Kye-Yeung, Kang Ye Ji, Park Hoon-Ki, Hwang Hwan-Sik. (2024). Exploring effective video-review strategies of patient encounters for medical students: precepted review versus peer discussion. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2024.2392428
title: Preceptor feedback template for communication and interpersonal skills
description: The study used a predetermined feedback template (Table 2) that structured preceptor oral feedback after each video review around five areas: effective listening and questioning, exploring the patient's illness experience and emotions, giving understandable explanations, creating a good relationship with the patient, and treating the patient respectfully with courtesy. The article states that "standardized feedback based on a predetermined template was consistently applied to overcome this issue" of single-provider variation. Specific items include appropriately using open-ended and close-ended questions, avoiding replicated questions, encouraging the patient to express emotions, avoiding medical jargon, checking for understanding, and hand hygiene. The template was applied after both video-viewing sessions in the preceptor feedback group.

Video recordings of the student's encounters as the basis for feedback
constraints: The article notes the use of a single preceptor feedback provider may have influenced results

examples: Template items included Appropriately used both open-ended questions and close-ended questions and Explained about the physical examination beforehand

description: Proficiency-based progression is a training model in which trainees advance through a simulation curriculum only after demonstrating predefined, quantitatively defined performance benchmarks verified by instructors. target_learning_goals: Surgical skills for CIED implantation, including incision, pocket creation, lead fixation, device-lead connection, and wound closure
examples: Trainees had to demonstrate the benchmark in the online module (unlimited attempts) before proceeding to the simulation-based module, and the surgical proficiency benchmark was defined as a maximum of two errors over the entire procedure

citation: Mascheroni J, Stockburger M, Patwala A, Mont L, Rao A, Retzlaff H, Garweg C, Gallagher AG, Verbelen T. (2024). The randomized trial supports this by showing far more PBP trainees reached the benchmark within the same training time.

Proficiency benchmarks derived from experienced operators' performance on the same tasks
Instructors trained to apply metrics-based feedback
constraints: PBP instruction is performance-based and adapts to learning speeds, so time-capped training may leave some trainees short of the benchmark
target_learners: Novice procedural operators, here novice CIED implanters
target_learning_goals: Acquiring safe surgical technique before supervised in vivo device implantation
examples: In the trial, formal surgical skills training and assessment using PBP was recommended to strengthen academic/institutional curricula and ensure skill acquisition prior to in vivo practice

title: Procedure-specific low-fidelity vaginal surgery simulation modules (didactic online module plus model training) for VH, AR and PR
description: The intervention combines a procedure-specific didactic online module covering "theory, informed consent, patient positioning, antibiotics and wound basics, anesthesia, relevant anatomy, procedural steps" with videos of the models and real OR procedures, followed by a written post-test requiring a passing grade. Residents then train on procedure-specific low-fidelity models designed at the authors' institution, through independent and supervised practice, with preceptors determining operative readiness by direct observation before proceeding to supervised OR cases. Initial validation of the models was previously published by the same group.

Surgeon preceptors at each site who determine operative readiness via direct observation of skills on the models

examples: Intervention residents completed the online module, passed a written post-test, trained on the low-fidelity models under supervision, and were then rated by blinded proctors during real OR cases

article_title: Capability to identify and manage critical conditions: effects of an interprofessional training intervention.
citation: Santesson Ia, Schell Carl Otto, Bjurling-Sjöberg Petronella. (2024). Capability to identify and manage critical conditions: effects of an interprofessional training intervention. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05567-z
title: proACT interprofessional training course
description: The proACT course is an interprofessional standardized training program developed by clinical healthcare professionals and managed by a non-profit association, "utilizing a cascade principle for implementation, with main instructors training local instructors who in turn train clinical staff." All participants, regardless of profession, read a theoretical textbook, complete digital exercises with interactive reflections and a self-test, and attend a one-day training combining a classroom seminar and interprofessional high-fidelity simulations (4 × 45 min) with pre-briefing, simulation, and three-phase debriefing. Content covers the ABCDEF-acronym, NEWS, CRM, communication techniques, and basic medical ethics.
requirements: Participants must testify they read the textbook and present a certificate of completed digital exercises before the one-day training
constraints: In the studied region the intervention only reached 26.5% of staff despite being mandatory, and most units lacked proACT-trained physicians
target_learning_goals: identifying deteriorating patients and critical conditions
NEWS use
non-technical team skills (CRM)
basic life-saving actions
examples: In the study setting, training was delivered via Clinical Training Centers with high-fidelity simulation guided by trained instructors

article_title: Beyond active learning: Using 3-Dimensional learning to create scientifically authentic, student-centered classrooms.
citation: Cooper M. M., Caballero M. D., Carmel J. H., Duffy E. M., Ebert-May D., Fata-Hartley C. L., Herrington D. G., Laverty J. T., Nelson P. C., Posey L. A., Stoltzfus J. R., Stowe R. L., Sweeder R. D., Tessmer S., Underwood S. M. (2024). Beyond active learning: Using 3-Dimensional learning to create scientifically authentic, student-centered classrooms. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0295887
title: Focus course transformation on 3D-aligned learning objectives, assessments, and materials rather than engagement techniques alone
description: This principle holds that transformation efforts should start from what students should know and be able to do with that knowledge, rather than from instructional methods such as clickers or group work. The authors "propose that focusing on creating 3DL aligned learning objectives, assessments, and instructional materials is a more fruitful approach to transforming a learning environment than the more common approach which focuses on instructional methods". Because 3DL tends to bring student engagement with it, designing for sensemaking of phenomena achieves both goals, whereas engagement alone may leave students active without meaningful engagement with core ideas.
requirements: Learning objectives, assessments, and instructional materials must all be aligned with the three dimensions, including disciplinary Core Ideas.
constraints: The authors caution that characterizing transformation solely by active learning, without investigating what is expected of students in terms of sensemaking and reasoning, may result in the illusion of transformation, or hands on without being minds on.
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory STEM gateway courses
target_learning_goals: coherent, connected, and useful disciplinary knowledge
mechanistic explanation and prediction of phenomena
examples: The meiosis example: converting a lecture into group work drawing cell-division stages is active but not 3D, while having students construct and use models to explain how the cell sorts genetic information, and predict what happens when the mechanism fails, makes the lesson three-dimensional.

title: Nursing skills training system combining procedural pathways with information management
description: A one-year in-service training system in which standardized operation pathways are built through collective and individual lesson preparation and delivered with information-technology support. Every operation procedure formed "different but regular operation pathways, including quality requirements, pre-operation preparation, operation process, post-operation treatment, and effect evaluation." A learning platform publishes appointment times, records practice via QR-code scans, and hosts recorded teaching videos; detailed scoring of operation assessment standards reduces invigilator subjectivity.

A learning platform supporting appointment scheduling, QR-code practice logging, and video replay

Nurse competency and clinical problem-solving ability

citation: Rai Amar, Shukla Shivani, Mehtani Nikita, Acharya Vikas, Tolley Neil. (2024). Does a junior doctor focused 'Bootcamp' improve the confidence and preparedness of newly appointed ENT registrars to perform their job roles? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05691-w
title: Preparedness as a state of readiness linked to confidence and negatively affected by fear and under-confidence
description: The article invokes an account, attributed to Caroll et al., in which preparedness is "a state of readiness that is negatively impacted by negative emotions such as fear and under-confidence". Accumulating knowledge and experience optimises future proficiency and performance, which the article describes as confidence; self-preparation is thereby associated with trainee self-confidence. The article uses this account to explain why the bootcamp's knowledge and simulation experience improved preparedness for complex technical skills, and why unfamiliar stations produce stress resembling a "fight or flight" response that may cause fear or task avoidance.
requirements: Requires trainees to accumulate knowledge and experience in the target skills for preparedness to develop
constraints: The article states that whether the bootcamp reduces the learning curve and negative emotions "still requires further investigation and assessment"
target_learners: Newly appointed ENT ST3 specialty trainee registrars
target_learning_goals: Preparedness and confidence in performing emergency, elective and ward-based ENT clinical tasks

title: Nursing training institutions should prioritise the development of educators' competence to enhance nursing students' development of clinical competence.
description: This principle holds that educator competence is the most significant lever for developing nursing students' clinical competence. The study argues that educators play the most significant role in developing the competence of nursing students and can shape and direct students' learning. It is recommended that nursing training institutions prioritise the recruitment of competent educators and the development of educators' competence.

title: Achieving sustained practitioner practice change requires more than education and training: provide social connection and coaching to build confidence and perceived competence
description: The article concludes that "Changing practice requires more than just education and training" and that "Opportunities for social connection and coaching to improve self-confidence and perceived competence are needed to overcome the fear of opening Pandora's box". Connection through a community of practice enabled peer coaching and support, and practitioners were more motivated to ask about adversity when they felt more supported. The importance of 'social influence' and 'beliefs about capabilities' across studies emphasises the need to create opportunities for practitioner social support, coaching and building relationships.

constraints: Barriers to connection included the physical building and part-time work patterns limiting co-presence

title: Preprocedural preparation for children should cover duration, location, sequence, discomfort, sensations and feelings about the procedure
description: The article argues that preprocedural preparation, such as interactive animated educational videos, tells the patient what would happen and lets them experience what they would feel, giving children the opportunity to "rehearse the process of going through a medical procedure". It then enumerates six pertinent points any such preparation should cover, from test duration to how the child may feel when the procedure is done. Exposure to this information lets children mentally practise the stressful event and develop accurate expectations.

constraints: The article notes no single intervention alone is enough to improve children's cooperativeness; parental involvement, preprocedural interventions and distraction during the scan all contribute.

target_learning_goals: Learning what will happen during a medical procedure
Coping with an unfamiliar and stressful procedure through mental rehearsal
examples: The trial's interactive animated video let patients help a panda go through an MRI scan using touch buttons, with pre-recorded MRI sounds incorporated, before the actual scan.

The Delphi results support using the 42 consensus competencies as "measurable learning objectives to guide the development of a health literacy curriculum," and the prioritized practices as indicators of competencies professionals should routinely use.

citation: Li Zi-Zhan, Lin Hao, Xu Yuan-Ming, Man Qi-Wen, Wu Tian-Fu, Shao Zhe, Liang Shanshan, Bu Lin-Lin, Liu Bing. (2024). Application of PRI-E–a combined learning method in oral and maxillofacial oncology education. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-58878-y
title: PRI-E: a step-by-step combined learning mode sequencing PBL, CBL and EBL under a Passion-Research-Innovation philosophy
description: PRI-E (Passion, Research, Innovation, Education) is a combined learning mode that sequences problem-based, case-based and evidence-based learning in three ordered steps: students first give a faculty-assigned PBL presentation, then a CBL presentation once the PBL content is delivered well, then receive an EBL task and join a higher-level contest. The article states that "PRI-E adopts a step-by-step approach to guide students through orderly progress" and that this individualized mode lets students grasp the essence of PBL, CBL and EBL. Sessions run 80 minutes weekly over a six-month rotation with identical content across arms.
requirements: PBL first requires little clinical experience and builds confidence before the heavier CBL and EBL presentations
CBL and EBL steps require more student experience and workload, so they are assigned only after the PBL content is delivered well
Staff must receive pre-job training and control the presentation delivery and clinical practice details
constraints: Weaknesses reported: lack of systematic teaching content leads to low efficiency in a single class and staff inexperience lowers initial efficiency
Extra time demands may cause student dissatisfaction and anxiety under exam-oriented education
Short internship time and busy clinical work can adversely affect learning outcomes
target_learners: postgraduate stomatology students rotating in oral and maxillofacial head and neck oncology
target_learning_goals: clinical presentation skills
critical thinking and problem solving
evidence-based clinical decision making
communication with patients

title: Use progressive evaluation with feedback in PBL so students can track their progress against objectives
description: The article argues that assessment in PBL should be ongoing rather than a one-time spot evaluation. It states that "Tutors should provide progressive evaluation and feedback that would allow students to determine whether they reached requirements, went off track from the objectives, and reflection on processes of learning." This principle responds to student complaints that end-of-module evaluation was unfair and did not reflect their efforts.

title: Preoperative surgical tracheostomy checklist developed through junior-doctor-led quality improvement
description: A quality-improvement artifact created by redeployed junior doctors after a clinical incident in which a patient's planned tracheostomy procedure was delayed by inappropriate anticoagulant administration. The checklist was enthusiastically adopted by specialist surgical teams and expanded to cover other ICU sites at two other hospitals within the authors' multicentre National Health Service Trust; similar checklists for intubation and proning followed. No outcome evaluation of the checklist is reported in the article.

constraints: Frequent changes in COVID-19 clinical guidelines can make audit and quality improvement challenging.

Quality improvement practice

article_title: Transferability of robotic console skills by early robotic surgeons: a multi-platform crossover trial of simulation training.
citation: Larkins Kirsten M., Mohan Helen M., Gray Matthew, Costello Daniel M., Costello Anthony J., Heriot Alexander G., Warrier Satish K. (2022). Transferability of robotic console skills by early robotic surgeons: a multi-platform crossover trial of simulation training. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-022-01475-w
title: Set multi-platform robotic credentialing to a proficiency-based rather than time-based standard
description: The article proposes that, following the aviation type-rating example, credentialing for each robotic platform type be based on demonstrated proficiency measured by objective simulation metrics rather than time-based standards. It reports that "overall risk and safety metrics are within acceptable limits regardless of the order of progression of console", supporting safe contemporaneous multi-console training. Individual credentialling for each platform would still be required.
requirements: Objective simulation metrics and pre-defined proficiency benchmarks for each exercise
Completion of exercises and passing pre-defined outcome metrics on two consecutive attempts to achieve proficiency
constraints: Based on a small pilot trial; the authors call for high-quality randomised data as the next step
Mimic simulation metrics have not been validated for the HUGO RAS operating system

target_learning_goals: basic robotic console operating skills including instrument and camera control, endowrist manipulation, two-handed dexterity and needle driving
examples: Ten participants completed four Mimic simulation exercises on the dV-Trainer and HUGO RAS in a counterbalanced crossover design, with proficiency defined as passing pre-defined metrics on two consecutive attempts

article_title: Effectiveness of a proficiency-based progression e-learning approach to training in communication in the context of clinically deteriorating patients: a multi-arm randomised controlled trial.
citation: McCarthy Nora, Neville Karen, Pope Andrew, Barry Lee, Livingstone Vicki. (2023). Effectiveness of a proficiency-based progression e-learning approach to training in communication in the context of clinically deteriorating patients: a multi-arm randomised controlled trial. BMJ Open 13(8):e072488. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2023-072488
title: Proficiency-based progression framework with steps, errors and critical errors
description: A training and assessment framework in which learning proceeds through intermediate levels on a planned pathway toward expert-determined proficiency benchmarks. Performance metrics are subdivided into three categories: a 'step' is a component of a task that should be performed; an 'error' is a component that should not be performed; and a 'critical error' is a component that could jeopardise the overall outcome of the domain event if omitted. The critical error category focuses evaluation on critical mistakes so that feedback can enable improved performance, and scaffolded exposure to the skill in increasingly complex situations aids learning and mastery.
requirements: Sufficiently detailed, properly integrated feedback used for remediation to move learners along the proficiency pathway
Expert-determined benchmarks defining steps, errors and critical error cut-offs for progression
constraints: Proficiency through predefined metrics had previously been demonstrated only in face-to-face simulation; this study tests its translation to e-learning
target_learners: novice learners moving toward proficiency in a defined skill
target_learning_goals: acquisition of a procedural or communication skill to an expert-determined proficiency level
examples: The 2019 face-to-face study by Breen et al. used the same metrics and benchmarks; this trial transferred them into e-learning with automatic feedback replacing the face-to-face instructor.
