BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02087-4

article_title: Use of profession-role exchange in an interprofessional student team-based community health service-learning experience.
citation: Wang J, Guo J, Wang Y, Yan D, Liu J, Zhang Y, Hu X. (2020). Use of profession-role exchange in an interprofessional student team-based community health service-learning experience. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02127-z
title: Profession-role exchange component in an interprofessional student team-based community health service-learning experience
description: An extracurricular IPE component in which health-care students from different professions perform one another's roles during a real community service activity. The article describes it as "an innovative simulation- based experiential learning method, in which health-care students from different professions play one another’s role in an environment similar to the clinical environment". Medical students acted as pharmacists or nurses, pharmacy students as physicians or nurses, and nursing students as physicians or pharmacists within interprofessional teams delivering diabetes self-management education. Role choices were based on students' own will and team negotiation; students could consult peers but not let others work instead of themselves.
requirements: An interprofessional student team-based community service activity in which each team includes members of the different professions, so exchanged roles have real counterparts to perform
constraints: The intervention was conducted only once; the small sample size and single-institution nature may limit generalizability, per the article's limitations section
target_learners: third-year medical, pharmacy and nursing students
target_learning_goals: role clarification and awareness of other professions' roles
attitudes toward interprofessional collaboration
examples: In the studied activity, one medical student in each team performed the pharmacy student's responsibilities and the other played the nursing students' role, while pharmacy students acted as student physician or nursing student
key_sources: Wang J, Guo J, Wang Y, Yan D, Liu J, Zhang Y, Hu X. (2020). Use of profession-role exchange in an interprofessional student team-based community health service-learning experience. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02127-z

article_title: Association of Physical Fitness with Intelligence and Academic Achievement in Adolescents.
citation: Gil-Espinosa F.J., Chillón P., Fernández-García J.C., Cadenas-Sanchez C. (2020). Association of Physical Fitness with Intelligence and Academic Achievement in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17124362
title: Do not reduce physical activity time in schools; support adolescents' physical fitness development as a potential contributor to intelligence and academic achievement
description: The article argues against the common practice of cutting physical education to increase academic instruction time. The authors conclude that "our study showed a positive association between cardiovascular fitness and general intelligence" and that fitness components "were associated with academic achievement in adolescents". They therefore recommend increasing the time adolescents spend in physical activity, noting that "physical activity interventions that promote improvements in fitness components could be very successful in enhancing academic achievement in the school setting".
requirements: Access to physical education and varied sports/physical activity opportunities during or after school
constraints: Cross-sectional design cannot establish causality
Confounders such as body mass index and maturational status were not included
Further studies or meta-analyses are needed on physical activity prescription for brain health in adolescents
target_learning_goals: General intelligence
Academic achievement in language, mathematics, humanities and other subjects
examples: The study used standardized EUROFIT fitness tests and school grades in 403 adolescents, finding cardiorespiratory fitness positively associated with both intelligence and achievement
key_sources: Gil-Espinosa F.J., Chillón P., Fernández-García J.C., Cadenas-Sanchez C. (2020). Association of Physical Fitness with Intelligence and Academic Achievement in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17124362

article_title: Practical lessons for phone-based assessments of learning.
citation: Angrist N, Bergman P, Evans DK, Hares S, Jukes MCH, Letsomo T. (2020). Practical lessons for phone-based assessments of learning. BMJ Global Health. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjgh-2020-003030
title: Protect children in phone-based assessments through low-stakes framing, caregiver awareness and supervisor monitoring of calls
description: Because few phone surveys gather data directly from children, face-to-face consent procedures and enumerator training must be adapted so children are not harmed. The article recommends making clear the questions are "low stakes" so adults do not discipline children who perform poorly, recording a random sample of calls for supervisor review, and relying on the caregiver's presence as "a layer of accountability and oversight".
requirements: Adapted consent procedures and enumerator training for phone administration
A mechanism for supervisors to monitor a sample of calls, such as automatic sending of recorded calls
target_learners: Children and youth in primary grades assessed remotely during school closures
target_learning_goals: Accurate, ethical measurement of student learning by phone
examples: In Botswana, assessors asked parents to give the child privacy and made clear the assessment had no rewards or consequences; supervisors could receive a random sample of recorded calls.
key_sources: Angrist N, Bergman P, Evans DK, Hares S, Jukes MCH, Letsomo T. (2020). Practical lessons for phone-based assessments of learning. BMJ Global Health. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjgh-2020-003030

article_title: Improving Cardiovascular Workforce Competencies in Cardio-Obstetrics: Current Challenges and Future Directions.
citation: Sharma G, Zakaria S, Michos ED, Bhatt AB, Lundberg GP, Florio KL, Vaught AJ, Ouyang P, Mehta L. (2020). Improving Cardiovascular Workforce Competencies in Cardio‐Obstetrics: Current Challenges and Future Directions. J Am Heart Assoc. https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.119.015569
title: Pregnancy heart team (PHT): multidisciplinary team-based care model for cardio-obstetric patients
description: A pregnancy heart team is a formal multidisciplinary care structure the article recommends establishing, including "cardiologists with expertise in cardio‐obstetrics, obstetricians, maternal‐fetal medicine specialists, primary healthcare providers, obstetric anesthesiologists, neonatologists, geneticists, pharmacists, social workers, nurses, and other care team members." Team-member involvement and prenatal visit frequency vary with CVD complexity (Tables 2 and 3). PHTs also run quality-improvement initiatives at monthly multidisciplinary meetings and provide trainees immersive outpatient clinic and inpatient labor-and-delivery educational experiences.
requirements: Strong partnerships and exposure to multidisciplinary team-based care; institutional collaboration between MFM/obstetrics, medicine, and anesthesia
constraints: For patients living far from a specialized high-risk delivery hospital, the PHT needs additional involvement before the third trimester with detailed antepartum and delivery plans
target_learners: Advanced trainees on labor and delivery rotations
target_learning_goals: Managing pregnant patients with heart disease
Recognizing effects of adverse pregnancy outcomes on long-term cardiovascular outcomes
examples: Tables 2 and 3 give suggested timetables and member involvement by condition: HDP, GDM, CAD, cardiomyopathy, and ACHD-modified WHO categories I–III
key_sources: Sharma G, Zakaria S, Michos ED, Bhatt AB, Lundberg GP, Florio KL, Vaught AJ, Ouyang P, Mehta L. (2020). Improving Cardiovascular Workforce Competencies in Cardio‐Obstetrics: Current Challenges and Future Directions. J Am Heart Assoc. https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.119.015569

article_title: Starting school: educational development as a function of age of entry and prematurity.
citation: Pettinger Katherine J, Kelly Brian, Sheldon Trevor A, Mon-Williams Mark, Wright John, Hill Liam J B. (2019). Starting school: educational development as a function of age of entry and prematurity. Archives of Disease in Childhood, 105(2), 160-165. https://doi.org/10.1136/archdischild-2019-317124
title: Health and education professionals should take a more proactive approach to supporting gestationally immature children through the transition into formal education
description: The article argues that because the EYFSP GLD measure can be treated as an estimate of a child's capacity to cope with the transition into formal education, findings of increased odds of failing to attain a GLD for preterm and early-starting children imply a need for proactive support. The authors state "our findings suggest the need for a more proactive approach by health and education professionals in supporting gestationally immature children through this transition". This principle targets the school-entry transition period for children born moderate-to-late preterm.
requirements: Health and education professionals able to identify gestationally immature children at school entry and coordinate support across services
constraints: The article notes this was not an analysis of the direct effect of delaying entry, as there were too few cases of delayed entry in the cohort
target_learners: children born moderate-to-late preterm entering formal schooling
target_learning_goals: developmental readiness for formal education including communication and language, physical development, personal social and emotional development, mathematics and literacy
examples: The authors suggest providing learning resources to teachers to help them support children born preterm in the classroom, tailored advice to families, and greater use of routine data linkage to monitor and support at-risk children across health and education services
key_sources: Pettinger Katherine J, Kelly Brian, Sheldon Trevor A, Mon-Williams Mark, Wright John, Hill Liam J B. (2019). Starting school: educational development as a function of age of entry and prematurity. Archives of Disease in Childhood, 105(2), 160-165. https://doi.org/10.1136/archdischild-2019-317124

article_title: Effect of hands-on interprofessional simulation training for local emergencies in Scotland: the THISTLE stepped-wedge design randomised controlled trial.
citation: Lenguerrand Erik, Winter Cathy, Siassakos Dimitrios, MacLennan Graeme, Innes Karen, Lynch Pauline, Cameron Alan, Crofts Joanna, McDonald Alison, McCormack Kirsty, Forrest Mark, Norrie John, Bhattacharya Siladitya, Draycott Tim. (2020). Effect of hands-on interprofessional simulation training for local emergencies in Scotland: the THISTLE stepped-wedge design randomised controlled trial. BMJ Quality & Safety 29(2):122-134. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjqs-2018-008625
title: PROMPT training package (Second edition) with Train the Trainers programme and local multiprofessional courses
description: PROMPT (PRactical Obstetric Multi-Professional Training) is an 'in-house', adaptable multiprofessional training day covering management of core obstetric emergencies including postpartum haemorrhage, sepsis and shoulder dystocia as well as fetal monitoring in labour and team-working. In THISTLE it was delivered as the Second edition package with a 2 day Train the Trainers programme at the Scottish Clinical Simulation Centre, after which each unit's in-house training team ran local PROMPT courses aiming to train all maternity staff within 12 months.
requirements: A multiprofessional in-house training team (recommended: two midwives, one obstetrician and one anaesthetist) attending the T3 programme before starting local courses
constraints: In THISTLE, units were allowed flexibility in course content to enhance local ownership, and no ongoing implementation support beyond phone or email was provided
target_learners: All maternity staff in large maternity units, multiprofessionally (midwives, obstetricians, anaesthetists)
target_learning_goals: Management of core obstetric emergencies (postpartum haemorrhage, sepsis, shoulder dystocia), fetal monitoring in labour, and team-working
examples: Each unit's training coordinator supplied course dates, attendee numbers by grade and role, and course programmes used to judge implementation fidelity.
key_sources: Lenguerrand Erik, Winter Cathy, Siassakos Dimitrios, MacLennan Graeme, Innes Karen, Lynch Pauline, Cameron Alan, Crofts Joanna, McDonald Alison, McCormack Kirsty, Forrest Mark, Norrie John, Bhattacharya Siladitya, Draycott Tim. (2020). Effect of hands-on interprofessional simulation training for local emergencies in Scotland: the THISTLE stepped-wedge design randomised controlled trial. BMJ Quality & Safety 29(2):122-134. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjqs-2018-008625

article_title: Impact of demonstration in a realistic simulation environment as a postoperative education in patients' experience.
citation: Barbosa Luciana Gardin, Frazão Cinthya da Silva. (2020). Impact of demonstration in a realistic simulation environment as a postoperative education in patients’ experience. Einstein (Sao Paulo). https://doi.org/10.31744/einstein_journal/2020AO4831
title: Practical Life Room — a simulated home environment for postoperative patient education through demonstration
description: The Practical Life Room, launched at the AACD hospital in December 2017, "simulates the rooms in a house" (living room, bedroom, kitchen, laundry and bathroom). In it, a physical therapist demonstrates and lets patients simulate activities of daily living, such as lying down and getting up from bed, using the toilet, showering, using a computer at a desk, or preparing a quick meal. The goal is to anticipate post-discharge difficulties, explain how to overcome them, and keep patients active within safety limits of their recovery.
requirements: Patients are taken to the space only when their clinical condition allows it, i.e., when there is no debilitating pain, symptoms or malaise of any nature
target_learners: adult orthopedic postoperative patients (cervical/lumbar disc herniation, idiopathic scoliosis, knee and hip arthroplasty)
target_learning_goals: safe performance of activities of daily living after hospital discharge
risk prevention and maintenance of functionality during the postoperative period
examples: Annex 2 lists the items addressed in the session, including stairs, ramps, bed transfers, kitchen, laundry room, closet and bathroom tasks tailored by surgery type
key_sources: Barbosa Luciana Gardin, Frazão Cinthya da Silva. (2020). Impact of demonstration in a realistic simulation environment as a postoperative education in patients’ experience. Einstein (Sao Paulo). https://doi.org/10.31744/einstein_journal/2020AO4831

article_title: Dynamic Balance, but Not Precision Throw, Is Positively Associated with Academic Performance in Children.
citation: Lima Rodrigo A., Stodden David F., Pfeiffer Karin A., Larsen Lisbeth R., Barros Mauro V. G., Bugge Anna, Andersen Lars B. (2020). Dynamic Balance, but Not Precision Throw, Is Positively Associated with Academic Performance in Children. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17082790
title: Promote the development of motor competence for all children because it is positively related to academic performance and other health-related outcomes
description: The article concludes that schools and practitioners should promote children's motor competence development, stating that "Our results and the results of others point to the importance of promoting the development of motor competence for all children". The recommendation rests on the study's longitudinal finding that dynamic balance was positively related to academic performance, partially mediated by waist circumference, and on broader evidence of health-related outcomes.
requirements: Motor competence must be assessed and developed, e.g., through gross motor tasks such as dynamic balance activities
constraints: The study assessed only two motor competence tests (dynamic balance and precision throw), which the authors state limits the generalizability of the results
The follow-up was only one year, which the authors describe as relatively short
target_learners: children in first through fifth grade (ages 7–11)
target_learning_goals: academic performance in Danish language and mathematics
examples: The CHAMPS-study DK measured children's dynamic balance with the KTK backward balance-beam test and academic performance with standardized Danish national tests, finding balance longitudinally associated with academic performance
key_sources: Lima Rodrigo A., Stodden David F., Pfeiffer Karin A., Larsen Lisbeth R., Barros Mauro V. G., Bugge Anna, Andersen Lars B. (2020). Dynamic Balance, but Not Precision Throw, Is Positively Associated with Academic Performance in Children. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17082790

article_title: The disaster worker resiliency training program: a randomized clinical trial.
citation: Mahaffey Brittain L., Mackin Daniel M., Rosen Jonathan, Schwartz Rebecca M., Taioli Emanuela, Gonzalez Adam. (2020). The disaster worker resiliency training program: a randomized clinical trial. International Archives of Occupational and Environmental Health. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00420-020-01552-3
title: Build disaster workers' coping resources in advance of trauma exposure rather than only intervening after a crisis
description: The article argues that prior disaster mental health interventions (CISM, Psychological First Aid) target mitigation of symptoms after a crisis, whereas resilience programs should build coping resources before exposure. The DWRT "encourages participants to think about ways to make themselves and their organizations more resilient to stress in advance of a crisis." The trial's trauma-exposed subgroup results support this timing: symptom increases appeared only in waitlist participants who later experienced trauma, not in trained participants.
requirements: Participants must remain active disaster workers likely to be called upon for future response efforts
constraints: The trial followed participants only 3 months, so durability of the preemptive benefit is unknown
Benefit on symptoms was observed only in the trauma-exposed subsample, not the full sample
target_learners: disaster responders such as police, firefighters, paramedics, Red Cross/FEMA personnel, and volunteers
target_learning_goals: adaptive coping skills and psychological resilience to future trauma exposure
examples: The study assessed change 3 months post-workshop to allow time for subsequent work-related trauma and stress exposure, finding symptom increases only among untrained trauma-exposed participants
key_sources: Mahaffey Brittain L., Mackin Daniel M., Rosen Jonathan, Schwartz Rebecca M., Taioli Emanuela, Gonzalez Adam. (2020). The disaster worker resiliency training program: a randomized clinical trial. International Archives of Occupational and Environmental Health. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00420-020-01552-3

article_title: Cardiac auscultation skills among junior doctors: effects of sound simulation lesson.
citation: Tokuda Yasuharu, Matayoshi Tetsutaro, Nakama Yasunori, Kurihara Masaru, Suzuki Tomoharu, Kitahara Yusuke, Kitai Yuya, Nakamura Takashi, Itokazu David, Miyazato Tatsuya. (2020). Cardiac auscultation skills among junior doctors: effects of sound simulation lesson. International Journal of Medical Education 11:107-110. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.5eb6.70c6
title: Combine pre-test, sound simulation lesson and post-test with gamification to teach cardiac auscultation to large groups
description: The article proposes an instructional design for auscultation skills consisting of "pre-test, sound simulation lesson, and post-test", delivered with a high-quality speaker for low-pitched sounds and scoring or gamification to motivate learners. It argues this suits teaching a large number of learners in limited time, and reports the design significantly improved accuracy in its own study.
requirements: A sound/murmur simulator with acoustic speaker capable of deep, low-pitched sound output in a quiet room
A multiple-choice assessment scored on correct auscultatory findings
constraints: The before-and-after design may carry regression-to-the-mean bias, and the separate contributions of lesson and tests are unclear
target_learners: junior doctors (first and second postgraduate year residents)
target_learning_goals: cardiac auscultation diagnostic accuracy
examples: 50 junior doctors heard seven abnormal cardiac recordings for about two minutes each (14 minutes total), chose diagnoses from nine multiple-choice items, and the top 10 scorers received commendation with medical book prizes.
key_sources: Tokuda Yasuharu, Matayoshi Tetsutaro, Nakama Yasunori, Kurihara Masaru, Suzuki Tomoharu, Kitahara Yusuke, Kitai Yuya, Nakamura Takashi, Itokazu David, Miyazato Tatsuya. (2020). Cardiac auscultation skills among junior doctors: effects of sound simulation lesson. International Journal of Medical Education 11:107-110. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.5eb6.70c6

article_title: Effect of structural training on surgical outcomes of residents' first operative laparoscopy: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Jokinen E, Mikkola TS, Härkki P. (2019). Effect of structural training on surgical outcomes of residents' first operative laparoscopy: a randomized controlled trial. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-018-06657-y
title: Simulator training curricula should be proficiency based rather than based on a fixed number of repetitions or fixed training time
description: The article recommends structuring surgical simulator curricula around reaching a defined proficiency criterion rather than a preset number of repetitions or sessions. In this trial, "Plateau was reached in two of the nine skill tasks", showing the fixed five-repetition program left most learning curves unfinished, and the authors conclude a proficiency-based curriculum could be more effective.
requirements: A defined expert or proficiency criterion level against which trainee performance is assessed
constraints: The article notes there is no fixed expert criterion, and the target level affects training length, skills level assessment, and training costs
target_learners: junior residents in Obstetrics and Gynecology
target_learning_goals: basic laparoscopic surgical skills
examples: In this trial all nine basic skills tasks were practiced five times each, and the learning-curve plateau was not reached in every task.
key_sources: Jokinen E, Mikkola TS, Härkki P. (2019). Effect of structural training on surgical outcomes of residents' first operative laparoscopy: a randomized controlled trial. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-018-06657-y

article_title: The Longitudinal Associations of Fitness and Motor Skills with Academic Achievement.
citation: Syväoja, H. J., Kankaanpää, A., Joensuu, L., Kallio, J., Hakonen, H., Hillman, C. H., & Tammelin, T. H. (2019). The Longitudinal Associations of Fitness and Motor Skills with Academic Achievement. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0000000000002031
title: Physical activity that enhances motor skills should be prioritized for its potential academic benefits.
description: Based on the finding that motor skills, rather than aerobic or muscular fitness, independently predicted future academic achievement, the authors highlight the importance of physical activity that enhances motor skills. They state these results "highlight the importance of such physical activity, which enhances motor skills." This principle suggests schools and health promoters should prioritize developing fundamental movement skills.
requirements: Programs should include activities that develop fundamental movement skills (locomotor and manipulative skills).
constraints: The evidence is based on observational longitudinal data, not intervention studies; the authors call for intervention studies to confirm the results.
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement (GPA)
Fundamental movement skills
examples: In the study, motor skills were measured with the 5-leaps test and a throwing–catching combination test, and better motor skills at T2 predicted better GPA at T3.
key_sources: Syväoja, H. J., Kankaanpää, A., Joensuu, L., Kallio, J., Hakonen, H., Hillman, C. H., & Tammelin, T. H. (2019). The Longitudinal Associations of Fitness and Motor Skills with Academic Achievement. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0000000000002031

article_title: Can simulation-based education and precision teaching improve paediatric trainees' behavioural fluency in performing lumbar puncture? A pilot study.
citation: Lydon Sinéad, Reid McDermott Bronwyn, Ryan Ethel, O’Connor Paul, Dempsey Sharon, Walsh Chloe, Byrne Dara. (2019). Can simulation-based education and precision teaching improve paediatric trainees’ behavioural fluency in performing lumbar puncture? A pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1553-7
title: Precision teaching as an educational framework for establishing behavioural fluency in procedural skills
description: Precision teaching is described as "an educational framework that facilitates the determination of when fluency is achieved, by ensuring monitoring of a learner’s performance". Its typical components are establishing a fluency criterion from expert performance, frequency building through repeated timed trials with feedback, monitoring progression on the standard celeration chart, and changing or supplementing instructional tactics when a participant is not progressing. Behavioural fluency itself is defined as the "combination of accuracy plus speed of responding", and fluent behaviour retains, is stable under distraction, and generalises to novel settings. In this study the framework was operationalised for infant lumbar puncture with a pinpointed task analysis and Chartlytics-generated celeration charts.
requirements: A pinpointed task analysis providing an objective written definition of the observable steps of the target behaviour
A fluency criterion set from expert performance (100% accuracy within the expert’s median duration plus 10%)
Timed trials with corrective feedback and standard celeration chart monitoring
constraints: The authors note the fluency criterion was set from the performance of just one consultant, and call for stronger experimental designs in evaluating simulation-based education incorporating precision teaching
target_learners: Paediatric trainees (senior house officers / junior residents) learning procedural skills
target_learning_goals: Performing infant lumbar puncture accurately and quickly enough to meet a behavioural fluency criterion
examples: Participants were given a booster session on infant positioning after celeration charts and observer notes revealed persistent inaccuracy on instructing the assistant to position the child
key_sources: Lydon Sinéad, Reid McDermott Bronwyn, Ryan Ethel, O’Connor Paul, Dempsey Sharon, Walsh Chloe, Byrne Dara. (2019). Can simulation-based education and precision teaching improve paediatric trainees’ behavioural fluency in performing lumbar puncture? A pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1553-7

article_title: Student progress decision-making in programmatic assessment: can we extrapolate from clinical decision-making and jury decision-making?
citation: Tweed M, Wilkinson T. (2019). Student progress decision-making in programmatic assessment: can we extrapolate from clinical decision-making and jury decision-making? BMC Medical Education 19:176. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1583-1
title: Progression decision-making in programmatic assessment as a parallel of clinical and jury decision-making
description: The article's organizing framework extrapolates from two familiar decision domains to student progression decisions. Decisions on whether a student is ready to progress have 'many parallels with patient diagnosis', including aggregating 'a mix of numerical and narrative/text with varying degrees of robustness' under high stakes. Jury decision-making supplies the group model: a panel weighing all evidence to reach a high-stakes pass/fail verdict where, unlike most group decisions, no correct answer is known.
requirements: Applies where programmatic assessment requires aggregation of information from multiple sources, which 'needs to be completed in a robust manner'.
constraints: The parallel is imperfect: 'The programmatic assessment panel may be closer to a Supreme Court panel of judges rather than a jury of lay-people and peers, but there is little research on the decision-making and deliberations of panels of Supreme Court judges'.
target_learners: healthcare professional students in programs using programmatic assessment
target_learning_goals: robust pass/progression decisions about student competence
protecting patients and society through competent graduates
examples: The article maps clinical practices (screening vs confirmatory testing, second opinions, multidisciplinary meetings) and jury phenomena (deliberation styles, foreperson influence, leniency) onto progression panel decision-making.
key_sources: Tweed M, Wilkinson T. (2019). Student progress decision-making in programmatic assessment: can we extrapolate from clinical decision-making and jury decision-making? BMC Medical Education 19:176. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1583-1

article_title: Using Low-Cost Virtual Reality Simulation to Build Surgical Capacity for Cervical Cancer Treatment.
citation: Bing EG, Parham GP, Cuevas A, Fisher B, Skinner J, Mwanahamuntu M, Sullivan R. (2019). Using Low-Cost Virtual Reality Simulation to Build Surgical Capacity for Cervical Cancer Treatment. Journal of Global Oncology. https://doi.org/10.1200/JGO.18.00263
title: Proficiency-based VR training with performance targets, feedback, and structured self-assessment
description: The training design sets movement and time targets for each substep, delivers immediate feedback (a chime, visual progression, and praise from an audio file of a senior surgeon's voice), and ends each simulation with a summary screen of step-specific scores and a composite proficiency score. Participants were "instructed to continue training on the simulator until they reached a proficiency score of 85 or higher five times in a row." After each session, participants identified areas needing improvement and reflected in writing on how to improve, which the authors intended to stimulate deliberate practice.
requirements: Access to the simulator near clinical settings during working hours; participants schedule sessions and can complete up to six simulations per session
A revised self-assessment asking participants to review each of the five substeps, identify the specific substep needing most improvement, and write an improvement plan
target_learners: Surgical novices and trainees learning complex procedures
target_learning_goals: Surgical procedural efficiency, instrument selection, and self-regulated skill improvement
examples: When the self-assessment form was revised to be more specific, participant reflections tended to focus more on studying pelvic anatomy and instrument placement before the next session
key_sources: Bing EG, Parham GP, Cuevas A, Fisher B, Skinner J, Mwanahamuntu M, Sullivan R. (2019). Using Low-Cost Virtual Reality Simulation to Build Surgical Capacity for Cervical Cancer Treatment. Journal of Global Oncology. https://doi.org/10.1200/JGO.18.00263

article_title: Family physicians' experience and understanding of evidence-based practice and guideline implementation in primary care practice, Cape Town, South Africa.
citation: Pather MK, Mash R. (2019). Family physicians' experience and understanding of evidence-based practice and guideline implementation in primary care practice, Cape Town, South Africa. Afr J Prm Health Care Fam Med. 11(1), a1592. https://doi.org/10.4102/phcfm.v11i1.1592
title: Guideline implementation training should be interactive, in workshop format, and recognise practitioners' readiness to change
description: The article recommends that implementation include "training that is interactive and in a workshop format that recognises the need to address individual practitioners' readiness to change as well as local barriers". Training should be a collaborative process that respects practitioners' autonomy and their choice of priorities rather than telling them what to follow, should provide evidence that the guideline has made a difference elsewhere, and should involve all practitioners involved in patient care, including both nurses and doctors.
requirements: Training should involve all practitioners involved in patient care, for example both nurses and doctors
Providing evidence that the guideline has made a difference elsewhere would also be helpful
constraints: Readiness to change varies among staff and is a huge problem in a busy and already overburdened primary care setting
target_learning_goals: adhering to adapted clinical guidelines
changing established clinical practice in line with current evidence
examples: Family physicians' reported experience was that workshop training on a guideline made adherence much more likely than a guideline simply passed down from the Department of Health
key_sources: Pather MK, Mash R. (2019). Family physicians' experience and understanding of evidence-based practice and guideline implementation in primary care practice, Cape Town, South Africa. Afr J Prm Health Care Fam Med. 11(1), a1592. https://doi.org/10.4102/phcfm.v11i1.1592

article_title: Improving developmental and educational support for children born preterm: evaluation of an e-learning resource for education professionals.
citation: Johnson S, Bamber D, Bountziouka V, Clayton S, Cragg L, Gilmore C, Griffiths R, Marlow N, Simms V, Wharrad HJ. (2019). Improving developmental and educational support for children born preterm: evaluation of an e-learning resource for education professionals. BMJ Open, 9(6): e029720. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-029720
title: Interactive e-learning resource about preterm birth for education professionals (www.pretermbirth.info)
description: A freely available, interactive e-learning resource (www.pretermbirth.info) comprising five discrete reusable learning objects (RLOs) covering what preterm birth is, educational, cognitive/motor, and behavioural/social/emotional outcomes, and how professionals can support affected children. RLOs combine "audio, video, animation, text, images, case studies and quizzes designed to engage the user in active learning and allowing individuals to set their own pace of learning". The resource represents about one hour of learning activity and is available non-commercially.
requirements: Delivered via an online platform; in the study participants needed an account and questionnaire access via the platform or JISC online surveys
constraints: Evaluated with a one-off use period of up to 30 days and no control group; effect on classroom practice and child outcomes unknown
target_learners: Primary school teachers and education professionals of children aged 4-11 years
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of long-term outcomes of preterm birth and practical strategies to support children's learning
examples: In the evaluation, 61 teachers were given up to 30 days' access and completed the PB-KS before and after use
key_sources: Johnson S, Bamber D, Bountziouka V, Clayton S, Cragg L, Gilmore C, Griffiths R, Marlow N, Simms V, Wharrad HJ. (2019). Improving developmental and educational support for children born preterm: evaluation of an e-learning resource for education professionals. BMJ Open, 9(6): e029720. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-029720

article_title: Exploring how medical students learn with the help of a digital presentation: a qualitative study.
citation: Hyll Mary, Schvarcz Robert, Manninen Katri. (2019). Exploring how medical students learn with the help of a digital presentation: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1569-z
title: Prezi digital presentation 'The Antibiotic Jungle' for orientation in bacteria and antibiotics
description: A web-based Prezi presentation created to provide "a basic orientation in common bacteria, related diseases, and antibiotics", based on a course leader's schematic explanation of which antibiotics are effective against which bacteria. It was divided into three main parts delineated by circles — common bacteria, groups of antibiotics, and the "antibiotic tree" — on a canvas with an orienteer running through a forest background, accessible via the LMS, the Prezi homepage, or a mobile app, and available in English online.
requirements: Access via LMS, Prezi homepage, or Prezi mobile app (which at the time only worked on Apple devices)
Student instruction in the software's pause, rewind and zoom functions
constraints: Some students experienced loading failures and slow playback; the pausing function often replayed an entire section, and the majority of students had not previously used Prezi
target_learning_goals: orientation in common bacteria, related diseases, and antibiotics
examples: The presentation was divided into three main parts delineated by circles: one part on common bacteria, one on different groups of antibiotics, and one part called the "antibiotic tree".
key_sources: Hyll Mary, Schvarcz Robert, Manninen Katri. (2019). Exploring how medical students learn with the help of a digital presentation: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1569-z

article_title: Process-Oriented Feedback through Process Mining for Surgical Procedures in Medical Training: The Ultrasound-Guided Central Venous Catheter Placement Case.
citation: Lira Ricardo; Salas-Morales Juan; Leiva Luis; de la Fuente Rene; Fuentes Ricardo; Delfino Alejandro; Hurtado Nazal Claudia; Sepúlveda Marcos; Arias Michael; Herskovic Valeria; Munoz-Gama Jorge. (2019). Process-Oriented Feedback through Process Mining for Surgical Procedures in Medical Training: The Ultrasound-Guided Central Venous Catheter Placement Case. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16111877
title: Observer-based process mining method for process-oriented feedback in procedural medical training
description: The article proposes a five-stage method — video recording, video tagging, event log generation, model discovery, and model analysis — inspired by the PM2 methodology, in which "event logs are not generated automatically" but are built from off-line observation of recorded videos by medical specialists. Discovery models of each student's execution are compared against expert (EXP) models to identify rework, incorrect activity order, and slow activities or transitions, complementing checklist- and GRS-based feedback with a process perspective.
requirements: Videos of procedure executions must be recorded and tagged by medical specialists to generate event logs
A validated reference process model of the correct procedure is needed for comparison
constraints: The main limitation is scalability when a large number of videos needs to be tagged
Procedures with more complex patterns, e.g., when order among some activities is not relevant, would require advanced conformance checking techniques
target_learners: medical residents learning surgical procedures in simulation
target_learning_goals: procedural skill execution including activity order, rework avoidance, and time performance
examples: Applied to the ultrasound-guided CVC placement course at the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, using the Celonis discovery algorithm and views comparing PRE, POST, and EXP models
key_sources: Lira Ricardo; Salas-Morales Juan; Leiva Luis; de la Fuente Rene; Fuentes Ricardo; Delfino Alejandro; Hurtado Nazal Claudia; Sepúlveda Marcos; Arias Michael; Herskovic Valeria; Munoz-Gama Jorge. (2019). Process-Oriented Feedback through Process Mining for Surgical Procedures in Medical Training: The Ultrasound-Guided Central Venous Catheter Placement Case. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16111877

article_title: Effect of a proficiency-based progression simulation programme on clinical communication for the deteriorating patient: a randomised controlled trial.
citation: Breen Dorothy, O'Brien Sinead, McCarthy Nora, Gallagher Anthony, Walshe Nuala. (2019). Effect of a proficiency-based progression simulation programme on clinical communication for the deteriorating patient: a randomised controlled trial. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-025992
title: Proficiency-based progression (PBP) training as an outcomes-based training model
description: Proficiency-based progression training is described as "a form of outcomes-based training that involves training individuals to achieve a proficiency benchmark". The process involves 'deliberate' practice against a set of clearly defined objective metrics, with the benchmark set as the mean performance of clinicians who undertake the procedure regularly in clinical practice. In this trial the model was applied for the first time to a non-technical skill, clinical communication, by having partners score each other's phone calls against predefined metrics and repeat cases until proficiency was reached.
requirements: A proficiency benchmark set from the mean performance of qualified personnel on each case
Operationally defined metrics quantified as steps, errors and critical errors for each case
Learners must reach the benchmark before progressing to the next case
constraints: The article notes the study was limited by restriction on training time, with 3.5 hours still restricted by the existing undergraduate curriculum
target_learners: qualified nurses and doctors (programme designed for them also)
target_learning_goals: clinical communication (ISBAR) for the deteriorating patient
escalation of care using the National Early Warning Score
examples: In the E+PBP arm, partners scored each other's simulated phone calls against predefined metrics and repeated cases until the proficiency benchmark was reached before progressing
key_sources: Breen Dorothy, O'Brien Sinead, McCarthy Nora, Gallagher Anthony, Walshe Nuala. (2019). Effect of a proficiency-based progression simulation programme on clinical communication for the deteriorating patient: a randomised controlled trial. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-025992

article_title: Using simulation to explore medical students' understanding of integrated care within geriatrics.
citation: Yang S, Chaudhary Z, Mylopoulos M, Hashmi R, Kwok Y, Colman S, Yogaparan T, Sockalingam S. (2019). Using simulation to explore medical students' understanding of integrated care within geriatrics. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1758-9
title: Productive struggle as a mechanism for simulation-based integrated care learning
description: The article applies productive struggle — experiences "where students first engage in problem solving before receiving instruction on underlying concepts, which is then followed by instruction to consolidate learning" — to explain why GPS-Care increases students' understanding of integrated care. Students experience the challenges of care delivery for patients with co-occurring physical and mental health needs across interprofessional contexts, then receive instruction through a facilitated debrief and reflection. The authors propose this sequence supports deeper learning of IC concepts before formal instruction.
requirements: A challenging experience exposing learners to crucial facets of the target concepts before instruction
A facilitated debrief and reflection after the experience to consolidate learning
constraints: The article states data had not fully examined this concept in GPS-Care prior to this study, and it remains unclear which preconditions triggered the transformative shift
target_learning_goals: understanding of integrated care concepts such as team-based care and care navigation
examples: In GPS-Care, students navigated five simulated appointments as patients or caregivers before the 45-min debrief
key_sources: Yang S, Chaudhary Z, Mylopoulos M, Hashmi R, Kwok Y, Colman S, Yogaparan T, Sockalingam S. (2019). Using simulation to explore medical students' understanding of integrated care within geriatrics. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1758-9

article_title: Surgeon Volume and Surgeon Age in Relation to Proficiency Gain Curves for Prognosis Following Surgery for Esophageal Cancer.
citation: Gottlieb-Vedi E, Mackenzie H, van Workum F, Rosman C, Lagergren P, Markar S, Lagergren J. (2018). Surgeon Volume and Surgeon Age in Relation to Proficiency Gain Curves for Prognosis Following Surgery for Esophageal Cancer. Annals of Surgical Oncology. https://doi.org/10.1245/s10434-018-6869-8
title: Proficiency gain curves with RA-CUSUM change-point analysis as a model of surgical skill acquisition
description: The article models surgical skill acquisition as a proficiency gain curve: a surgeon's risk-adjusted outcome trajectory over consecutive cases, reaching a plateau (change point) where outcome improves from worse to better than expected. Change points are identified graphically on RA-CUSUM curves as "the maximal deflection of the curve, i.e. the point at which the outcome changed from worse to better than expected", with expected probabilities from multivariable logistic regression adjusting for seven confounders. The model is applied to mortality, reoperation, margin, and lymph-node outcomes.
requirements: A sufficient cumulative case series per surgeon to reach a plateau; the 103 surgeons with insufficient volume were excluded
constraints: Retrospective observational design; cut-offs based on median values may not generalize to other datasets; results precede centralization and team-based operating
target_learners: surgeons in training for complex procedures (esophagectomy)
target_learning_goals: acquisition of proficiency in complex surgical procedures to reduce learning-associated patient harm
examples: Change points identified at 14 vs 31 cases (volume) and 13 vs 48 cases (age) for 1- to 5-year mortality
key_sources: Gottlieb-Vedi E, Mackenzie H, van Workum F, Rosman C, Lagergren P, Markar S, Lagergren J. (2018). Surgeon Volume and Surgeon Age in Relation to Proficiency Gain Curves for Prognosis Following Surgery for Esophageal Cancer. Annals of Surgical Oncology. https://doi.org/10.1245/s10434-018-6869-8

article_title: Simulation-enhanced nurse mentoring to improve preeclampsia and eclampsia care: an education intervention study in Bihar, India.
citation: Raney Julia H., Morgan Melissa C., Christmas Amelia, Sterling Mona, Spindler Hilary, Ghosh Rakesh, Gore Aboli, Mahapatra Tanmay, Walker Dilys M. (2019). Simulation-enhanced nurse mentoring to improve preeclampsia and eclampsia care: an education intervention study in Bihar, India. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-019-2186-x
title: PRONTO simulation-based nurse mentoring program embedded in AMANAT, Bihar
description: A high-fidelity in-situ simulation training program developed by PRONTO International and implemented with CARE India within the AMANAT nurse mentoring program at 320 primary health centers in Bihar between 2015 and 2017. Nurse mentors rotated in pairs between facilities, facilitating video-recorded emergency obstetric simulations, each "followed by a video-guided debrief, led by the nurse mentor." The curriculum included 31 simulation scenarios, including two PE/E scenarios, and 3422 mentees were trained statewide across four phases.
requirements: Nurse mentors completed four weeks of CARE India training including one week on simulation facilitation and debriefing, plus a four-day advanced simulation facilitation course four months later
constraints: Evaluation was based on simulated scenarios; generalizability of findings to actual clinical practice is unknown
target_learners: Nurse mentees (ANM/GNM-qualified nurses) at primary health centers in Bihar, India
target_learning_goals: Diagnosis and management of preeclampsia and eclampsia using evidence-based practices
examples: During week four of each phase, mentees received PE/E training through lectures, skills stations, and simulations of a 17-year-old woman with severe headache, BP 170/112, and 3+ urine protein
key_sources: Raney Julia H., Morgan Melissa C., Christmas Amelia, Sterling Mona, Spindler Hilary, Ghosh Rakesh, Gore Aboli, Mahapatra Tanmay, Walker Dilys M. (2019). Simulation-enhanced nurse mentoring to improve preeclampsia and eclampsia care: an education intervention study in Bihar, India. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-019-2186-x

article_title: Problems of problem-based learning: Towards transformative critical pedagogy in medical education.
citation: Cavanagh A, Vanstone M, Ritz S. (2019). Problems of problem-based learning: Towards transformative critical pedagogy in medical education. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40037-018-0489-7
title: Broaden PBL so students problematize structural and political causes of ill health rather than only recognizing social context
description: The paper recommends that medical curricula go beyond invoking social determinants of health for students to 'recognize' or 'acknowledge', and instead have students probe the structural causes of ill health seen in the clinic, questioning how professional roles and socio-political structures uphold disparities. This positions social context as a site of professional intervention and advocacy rather than secondary to biomedical learning objectives.
requirements: Requires re-centering the struggle against social causes of illness within curricula, including rethinking hierarchical clinic dynamics and students' relationships to biomedical knowledge
constraints: The paper acknowledges Freire's pedagogy remains beyond the boundaries of medical education as it is imagined today
target_learning_goals: Health advocacy
Health equity
Critical analysis of social determinants of health
examples: The paper proposes students develop richer understanding of how lived experiences of race, gender, migration status and other social identities combine to affect patients
key_sources: Cavanagh A, Vanstone M, Ritz S. (2019). Problems of problem-based learning: Towards transformative critical pedagogy in medical education. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40037-018-0489-7

article_title: Design and evaluation of a clinical competency committee.
citation: Duitsman ME, Fluit CRMG, van Alfen-van der Velden JAEM, de Visser M, ten Kate-Booij M, Dolmans DHJM, Jaarsma DADC, de Graaf J. (2019). Design and evaluation of a clinical competency committee. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40037-018-0490-1
title: Prototype CCC meeting at Amalia Children's Hospital
description: A prototype clinical competency committee meeting developed in the prototyping phase of a design-based approach at a Dutch university children's hospital. It combined "previously gathered scores from multiple frontline workplace assessors" with written independent judgments from CCC members, structured discussion led by a neutral chair, and formulation of feedback comprising positive feedback and three points for improvement for each resident. It was evaluated with observations, member interviews and resident questionnaires over two cycles.
requirements: CCC members trained in providing feedback
Program director briefs members beforehand on the CCC's purpose, assessment forms, and interpretation of EPA levels and CanMEDS competencies
Residents deliver multiple assessment data prior to the meeting
constraints: Evaluated in a single paediatrics program with a relatively small sample of CCC members and residents; the authors note future research should focus on CCCs in different contexts
target_learners: paediatrics residents (24 at the time of study)
target_learning_goals: developmental assessment of clinical competence across CanMEDS competencies and EPAs
examples: Two meetings were evaluated: October 2016 (24 residents, 150 min) and February 2017 (12 residents, 120 min), with modifications made between cycles.
key_sources: Lb0

article_title: SVI Self-Study Guide: A Study Tool for Independent Preparation for the AAMC Standardized Video Interview.
citation: Mayer-Hirshfeld Ilana, Agarwal Gauri G., Jackson Jennifer S. (2019). SVI Self-Study Guide: A Study Tool for Independent Preparation for the AAMC Standardized Video Interview. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10805
title: Preparation resources for a novel testing format should prioritize practice in that format, since format familiarity drives preparedness gains more than content review
description: Based on their evaluation, the authors conclude that "in creating resources to prepare for the SVI, it is most useful to provide tools to practice using the SVI testing format." The guide operationalizes this by including eight practice questions in the SVI's format (30 seconds to prepare, 3 minutes to deliver a recorded oral answer), and the largest preparedness gains occurred on format-dependent components such as delivering a complete answer within 3 minutes.
requirements: Practice questions should be written in a style similar to the assessment's published example questions
constraints: The guide includes only a limited number of practice questions and does not give individualized feedback; the authors state students would benefit from individual counseling and feedback on their responses as well as from additional practice questions
target_learners: medical students preparing for the AAMC Standardized Video Interview
target_learning_goals: preparedness for a novel oral video-recorded testing format
verbal explanation of professionalism and communication topics using personal examples
examples: The guide's eight practice questions were written in a style similar to the AAMC's example questions, informed also by the Emergency Medicine Residents' Association's Residency Interview Guide
key_sources: Mayer-Hirshfeld Ilana, Agarwal Gauri G., Jackson Jennifer S. (2019). SVI Self-Study Guide: A Study Tool for Independent Preparation for the AAMC Standardized Video Interview. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10805

article_title: Self-handicapping among nursing students: an interventional study.
citation: Zarshenas Ladan, Jahromi Leila Ashrafean, Jahromi Mohsen Faseleh, Manshadi Marieh Dehghan. (2019). Self–handicapping among nursing students: an interventional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1441-6
title: Incorporate problem solving skills training into nursing and medical students' curricula to reduce self-handicapping
description: The article recommends that universities teach problem solving skills as a cognitive-behavioral approach to reduce students' self-handicapping. It states that "teaching cognitive-behavioral approaches is recommended to be considered among the ten life skills used in curricular design for medical students, including nurses," and that officials should "incorporate problem solving skills training in the students' curricula or introduce it as a course." The recommendation rests on the trial's finding of a significant decline one month after training.
requirements: Students with elevated self-handicapping (in the trial, scores higher than 50 on Jones and Rodwalt's scale)
constraints: The between-group difference was significant only one month after the intervention, not immediately
The sample was limited to one city, which the authors state might affect generalizability
target_learning_goals: problem solving skills
reduced self-handicapping
psychological health
examples: The intervention delivered six two-hour weekly sessions based on the Dezorilla and Goldfried model, using lecture, group discussion, question and answer, brain-storming, scenario, and role play
key_sources: Zarshenas Ladan, Jahromi Leila Ashrafean, Jahromi Mohsen Faseleh, Manshadi Marieh Dehghan. (2019). Self–handicapping among nursing students: an interventional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1441-6

article_title: Fostering critical thinking and collaborative learning skills among medical students through a research protocol writing activity in the curriculum.
citation: Sahoo Soumendra; Mohammed Ciraj Ali. (2018). Fostering critical thinking and collaborative learning skills among medical students through a research protocol writing activity in the curriculum. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2018.86
title: Proposal Wizard protocol template
description: Proposal Wizard is a standard protocol template developed by the ophthalmology department and used by participants in the study. The article states the proposal wizard had five headings: title, rationale, objectives, study design, and references. It structured the groups' protocol writing during the clinical posting.
requirements: Used with an orientation on literature search and retrieval of at least five references
target_learning_goals: research proposal writing
critical thinking
examples: Students used the template to write proposals for clinical studies answering two hypothetical research questions
key_sources: Sahoo Soumendra; Mohammed Ciraj Ali. (2018). Fostering critical thinking and collaborative learning skills among medical students through a research protocol writing activity in the curriculum. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2018.86

article_title: Ten years of simulation-based shoulder dystocia training- impact on obstetric outcome, clinical management, staff confidence, and the pedagogical practice - a time series study.
citation: Dahlberg Johanna, Nelson Marie, Dahlgren Madeleine Abrandt, Blomberg Marie. (2018). Ten years of simulation-based shoulder dystocia training- impact on obstetric outcome, clinical management, staff confidence, and the pedagogical practice - a time series study. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-018-2001-0
title: PROBE (Practical Obstetric team-training): a mandatory, recurring simulation-based shoulder dystocia team-training program
description: PROBE is the simulation-based team-training program introduced in 2008 at the Linköping delivery ward, with objectives "to improve obstetric emergency skills and develop interprofessional teamwork, thus promoting better patient outcome". Participation is mandatory, sessions run six times yearly at an interval of 1.5 years during working hours, each 3-hour session includes two scenarios plus a skills station, and a 40-minute shoulder dystocia scenario has been part of every event. Teams of one or two midwives, a doctor and a nurse assistant work scenarios led by ALSO-trained certified instructors, preceded by individual theoretical study.
requirements: Mandatory, scheduled participation during working hours for all delivery-ward obstetricians, midwives and nurse assistants
A simulation center with an obstetric skills laboratory and certified experienced instructors
constraints: The HELPERR management mnemonic and clinical guidelines remained unchanged after PROBE introduction, so outcome changes are attributed to training rather than protocol change
target_learners: Delivery-unit obstetricians, midwives and nurse assistants
target_learning_goals: Recognition and standardized management of shoulder dystocia and obstetric emergencies
Interprofessional teamwork and communication
examples: Teams trained in the HELPERR mnemonic scenario; the shoulder dystocia scenario included in every PROBE event since 2008.
key_sources: Dahlberg Johanna, Nelson Marie, Dahlgren Madeleine Abrandt, Blomberg Marie. (2018). Ten years of simulation-based shoulder dystocia training- impact on obstetric outcome, clinical management, staff confidence, and the pedagogical practice - a time series study. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-018-2001-0

article_title: Elimination testing with adapted scoring reduces guessing and anxiety in multiple-choice assessments, but does not increase grade average in comparison with negative marking.
citation: Vanderoost J, Janssen R, Eggermont J, Callens R, De Laet T. (2018). Elimination testing with adapted scoring reduces guessing and anxiety in multiple-choice assessments, but does not increase grade average in comparison with negative marking. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0203931
title: Use elimination testing with adapted scoring instead of negative marking when the goal is to discourage guessing without grade inflation or risk-aversion bias
description: The article concludes that "elimination testing with adapted scoring is a valuable alternative for negative marking when looking for a scoring method that discourages guessing", because it avoids grade inflation, reduces blank answers and guessing, and lowers reported stress. Examiners seeking an alternative to negative marking should adopt this scoring rule, since traditional elimination scoring inflates average scores and would require adjusting test difficulty or pass thresholds.
requirements: Students must receive instruction and practice opportunities with the adapted scoring rule before the exam.
constraints: The gender-gap reduction in blank answers was observed only in one of the two courses.
Adapted scoring requires more exam time according to students.
target_learners: higher education students, especially in medicine and life sciences with large enrolments
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of mastery without guessing artefacts
fair assessment independent of risk-aversion
examples: The study implemented the method on final high-stakes exams in two courses with a crossed between-group design across 683 students.
key_sources: Vanderoost J, Janssen R, Eggermont J, Callens R, De Laet T. (2018). Elimination testing with adapted scoring reduces guessing and anxiety in multiple-choice assessments, but does not increase grade average in comparison with negative marking. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0203931

article_title: Proficiency-based progression training: an 'end to end' model for decreasing error applied to achievement of effective epidural analgesia during labour: a randomised control study.
citation: Kallidaikurichi Srinivasan Karthikeyan, Gallagher Anthony, O'Brien Niall, Sudir Vinod, Barrett Nick, O'Connor Raymund, Holt Francesca, Lee Peter, O'Donnell Brian, Shorten George. (2018). Proficiency-based progression training: an 'end to end' model for decreasing error applied to achievement of effective epidural analgesia during labour: a randomised control study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2017-020099
title: Proficiency-based progression 'end-to-end' training methodology
description: Proficiency-based progression (PBP) is a training methodology in which "the learner is required to demonstrate a proficiency benchmark in procedure performance before progressing". The article implements it end-to-end: experts define unambiguous, dichotomously scored procedure-specific metrics and errors; the metrics are validated for reliability and construct validity; trainees practise on a simulator with focused feedback until they reach a predetermined proficiency benchmark on two consecutive procedures; only then do they perform clinical procedures. In this study the benchmark required absence of critical errors and an error count not exceeding the average expert-derived error count.
requirements: Procedure-specific metrics defined as unambiguous descriptions of observable behaviours by experts
A validated assessment tool with inter-rater reliability above 0.8
A predetermined, unambiguous proficiency benchmark
Simulator practice with focused feedback on errors until the benchmark is attained on two consecutive procedures
constraints: The authors acknowledge the resource intensiveness of this intervention, describing the study as a proof-of-concept and calling for research on mitigating or optimising resource use
The study did not measure skill of optimising epidural analgesia such as timing, dose and selection of agents for top-ups
target_learners: Novice anaesthetic trainees with fewer than 2 years of experience and fewer than 50 epidural catheter insertions
target_learning_goals: Safe and effective performance of labour epidural catheter placement, reducing procedural errors and clinical failure
examples: Experts attended five face-to-face meetings to define 74 metrics, of which 12 were classified as critical errors; group P trainees achieved proficiency following three trials on a manikin
key_sources: Kallidaikurichi Srinivasan Karthikeyan, Gallagher Anthony, O'Brien Niall, Sudir Vinod, Barrett Nick, O'Connor Raymund, Holt Francesca, Lee Peter, O'Donnell Brian, Shorten George. (2018). Proficiency-based progression training: an 'end to end' model for decreasing error applied to achievement of effective epidural analgesia during labour: a randomised control study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2017-020099

article_title: Effect of a 20-week physical activity intervention on selective attention and academic performance in children living in disadvantaged neighborhoods: A cluster randomized control trial.
citation: Gall S, Adams L, Joubert N, Ludyga S, Müller I, Nqweniso S, Pühse U, du Randt R, Seelig H, Smith D, Steinmann P, Utzinger J, Walter C, Gerber M. (2018). Effect of a 20-week physical activity intervention on selective attention and academic performance in children living in disadvantaged neighborhoods: A cluster randomized control trial. PLoS ONE 13(11): e0206908. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0206908
title: Protect regular physical activity lessons in the school curriculum to help maintain academic performance during academically demanding transitions
description: The authors conclude that school-based physical activity can counteract academic decline in disadvantaged settings: "Participation in a 20-week physical activity intervention implemented in disadvantaged schools in Port Elizabeth, South Africa, was positively associated with children’s academic performance." They recommend that school administrators ensure staff deliver compulsory physical activity lessons. The intervention combined PE lessons, moving-to-music, in-class activity breaks, and infrastructure adaptation.
requirements: School staff must implement physical activity lessons, which the curriculum already makes a compulsory component
constraints: The 20-week period was short, teacher compliance was uneven, and baseline academic differences between groups existed; the authors state the conclusion "needs to be interpreted with caution"
target_learners: Disadvantaged (quintile three) South African primary school children aged 8–13
target_learning_goals: Maintenance of end-of-year academic performance across home language, additional language, mathematics, and life skills
examples: Three intervention schools received two weekly PE lessons, one weekly moving-to-music class, regular in-class activity breaks, and a low-cost physical-activity-friendly environment over 20 weeks
key_sources: Gall S, Adams L, Joubert N, Ludyga S, Müller I, Nqweniso S, Pühse U, du Randt R, Seelig H, Smith D, Steinmann P, Utzinger J, Walter C, Gerber M. (2018). Effect of a 20-week physical activity intervention on selective attention and academic performance in children living in disadvantaged neighborhoods: A cluster randomized control trial. PLoS ONE 13(11): e0206908. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0206908

article_title: Improvement in children's fine motor skills following a computerized typing intervention.
citation: McGlashan H.L., Blanchard C.C.V., Sycamore N.J., Lee R., French B., Holmes N.P. (2017). Improvement in children's fine motor skills following a computerized typing intervention. Human Movement Science. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.humov.2017.10.013
title: Process-oriented versus task-oriented approaches to motor-skill intervention
description: The article organises prior motor intervention research into two approaches: a "process-oriented" approach that "focuses on the suspected underlying process of the motor deficit such as sensory functions, memory, attention, planning, and formulating motor programs", and a "task-oriented" approach involving "remediation through the practice of a specific task that results in skill generalization". The authors interpret their finding that typing practice improved general manual dexterity but not the task-specific tapping measure as "giv[ing] more support to the process-oriented approach".
requirements: Interventions should be matched to whether the goal is underlying process improvement or specific-task remediation
constraints: The authors note that although there is strong evidence for both approaches, "the reason for their success is not clear"
target_learners: school-aged children with fine motor difficulties
target_learning_goals: fine motor skill remediation and generalisation
examples: The typing game shared finger-tapping practice with the tapping task but required broader motor processes like planning and control, matching the MABC-2
key_sources: McGlashan H.L., Blanchard C.C.V., Sycamore N.J., Lee R., French B., Holmes N.P. (2017). Improvement in children's fine motor skills following a computerized typing intervention. Human Movement Science. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.humov.2017.10.013

article_title: The Effects of Practice-Based Training on Graduate Teaching Assistants' Classroom Practices.
citation: Becker Erin A., Easlon Erin J., Potter Sarah C., Guzman-Alvarez Alberto, Spear Jensen M., Facciotti Marc T., Igo Michele M., Singer Mitchell, Pagliarulo Christopher. (2017). The Effects of Practice-Based Training on Graduate Teaching Assistants' Classroom Practices. CBE—Life Sciences Education 16(4):ar58. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-05-0162
title: Practice-based teacher-training framework (deliberate practice of component skills with feedback)
description: A K–12-derived teacher-training framework the authors transferred to higher education, in which "Complex teaching practices are first broken down into learnable component skills" and novices receive "repeated and progressive practice of these skills to develop automaticity." Component skills are modeled by trainers, drilled in simplified mock classrooms with peers, then implemented in authentic classrooms under observation with coaching. The program paired task repetition (weekly drills) with a comprehensive feedback program built on an explicit task standard, which the authors argue fulfills the demonstrated requirements for effective deliberate practice.
requirements: A core set of high-frequency, portable target techniques; repeated drill cycles; and timely, goal-directed feedback focused on an explicit task standard
constraints: Drills are simplified mock-classroom situations and, as the article notes, are not accurate representations of authentic classroom experiences
target_learners: Novice higher education instructors (graduate teaching assistants)
target_learning_goals: Implementation of evidence-based active-learning instructional practices
examples: Weekly 2-hour training sessions in which the first hour was a mock warm-up with trainers modeling techniques and GTAs acting as students, and the second hour was dedicated to drilling one technique per week (cold call, stretch it variants, right is right, circulate)
key_sources: Becker Erin A., Easlon Erin J., Potter Sarah C., Guzman-Alvarez Alberto, Spear Jensen M., Facciotti Marc T., Igo Michele M., Singer Mitchell, Pagliarulo Christopher. (2017). article_title: Predictive validity of pre-admission assessments on medical student performance.
citation: Dabaliz Al-Awwab, Kaadan Samy, Dabbagh M. Marwan, Barakat Abdulaziz, Shareef Mohammad Abrar, Al-Tannir Mohamad, Obeidat Akef, Mohamed Ayman. (2017). Predictive validity of pre-admission assessments on medical student performance. International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.5a10.04e1
title: The progress test as a longitudinal indicator of functional knowledge in medical education
description: The progress test (PT) is presented as a longitudinal assessment method that, unlike the cGPA, "assesses student achievement and progression". First introduced at Maastricht in the early 1970s to assess a problem-based learning curriculum, it "focuses on functional knowledge (knowledge that comes with repetition), provides valuable information that can be used for feedback and has research potential". The article uses it as a performance indicator against which pre-admission variables' predictive validity was tested.

constraints: The article notes the literature investigating the relationship between PT and cGPA is quite deficient

article_title: How frequent are non-evidence-based health care beliefs in chiropractic students and do they vary across the pre-professional educational years.
citation: Innes SI, Leboeuf-Yde C, Walker BF. (2018). How frequent are non-evidence-based health care beliefs in chiropractic students and do they vary across the pre-professional educational years. Chiropractic & Manual Therapies. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12998-018-0178-y
title: Professional-identity 'philosophy' as a cognitive lens that inverts the evidence pyramid
description: The article draws on osteopathic research to propose an explanatory account of why students hold guideline-inconsistent beliefs: some manual therapy professions carry a professional identity based on principles perceived as "unique, complex, and distinct". This 'philosophy' is deemed superior to science and acts as a cognitive lens through which students judge and reject research evidence, elevating personal experience and expert teachings while diminishing systematic reviews. The authors state this is often the case in chiropractic too.
requirements: A strong professional identity underpinned by a profession-specific philosophy
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation, drawn from qualitative osteopathic research (Figg-Latham and Rajendran), not tested in this study
target_learning_goals: evidence-based practice attitudes and guideline adherence
examples: The article cites UK osteopaths who reject low back pain guidance as the source of the lens account

article_title: Early musculoskeletal classroom education confers little advantage to medical student knowledge and competency in the absence of clinical experiences: a retrospective comparison study.
citation: Khorsand Derek D, Khwaja A, Schmale GA. (2018). Early musculoskeletal classroom education confers little advantage to medical student knowledge and competency in the absence of clinical experiences: a retrospective comparison study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1157-7
title: Direct musculoskeletal education reform efforts toward providing clinical experiences with patients rather than earlier classroom instruction
description: The article concludes that preclinical classroom changes, including moving the introductory musculoskeletal course to the first year, did not improve knowledge, and that "further efforts to improve the education of medical students in musculoskeletal medicine should be directed towards providing more clinical experiences with patients having musculoskeletal concerns". It suggests a comprehensive reform with routine early patient exposure continued into the clinical years.
requirements: Requires access to clinical settings with patients having musculoskeletal concerns, which the authors note was neither routine nor predictable in the preclinical years studied.
constraints: The article reports this as level III retrospective evidence from one institution with an 11% survey response rate; a more comprehensive reform including routine early exposure may be required to achieve optimum proficiency.
target_learning_goals: musculoskeletal medicine knowledge and proficiency
examples: Students who took a musculoskeletal-focused elective clerkship in their third or fourth years scored significantly higher (63% vs. 53%, p = 0.047) than students without these clinical experiences.

article_title: Impact Evaluation of PRONTO Mexico: A Simulation-Based Program in Obstetric and Neonatal Emergencies and Team Training.
citation: Walker Dilys M. MD, Cohen Susanna R. CNM, DNP, Fritz Jimena MD, MSc, Olvera-García Marisela MSc, Zelek Sarah T. MPH, Fahey Jenifer O. CNM, MSN, MPH, Romero-Martínez Martín PhD, Montoya-Rodríguez Alejandra MSc, Lamadrid-Figueroa Héctor MD, ScD. (2016). Impact Evaluation of PRONTO Mexico: A Simulation-Based Program in Obstetric and Neonatal Emergencies and Team Training. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000106
title: PRONTO: a low-cost, high-fidelity, in-situ simulation-based obstetric and neonatal emergency and team training program
description: PRONTO (Programa de Rescate Obstétrico y Neonatal) provides "high-fidelity, low-cost training for interprofessional obstetric and neonatal teams." Sessions have minimal didactic content and consist of interactive team and communication exercises, targeted skill-building, simulation of emergencies, video-guided debriefings, and strategic planning. Simulations use the PartoPants hybrid birth simulator worn by a patient actress and the Laerdal NeoNatalie, conducted in situ with locally available resources. Training spans a 2-day Module I and a 1-day Module II 2–3 months later.
requirements: Trainers must be flexible on some aspects of the training while maintaining fidelity to the curriculum as a whole
constraints: The program was evaluated in government-run level 2 or 3 hospitals with 500 to 3000 annual deliveries in resource-limited Mexican states
target_learners: interprofessional obstetric and neonatal care providers (physicians, nurses, and related personnel) in public hospitals
target_learning_goals: teamwork and communication in obstetric and neonatal emergencies
management of obstetric hemorrhage, neonatal resuscitation, shoulder dystocia, preeclampsia, and eclampsia
examples: 450 of 3228 eligible personnel (mean 20.5%) were trained across 12 intervention hospitals between August 2010 and January 2012
