article_title: Effectiveness of an individual, online e-learning program about sexually transmitted infections: a prospective cohort study.
citation: Bos-Bonnie Linda H. A., van Bergen Jan E. A. M. J., te Pas Ellen, Kijser Michael A. M., van Dijk Nynke. (2017). Effectiveness of an individual, online e-learning program about sexually transmitted infections: a prospective cohort study. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-017-0625-1
title: Three-stage design for behaviour change in CME: priming, focusing, and follow-up
description: The article organises behaviour change in CME into three stages: "confrontation with activities that trigger the consideration of change (priming), experiencing strategies to motivate or facilitate the change (focusing), and maintaining the behavioral change by means of a supportive activity (follow-up)". The e-learning program maps didactic methods onto these stages: the quickscan (priming), videotaped case-studies with examples of good and less appropriate behaviour (priming and focusing), and the CtC-method (follow-up).
requirements: A priming activity that triggers consideration of change
A focusing activity with strategies to motivate or facilitate the change
A follow-up supportive activity to maintain the behavioural change
target_learning_goals: Knowledge, attitude, and behaviour change concerning the STI-consultation
examples: The quickscan triggered consideration of change and evaluated knowledge and attitude; videotaped case-studies introduced role models; the CtC-method served as follow-up

article_title: A qualitative evaluation of scalpel skill teaching of podiatry students.
citation: Causby RS, McDonnell MN, Reed L, Fryer CE, Hillier SL. (2017). A qualitative evaluation of scalpel skill teaching of podiatry students. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13047-017-0202-9
title: Progressive low-to-high fidelity scalpel skill training sequence: demonstration, part-task practice on inanimate objects, low-fidelity wax simulation on a colleague's foot, then real callus and public patients
description: The article describes a commonly used structured progression for teaching scalpel skills in podiatry programs. Teaching typically begins with theoretical content and demonstration, followed by part-task training on inanimate objects such as oranges, soap, cork, potatoes, fleecy web, wax or candles. Training then progresses to low-fidelity simulation such as debriding wax from wax impregnated materials attached to a colleague's foot, then to debriding actual callus from fellow students, and finally to treating members of the public in the university clinic.
requirements: Requires access to inanimate practice materials, wax impregnated simulation bases, willing peer partners, and a university clinic with patients
constraints: The article notes many students were too young to have developed significant skin pathology, limiting practice on real callus from peers
target_learning_goals: safe and competent scalpel handling and callus debridement technique
examples: One program taught students to use the scalpel handle without a blade attached first; another embedded small seeds within the wax to replicate corns and another used rubberised feet to increase fidelity

article_title: Improving Exam Performance in Introductory Biology through the Use of Preclass Reading Guides.
citation: Lieu, R., Wong, A., Asefirad, A., & Shaffer, J. F. (2017). Improving Exam Performance in Introductory Biology through the Use of Preclass Reading Guides. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5589426/
title: Custom preclass reading guides for introductory biology textbook reading
description: Reading guides are two-to-five-page documents (average 3.5 ± 1.0 pages, n = 24), created per lesson by the instructor and posted at least one week before class. They direct students which pages and sections to read and ask them to "defin[e] terms, explaining concepts, making tables and drawings, or answering in-chapter textbook questions." Guides were optional, ungraded, never posted with answers, and supported by a course discussion board where students could ask questions.
requirements: Correct page numbers, section titles, and figures must be cited, and specific questions tied to the textbook must be written, requiring a significant time commitment to develop
Students must have time to complete them; about 70% of students spent 30–120 minutes per guide
constraints: Developed for a specific textbook (Campbell Biology, 10th ed.), so new textbook editions may require updating the guides
target_learners: Primarily first-quarter freshman biological sciences majors in large-enrollment introductory biology
target_learning_goals: Acquiring course content before class (cell biology, molecular biology, genetics) in support of high-structure flipped instruction
examples: Guides were used in two Fall 2015 sections of a 400+ student introductory biology course at an R1 institution, taught with daily preclass Mastering Biology assignments, clicker questions, group work, and weekly review quizzes
key_sources: Lieu, R., Wong, A., Asefirad, A., & Shaffer, J. F. (2017). Improving Exam Performance in Introductory Biology through the Use of Preclass Reading Guides. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5589426/

article_title: Comparison of formula and number-right scoring in undergraduate medical training: a Rasch model analysis.
citation: Cecilio-Fernandes D, Medema H, Collares CF, Schuwirth L, Cohen-Schotanus J, Tio RA. (2017). Comparison of formula and number-right scoring in undergraduate medical training: a Rasch model analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1051-8
title: Prefer number-right scoring for MCQ progress tests on psychometric grounds, while considering test-taking strategies
description: The article concludes that Rasch analyses favor number-right scoring: "Rasch model analyses showed that tests with number-right scoring have better psychometric properties than formula scoring." It recommends number-right scoring "based on our psychometric analysis alone", while cautioning that the choice "should depend not only on psychometric properties but also on self-directed test-taking strategies and metacognitive skills."
requirements: The comparison was established with Rasch model analysis of progress-test-style MCQs in a crossover design
constraints: The authors state the choice of scoring method should also weigh self-directed test-taking strategies and metacognitive skills, not psychometrics alone
Further studies are necessary to investigate whether findings transfer to other years in medical school
target_learners: medical students in years 2–4 of undergraduate medical education
target_learning_goals: valid and reliable assessment of end-of-curriculum medical knowledge via progress testing
examples: A 2×2 crossover experiment in which 298 students took the same 100-item sets under both scoring conditions, analyzed with the Rasch model in Winsteps

article_title: Comparison between three option, four option and five option multiple choice question tests for quality parameters: A randomized study.
citation: Vegada Bhavisha, Shukla Apexa, Khilnani Ajeetkumar, Charan Jaykaran, Desai Chetna. (2016). Comparison between three option, four option and five option multiple choice question tests for quality parameters: A randomized study. Indian Journal of Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.4103/0253-7613.190757
title: Prefer three-option MCQs over four- and five-option formats for knowledge assessment
description: The article recommends constructing single-best-answer MCQ tests with three options per item rather than four or five, because three-option tests produced higher scores, shorter completion times, higher facility values, and fewer nonfunctioning distracters, while validity, reliability, and item discrimination were equivalent across formats. As the conclusion states, "Assessment based on three option MCQs can be preferred over four option and five option MCQS."
requirements: Items must have plausible distracters; the test should be validated by subject experts as in the study's expert-validation procedure.
constraints: The study was conducted on second-year M.B.B.S. students for ANS pharmacology assessment with a small sample, so results "should be interpreted cautiously for other specialty, subject, and content."
Random distracter elimination may have affected scores and facility values.
target_learning_goals: assessment of pharmacology knowledge
examples: 132 students were randomized to three-, four-, or five-option versions of the same 30-item test, with scores, time, and item statistics compared.

Indian Journal of Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.4103/0253-7613.190757

article_title: Certainty rating in pre-and post-tests of study modules in an online clinical pharmacy course - A pilot study to evaluate teaching and learning.
citation: Luetsch Karen, Burrows Judith. (2016). Certainty rating in pre-and post-tests of study modules in an online clinical pharmacy course - A pilot study to evaluate teaching and learning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0783-1
title: Combine formative pre- and post-module certainty-rated MCQ tests with automated feedback and sign-posting to learning resources so learners self-regulate and focus their study
description: The article describes restructuring formative e-assessment into identical pre- and post-module certainty-rated MCQ tests with automated feedback that identifies correctness and sign-posts relevant module resources without revealing answers. The authors state that adding pre-module tests "integrates feeding forward and allows e-learners to self-regulate and focus their learning through the online study content". Survey responses indicated the tests directed learning (67%) and were useful for revision (67%).
requirements: Identical CRMCQ sets administered at module start and completion, with automated feedback identifying correctness and pointing to relevant learning resources without revealing the exact answer in pre-tests
constraints: Test availability was temporally restricted; the study lacked a control group without certainty ratings, and sign-posting was not investigated separately from CRMCQ use
target_learners: practising pharmacists in postgraduate online coursework programs
target_learning_goals: clinical pharmacotherapeutic knowledge application
self-assessment and self-regulation of study
examples: Sets of 10 MCQs per module were administered pre- and post-module over a one-year pharmacotherapeutics course, with feedback sign-posting lectures, guidelines or journal articles linked in the module

article_title: Sustained effect of simulation-based ultrasound training on clinical performance: a randomized trial.
citation: Tolsgaard M G, Ringsted C, Dreisler E, Nørgaard L N, Petersen J H, Madsen M E, Freiesleben N L C, Sørensen J L, Tabor A. (2015). Sustained effect of simulation-based ultrasound training on clinical performance: a randomized trial. Ultrasound in Obstetrics & Gynecology. https://doi.org/10.1002/uog.14780
title: Provide proficiency-based simulation training to an expert level before clinical training in operator-dependent skills
description: The article's intervention concept was "'proficiency-based training' in accordance with current recommendations", meaning residents trained on a virtual-reality TVS simulator and then a pelvic mannequin until a predefined expert performance level was attained, before starting supervised clinical practice. This initial simulation produced sustained performance advantages at 2 months into residency. The principle is to front-load deliberate, safe-environment practice with continuous assessment until a competence criterion is reached.
requirements: Training must continue until a predefined expert performance level is attained, with continuous performance assessment
Access to both a virtual-reality simulator with validated metrics and a physical mannequin for equipment handling practice
constraints: The effect cannot be attributed to either simulator type individually
Generalizability to other examination types such as abdominal ultrasound requires further study
Effects on diagnostic error, patient satisfaction, costs and long-term outcomes were not explored
target_learners: new obstetrics and gynecology residents without prior ultrasound experience
target_learning_goals: transvaginal ultrasound competence including image optimization, systematic examination, interpretation, documentation and medical decision-making
examples: Residents trained on seven selected simulator modules until they passed an expert level corresponding to 88.4% of the maximum total score, taking on average 3 h 16 min, then continued on a pelvic mannequin until proficiency
key_sources: Tolsgaard M G, Ringsted C, Dreisler E, Nørgaard L N, Petersen J H, Madsen M E, Freiesleben N L C, Sørensen J L, Tabor A. (2015). article_title: Incorporating prognosis in the care of older adults with multimorbidity: description and evaluation of a novel curriculum.
citation: Schoenborn Nancy L., Boyd Cynthia, Cayea Danelle, Nakamura Kelly, Xue Qian-Li, Ray Anushree, McNabney Matthew. (2015). Incorporating prognosis in the care of older adults with multimorbidity: description and evaluation of a novel curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0488-x
title: Prognosis curriculum pattern: small-group sessions plus guided experiential exercise with real patients, built on Kolb's experiential learning model
description: A curriculum pattern combining three small-group sessions with a clinical exercise: case-based teaching of prognostic tools, role play with standardized patients for prognosis communication, then a real-patient exercise in which residents assess a patient's prognosis, use it to frame a clinical decision, and discuss it, followed by reflection and group feedback. The authors state it is "innovative in combining role play with subsequent guided experiential learning with actual patients in clinical practice" and that development "drew from Kolb's model of experiential learning".
requirements: An existing required rotation in which the clinical exercise can be embedded
A summary of prognostic tools and resources provided to residents to facilitate application
constraints: Implemented at one institution; results may not reflect residents or patients elsewhere
Evaluation focused on short-term outcomes; long-term impact not assessed
target_learning_goals: Assess prognosis using evidence-based tools
Communicate prognosis explicitly and within benefits/harms discussions
Apply prognosis to inform clinical decisions in older adults with multimorbidity
examples: Session 2 used role play exercises with standardized patients; in the clinical exercise residents assessed prognosis for one of their primary care patients and discussed it with the patient

article_title: How do case presentation teaching methods affect learning outcomes?--SNAPPS and the One-Minute preceptor.
citation: Seki Masayasu, Otaki Junji, Breugelmans Raoul, Komoda Takayuki, Nagata-Kobayashi Shizuko, Akaishi Yu, Hiramoto Jun, Ohno Iwao, Harada Yoshimi, Hirayama Yoji, Izumi Miki (2016). How do case presentation teaching methods affect learning outcomes?-SNAPPS and the One-Minute preceptor. BMC Medical Education 16. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0531-6
title: Preceptors need a deep understanding of the teaching method and the ability to teach that considers learner characteristics
description: The article concludes that either structured case-presentation technique depends on the preceptor: "preceptors require a deep understanding of the teaching method and an ability to teach that considers the characteristics of the learner." Because there were individual resident differences in teaching outcomes within each group, instruction should be adapted to the individual learner rather than delivered mechanically.
requirements: The study preceptor prepared by reviewing both models in a pilot study before teaching, indicating deliberate familiarization with the chosen method is needed.
constraints: The authors stress taking "national and regional cultural differences sufficiently into account when disseminating educational theories," noting that East Asian "cultural reticence" may affect results and that further studies in other regions are needed.
target_learning_goals: case presentation in outpatient clinical settings
examples: A single preceptor taught both groups after reviewing both models in a pilot study, and reminded residents of the correct sequence as needed during presentations.

article_title: Computer-supported feedback message tailoring: theory-informed adaptation of clinical audit and feedback for learning and behavior change.
citation: Landis-Lewis Zach, Brehaut Jamie C, Hochheiser Harry, Douglas Gerald P, Jacobson Rebecca S. (2015). Computer-supported feedback message tailoring: theory-informed adaptation of clinical audit and feedback for learning and behavior change. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-014-0203-z
title: Prototype computer-supported feedback message tailoring system generating a menu of graphical and textual messages
description: The article describes a prototype system that "supports the provision of tailored feedback messages by generating a menu of graphical and textual messages with associated descriptions of targeted barriers to behavior change." Supervisors review the menu and select messages matching their beliefs about a recipient's barriers. The system would use facts about performance history, theoretical constructs, and clinical context to generate messages such as truncated-scale graphs, peer benchmarks, and historical peer comparisons, and creating a knowledge-base of such facts is described as an initial development step.
requirements: A valid classification of feedback message elements
Performance thresholds matching health-care providers' expectations
A knowledge-base of tailoring facts
constraints: The approach focuses on message selection and visualization, not the audit of clinical performance
It is unknown whether different visualizations moderate the effect of feedback on performance
target_learners: health-care providers receiving individually tailored audit and feedback
target_learning_goals: improving clinical performance through relevant feedback
examples: Figure 2 shows a prototype menu of three graphical messages based on published AF studies: scale truncation, peer benchmarking, and historical peer comparison, all generated from the same performance data in Table 2.

article_title: Turkish students' perceptions of professionalism at the beginning and at the end of medical education: a cross-sectional qualitative study.
citation: Kavas Mustafa Volkan; Demirören Meral; Koşan Ayşen Melek Aytuğ; Karahan Süleyman Tuna; Yalim Neyyire Yasemin. (2015). Turkish students' perceptions of professionalism at the beginning and at the end of medical education: a cross-sectional qualitative study. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4368711/
title: Proto-professionalism as a dynamic of attainment and attrition in medical students' professional identity development
description: The article adopts Hilton and Slotnick's concept of proto-professionalism, in which developing a professional identity is 'a lengthy state in which the learner develops the skills and knowledge, and gains the experience needed to acquire professionalism'. Two opposite forces operate during this process: attainment, the progress of novices from naïveté to practical wisdom (phronesis), and attrition, the inclination from idealism toward lack of motivation and cynicism. The authors use this dynamic to interpret the difference between Grade-1 and Grade-6 focus-group accounts in their data and in earlier studies.
requirements: Professional identity development unfolds over the education continuum and is shaped by formal, informal, and hidden curriculum influences
constraints: The study's cross-sectional design prevents attributing observed G1–G6 differences directly to professional education at a single institution (AUFM)
target_learning_goals: professional identity development and medical professionalism
examples: Focus-group accounts of G6 students describing how negative internship experiences, unskilled role models, and workload eroded their ideals of being a good doctor

article_title: Competence acquisition for single-incision laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
citation: Deutsch G.B., Sathyanarayana S.A., Giangola M., Akerman M., DeNoto G., Klein J.D.S., Zemon H., Rubach E. (2015). Competence Acquisition for Single-Incision Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy. JSLS: Journal of the Society of Laparoendoscopic Surgeons. https://doi.org/10.4293/JSLS.2014.00116
title: Total prior laparoscopic experience, rather than fellowship training alone, should guide expectations for SILC competence acquisition
description: The article proposes that a surgeon's accumulated laparoscopic experience determines whether a SILC learning curve is needed: "Total surgical experience level may be the most important factor in achieving competence in SILC." Surgeons with more than 5 years of laparoscopic experience showed no learning curve, while the least experienced surgeon needed about 15 cases. The authors conclude general surgeons do not require a laparoscopic fellowship specifically for SILC.
requirements: Surgeons should have substantial prior conventional laparoscopic experience (the article's experienced group had >5 years) or, if less experienced, expect a short learning curve of roughly 15 cases
constraints: Based on retrospective, nonrandomized data from 3 institutions with variable resident involvement; the authors call for prospective randomized studies to confirm
target_learners: general surgeons transitioning from conventional laparoscopic to single-incision laparoscopic surgery
surgical residents and fellows training in minimally invasive techniques
target_learning_goals: acquiring technical proficiency in single-incision laparoscopic cholecystectomy
plaining surgical training and case sequencing for new procedural techniques
examples: In the retrospective review, the three surgeons with >5 years' experience showed no significant downward trend in procedure times, while the fellowship-trained surgeon with <5 years' experience reached proficiency after about 15 cases

article_title: Progress testing in the medical curriculum: students' approaches to learning and perceived stress.
citation: Chen Yan, Henning Marcus, Yielder Jill, Jones Rhys, Wearn Andy, Weller Jennifer. (2015). Progress testing in the medical curriculum: students' approaches to learning and perceived stress. BMC Medical Education 15:147. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0426-y
title: Progress testing: repeated assessment of all students against graduate-level applied medical knowledge
description: Progress testing (PT) is an assessment regime in which a common question bank of applied medical knowledge at the level of a new graduate is administered to all students across all years of a programme. The article describes PTs as intended to discourage students from preparing specifically for a test and then 'discarding' that knowledge, to demonstrate knowledge growth longitudinally, and to provide comprehensive feedback that facilitates self-directed learning. At the University of Auckland, PTs contributed 15 % in Year 2 and 40 % in Year 3 to final marks for applied medical knowledge, and 100 % in Years 4–6.
requirements: A common question bank covering the major areas of basic, clinical and behavioural science, and public health expected of a graduating doctor
Administration at multiple step-points across the programme so judgements are not made at a single end-of-year examination
constraints: the impact of PTs on student learning can vary with context and curriculum structure
the relatively low PT scores that students obtain in the first few years are not as rewarding as the potentially high grades they receive from traditional summative examinations
target_learners: undergraduate medical students (Years 2–5, University of Auckland MBChB programme)
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of applied medical knowledge at the level of a new graduate
self-directed learning through comprehensive feedback on knowledge gaps
examples: PTs were introduced to Years 2 and 4 in 2013 while Years 3 and 5 sat traditional end-of-year assessments, creating a quasi-experimental comparison in a single medical programme
key_sources: Chen Yan, Henning Marcus, Yielder Jill, Jones Rhys, Wearn Andy, Weller Jennifer. (2015). Progress testing in the medical curriculum: students' approaches to learning and perceived stress. BMC Medical Education 15:147. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0426-y
